title: AI interview prep: GenAI roadmap and ML system design questions · FAANGrind
description: A 24-lesson GenAI and agentic AI roadmap with quizzes and runnable code, plus 40 interview problems on RAG, agents, LLM serving, ML system design and implement-it coding.
markdown:
AI

# GenAI, agents and ML systems.

24 lessons (70.5 h of study) and 40 interview problems: RAG, agents, LLM serving, ML system design and implement-it coding.

16 to study, 2 to skim, 6 for later 6 easy, 18 medium, 16 hard

## Roadmap

Read the modules in order. Each lesson has a worked example, runnable code, interview questions and a quiz.

[Jump to problems](#problems)

1

### Foundations

6 lessons · 14 h

1. [#1SkimBeginner 45 minHistory - how AI got to transformersAI did not jump straight to LLMs (large language models). Each generation of methods hit a wall, and the next idea was built to get past it: hand-written rules, then learning from data, then deep networks on GPUs, then attention, then transformers pretrained on huge amounts of text. This lesson walks that chain in order, so you can explain why a transformer looks the way it does and which problem each part solves.Open lesson](/ai/learn/history-ai-to-transformers)
2. [#2StudyBeginner 3.5 hNeural networks and backpropA neural network is a stack of simple units. Each unit multiplies its inputs by weights, adds a bias and applies a non-linear function. Training means finding weights that make a loss number small. Backpropagation computes how much each weight contributed to the loss, and gradient descent moves each weight a small step in the direction that lowers it. This lesson covers both, plus the basics interviewers check: activations, losses, optimisers, regularisation, normalisation and metrics.Open lesson](/ai/learn/neural-networks-backprop)
3. [#3SkimBeginner 1 hRNNs, LSTMs, CNNsRNNs, LSTMs and CNNs are the three network designs that came before the transformer. An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a memory vector forward. An LSTM is an RNN with gates that protect that memory. A CNN slides small filters over an image. This lesson explains what each one solved, the limit each one hit, and which parts are still inside the models you use today.Open lesson](/ai/learn/rnns-lstms-cnns)
4. [#4StudyBeginner 3 hLLM fundamentals - tokens, embeddings, decodingAn LLM (large language model) is a neural network trained to do one thing: predict the next token. This lesson follows a piece of text through the whole machine. Text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors, a stack of transformer blocks mixes those vectors, and a decoding rule picks the next token from the output probabilities. You will work each stage with small numbers.Open lesson](/ai/learn/llm-fundamentals)
5. [#5StudyIntermediate 2.5 hCoding simple attentionSelf-attention lets every token update its vector using the other tokens in the sequence. This lesson builds it in small steps: measure similarity with a dot product, turn the scores into weights with softmax, and take a weighted sum. Then it adds the three things a real layer needs: the scaling by the square root of d\_k, the causal mask and multiple heads. Every step is worked with numbers you can check by hand.Open lesson](/ai/learn/coding-simple-attention)
6. [#6StudyBeginner 3 hHugging Face end to endHugging Face is where open models live and the set of Python libraries used to run them. This lesson follows one path from start to finish: find a model on the Hub, read its card and licence, load the tokenizer and the weights, format a chat with the model's template, generate text, measure the output, and save or push your own version. Every step names the object you get back.Open lesson](/ai/learn/hugging-face-end-to-end)

2

### Build with LLMs

4 lessons · 13.5 h

1. [#7StudyBeginner 2.5 hPrompting and context engineeringPrompt engineering is writing a good instruction. Context engineering is deciding everything that enters the context window: instructions, examples, retrieved data, tool definitions and history. This lesson covers both: the parts of a prompt, when to use few-shot examples or step-by-step reasoning, how to get valid JSON every time, how to keep a long conversation inside a token budget, and how to prove a prompt change helped.Open lesson](/ai/learn/prompting-context-engineering)
2. [#8StudyIntermediate 4 hVector DBs and RAGRAG (retrieval-augmented generation) fetches relevant text at query time and puts it in the prompt, so a model answers from your data without being retrained. A vector database makes the fetching fast: it stores an embedding for every chunk of text and finds the nearest ones to a query in milliseconds. This lesson covers both, from chunking to evaluation.Open lesson](/ai/learn/vector-dbs-rag)
3. [#9StudyIntermediate 3 hWhat is fine-tuning - LoRA, QLoRA, DoRAFine-tuning changes how a model behaves by updating its weights on your examples. Updating every weight of a large model is expensive, so the LoRA family freezes the base model and trains a small add-on called an adapter, usually under 1% of the parameters. This lesson explains LoRA from the formula up, then QLoRA, DoRA and rsLoRA, and how to choose between them.Open lesson](/ai/learn/fine-tuning-lora-qlora-dora)
4. [#10StudyIntermediate 4 hFine-tuning a model for a real use caseThis lesson takes one real task, a model that sorts support tickets and drafts a reply, and walks the whole fine-tuning job from start to finish. You decide whether to fine-tune at all, build and clean the dataset, format it with the chat template, split it, train a QLoRA adapter, read the loss curves, compare with the base model, serve the adapter, and debug a run that made things worse.Open lesson](/ai/learn/fine-tuning-real-use-case)

3

### Serving

1 lessons · 3.5 h

1. [#11StudyIntermediate 3.5 hInference and serving - KV cache, batching, vLLMInference is running a trained model to produce output. Serving is doing that for many users at once, fast and cheaply. This lesson follows one request through an LLM server: the prefill and decode phases, the KV cache that makes decode fast, batching that keeps the GPU busy, quantization that shrinks the model, and the metrics and engines you use to run it in production.Open lesson](/ai/learn/inference-serving)

4

### Agents

4 lessons · 15.5 h

1. [#12StudyIntermediate 4 hAgents from first principles - build a mini frameworkAn agent is an LLM running in a loop with tools: it chooses an action, sees the result, and repeats until the goal is met. A chatbot answers; an agent acts. This lesson builds a small agent framework piece by piece (message list, tools, registry, loop, error handling, limits), so you can explain what any agent framework is doing underneath.Open lesson](/ai/learn/agents-first-principles)
2. [#13StudyIntermediate 4 hAgent frameworks - LangChain, LangGraphAn agent framework gives you the loop, the state and the tool plumbing from the previous lesson as ready-made parts. This lesson names the eight frameworks interviewers expect you to recognise, then teaches you to read LangChain and LangGraph code line by line: tools, `create\_agent`, state, reducers, nodes, conditional edges, checkpointers and interrupts.Open lesson](/ai/learn/agent-frameworks-langchain-langgraph)
3. [#14StudyIntermediate 3.5 hTools, MCP and memoryA tool is a function your application offers to a model: a name, a description and a schema for the arguments. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for packaging tools and data so any compatible AI application can use them. Memory is how an agent keeps facts beyond one context window. This lesson covers how to design all three, and what each one costs in tokens.Open lesson](/ai/learn/tools-mcp-memory)
4. [#15StudyAdvanced 4 hAgents in depth - patterns, reliability, securityThis lesson is about agents in production. It covers the seven architecture patterns and how each one fails, why long tasks fail more often than short ones, how to manage context over hours, how to make actions safe to retry with idempotency keys and checkpoints, how to evaluate an agent, and how to keep it from leaking data. It ends with a full design of a customer support agent.Open lesson](/ai/learn/agents-in-depth)

5

### Ship

3 lessons · 9 h

1. [#16StudyIntermediate 3.5 hEvals, tracing and guardrailsAn eval is a repeatable test that tells you whether a change made an LLM system better or worse. A trace is the record of one request: every prompt, retrieval, tool call, token count, latency and cost. A guardrail is a check on what goes into the model or comes out of it. This lesson shows how to build all three, with the numbers and the wording interviewers expect.Open lesson](/ai/learn/evals-tracing-guardrails)
2. [#17StudyIntermediate 3 hLLM system designLLM system design is the interview round where you design a whole product around a model: a chat service, document Q&A, a support agent or a serving platform. Almost every answer uses the same five layers and the same seven steps. This lesson gives you the layers, the steps, the arithmetic for capacity, cost and latency, and the points each common question expects.Open lesson](/ai/learn/llm-system-design)
3. [#18StudyIntermediate 2.5 hWhat is new in 2026 + revisionThis is the last stop before the interview. It lists the eleven 2026 trends an interviewer may probe, each with what it is, why it matters to someone who builds systems, and a line you can say. It then gives the 37-term revision sheet for the rapid-fire round, and a structure for answering "what have you been following lately?" in two minutes.Open lesson](/ai/learn/whats-new-2026-revision)

6

### Later

6 lessons · 15.5 h

1. [#19LaterAdvanced 1.5 hAttention variations - GQA, MLAStandard multi-head attention stores a key and a value for every head, every layer and every past token. That store, the KV cache, is the main memory cost of serving besides the weights. This lesson covers the variants that shrink it: multi-query attention, grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-head latent attention (MLA). It also places FlashAttention and sliding-window attention, which solve different problems.Open lesson](/ai/learn/attention-variations-gqa-mla)
2. [#20LaterAdvanced 1.5 hRL fine-tuningSupervised fine-tuning needs the right answer written out for every example. Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning needs only a score: which of two answers a person preferred, or whether a program accepted the answer. This lesson explains policy, reward and policy gradient in plain words, then the three methods used on LLMs: RLHF with PPO, DPO and GRPO, with what each needs and how each fails.Open lesson](/ai/learn/rl-fine-tuning)
3. [#21LaterAdvanced 1.5 hComputer use and multimodal agentsA multimodal model reads images and audio as well as text, by turning each of them into tokens. A multimodal agent uses that ability to act: answer from documents with charts, hold a voice call, or operate a computer by looking at screenshots and clicking. This lesson explains how an image becomes tokens, how voice and computer-use agents are built, why they are slow and easy to break, and how to test and secure them.Open lesson](/ai/learn/computer-use-multimodal-agents)
4. [#22LaterAdvanced 1.5 hAdvanced topicsThis lesson is a map of what to study after the core roadmap. It covers ten topics that sit one level below the basics: reasoning models, mixture of experts, distillation, constrained decoding, speculative decoding, long-running agents, harness engineering, open-weight models, the small tuned model plus RAG pattern, and GraphRAG. For each one you get what it is, why a system builder cares, and what to learn first.Open lesson](/ai/learn/advanced-topics)
5. [#23LaterIntermediate 8 hProjects - RAG app, fine-tuned model, agent + evalsThree small projects turn the rest of this course into things you can talk about: a RAG app, a fine-tuned model, and an agent with an eval harness. This lesson gives each one a scope, milestones, numbers to measure with targets a student can reach, a README outline, and a way to present it in two minutes: problem, design, trade-offs, numbers.Open lesson](/ai/learn/projects)
6. [#24LaterIntermediate 1.5 hLLMs on cloud - Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Vertex AIAmazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI and Google Vertex AI each give you one managed API to many models inside your own cloud account. The product names differ, but the ideas are the same: pay per token or reserve capacity, live inside quotas, choose where data is processed, lock access down with cloud identity and private networking, and add managed retrieval, agents, guardrails, tuning and evals. This lesson teaches the shared ideas and when to self-host instead.Open lesson](/ai/learn/llms-on-cloud)

# Advanced topics

This lesson is a map of what to study after the core roadmap. It covers ten topics that sit one level below the basics: reasoning models, mixture of experts, distillation, constrained decoding, speculative decoding, long-running agents, harness engineering, open-weight models, the small tuned model plus RAG pattern, and GraphRAG. For each one you get what it is, why a system builder cares, and what to learn first.

reasoning modelsmixture of expertsdistillationconstrained decodingspeculative decodingharness engineeringgraphrag

## Why it matters

Senior interviews go one question deeper than the definition. After "how do you get JSON out of a model?" comes "how does the server guarantee it?". After "what is an agent?" comes "what is in the code around the model?". These ten topics are where those second questions come from. They are also the levers you pull in real work: most of them trade cost, latency or reliability against quality. You do not need all ten at once. Use the table to pick the two or three that match the system you are building, and learn those properly.

Read first: [LLM fundamentals - tokens, embeddings, decoding](/ai/learn/llm-fundamentals), [Vector DBs and RAG](/ai/learn/vector-dbs-rag), [What is fine-tuning - LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA](/ai/learn/fine-tuning-lora-qlora-dora), [Inference and serving - KV cache, batching, vLLM](/ai/learn/inference-serving), [Agents in depth - patterns, reliability, security](/ai/learn/agents-in-depth), [What is new in 2026 + revision](/ai/learn/whats-new-2026-revision)

## Lesson

### The map

| Topic | One-line idea | Learn it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reasoning models | The model thinks before answering; effort is a setting | Hard tasks fail, or thinking costs too much |
| Mixture of experts | Many expert networks, a few run per token | You size hardware for an open model |
| Distillation | A small student learns from a large teacher's outputs | A large model works but costs too much |
| Constrained decoding | Invalid tokens cannot be sampled | Code parses the model's output |
| Speculative decoding | A small model drafts, the large one verifies | You self-host and latency is the limit |
| Long-running agents | Agents that work for hours and keep state | Tasks outgrow one context window |
| Harness engineering | The code around the model: skills, hooks, sub-agents, compaction | Your agent works in demos but not in production |
| Open-weight models | Open models are close to closed ones | Cost, privacy or control matter |
| Small tuned model plus RAG | Tuning for behaviour, retrieval for facts | One narrow task has high volume |
| GraphRAG | Retrieve over a graph of entities and relations | Answers need facts joined across documents |

### Reasoning models and adaptive reasoning

Reasoning models think before answering: they write reasoning tokens first, then the answer. Training adds reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The focus has moved from raw ability to efficiency: effort adjusts to how hard the prompt is.

Reasoning tokens are generated like any other output tokens. You pay for them and you wait for them before the answer starts. So treat effort as a setting per task: low for extraction and routing, high for planning and debugging. A line to say aloud: "I set the thinking level per task, because reasoning tokens cost latency and money." These models need a clear goal more than a step-by-step script. Learn first: run one eval set at two effort levels and compare pass rate, latency and tokens.

### Mixture of experts (MoE)

The feed-forward layer is split into many expert networks, and a router sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many parameters but uses a small part per token, so quality rises without the same rise in compute. Many recent open-weight models use sparse MoE designs.

![A mixture-of-experts router sending one token to 2 of 8 expert networks](/ai/img/moe-router-top2-of-8.svg)A mixture-of-experts router sending one token to 2 of 8 expert networks

Formula

y=i∈top-k∑​gi​Ei​(x)

Here E\_i is expert i and g\_i is the weight the router gives it. For a builder the point is two different numbers. Speed follows the active parameters, the experts that run. Memory follows the total parameters, because every expert stays loaded. Training adds a load-balancing loss so the router does not send everything to the same few experts. Learn first: top-k routing, and total versus active parameters.

### Distillation

A large teacher model generates outputs and a small student model is trained to match them. This is how small models get close to large-model quality on a narrow task. The classic form matches the teacher's whole probability distribution, softened with a temperature. These soft targets carry more signal than one label: a teacher that gives 70% to one answer and 25% to another shows the student which wrong answer is nearly right. With an API teacher you only see text, so you fine-tune the student on the teacher's answers.

It is the standard move when a large model works but costs too much at volume. The risk: the student copies the teacher's mistakes, so filter the teacher's outputs and evaluate on human-checked examples. Learn first: generate 1,000 to 2,000 teacher answers for one task and fine-tune a small model on them.

### Constrained (structured) decoding

At each step the model gives a score to every token in the vocabulary. In constrained decoding, a grammar or JSON schema is compiled into a state machine that knows which tokens are legal next. Every other token is masked (its score is set to minus infinity) before sampling, so invalid tokens cannot be sampled.

This guarantees the form, not the content: the output parses and matches the schema, but a value can still be wrong. Output can also be cut off by the token limit. So validate in code, and retry with the error message if validation fails.

Two practical points. The mask is needed at every step over a vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens or more, so engines compile the grammar once and reuse it. And the schema shapes quality: if a field for the reasoning comes after the answer field, the model must answer before it has thought, so put reasoning fields first. Learn first: the structured output option of your provider or serving engine. SGLang is known for fast constrained decoding.

### Speculative decoding

A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. Accepted tokens are free speed, and the output distribution stays the same, because the large model verifies every drafted token and rejects the ones it would not have produced.

The rule that makes this exact: a drafted token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x) / q(x)), where p is the large model's probability and q is the draft's. On the first rejection, the large model samples a replacement from a corrected distribution and the rest of the draft is dropped. The large model needs no retraining.

You only gain when the draft guesses right often, so it works best on predictable text such as code and boilerplate. The price is a second model in memory. Learn first: the acceptance rate and the expected-tokens formula in the worked example.

### Long-running and persistent agents

These are agents that work for hours and keep state. Reliability and security are the open problems. Errors compound over long tasks, so add checkpoints, limits and approvals. The state must live outside the context window: a progress file the agent re-reads, saved checkpoints, and a memory store. Then a run can stop, resume a day later, or survive a crash. More hours also means more untrusted content read, so the injection risk grows with run length. Learn first: checkpoint and resume, idempotent writes (a retry has no extra effect), and budgets for steps, tokens, time and money.

### Harness engineering

The harness is everything around the model: the loop, the tools, context management, permissions and checks. With the same model, a better harness often finishes more tasks. Four parts to know:

* **Skills:** packaged instructions, a folder with an instruction file and sometimes scripts, that the agent loads when a task needs them. Until then only a short description sits in the context.
* **Hooks:** your own checks that run before or after a tool call. A before-hook can block a call, such as a delete outside the project folder. An after-hook can run tests. The rule lives in code, not in the prompt.
* **Sub-agents:** a sub-agent explores in its own window and returns a short summary, so the lead agent's context stays clean. The cost is more total tokens, more latency if they run in sequence, and lost detail when results are summarised. They pay off when sub-tasks are independent and large.
* **Compaction:** when the window is nearly full, summarise the history and keep decisions, open items and key facts.

Learn first: write the agent loop yourself, then add one hook and compaction.

### Open-weight models closing the gap

Open models are close to closed ones on many benchmarks, often with sparse MoE designs and long context. Self-hosting is now a real option when cost, privacy or control matter. You take on the serving work in exchange: GPUs, autoscaling, upgrades and your own evals. Learn first: serve one open model and compare it with a hosted model on your eval set.

### Small fine-tuned model plus RAG

A QLoRA-tuned small open model with good retrieval is a common cost-for-quality choice. Fine-tuning teaches the behaviour (format, tone, tool-call style) and retrieval supplies the facts. The usual split: a large model for hard reasoning and a small tuned one for high-volume tasks, with a router between them. Learn first: the router and the eval that proves the small model is good enough.

### GraphRAG

Build a knowledge graph of entities and relations from the documents, then retrieve over the graph. It helps with questions that need facts joined across many documents, such as "which suppliers are shared by our three largest customers?". One published design also writes a summary in advance for each cluster of closely related entities, which answers corpus-wide questions such as "what are the main themes?". The cost is at indexing: a model must read every chunk to extract entities and relations, and again when documents change. Learn first: plain hybrid RAG. Add a graph only when your eval shows multi-document questions failing.

## Diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Worked example

**Is speculative decoding worth it?** A draft model proposes 4 tokens per round (call this g = 4). The large model accepts each drafted token with probability a, and stops at the first rejection. Every round also yields one token from the large model itself: the correction after a rejection, or a bonus token when all four are accepted. So the expected number of tokens per round is

Formula

E=1+a+a2+⋯+ag=1−a1−ag+1​

With a = 0.8: E = (1 - 0.8^5) / 0.2 = (1 - 0.328) / 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per round, against 1 token per pass without drafting.

The draft is not free. Assume one draft step costs 5% of a large-model pass. A round costs 4 x 0.05 + 1 = 1.2 large passes. Speed-up = 3.36 / 1.2 = 2.8 times.

| Assumed acceptance rate a | Tokens per round | Speed-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.8 (predictable text) | 3.36 | 2.8x |
| 0.5 | 1.94 | 1.6x |
| 0.3 (unpredictable text) | 1.43 | 1.2x |

The method pays off only when the draft is right most of the time. Measure the acceptance rate on your own traffic before you deploy it.

**MoE sizing.** Take a layer with width 4,096 and a feed-forward hidden size of 16,384. One expert has 2 x 4,096 x 16,384 = 134 million weights. Eight experts hold 1.07 billion weights in this layer, and all of them use GPU memory. With top-2 routing, a token passes through 268 million of them, which is 25% of the feed-forward compute. Size memory from the total and speed from the active part.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""Constrained decoding in miniature.

A tiny state machine tracks where we are inside a JSON object with the schema
{"city": string, "temp": number}. At every step it lists the tokens that keep
the output valid, masks every other token to minus infinity, and picks the
best token that is left. The model scores are scripted, so this runs anywhere.
"""
import json
import math

VOCAB = ["Sure", "!", "{", "}", '"city"', '"temp"', ":", ",", '"Pune"', '"hot"', "31", "<eos>"]
SCHEMA = {'"city"': "string", '"temp"': "number"}       # every key is required
STRINGS = {'"Pune"', '"hot"'}
NUMBERS = {"31"}

def allowed_tokens(state):
    """Return the set of tokens that keep the output inside the grammar."""
    phase, used, key = state["phase"], state["used"], state["key"]
    if phase == "start":
        return {"{"}
    if phase == "key":                                   # a key not used yet
        return set(SCHEMA) - used
    if phase == "colon":
        return {":"}
    if phase == "value":                                 # type comes from the schema
        return STRINGS if SCHEMA[key] == "string" else NUMBERS
    if phase == "after_value":                           # "}" only when all keys are present
        return {"}"} if used == set(SCHEMA) else {","}
    if phase == "end":
        return {"<eos>"}
    return set()

def advance(state, token):
    """Move the state machine forward by one emitted token."""
    phase = state["phase"]
    if phase == "start":
        state["phase"] = "key"
    elif phase == "key":
        state["key"] = token
        state["used"] = state["used"] | {token}
        state["phase"] = "colon"
    elif phase == "colon":
        state["phase"] = "value"
    elif phase == "value":
        state["phase"] = "after_value"
    elif phase == "after_value":
        state["phase"] = "end" if token == "}" else "key"
    elif phase == "end":
        state["phase"] = "done"

# Scripted "model" scores (logits) for each step. The top choice is often a
# token that would break the JSON, which is what real models sometimes do.
# A real model would react to its earlier tokens; this script does not.
SCRIPT = [
    {"Sure": 3.1, "{": 2.4, '"city"': 0.3},              # wants to chat first
    {'"temp"': 1.9, '"city"': 1.7, "}": 2.2},            # wants to close early
    {":": 4.0, ",": 0.5},
    {"31": 2.0, '"hot"': 1.5, "}": 0.2},                 # schema says number here
    {"}": 2.6, ",": 1.1, "!": 0.4},                      # "city" is still missing
    {'"temp"': 2.8, '"city"': 1.0},                      # would repeat a key
    {":": 3.5},
    {"31": 2.2, '"Pune"': 2.1, '"hot"': 0.9},            # schema says string here
    {",": 1.8, "}": 1.6, "!": 1.0},
    {"!": 2.0, "<eos>": 1.9},
]

def decode(constrained):
    state = {"phase": "start", "used": set(), "key": None}
    out = []
    for step, scores in enumerate(SCRIPT, start=1):
        logits = {tok: scores.get(tok, -5.0) for tok in VOCAB}     # unlisted tokens score low
        free_pick = max(logits, key=logits.get)
        if not constrained:
            out.append(free_pick)
            continue
        allowed = allowed_tokens(state)
        masked = {tok: (s if tok in allowed else -math.inf) for tok, s in logits.items()}
        pick = max(masked, key=masked.get)
        note = "" if pick == free_pick else f"   (model wanted {free_pick})"
        print(f"step {step:>2}  allowed = {sorted(allowed)}  ->  pick {pick}{note}")
        out.append(pick)
        advance(state, pick)
        if state["phase"] == "done":
            break
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    free = decode(constrained=False)
    print("unconstrained:", " ".join(free))
    try:
        json.loads("".join(t for t in free if t != "<eos>"))
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        print("  json.loads fails:", e.msg, "\n")

    tokens = decode(constrained=True)
    text = "".join(t for t in tokens if t != "<eos>")
    parsed = json.loads(text)
    print("\nconstrained  :", text)
    assert parsed == {"temp": 31, "city": "Pune"}
    assert set(parsed) == {"city", "temp"} and isinstance(parsed["temp"], int)
    print("parses, has both keys, types match the schema")
```

## Key takeaways

* Reasoning effort is a setting per task: reasoning tokens cost latency and money, so spend them only on hard steps.
* MoE splits the feed-forward layer into experts and runs a few per token. Compute follows active parameters; memory follows total parameters.
* Distillation trains a small student on a large teacher's outputs to cut cost on a narrow task.
* Constrained decoding masks every token that would break the grammar, so the output always parses. It does not make the values correct.
* Speculative decoding keeps the large model's output distribution and gains speed only when the draft is accepted often.
* Long-running agents need checkpoints, limits and approvals because errors compound.
* The harness (skills, hooks, sub-agents, compaction) decides how reliable an agent is as much as the model does.
* A small fine-tuned model plus RAG, behind a router, is a common cost-for-quality design; GraphRAG is for questions that join facts across documents.

## Common mistakes

* Running every request at maximum reasoning effort, then being surprised by latency and cost.
* Sizing GPU memory for an MoE model from its active parameters. All experts must be loaded.
* Treating schema-valid JSON as correct JSON and skipping validation of the values.
* Turning on speculative decoding without measuring the acceptance rate on real traffic.
* Putting a hard safety rule only in the system prompt when a hook in code could enforce it.
* Building GraphRAG before plain hybrid retrieval has been measured and shown to fail.

## Practice

* Extend the code example: add a third required key `"unit"` whose value must be `"C"` or `"F"`, and confirm the output still parses.
* Compute the speculative decoding speed-up for a = 0.6 and 0.9 with g = 4 and a 5% draft cost (expected: about 1.9x and 3.4x).
* Run 30 eval tasks on a reasoning model at low and high effort. Report pass rate, median latency and output tokens for each.
* Add one before-hook to an agent loop that blocks a named tool call, and a test that proves the block works.

## Interview questions (10)

1.What is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model?Easy

The feed-forward layer is split into many expert networks and a router sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many parameters but uses a small part per token, so quality rises without the same rise in compute. Many recent open-weight models use sparse MoE designs. One detail matters for serving: all experts must stay in memory, so I size the GPU from total parameters and estimate speed from the active ones. Training also needs a load-balancing loss so the router spreads tokens across experts.

2.How do you get reliable JSON from an LLM?Medium

Use the provider's structured output or constrained decoding with a JSON schema, so invalid tokens cannot be sampled. Under the hood the schema becomes a state machine; at each step it masks every token that would break the grammar, and the model samples only from what is left. Then validate the result in code and retry with the error message if validation fails, because the schema guarantees the form, not the values, and output can still be cut off by the token limit. Never rely on "please return JSON" alone.

3.How does speculative decoding keep quality the same?Hard

The large model verifies every drafted token and rejects the ones it would not have produced. The draft model proposes a few tokens, and the large model scores all of them in one parallel pass. Each drafted token is accepted with probability min(1, p / q), where p is the large model's probability for it and q is the draft's. At the first rejection the large model samples a replacement from a corrected distribution and the rest of the draft is dropped, which makes the output distribution exactly the large model's. You only gain speed when the draft model guesses right often, so it works best on predictable text. With an 80% acceptance rate and 4 drafted tokens, you get about 3.4 tokens per large-model pass.

4.What do sub-agents cost you?Medium

More total tokens, more latency if they run in sequence, and lost detail when results are summarised. They pay off when sub-tasks are independent and large enough to pollute the lead agent's context. A sub-agent explores in its own window and returns a short summary, so the lead agent stays clean. I use them for broad search or research, and avoid them when steps are tightly coupled, because then the lead agent needs the detail that the summary drops.

5.When do you turn reasoning effort up, and when down?Medium

Reasoning models think before answering, and those reasoning tokens are billed as output and delay the visible answer. So I set the thinking level per task. Low or off for extraction, classification, routing and simple lookups. High for planning, debugging, multi-step maths and decisions that are costly to get wrong. I check the choice with an eval: run the same set at two effort levels and compare pass rate, latency and tokens. If the pass rate does not move, the extra thinking is wasted money. I also give these models a clear goal, not a step-by-step script.

6.What is distillation, and how is it different from ordinary fine-tuning?Medium

Distillation is fine-tuning where the labels come from a larger model. A large teacher generates outputs and a small student is trained to match them. In the classic form the student matches the teacher's full probability distribution, softened with a temperature, which carries more signal than one correct label. With an API teacher you only get text, so you train on its answers. It is how small models get close to large-model quality on a narrow task. The risks are copying the teacher's errors and drifting from real inputs, so I filter the teacher's outputs and evaluate on human-checked examples.

7.What is harness engineering? Give an example of a hook.Medium

The harness is all the code around the model: the loop, tool execution, context management, permissions and checks. Harness engineering is improving that code, and it often raises the task pass rate more than a model change. A hook is my own check that runs before or after a tool call. For example, a before-hook inspects every shell command and blocks a delete outside the project folder, and an after-hook runs the tests after each file edit and feeds failures back. The rule is enforced in code, so a confused or injected model cannot talk its way past it.

8.How do you manage context for an agent that runs for hours?Hard

Compact the history when the window fills, clear old tool results, keep notes in an external file, and push exploration into sub-agents that return summaries. I also keep the start of the context stable so the prompt cache keeps working. For the run itself I checkpoint state after each step so a crash resumes instead of restarting, make write actions idempotent, and set budgets for steps, tokens, time and money. Errors compound over long tasks, so I add approvals before anything irreversible.

9.Open-weight model or hosted API: how do you decide?Medium

Open models are now close to closed ones on many benchmarks, so self-hosting is a real option when cost, privacy or control matter. I would self-host when data cannot leave our environment, when volume is high and steady enough to keep GPUs busy, or when I need a fine-tuned adapter or fixed model version. I would stay on a hosted API when traffic is low or spiky, when the hardest reasoning is needed, or when the team cannot run GPUs. Either way I decide on my own eval set, not on public benchmarks.

10.When is GraphRAG worth building?Medium

GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph of entities and relations from the documents and retrieves over the graph. It helps with questions that need facts joined across many documents, where no single chunk holds the answer. The cost is indexing: a model reads every chunk to extract entities and relations, and updates repeat that work. So I start with hybrid retrieval and a reranker, build an eval set that includes multi-document questions, and add a graph only if those questions keep failing.

## Quiz

1.An MoE model has 8 experts per layer and routes each token to 2. What is true?

2.What does constrained decoding guarantee?

3.Speculative decoding gives a small speed-up on your traffic. What is the most likely cause?

4.A coding agent must never delete files outside the project folder. Where should this rule live?

# Agent frameworks - LangChain, LangGraph

An agent framework gives you the loop, the state and the tool plumbing from the previous lesson as ready-made parts. This lesson names the eight frameworks interviewers expect you to recognise, then teaches you to read LangChain and LangGraph code line by line: tools, `create_agent`, state, reducers, nodes, conditional edges, checkpointers and interrupts.

langchainlanggraphagent frameworksstate graphcheckpointerhuman in the loop

## Why it matters

Many job descriptions for AI engineers name LangChain or LangGraph, and interviewers often hand you a short snippet and ask what each line does. You also review code like this at work, written by a teammate or by an AI assistant. The questions that separate candidates are specific: what a reducer does, why the loop ends, what a checkpointer saves, and what happens when a paused run resumes. If you can answer those on a 20-line graph, you can pick up any other framework quickly, because they all wrap the same loop.

Read first: [Prompting and context engineering](/ai/learn/prompting-context-engineering), [Vector DBs and RAG](/ai/learn/vector-dbs-rag), [Agents from first principles - build a mini framework](/ai/learn/agents-first-principles)

## Lesson

You do not need to write this code from memory, but you must be able to read it and say what each line does. LangChain gives you a ready-made agent. LangGraph is the engine underneath, where the agent is drawn as a graph.

### Frameworks to recognise

| Framework | Known for | Choose it when your main constraint is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LangGraph | Agent as a graph with shared state and checkpoints; strong control and human-approval steps | Control: audit, approvals, long-running flows |
| CrewAI | Role-based teams of agents; fastest route to a multi-agent prototype | Time to a multi-agent demo |
| Microsoft Agent Framework | Merged AutoGen and Semantic Kernel into one SDK in April 2026; fits Azure and .NET | An Azure or .NET stack |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | Lightweight, minimal abstraction, OpenAI-centred | A small API to learn, on OpenAI models |
| Google ADK | Code-first toolkit for Gemini and Google Cloud | A Gemini and Google Cloud stack |
| LlamaIndex Workflows | Event-driven agents over large document sets | Document-heavy work |
| Pydantic AI | Type-safe Python with validated structured output | Type safety and validated output |
| Claude Agent SDK | Anthropic-native agents with sub-agents | Anthropic models with sub-agents |

AutoGen itself is now effectively in maintenance mode, so say "Microsoft Agent Framework" if asked about it.

To choose, name the one constraint that dominates your project and take the framework built around it. Then check that it covers what every production agent needs: saved state, a pause for approval, step limits and tracing. If you need none of these, plain SDK code is the right choice.

### How the LangChain products fit together

| Product | Layer | What it gives you | Reach for it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LangChain | Agent framework | One interface to models, tools and embeddings across providers, plus `create_agent` | You want a working agent quickly and will customise it |
| LangGraph | Orchestration runtime | State, nodes, edges, persistence, human-in-the-loop, streaming | You need control over the flow, mixing fixed steps with model-driven steps |
| Deep Agents | Agent harness on top of LangChain agents | Planning, sub-agents, a virtual filesystem, automatic context compression | Long tasks where you want those features ready-made |
| LangSmith | Platform | Tracing, evaluation, deployment | Always, for debugging and evals; it works with all three |

LangChain's agents are built on LangGraph, so a LangChain agent is a LangGraph graph inside.

### LangChain words you will see in code

* **Chat model:** one interface for every provider. Changing provider is changing a string.
* **Messages:** system, user, AI and tool messages. A conversation is a list of these.
* **Tool:** a normal Python function. Its name, docstring and type hints become the schema the model sees.
* **create\_agent:** takes a model, tools and a system prompt, and returns a ready agent with the tool-calling loop built in.
* **Middleware:** hooks that run around model and tool calls. Guardrails, retries, summarising and approval steps are added this way.
* **Structured output:** asking the model to return a typed object, not free text.
* **Loader, splitter, embeddings, vector store, retriever:** the RAG pieces from the Vector DBs and RAG lesson.
* **invoke, stream, batch:** run once, stream the output as it is produced, or run many inputs.
* **Pipe syntax (`prompt | model | parser`):** the older chain style, still common in existing codebases. Each piece passes its output to the next.

### Reading a LangChain agent

```
# needs: langchain
from langchain.agents import create_agent

def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up the delivery status of an order."""
    return lookup(order_id)

agent = create_agent(
    model="provider:model-name",
    tools=[get_order_status],
    system_prompt="You are a support assistant.",
)

result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order 123?"}]}
)
```

1. The function is the tool. The docstring tells the model when to use it; the type hints define its arguments.
2. `create_agent` wires the model, the tools and the prompt into a loop.
3. `invoke` sends the user message. The agent calls the model, runs any tool the model asks for, feeds the result back, and repeats until the model answers without a tool call.
4. `result["messages"]` holds the whole exchange, including tool calls. The last message is the answer.

### LangGraph words you will see in code

* **State:** a shared, typed dictionary. Every node reads it and returns only the part it changes.
* **Reducer:** the rule for merging an update into a state key. The default overwrites. `add_messages` appends, which is why chat history grows.
* **Node:** a Python function that takes the state and returns an update. It can be an LLM call or plain code.
* **Edge:** a fixed rule, "after A, go to B".
* **Conditional edge:** a function that looks at the state and returns the name of the next node. Branches and loops come from here.
* **START and END:** the entry and exit points.
* **compile:** turns the definition into something you can run. The checkpointer is attached here.
* **Checkpointer:** saves the state after every step, per `thread_id`. It gives conversation memory, recovery after a crash, human-in-the-loop and replay. In-memory for development; SQLite or Postgres for production. The LangGraph docs suggest SQLite for local workflows and Postgres for a production service.
* **interrupt:** pauses inside a node and waits for a person. You resume by invoking the graph with `Command(resume=...)`. It needs a checkpointer.
* **Command:** lets a node return a state update and the next node together.
* **Send:** starts many parallel runs of a node, one per item. Reducers merge the results. This is map-reduce.
* **Subgraph:** a graph used as a node inside another graph. Multi-agent systems are built this way.
* **ToolNode:** a prebuilt node that executes the tool calls in the last AI message.
* **Store:** long-term memory shared across threads. The checkpointer is memory within one thread.

### The agent loop as a graph

![The LangGraph agent loop from START through the model node, the tool calls decision and the tools node to END, with a checkpointer saving the state after every step](/ai/img/langgraph-loop-checkpointer.svg)The LangGraph agent loop from START through the model node, the tool calls decision and the tools node to END, with a checkpointer saving the state after every step

The loop is START, model node, a "tool calls?" decision, then either END or the tools node, whose results join the state before the model runs again. A checkpointer saves the state after every step, keyed by `thread_id`.

The conditional edge after the model node is the whole agent: tool calls send the run to the tools node and back, and no tool calls send it to END.

### Reading a LangGraph agent

```
# needs: langgraph
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]

def call_model(state: State):
    reply = model_with_tools.invoke(state["messages"])
    return {"messages": [reply]}

def route(state: State):
    last = state["messages"][-1]
    return "tools" if last.tool_calls else END

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("model", call_model)
builder.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))
builder.add_edge(START, "model")
builder.add_conditional_edges("model", route)
builder.add_edge("tools", "model")

graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
graph.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order 123?"}]},
    config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}},
)
```

1. **State:** one key, `messages`. `add_messages` means new messages are appended, not overwritten. `Annotated[list, add_messages]` is how a reducer is attached to a key.
2. **call\_model:** sends all messages to the LLM and returns its reply as the update. `model_with_tools` is defined outside the snippet: it is the chat model with the tool schemas attached, usually by `model.bind_tools(tools)`, so the model knows which tools it may ask for.
3. **route:** if the reply asks for a tool, go to `tools`. Otherwise finish.
4. **add\_node:** registers the two nodes. `ToolNode` runs the requested tools and adds their results as tool messages.
5. **Edges:** START to model; model to wherever `route` says; tools back to model. That last edge creates the loop.
6. **compile with a checkpointer:** the state is saved after every step.
7. **invoke with a thread\_id:** calling again with the same id continues the same conversation.

If the model never stops asking for tools, the recursion limit ends the run. It caps the steps of one run, raises `GraphRecursionError` when reached, and is set per call with `config={"recursion_limit": 25}`.

### What a reducer does: a two-node example

Take a state with one key, `results`, and two nodes. Node A returns `{"results": ["a"]}`. Node B returns `{"results": ["b"]}`.

| Setup | `results` at the end |
| --- | --- |
| No reducer, A runs and then B | `["b"]`. A's value is lost |
| Reducer `operator.add`, A runs and then B | `["a", "b"]` |
| No reducer, A and B run in the same step | Error: two writes to one key and no rule to merge them |
| Reducer `operator.add`, A and B run in the same step | Both values are kept |

```
# needs: langgraph
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict

class State(TypedDict):
    results: Annotated[list, operator.add]   # reducer: old + new
    status: str                               # no reducer: the new value replaces the old one
```

`add_messages` is a reducer written for chat history. It appends new messages, and when an update carries the id of an existing message it replaces that message.

### What a checkpointer stores per thread

A thread is the chain of checkpoints saved under one `thread_id`. Each checkpoint is a snapshot with these parts:

| Part | Holds | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Values | The full state at that point, such as the message list | Memory: the next call starts from here |
| Next | The node or nodes due to run next; empty when the run has finished | Resuming a crashed or paused run |
| Config | The thread id and this checkpoint's id | Loading one exact checkpoint |
| Metadata | The step counter and what wrote the checkpoint | Debugging |
| Parent | A pointer to the previous checkpoint | Walking the history, replay |
| Tasks | Pending work, including a waiting interrupt or an error | Human approval |

`graph.get_state(config)` returns the latest snapshot of a thread and `graph.get_state_history(config)` returns all of them, newest first. Replaying from an older checkpoint skips the nodes before it and runs the later ones again, LLM calls included.

### Reading a human approval step

```
# needs: langgraph
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command

def approve_refund(state: State):
    decision = interrupt({"refund": state["amount"]})
    return {"approved": decision == "yes"}

graph.invoke(Command(resume="yes"), config)
```

In this snippet `State` also has the keys `amount` and `approved`, and `config` is the same `thread_id` config that started the run.

`interrupt` saves the state and stops the run. Hours later, the second call resumes it with the person's answer. On resume the node runs again from its first line, so anything before the `interrupt` must be safe to repeat.

How the resume works, step by step:

1. The node calls `interrupt(payload)`. LangGraph saves a checkpoint and the first `invoke` returns, with the payload under `result["__interrupt__"]`.
2. Your application shows the payload to a person. Nothing is running while it waits.
3. The application calls `invoke` with `Command(resume="yes")` and the same `thread_id`.
4. LangGraph loads the checkpoint and restarts the node. This time `interrupt` returns `"yes"` and the node finishes.

Two rules follow. Put side effects after the `interrupt`, never before it. Do not wrap `interrupt` in a bare `try/except`, because the pause is raised as an exception.

### When someone else, or an AI, writes the code: five things to check

1. **State and reducers:** which keys exist, and which append instead of overwrite?
2. **Exits:** where can the loop end, and what stops it if the model keeps calling tools?
3. **Checkpointer:** is one attached, and is it a production one, not in-memory?
4. **Tools:** does each have a clear docstring and typed arguments?
5. **Side effects:** is there an approval step before anything that spends money or cannot be undone?

## Worked example

**Tracing one thread.** Run the graph above on "Where is order 123?" with `thread_id` "user-42". The input is merged first, so the state starts with 1 message.

| Step | Node that ran | Update it returned | Messages after the merge | Next node | Checkpoints in the thread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | model | 1 AI message with a tool call | 2 | tools | 1 |
| 2 | tools | 1 tool message: "out for delivery" | 3 | model | 2 |
| 3 | model | 1 AI message: the answer | 4 | END | 3 |

`route` ran twice. After step 1 the last message had a tool call, so it returned "tools". After step 3 it had none, so it returned END.

The last column counts one checkpoint per node step, as the small engine below does. Real LangGraph also saves two at the start of a run, an empty one and one that holds the input, so `get_state_history` returns 5 snapshots after this first call.

**Second call, same thread.** The user sends "Thanks!" with `thread_id` "user-42". The engine loads checkpoint 3 (4 messages), appends the new message (5), and runs the model once (6 messages, next is END). The thread now holds 4 checkpoints. A call with `thread_id` "user-7" starts from an empty state and ends with 2 messages: threads share nothing.

**The same run without the reducer.** Remove `add_messages`, so `messages` is overwritten. Step 1 replaces the user's question with the AI message: 1 message. Step 2 replaces that with the tool result: 1 message. At step 3 the model sees only "out for delivery" and has no idea what was asked. One missing annotation breaks the agent, and nothing raises an error.

**The loop that never ends.** If `route` always returns "tools", the run goes model, tools, model, tools. With a recursion limit of 4 it is stopped after step 4, with 4 checkpoints saved that show where it was going wrong.

The code example below is this exact run on a small engine written from scratch, and it prints the same numbers.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""A tiny state-graph engine in the style of LangGraph, standard library only.

Nodes read the state and return an update. A reducer merges each update. A conditional edge picks
the next node. A checkpointer saves the state after every step, keyed by thread id. No network.
"""
import copy

START, END = "__start__", "__end__"

class StateGraph:
    def __init__(self, reducers):
        self.reducers = reducers                      # key -> merge rule; other keys are overwritten
        self.nodes, self.edges, self.routers = {}, {}, {}

    def add_node(self, name, fn):
        self.nodes[name] = fn

    def add_edge(self, src, dst):                     # fixed: after src, always go to dst
        self.edges[src] = dst

    def add_conditional_edges(self, src, router):     # router(state) returns the next node's name
        self.routers[src] = router

    def merge(self, state, update):
        for key, value in update.items():
            reducer = self.reducers.get(key)
            state[key] = reducer(state[key], value) if reducer and key in state else value
        return state

    def invoke(self, update, thread_id, checkpointer, recursion_limit=10):
        history = checkpointer.setdefault(thread_id, [])              # one checkpoint list per thread
        state = copy.deepcopy(history[-1]["state"]) if history else {}
        state = self.merge(state, update)                             # the input is merged like any update
        node, step = self.edges[START], 0
        while node != END:
            step += 1
            if step > recursion_limit:
                raise RecursionError(f"no END after {recursion_limit} steps (recursion limit)")
            state = self.merge(state, self.nodes[node](state))        # run the node, merge what it returns
            nxt = self.routers[node](state) if node in self.routers else self.edges[node]
            history.append({"node": node, "next": nxt, "state": copy.deepcopy(state)})   # checkpoint
            last = state["messages"][-1]
            print(f"  step {step}: ran {node:5} next {nxt:7} | {len(state['messages'])} messages, "
                  f"model_calls={state['model_calls']} | last = {last['role']}: {last.get('tool_calls') or last['content']}")
            node = nxt
        return state

def add_messages(old, new):                           # reducer: append, do not overwrite
    return old + new

def call_model(state):                                # scripted fake model: decides from the last message
    last = state["messages"][-1]
    if last["role"] == "user" and "order" in last["content"]:
        reply = {"role": "ai", "content": "", "tool_calls": [{"name": "get_order_status", "args": {"order_id": "123"}}]}
    elif last["role"] == "tool":
        reply = {"role": "ai", "content": f"Order 123 is {last['content']}."}
    else:
        reply = {"role": "ai", "content": "You are welcome."}
    return {"messages": [reply], "model_calls": state.get("model_calls", 0) + 1}

def run_tools(state):                                 # like ToolNode: run every call in the last AI message
    tools = {"get_order_status": lambda order_id: "out for delivery"}
    calls = state["messages"][-1].get("tool_calls", [])
    return {"messages": [{"role": "tool", "content": tools[c["name"]](**c["args"])} for c in calls]}

def route(state):                                     # the conditional edge: tools, or finish
    return "tools" if state["messages"][-1].get("tool_calls") else END

def build(router):
    g = StateGraph(reducers={"messages": add_messages})   # model_calls has no reducer: it is overwritten
    g.add_node("model", call_model)
    g.add_node("tools", run_tools)
    g.add_edge(START, "model")
    g.add_conditional_edges("model", router)
    g.add_edge("tools", "model")
    return g

if __name__ == "__main__":
    saver, graph = {}, build(route)                   # saver: in-memory checkpointer, thread_id -> checkpoints
    for thread, text in [("user-42", "Where is order 123?"), ("user-42", "Thanks!"), ("user-7", "Hello")]:
        print(f"thread {thread}: {text}")
        out = graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": text}]}, thread, saver)
    assert len(saver["user-42"][-1]["state"]["messages"]) == 6 and len(out["messages"]) == 2
    print("checkpoints per thread:", {t: len(h) for t, h in saver.items()})
    try:                                              # a broken router that never returns END
        build(lambda state: "tools").invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}]}, "user-9", saver, 4)
    except RecursionError as exc:
        print("stopped:", exc)
```

## Key takeaways

* LangChain is the high-level framework with a prebuilt agent (`create_agent`). LangGraph is the runtime underneath: state, nodes, edges, persistence, interrupts.
* A LangGraph agent is two nodes and one conditional edge: tool calls go to the tools node and back, no tool calls go to END.
* A node returns only the keys it changes. The reducer decides how that update merges: overwrite by default, append with `add_messages`.
* The checkpointer saves the state after every step under a `thread_id`. It gives memory, crash recovery, human approval and replay.
* `interrupt` pauses a node; `Command(resume=...)` restarts that node from its first line, so code before the interrupt must be safe to repeat.
* Loops end through the conditional edge, a counter in the state, or the recursion limit. Set the limit yourself.
* Pick a framework by your dominant constraint, and use plain SDK code when a single call or a fixed pipeline is enough.
* Microsoft Agent Framework merged AutoGen and Semantic Kernel in April 2026; AutoGen itself is effectively in maintenance mode.

## Common mistakes

* Forgetting the reducer on `messages`, so each node overwrites the history and the model loses the question.
* Shipping with `InMemorySaver`. Every thread is lost when the process restarts, and paused approvals can never resume.
* Putting a side effect such as "send email" or "charge card" before `interrupt` in the same node. It runs again on resume.
* Using a new `thread_id` on every call and then wondering why the agent has no memory.
* Relying only on the conditional edge to end the loop, with no step counter and no explicit recursion limit.
* Reaching for a graph framework when one model call or a three-step fixed pipeline would do.

## Practice

* Run the code example, then change the engine so `messages` has no reducer. Record how many messages the model sees at step 3 (it should be 1) and explain the printed trace.
* Add an `interrupt` to the engine: a node may return `{"__interrupt__": payload}`, the engine saves a checkpoint and returns, and a second `invoke` with `resume=value` reruns that node. Add a refund approval node and show both the yes path and the no path.
* Take the LangGraph agent from this lesson and write, for each of the five review questions, the exact line that answers it. Note the two questions the snippet fails (no production checkpointer, no approval step).
* Build the same order-status agent twice, once with `create_agent` and once as your own graph, and list three things the second version lets you control that the first hides.

## Interview questions (14)

1.LangGraph or CrewAI?Easy

LangGraph when you need explicit control, state, auditability and long-running flows. CrewAI when the work splits into roles and you want a prototype quickly. Teams often prototype in one and move critical paths to the other. The difference is the core idea: LangGraph makes you draw the flow as nodes and edges with saved state, while CrewAI makes you describe a team of agents with roles and lets them coordinate.

2.LangChain vs LangGraph?Easy

LangChain is the high-level framework: standard components and a prebuilt agent. LangGraph is the low-level runtime: you define state, nodes and edges yourself and get persistence, interrupts and streaming. LangChain agents run on LangGraph. I start with `create_agent` and drop to LangGraph when I need custom control flow.

3.What is a reducer, and why does it matter?Medium

It decides how a node's update merges into the state. Without one, a new value replaces the old one. If two parallel nodes write the same key with no reducer, LangGraph cannot choose a winner and raises an error. So keys that accumulate, such as messages or results, need a reducer. The classic bug is a `messages` key without `add_messages`: every node overwrites the history, and the model stops seeing the user's question.

4.Edge vs conditional edge?Easy

An edge always goes to the same next node. A conditional edge runs a function on the state and picks the next node at run time. Every loop and branch in a graph is a conditional edge. In the standard agent graph there is exactly one: after the model node, go to the tools node if the last message has tool calls, otherwise go to END.

5.What do you lose without a checkpointer?Medium

Memory between calls, the ability to resume after a failure, interrupts for human approval, and the history you need for replay and debugging. I would not ship an agent without one. I would also make sure it is a database-backed checkpointer such as Postgres, because the in-memory one loses every thread when the process restarts.

6.Checkpointer vs store?Easy

The checkpointer keeps the state of one thread, which is short-term memory. The store keeps data across threads, such as user preferences, which is long-term memory. A support agent uses both: the checkpointer holds the messages of this conversation under its `thread_id`, and the store holds the fact that this customer prefers replies in Hindi, which every future conversation can read.

7.How do you run steps in parallel?Medium

Give one node several outgoing edges, or return `Send` objects to start one run per item. The parallel results merge through the reducer on the state key. For example, to summarise 10 documents I return 10 `Send` objects that each run the summarise node on one document, and a list key with an append reducer collects the 10 summaries. Without the reducer the parallel writes would conflict.

8.How do you stop an infinite loop?Medium

LangGraph enforces a recursion limit on steps. I also keep a counter in the state and make the conditional edge exit when it passes a threshold. The counter gives a clean exit with a useful message, and the recursion limit is the backstop that raises `GraphRecursionError`. I set the limit explicitly per run, because the default is high: the documentation gives 1,000 steps from version 1.0.6.

9.How do you debug a LangGraph agent?Medium

Turn on LangSmith tracing to see every node, tool call and state change. Inspect the saved state and its history for a thread, and replay from an earlier checkpoint to reproduce a failure. In practice I find the first step where the state looks wrong, check which node wrote it, and read that node's input. Replay matters because agents are not deterministic, so re-running from the top may not reproduce the bug.

10.create\_agent or your own graph?Medium

`create_agent` when the standard model-and-tools loop fits and I only need to add behaviour through middleware. My own graph when the flow has fixed business steps, several branches, approvals in specific places, or multiple agents. A refund flow is a good example of the second: verify identity, then check the policy, then ask for approval above a set amount. Those steps must happen in that order every time, so I code them as nodes.

11.When would you not use these frameworks?Medium

For a single model call or a simple fixed pipeline, plain SDK code is clearer. Frameworks add abstraction to learn and APIs that change between versions, so they have to pay for themselves in persistence, tracing or orchestration. My test is simple: if I do not need saved state, a pause for approval, or a loop the model controls, I do not need a graph runtime.

12.What happens, step by step, when a graph resumes after an interrupt?Hard

When the node calls `interrupt`, LangGraph saves a checkpoint for the thread and the `invoke` call returns with the interrupt payload. Nothing runs while the person decides. The application then invokes the graph with `Command(resume=answer)` and the same `thread_id`. LangGraph loads the checkpoint and runs the interrupted node again from its first line, and this time `interrupt` returns the answer. Two consequences: code before the interrupt runs twice, so it must be safe to repeat, and the whole thing needs a checkpointer that survives a restart.

13.How do you choose an agent framework for a new project?Medium

I name the dominant constraint first. Control, audit and approvals point to LangGraph. A quick multi-agent prototype points to CrewAI. An Azure or .NET stack points to Microsoft Agent Framework, and a Google Cloud stack to Google ADK. Document-heavy work points to LlamaIndex Workflows, and strict typing to Pydantic AI. Then I check four things in the candidate: saved state, a way to pause for approval, step limits and tracing. If the task is one call or a fixed pipeline, I use no framework.

14.An interviewer asks about AutoGen. What do you say?Easy

I would say that AutoGen was merged with Semantic Kernel into Microsoft Agent Framework in April 2026, and that AutoGen itself is now effectively in maintenance mode. So for new work on a Microsoft stack I would name Microsoft Agent Framework, which fits Azure and .NET. The idea AutoGen made popular, several agents solving a task by exchanging messages, still matters as a pattern.
