# History - how AI got to transformers

AI did not jump straight to LLMs (large language models). Each generation of methods hit a wall, and the next idea was built to get past it: hand-written rules, then learning from data, then deep networks on GPUs, then attention, then transformers pretrained on huge amounts of text. This lesson walks that chain in order, so you can explain why a transformer looks the way it does and which problem each part solves.

historyperceptrondeep learningattentiontransformersllm

## Why it matters

Interviewers rarely ask for dates. They ask "why": why did transformers replace RNNs, why did deep learning take off only in 2012, why do we pretrain. Those are history questions in disguise, and the strong answer is always "the older method had this limit, and the new one removed it". The same habit helps in design rounds. RAG, agents and reasoning models each exist because a plain LLM has a specific limit, and you choose between them by naming that limit. Skim this lesson once and keep the table.

## Lesson

### Rules first: symbolic AI and the perceptron

The field got its name at a summer workshop in 1956, six years after the Turing test was proposed. Early systems were symbolic: a programmer wrote facts and if-then rules, and the program searched through them. This worked on closed problems such as logic puzzles. It failed on real input, because nobody can write a rule for every way a cat can appear in a photo.

The perceptron (1958) was the first well-known alternative: one artificial neuron that learns its weights from labelled examples. In 1969 its limit was shown clearly. A single layer can only separate classes with a straight line, so it cannot learn even XOR. More layers would fix that, but nobody had a practical way to train them.

![Timeline of AI from 1950 to today with the years since 2012 enlarged into eight steps](/ai/img/ai-history-timeline.svg)Timeline of AI from 1950 to today with the years since 2012 enlarged into eight steps

### AI winters and expert systems

Promises ran ahead of results, and funding collapsed twice: in the mid-1970s and again in the late 1980s. These periods are called AI winters. Between them, the 1980s belonged to expert systems: thousands of if-then rules collected from human specialists, for narrow jobs such as diagnosing faults. They earned money, but every rule was written and maintained by hand, and they broke on any case their authors had not foreseen.

### Backpropagation and statistical machine learning

In 1986 backpropagation was shown to train networks with hidden layers: pass the error backward with the chain rule and adjust every weight. That removed the XOR limit. The networks stayed small, though. Datasets were tiny, computers were slow, and gradients faded in deep stacks.

So the 1990s and 2000s went to statistical machine learning: support vector machines (SVMs), decision trees, random forests and boosting. They learn the decision from data, and boosted trees are still a top choice for tables of numbers. Their limit was the input. People had to design the features for each task, such as edge detectors for images or word counts for text.

### 2012: deep learning works at scale

In 2012 a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) won the main image classification contest with 15.3% top-5 error. The runner-up, built on hand-designed features, scored 26.2%. Three things came together: 1.2 million labelled images, GPUs fast enough to train on them, and training tricks such as ReLU and dropout. The network learned its own features from raw pixels, so the hand-design step disappeared. Two limits remained: it needed very large labelled datasets, and language was still unsolved.

### Words, sequences and attention

Word embeddings (2013) gave every word a dense vector learned from raw, unlabelled text. Similar words sit close together, and king - man + woman lands near queen. The limit: one fixed vector per word, so "bank" means the same thing next to "river" and next to "loan".

Sequence-to-sequence models (2014) used one recurrent neural network (RNN) to read a sentence into a single vector and a second one to write the translation. Long sentences did not fit through that one vector. Attention, added the same year, let the decoder look back at every input word at each step. The RNN underneath still read one token at a time, which is slow to train and loses long-range context.

### The transformer and pretraining

The transformer (2017) dropped recurrence and kept only attention. Any two tokens connect in one step, and all positions train in parallel on GPUs. Its costs: attention grows with the square of the sequence length, and each task still needed its own labelled data.

Pretraining (2018 onward) fixed the data problem. Train a transformer on raw text to predict hidden or next tokens, then fine-tune it on a small labelled set. Encoder models (BERT style) became the standard for classification and search, decoder models (GPT style) for generation. The limit: one fine-tune per task.

In 2020 a decoder with 175 billion parameters showed that a large enough model can do a new task from a few examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. This is few-shot learning. It was still hard to steer, it made things up, and it knew nothing after its training data ended.

### Chat assistants, retrieval, agents and reasoning

Chat assistants (2022) added instruction tuning and alignment from human feedback, so the model follows a plain request. What a chat model still cannot do explains most of today's stack:

* **Stale or missing knowledge, invented facts:** retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fetches documents at query time.
* **It can only write text:** agents let the model call tools in a loop and act on the results.
* **Mistakes on multi-step problems:** reasoning models think before they answer, trained with reinforcement learning on rewards that can be checked automatically.

Still open: cost, latency, reliability over long tasks, and security.

### The chain in one table

| Era | Main idea | What limited it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1950s to 1960s: symbolic AI | Hand-written rules and search | Rules cannot cover messy real input |
| 1958: perceptron | Learn weights from examples | One layer: straight-line boundaries only, no XOR |
| 1980s: expert systems | Thousands of rules from specialists | Costly to maintain, brittle outside a narrow domain |
| 1986: backpropagation | Train hidden layers with the chain rule | Little data, slow computers, vanishing gradients |
| 1990s to 2000s: statistical ML | SVMs, trees, boosting | Features designed by hand for every task |
| 2012: deep learning | Deep CNN, GPUs, 1.2 million labelled images | Needs huge labelled sets; text unsolved |
| 2013: word embeddings | Word vectors from raw text | One vector per word, whatever the context |
| 2014: seq2seq and attention | RNN encoder-decoder that looks back at the input | Token by token: slow, forgets long-range context |
| 2017: transformer | Attention only, parallel training | Quadratic cost; labelled data per task |
| 2018: pretraining | Pretrain on raw text, then fine-tune | A separate fine-tune for every task |
| 2020: few-shot LLMs | The task is given in the prompt | Hard to steer, invents facts, frozen knowledge |
| 2022: chat assistants | Tuned to follow instructions | Stale knowledge, text only, weak multi-step reasoning |
| After 2022 | Retrieval, agents, reasoning models | Cost, latency, long-task reliability, security |

## Diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Worked example

**Why one perceptron cannot learn XOR, and how a hidden layer fixes it.** This small proof is the first "limit, then idea" step in the chain, and you can do it on paper.

A perceptron outputs 1 when w1 x1 + w2 x2 + b is greater than 0, and 0 otherwise. XOR outputs 1 only when exactly one input is 1. For a perceptron to compute XOR, four conditions must hold:

1. Input (0, 0) gives 0, so b is at most 0.
2. Input (0, 1) gives 1, so w2 + b is greater than 0.
3. Input (1, 0) gives 1, so w1 + b is greater than 0.
4. Input (1, 1) gives 0, so w1 + w2 + b is at most 0.

Add conditions 2 and 3: w1 + w2 + 2b is greater than 0, so w1 + w2 + b is greater than -b. Condition 1 says -b is at least 0. So w1 + w2 + b is greater than 0, which contradicts condition 4. No weights exist. In a picture: no single straight line puts (0, 1) and (1, 0) on one side and (0, 0) and (1, 1) on the other.

Now add two hidden units with the same step rule:

* h1 = step(x1 + x2 - 0.5), which is OR
* h2 = step(x1 + x2 - 1.5), which is AND
* output = step(h1 - h2 - 0.5), which is "OR and not AND"

| x1 | x2 | h1 | h2 | h1 - h2 - 0.5 | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | -0.5 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0.5 | 1 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0.5 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | -0.5 | 0 |

All four rows are correct. So a hidden layer has enough capacity. The open problem was how to learn those hidden weights, because the step function has zero slope and gives no signal about which way to move. Smooth activations plus backpropagation (1986) answered that, which is the next link in the chain.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""Why the field needed hidden layers: a perceptron learns AND but never XOR.

Part 1 trains a single perceptron with the classic learning rule.
Part 2 shows that two hidden units with hand-set weights solve XOR.
"""
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]])
AND = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])
XOR = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])

def step(z):
    return (z > 0).astype(int)

def train_perceptron(X, y, epochs=100, lr=0.1):
    """Perceptron rule: on each mistake, move the weights toward the example."""
    w, b = np.zeros(2), 0.0
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        mistakes = 0
        for xi, target in zip(X, y):
            pred = int(w @ xi + b > 0)
            if pred != target:
                w += lr * (target - pred) * xi
                b += lr * (target - pred)
                mistakes += 1
        if mistakes == 0:                      # a full pass with no mistake: converged
            return w, b, epoch
    return w, b, None

def two_layer_xor(X):
    """Hidden unit 1 computes OR, hidden unit 2 computes AND, output = OR and not AND."""
    h1 = step(X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - 0.5)         # OR
    h2 = step(X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - 1.5)         # AND
    return step(h1 - h2 - 0.5)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for name, y in [("AND", AND), ("XOR", XOR)]:
        w, b, epoch = train_perceptron(X, y)
        acc = (step(X @ w + b) == y).mean()
        status = f"converged in {epoch} epochs" if epoch else "never converged in 100 epochs"
        print(f"perceptron on {name}: {status}, accuracy {acc:.2f}")
        assert (acc == 1.0) == (name == "AND")

    out = two_layer_xor(X)
    print("two-layer network on XOR:", out, "target:", XOR)
    assert (out == XOR).all()
    print("one hidden layer solves XOR; a single perceptron cannot")
```

## Key takeaways

* The history is a chain: each method had a clear limit, and the next idea removed it.
* Rules and expert systems failed because people had to write every rule. Statistical ML learned the decision but still needed hand-designed features.
* Deep learning took off in 2012 when large labelled data, GPUs and better training tricks met. Backpropagation itself dates from 1986.
* Attention (2014) was added to RNNs to remove the single-vector bottleneck. The transformer (2017) kept attention and removed the RNN.
* Pretraining on raw text removed the need for labelled data per task. Large models then made the prompt the interface.
* RAG, agents and reasoning models each answer one limit of a plain chat model: stale knowledge, no actions, weak multi-step reasoning.

## Common mistakes

* Saying deep learning was invented in 2012. The ideas were decades old; data and GPUs made them work.
* Saying the transformer invented attention. Attention came three years earlier, on top of RNNs.
* Treating classical ML as obsolete. Boosted trees still win on many tabular problems and cost far less to run.
* Reciting dates without the reason. The interviewer wants the limit and the fix, not the year.

## Practice

* Close the lesson and write the "era, main idea, what limited it" table from memory. Aim for at least 10 of the 13 rows with the correct limit.
* Explain aloud, in under two minutes, the path from the perceptron to the transformer. Record it and check that you named at least six "limit, then fix" steps.
* Run the code example, then change the target to OR and to NAND. Record how many epochs the perceptron needs for each, and explain why both converge when XOR does not.

## Interview questions (6)

1.Why did transformers replace RNNs and LSTMs?Easy

RNNs process tokens one by one, so they cannot be parallelised and they forget long-range context. Attention connects any two tokens directly and trains in parallel on GPUs. To add detail: in an RNN, information from token 1 must survive every step to reach token 100, and the gradient has to travel the same path back, so it fades. LSTMs reduce that with gates but still run step by step. In a transformer the path between any two tokens is one attention step, and a whole sequence is processed in one pass. That made it practical to train on far more text, which is what later made pretraining and LLMs possible. The price is attention cost that grows with the square of the sequence length.

2.Backpropagation dates from 1986. Why did deep learning only take off in 2012?Medium

Three ingredients were missing. Data: deep networks need a lot of labelled examples, and a dataset with over a million labelled images only arrived around 2010. Compute: training on that much data was too slow on CPUs, and GPUs made it many times faster. Training methods: sigmoid networks suffered from vanishing gradients, and ReLU, better initialisation and dropout made deeper stacks trainable. In 2012 all three came together and a deep convolutional network cut the top-5 error on the main image benchmark to 15.3%, against 26.2% for the best system built on hand-designed features. After that result most of the field moved to deep learning.

3.What were the AI winters, and what caused them?Easy

They were two periods, in the mid-1970s and the late 1980s, when funding and interest in AI dropped sharply. Both followed the same pattern: large promises, systems that worked in demos but not on real problems, then disappointment. The first followed the limits of early symbolic AI and of the single-layer perceptron. The second followed expert systems, which were expensive to build and maintain because every rule was written by hand, and which broke outside their narrow domain. The lesson I take from it is to judge a method by measured results on real tasks, which is why I care about evals for LLM systems.

4.What did pretraining change, and how do encoder and decoder models differ?Medium

Before pretraining, each task needed its own model trained on its own labelled data. Pretraining trains one transformer on raw text with a self-supervised objective, so the labels come for free from the text itself. The model learns general language knowledge once, and a small labelled set is enough to adapt it. Encoder models hide some tokens and predict them using context on both sides, so they produce good representations for classification, search and reranking. Decoder models predict the next token using only the left context, so they generate text. Scaling up decoders led to few-shot LLMs, where the task is described in the prompt and no fine-tune is needed.

5.Which limits of a plain LLM led to RAG, agents and reasoning models?Medium

A plain LLM only knows its training data, so it is out of date, it has never seen private documents, and it fills gaps with fluent guesses. RAG addresses that by retrieving relevant text at query time and putting it in the prompt. A plain LLM also only produces text. Agents address that by letting the model call tools in a loop: search, run code, call an API, then read the result and decide the next step. Finally, a model that answers in one pass makes mistakes on multi-step problems. Reasoning models spend tokens thinking before the answer. What is still open is cost, latency, reliability over long tasks and security.

6.Are classical ML models still worth knowing now that LLMs exist?Easy

Yes. For structured tables with numeric and categorical columns, such as fraud scores, credit risk or click prediction, gradient-boosted trees are often the most accurate option, and they often train in minutes on a CPU. They are cheap to serve and easier to explain. Logistic regression is still the usual baseline and the final layer of many systems. LLMs are the right tool for open-ended language tasks. A common production design uses both: a small classical model or small neural model for high-volume narrow decisions, and an LLM for the cases that need language understanding.

## Quiz

2.What did statistical ML methods such as SVMs and boosted trees still depend on people for?

FoundationsLesson #6StudyBeginner 3 h

# Hugging Face end to end

Hugging Face is where open models live and the set of Python libraries used to run them. This lesson follows one path from start to finish: find a model on the Hub, read its card and licence, load the tokenizer and the weights, format a chat with the model's template, generate text, measure the output, and save or push your own version. Every step names the object you get back.

hugging facetransformerstokenizerchat templategenerationquantizationdatasets

## Why it matters

Almost every open-model project starts with `from_pretrained`. Interviewers who ask about fine-tuning or serving expect you to know what sits underneath: what a tokenizer returns, why a batch needs an attention mask, what a chat template is, and how an 8-billion-parameter model fits on a 16 GB GPU. The same knowledge saves hours of real work. Most "my model outputs garbage" reports come from a wrong template, a missing generation prompt or a default of 20 new tokens, not from the model. If you can run, measure and publish a model yourself, lessons 9 to 11 on fine-tuning and serving become much easier.

Read first: [LLM fundamentals - tokens, embeddings, decoding](/ai/learn/llm-fundamentals)

## Lesson

### The Hub: what you are downloading

The Hub is a hosting site for three kinds of repository: models, datasets and demo apps (called Spaces). A model repository is a versioned folder of files. Versioning is based on Git, so you can load an exact commit with the `revision` argument.

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `config.json` | Architecture: layer count, hidden size, vocabulary size |
| `model.safetensors` | The weights. Large models are split into shards such as `model-00001-of-00006.safetensors` |
| Tokenizer files | The vocabulary, the special tokens and the chat template |
| `generation_config.json` | Default generation settings for this model |
| `README.md` | The model card |
| `*.gguf` | Optional: the same model packed for llama.cpp |

Read the **model card** before anything else. It is the `README.md`, with a YAML block at the top that the Hub indexes: `license`, `base_model`, `datasets`, `language`, `tags`. Check three things: the licence (some forbid commercial use; `license: other` means a custom licence you must read), the `base_model` (is this a fine-tune, an adapter or a quantized copy of something else?), and the prompt format. Some models are **gated**: you accept the author's terms in the browser, then log in on your machine by running `hf auth login`, which stores an access token.

Two weight formats matter.

| Format | Contains | Loaded by | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| safetensors | Tensors only, no executable code | transformers, vLLM, most Python tools | Training, fine-tuning, GPU serving |
| GGUF | Tensors plus standard metadata in one binary file, usually quantized | llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio | Laptops, CPUs, edge devices |

Older PyTorch weights were stored with Python's pickle, which can run code when a file is loaded. Safetensors cannot, and it loads faster, so `from_pretrained` picks it when available. Some repositories ship their own model code and need `trust_remote_code=True`. Pass it only for code you have read, and pin a `revision`.

### The libraries, and the shortest path

* **transformers:** model classes, tokenizers, `generate`, `pipeline`.
* **accelerate:** places weights across GPU, CPU and disk. `device_map="auto"` needs it.
* **datasets:** load, transform and split data.
* **peft:** LoRA and other adapter methods (lesson 9).
* **trl:** training loops such as `SFTTrainer` (lesson 10).
* **bitsandbytes:** 8-bit and 4-bit loading.

`pipeline` is the shortest path. It loads the tokenizer and model, applies the chat template, generates and decodes.

```
# needs: transformers, accelerate, torch
from transformers import pipeline

chat = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful science assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain gravity in two sentences."},
]
pipe = pipeline(task="text-generation", model="HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct",
                dtype="auto", device_map="auto")
response = pipe(chat, max_new_tokens=128)
print(response[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])
```

Use `pipeline` to try a model. Use the explicit classes below when you need to see the tokens, batch prompts or train.

### What the tokenizer returns

`AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)` reads the repository and builds the right tokenizer. Calling it on text returns a dictionary. Two entries matter for a decoder model.

* `input_ids`: one integer per token. This is what the model reads.
* `attention_mask`: same shape, 1 for a real token and 0 for padding.

The tokenizer also adds **special tokens**, which mark structure and are not words: beginning of sequence, end of sequence, padding. Each model defines its own set. `decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True)` strips them on the way back.

A tensor must be a rectangle, so a batch of prompts with different lengths needs padding and sometimes truncation.

| Argument | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `padding` | `True` or `"longest"` | Pad to the longest sequence in the batch |
| `padding` | `"max_length"` | Pad every row to `max_length` |
| `truncation` | `True` | Cut rows longer than `max_length`; trailing tokens are lost |
| `max_length` | integer | The limit used by both |
| `return_tensors` | `"pt"` | Return PyTorch tensors, not Python lists |

Both `padding` and `truncation` are off by default. For generation, pad on the **left** by loading the tokenizer with `padding_side="left"`. A decoder continues from the last position, and it was never trained to continue from padding tokens. Many decoder tokenizers ship without a padding token, and padding then raises an error. For generation, the usual fix is `tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token`. Truncation cuts the end of a prompt, which for a chat is the newest question. Trim old turns yourself before tokenizing.

### Chat templates

A chat model is still a next-token predictor. During fine-tuning, every conversation was flattened into one string with control tokens that mark who is speaking. A **chat template** is the code, stored with the tokenizer, that rebuilds that exact string from a list of `{"role", "content"}` messages.

Formats differ between models, even between fine-tunes of the same base. One family marks a user turn with `[INST]` and `[/INST]`, another writes `<|user|>` and `<|assistant|>`, a third wraps each message in `<|im_start|>` and `<|im_end|>`. Feed a model the wrong format and it sees text unlike anything in its training data. It does not raise an error. It answers worse, rambles or continues the user's message. This is why a wrong template is the most common cause of bad output, in inference and in fine-tuning: when a fine-tuned model is worse than its base, check the template and special tokens first.

```
# needs: transformers, accelerate, torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype="auto", device_map="auto")

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    chat, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt"
).to(model.device)
input_length = inputs.input_ids.shape[1]

generated_ids = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=128)
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(generated_ids[:, input_length:], skip_special_tokens=True)[0])
```

Three rules prevent most template bugs.

1. Always call `apply_chat_template`. Never hand-write the control tokens.
2. Set `add_generation_prompt=True` for inference. It appends the tokens that open the assistant's turn. For training data set it to `False`, because the assistant's reply is already in the text.
3. Do not add special tokens twice. The template already contains them. If you render with `tokenize=False` and tokenize later, pass `add_special_tokens=False`. Using `tokenize=True` avoids the problem.

### Device and precision

`AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained` picks the model class from `config.json` and loads the weights. Two arguments decide where and how.

* `device_map="auto"` places the weights on the fastest device available, GPU first. What does not fit spills to CPU memory and then to disk, which is much slower.
* `dtype` sets the number format. `"auto"` uses the type stored in the checkpoint; `torch.bfloat16` forces 16-bit floats. Older code spells this argument `torch_dtype`.

Memory for weights is parameters times bytes per parameter. For an 8-billion-parameter model:

| Precision | Bytes per parameter | Weights |
| --- | --- | --- |
| float32 | 4 | about 32 GB |
| bfloat16 or float16 | 2 | about 16 GB |
| 4-bit | 0.5 | about 4 GB, plus the layers left unquantized |

To load in 4-bit, pass a quantization config. The weights are stored in 4 bits and computed in 16-bit.

```
# needs: transformers, accelerate, bitsandbytes, torch
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, device_map="auto", quantization_config=quantization_config
)
print(model.get_memory_footprint())
```

The printed footprint is larger than parameters x 0.5 bytes. Only the linear layers are replaced by 4-bit layers. The embedding table is not a linear layer, and the output head of a causal model keeps its original type. On a model with a large vocabulary these add 1 GB or more.

NF4 is the 4-bit scheme QLoRA uses. A model loaded this way cannot be fully fine-tuned; you can only train extra parameters such as LoRA adapters on top of it.

### Generation settings

`generate` runs the decode loop: forward pass, choose a token, append, repeat. Its defaults surprise people. Unless the model's `generation_config.json` says otherwise, decoding is greedy and stops after 20 new tokens.

| Argument | What it controls | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_new_tokens` | Upper limit on generated tokens, not counting the prompt | Always set it |
| `do_sample` | `False`: greedy, take the top token. `True`: sample | Greedy for extraction and evals |
| `temperature` | Flattens (above 1) or sharpens (below 1) the distribution | Ignored unless `do_sample=True` |
| `top_p` | Sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose probability reaches p | Default 1.0, which keeps everything |
| `top_k` | Sample only from the k most likely tokens | Default 50 |
| `repetition_penalty` | Above 1.0 discourages repeats | 1.0 means off |

A decoder-only model returns the prompt ids followed by the new ids. Slice from the input length, as in the code above, or the prompt appears in your answer.

### Datasets: load, map, split

A dataset is a table with named columns. `load_dataset` downloads one from the Hub, `map` applies a function to every row, and `train_test_split` creates a held-out set. Shuffling once with a fixed seed and then splitting with `shuffle=False` gives the same split on every run. In the sketch below, replace `your-name/support-chats` with any dataset that has a `messages` column.

```
# needs: datasets, transformers
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("your-name/support-chats", split="train")
dataset = dataset.shuffle(seed=42).train_test_split(test_size=0.1, shuffle=False)

def to_text(example):
    text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        example["messages"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False
    )
    return {"text": text}

dataset = dataset.map(to_text)
print(dataset["train"][0]["text"])
```

Printing one formatted row and reading it is the cheapest check in the whole pipeline. With `batched=True`, `map` passes 1,000 rows at a time, which is much faster for tokenizing.

### Where PEFT and TRL fit

Inference stops at `generate`. To change the model you add two libraries. PEFT wraps the loaded model with small trainable adapter matrices: build a `LoraConfig`, call `get_peft_model`, and the base weights stay frozen. TRL supplies the training loop. `SFTTrainer` takes a model, a `train_dataset` and an optional `peft_config`, and applies the chat template for you when the dataset has a `messages` column. Lessons 9 and 10 cover the choices.

### Evaluating outputs

Before you call your version better, measure it.

1. Hold out data the model never trains on. The `test` split above is enough to start.
2. Fix the generation settings. Use `do_sample=False` so two runs give the same text.
3. Score with the cheapest check that fits the task: exact match for labels, valid JSON for extraction, a unit test for code, a judge model with a rubric for free text.
4. Run the base model and your model on the same prompts and compare the two numbers.
5. Read 20 raw outputs. A metric will not tell you that every answer starts with a stray token.

### Saving and pushing

`save_pretrained` writes the files to a local folder. `push_to_hub` creates a repository under your account and uploads them. Save the tokenizer with the model, or the next user gets no chat template.

```
# needs: transformers, huggingface_hub (run `hf auth login` first)
model.save_pretrained("my-model")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("my-model")

model.push_to_hub("your-name/my-model")
tokenizer.push_to_hub("your-name/my-model")
```

A PEFT model saves only the adapter: `adapter_config.json` and `adapter_model.safetensors`, usually a few megabytes. Then write the model card: base model, training data, licence, prompt format and your eval numbers.

## Worked example

**Fitting and running an 8-billion-parameter chat model on one 16 GB GPU.**

**Step 1: memory.** In float32 the weights need 8 billion x 4 bytes = 32 GB. In bfloat16 they need 8 billion x 2 = 16 GB, which fills the card and leaves nothing for activations or the KV cache. In 4-bit they need 8 billion x 0.5 = 4 GB, plus the embedding table and output head, which stay unquantized. With a 128,000-token vocabulary and a hidden size of 4,096, each of those is 128,000 x 4,096 x 2 bytes = about 1 GB in 16-bit, so plan for about 6 GB. So load in 4-bit.

**Step 2: a batch.** Three chats go through the template and the tokenizer and come out as 22, 9 and 14 token ids. With `padding=True` every row becomes 22 long. The batch has 3 x 22 = 66 slots, of which 22 + 9 + 14 = 45 are real tokens and 21 are padding, so 32% of the batch is padding. The attention mask has 45 ones and 21 zeros. With left padding, the last column holds a real token in all three rows, which is where generation continues.

**Step 3: generate.** With `max_new_tokens=50` the output has at most 22 + 50 = 72 columns. Slicing from column 22 leaves at most 50 new tokens per row. Rows that finish early are filled with padding after their end-of-sequence token, and `skip_special_tokens=True` removes it.

**Step 4: measure.** On 200 held-out prompts with greedy decoding, suppose the base model gets 124 exactly right: 124 / 200 = 62%. After training an adapter, 163 are right: 163 / 200 = 81.5%. That is a gain of 19.5 points on the same prompts and the same settings.

**Step 5: save.** The PEFT documentation's example adapter on a model with 1,236,338,688 parameters trains 524,288 of them, which is 0.0424%. In float32 that adapter is 524,288 x 4 bytes = about 2.1 MB. The full model in 16-bit is 1,236,338,688 x 2 bytes = about 2.5 GB. You push megabytes, and the card names the base model.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""A chat template and a padded batch, in miniature.

The tokenizer here is a toy (one id per word or special token). It stands in
for a real subword tokenizer so every step runs with NumPy alone.
"""
import re

import numpy as np

def render_chatml(messages, add_generation_prompt=True):
    """ChatML-style template: <|im_start|>role, newline, content, <|im_end|>."""
    text = ""
    for m in messages:
        text += f"<|im_start|>{m['role']}\n{m['content']}<|im_end|>\n"
    if add_generation_prompt:
        text += "<|im_start|>assistant\n"      # tells the model: your turn starts here
    return text

def render_zephyr(messages, add_generation_prompt=True):
    """A different model family: same messages, different control tokens."""
    text = ""
    for m in messages:
        text += f"<|{m['role']}|>\n{m['content']}</s>\n"
    if add_generation_prompt:
        text += "<|assistant|>\n"
    return text

class ToyTokenizer:
    """Maps each special token, word or punctuation mark to an integer id."""

    SPECIAL = ["<pad>", "<|im_start|>", "<|im_end|>"]

    def __init__(self):
        self.vocab = {tok: i for i, tok in enumerate(self.SPECIAL)}
        self.pad_token_id = self.vocab["<pad>"]

    def tokenize(self, text):
        return re.findall(r"<\|im_start\|>|<\|im_end\|>|\n|\w+|[^\w\s]", text)

    def encode(self, text):
        ids = []
        for tok in self.tokenize(text):
            if tok not in self.vocab:
                self.vocab[tok] = len(self.vocab)
            ids.append(self.vocab[tok])
        return ids

    def decode(self, ids, skip_special_tokens=False):
        inv = {i: t for t, i in self.vocab.items()}
        toks = [inv[i] for i in ids]
        if skip_special_tokens:
            toks = [t for t in toks if t not in self.SPECIAL]
        return " ".join(toks).replace("\n", "\\n")

def pad_batch(sequences, pad_id, side="left", max_length=None):
    """Return (input_ids, attention_mask) as rectangular integer arrays."""
    if max_length is not None:                       # truncation keeps the first max_length ids,
        sequences = [s[:max_length] for s in sequences]   # so the END of a long prompt is lost
    width = max(len(s) for s in sequences)
    input_ids = np.full((len(sequences), width), pad_id, dtype=np.int64)
    attention_mask = np.zeros((len(sequences), width), dtype=np.int64)
    for row, seq in enumerate(sequences):
        if side == "left":
            input_ids[row, width - len(seq):] = seq
            attention_mask[row, width - len(seq):] = 1
        else:
            input_ids[row, :len(seq)] = seq
            attention_mask[row, :len(seq)] = 1
    return input_ids, attention_mask

def mean_pool(input_ids, attention_mask, table):
    """Average the token vectors of each row, counting only positions where mask is 1."""
    vectors = table[input_ids]                       # (batch, width, dim)
    mask = attention_mask[:, :, None]
    return (vectors * mask).sum(axis=1) / mask.sum(axis=1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    chats = [
        [{"role": "system", "content": "Answer in one word."},
         {"role": "user", "content": "Capital of India?"}],
        [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],
        [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2 + 2?"}],
    ]

    print("STEP 1. One list of messages, two templates")
    print(render_chatml(chats[0]))
    print(render_zephyr(chats[0]))

    print("STEP 2. Template string to token ids")
    tok = ToyTokenizer()
    batch = [tok.encode(render_chatml(c)) for c in chats]
    for ids in batch:
        print(f"  {len(ids):2d} ids: {ids}")

    print("STEP 3. Pad to a rectangle and build the attention mask")
    for side in ("right", "left"):
        ids, mask = pad_batch(batch, tok.pad_token_id, side=side)
        print(f"  padding_side={side}, shape={ids.shape}, "
              f"real tokens={int(mask.sum())}, padding={int((1 - mask).sum())}")
        print("  input_ids:\n" + "\n".join("    " + str(r) for r in ids))
        print("  attention_mask:\n" + "\n".join("    " + str(r) for r in mask))
        last_is_real = bool(mask[:, -1].all())
        print(f"  last column is a real token in every row: {last_is_real}")
        assert mask.sum(axis=1).tolist() == [len(s) for s in batch]

    print("STEP 4. Truncation: max_length=8 keeps the first 8 ids of each row")
    ids, mask = pad_batch(batch, tok.pad_token_id, side="left", max_length=8)
    print("  shape:", ids.shape, "real tokens per row:", mask.sum(axis=1).tolist())

    print("STEP 5. Why the mask matters")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    table = rng.normal(size=(len(tok.vocab), 4))     # one 4-number vector per token id
    ids, mask = pad_batch(batch, tok.pad_token_id, side="left")
    alone = table[np.array(batch[1])].mean(axis=0)   # the short chat on its own
    with_mask = mean_pool(ids, mask, table)[1]
    no_mask = mean_pool(ids, np.ones_like(mask), table)[1]
    print("  short chat alone      :", np.round(alone, 3))
    print("  in batch, with mask   :", np.round(with_mask, 3))
    print("  in batch, mask ignored:", np.round(no_mask, 3))
    assert np.allclose(alone, with_mask) and not np.allclose(alone, no_mask)

    print("STEP 6. Decode ids back to text")
    print("  with special tokens   :", tok.decode(batch[1]))
    print("  skip_special_tokens   :", tok.decode(batch[1], skip_special_tokens=True))
```

## Key takeaways

* A model repository is a folder: config, weights, tokenizer files with the chat template, generation defaults and a model card. Read the card and the licence first.
* Safetensors is the format transformers loads: tensors only, no executable code. GGUF is one file with metadata for llama.cpp-style runtimes, usually quantized.
* A tokenizer returns `input_ids` and `attention_mask`. The mask is 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding. Pad on the left for generation.
* The chat template rebuilds the exact string format the model was trained on. A wrong or missing template is the first thing to check when output is bad.
* Weights memory is parameters times bytes per parameter: 8 billion parameters is 32 GB in float32, 16 GB in 16-bit, and about 4 GB in 4-bit plus the layers left unquantized.
* `generate` is greedy and stops after 20 new tokens unless told otherwise. Set `max_new_tokens`, and remember `temperature` and `top_p` do nothing without `do_sample=True`.
* Compare your model with the base on the same held-out prompts with fixed settings before you push it.
* Push the tokenizer with the model. After a LoRA run, the adapter is two small files.

## Common mistakes

* Writing the prompt as a plain string for a chat model, or copying another model's control tokens, when `apply_chat_template` exists.
* Leaving out `add_generation_prompt=True` at inference, so the model continues the user's message.
* Tokenizing a templated string with special tokens added again, which doubles the beginning-of-sequence token.
* Batching prompts with right padding, so short rows generate from padding tokens.
* Not setting `max_new_tokens`, then concluding the model "cuts off mid-sentence".
* Decoding the full output and reporting the prompt as part of the answer.

## Interview questions (11)

1.What does a tokenizer return, and what is the attention mask for?Easy

It returns a dictionary. `input_ids` holds one integer per token, and that is what the model reads. `attention_mask` has the same shape, with 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding. A batch must be rectangular, so short prompts are padded to the length of the longest one. Attention looks at every position, so without the mask the padding tokens would change the result for the short rows. The mask tells the attention layers to ignore those positions. The tokenizer also adds the model's special tokens, such as beginning of sequence.

2.What is a chat template, and why does the wrong one hurt?Medium

A chat model only continues a token sequence. In fine-tuning, each conversation was flattened into one string with control tokens marking the roles, and the format differs per model: one uses `[INST]` tags, another uses `<|im_start|>` and `<|im_end|>`. The chat template is stored with the tokenizer and rebuilds that format from a list of role and content messages. With the wrong format the model sees input unlike its training data. Nothing crashes, the answers just get worse: it ignores the system prompt, rambles or continues the user's turn. So I always call `apply_chat_template` and never hand-write the tokens.

3.Your model's output is bad after loading it or fine-tuning it. What do you check first?Medium

The chat template, because it is the most frequent bug. I print the exact string the model receives and compare it with the format on the model card. I look for three things: the right control tokens, special tokens that appear twice, and the generation prompt at the end for inference. For a fine-tune I check that training and inference used the same template and the same end-of-turn token. Then I check generation settings: `max_new_tokens`, sampling, left padding for batches. Only after that do I suspect learning rate, epochs or the data.

4.Why do you pad on the left for generation?Medium

A decoder-only model predicts the next token from the last position of each row. With right padding, a short row ends in padding tokens, and the model was never trained to continue from padding, so the continuation is poor. With left padding, every row ends with its real last token and the padding sits at the start, where the attention mask hides it. For training the side matters less, because the loss ignores padded positions, but for batched generation it must be left.

5.safetensors or GGUF: what is the difference?Easy

Both store model weights. Safetensors stores only tensors and cannot run code when loaded, unlike the older pickle-based files, and it loads fast. It is what transformers, PEFT and GPU servers such as vLLM read. GGUF is a single binary file that holds the tensors plus standard metadata, and it is the format llama.cpp and tools built on it use. GGUF files are usually quantized, for example to about 4.5 bits per weight. I use safetensors to train or serve on GPUs and GGUF to run on a laptop or CPU.

6.How do you fit an 8-billion-parameter model on a 16 GB GPU?Medium

Start with the arithmetic. Float32 is 4 bytes per parameter, so 32 GB. 16-bit halves that to 16 GB, which fills the card with no room for activations or the KV cache. So I load it in 4-bit with a `BitsAndBytesConfig`, which stores the linear layers in about 4 GB and computes in bfloat16. The embeddings and output head stay in 16-bit, so the real footprint is nearer 6 GB. I pass `device_map="auto"` so placement is handled for me. The cost is some quality, more on reasoning and long outputs, so I compare against the 16-bit model on my own eval set if I can run it somewhere.

7.Which generation settings do you set, and what are the defaults?Easy

By default `generate` is greedy and stops after 20 new tokens unless the model's generation config says otherwise. So I always set `max_new_tokens`. For extraction, classification and evals I keep `do_sample=False`, so runs are repeatable. For chat or creative text I set `do_sample=True` with a temperature around 0.7 and `top_p` around 0.9. Temperature and top-p are ignored when sampling is off, which is a common confusion. I also remember that the output contains the prompt, so I slice it off before decoding.

8.pipeline or AutoModel with generate: when do you use each?Easy

`pipeline` is one call that loads the tokenizer and model, applies the chat template, generates and decodes. I use it to try a model or build a quick demo. I switch to `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModelForCausalLM` when I need control: inspecting token ids, batching prompts with padding, custom stopping, reading logits, or training. In production I usually use neither for serving. A dedicated engine such as vLLM handles batching and caching far better than a Python loop around `generate`.

9.How do you show that your version of a model is better than the base?Medium

I hold out data the model never trained on, usually 10 to 20 percent. I run the base and my model on the same prompts with the same template and greedy decoding, so differences come from the weights and not from sampling. I score with the cheapest check that fits: exact match, schema validity, unit tests, or a judge model with a rubric. I also run a small set of general prompts to catch forgetting, and I read a sample of raw outputs. If the gain is not clear, I do not ship.

10.After a LoRA fine-tune, what do you push to the Hub?Medium

Usually only the adapter. A PEFT model's `save_pretrained` and `push_to_hub` write two files, `adapter_config.json` and `adapter_model.safetensors`, a few megabytes against gigabytes for the base. The config records the base model, and I set `base_model` in the card so the Hub links them. I push the tokenizer too if I changed the template or added tokens. I push merged full weights only when the serving stack cannot load adapters, because that costs the full model size per variant.

11.What do you check on a model card before using a model?Easy

The licence first: whether commercial use is allowed and whether the model is gated. Then the base model and what was changed, the training data, the prompt format or chat template, the context length, and any eval numbers with how they were measured. I also look at the files tab: is there a safetensors file, does the repository need `trust_remote_code`, and how large are the weights. If code must be trusted, I read it and pin a commit.

# Inference and serving - KV cache, batching, vLLM

Inference is running a trained model to produce output. Serving is doing that for many users at once, fast and cheaply. This lesson follows one request through an LLM server: the prefill and decode phases, the KV cache that makes decode fast, batching that keeps the GPU busy, quantization that shrinks the model, and the metrics and engines you use to run it in production.

inferencekv cachecontinuous batchingvllmquantizationlatencyautoscaling

## Why it matters

Serving questions test whether you can reason with numbers. "Serve an open model to 1,000 users" and "design a batching system for one GPU" are asked at AI labs and platform teams, and the follow-ups are always the same: where does the memory go, why is the first token slow, what happens to latency when you raise the batch size. In real work the same ideas decide your GPU bill. A team that understands the KV cache, continuous batching and prefix caching can serve the same traffic on a fraction of the hardware.

Read first: [LLM fundamentals - tokens, embeddings, decoding](/ai/learn/llm-fundamentals), [Coding simple attention](/ai/learn/coding-simple-attention)

## Lesson

Serving comes down to three numbers: latency, throughput and cost per token. Almost every technique here trades one for another, and saying which trade you are making is what interviewers listen for.

### Two phases: prefill and decode

* **Prefill** processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass and saves what it computed for every prompt token. Prefill sets time to first token.
* **Decode** then generates one token at a time. Each step feeds in only the newest token. Decode sets tokens per second.

```
Prompt: "The capital of France is"   (5 tokens)

Prefill   [The][capital][of][France][is]   one parallel pass      -> " Paris"   cache: 5 tokens
Decode 1  [ Paris]                         reads 5 cached tokens  -> "."        cache: 6 tokens
Decode 2  [.]                              reads 6 cached tokens  -> <eos>      cache: 7 tokens
```

Prefill can be parallel because every prompt token is already known. Decode cannot: token 2 of the answer depends on token 1. So a 2,000-token prompt costs one pass, and a 300-token answer costs 300 passes, one after another. That is why capping output length cuts total latency more than trimming the prompt does.

Each decode pass reads every weight of the model to produce a single token. If 32 requests share the pass, the weights are read once and 32 tokens come out. This is the reason batching helps decode so much.

### The KV cache

Attention compares the new token's query with a key and a value from every earlier token. A decoder token only looks backwards, so those keys and values never change once computed. During decode, the keys and values of all earlier tokens are stored for every layer, so each new token only computes its own. Without the cache, every step would push the full sequence through the model again. For a 2,000-token prompt and a 300-token answer that is 2,000 + 2,001 + ... + 2,299 = 644,850 token positions through the layers. With the cache it is 2,299: the prompt once, then one position per step. The cache makes generation fast, and it is the main memory cost besides the weights.

Formula

KV bytes=2×layers×heads×head dim×sequence length×batch×bytes per value

The 2 is for keys plus values. Heads x head dim equals the hidden size in a standard model. Models with grouped-query attention share keys and values between heads, so count the KV heads only. The cache is not shared between requests: every concurrent request holds its own.

### Memory maths you should be able to do

Weights = parameters x bytes per parameter. A 7B model in FP16 (2 bytes) needs about 14 GB. In 4-bit it needs about 3.5 GB. A 70B model in FP16 needs about 140 GB. Then add the KV cache, which grows with layers x sequence length x batch size.

**Quantization** stores weights in fewer bits (FP16 to INT8 to 4-bit). Memory drops and speed rises, with a small quality loss.

| Precision | Bytes per parameter | 7B model | Quality |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FP32 | 4 | 28 GB | Training precision; rarely served |
| FP16 or BF16 | 2 | 14 GB | The serving default |
| INT8 | 1 | 7 GB | Usually near lossless |
| 4-bit | 0.5 | 3.5 GB | Fine for many tasks; can hurt reasoning, maths and long outputs |

Names to know:

* **GPTQ and AWQ** are post-training methods: they quantize an already trained model using a small calibration set, with no retraining. GPTQ goes layer by layer and adjusts the remaining weights to cancel each rounding error. AWQ looks at activations to find the small share of weights that matter most and protects them.
* **GGUF** is the file format llama.cpp uses. One file holds the quantized weights, the tokenizer and the metadata, at a bit width you choose when you download it.
* **NF4** is the 4-bit data type used by QLoRA.

GPU engines such as vLLM load a GPTQ or AWQ checkpoint; llama.cpp and Ollama load GGUF; TensorRT-LLM compiles the model into an engine file built for one GPU type. Quantizing the weights does not shrink the KV cache, so long contexts stay expensive.

### The metrics

* **TTFT** (time to first token): queue wait plus prefill.
* **TPOT** (time per output token): the gap between streamed tokens.
* **Tokens per second:** 1 / TPOT for one request.
* **End-to-end latency:** from request to last token.
* **Throughput:** total tokens per second across all requests on the server.

Formula

latency=TTFT+(N−1)×TPOT,throughput≈TPOT at that batch sizebatch size​

N is the number of output tokens. With streaming, users feel TTFT first and TPOT after that, so a chat product sets a target for each. A batch job cares only about throughput. Always quote p95 or p99, not the average. p95 is the latency that 95% of requests beat. Latency has a long tail, and the slowest 5% of requests are the ones users complain about.

### Batching: static and continuous

A GPU can run many requests in one forward pass for little extra time, so batching is where throughput comes from.

**Static batching** waits to fill a batch and holds every request until the longest finishes. A request that needs 2 tokens sits in a batch with one that needs 8, and its slot does nothing for 6 steps.

**Continuous batching** adds new requests and removes finished ones at every decode step, so the GPU stays busy.

![Two timelines of six requests on three GPU slots: static batching leaves slots idle, continuous batching refills them](/ai/img/batching-static-vs-continuous.svg)Two timelines of six requests on three GPU slots: static batching leaves slots idle, continuous batching refills them

In the picture, six requests need 2, 8, 4, 3, 5 and 2 tokens on three slots. Static batching finishes at step 13 with the GPU 61.5% busy. Continuous batching finishes at step 9 with the GPU 88.9% busy, and the average wait drops from 4.0 steps to 1.8. The gap widens when output lengths vary more, which is the normal case for chat.

What limits the batch is memory first and latency second. Every running request needs room for its KV cache, and every extra request slows each step a little.

**The one-GPU batching question.** "Design an inference batching system for one GPU while users wait" is reported again and again at AI labs. The expected answer: requests enter a queue, and a scheduler fires a batch when either the maximum batch size or a short maximum wait window is reached. Call the wait window your latency-throughput dial. Group requests by length so padding does not dominate, add backpressure when the queue grows, and mention continuous batching for token generation. Padding is the filler that brings every prompt in a batch up to the longest one. Backpressure means the server rejects or delays new requests once the queue is too long.

### PagedAttention and prefix caching

A request's cache grows one token at a time, and the server cannot know the final length. Older engines reserved one contiguous block per request, sized for the longest possible output. Most of that reservation stayed empty, and the gaps between blocks were too small to reuse.

**PagedAttention** stores the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks, like virtual memory pages, instead of one contiguous block per request. A block is handed out only when the sequence needs it, and a table maps each request to its blocks. Less fragmentation means bigger batches on the same GPU.

**Prefix caching** reuses the KV cache for a shared prompt prefix (system prompt, few-shot examples, chat history) across requests. The second request with the same first 1,500 tokens skips prefill for them, so TTFT drops. The match must be exact from the first token, so put stable text first and anything that changes (the user message, the time) last.

### Speculative decoding, FlashAttention and multi-GPU

* **Speculative decoding:** a small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. Accepted tokens are free speed; the output distribution stays the same. Say the draft proposes 4 tokens and the large model agrees with the first 3. It keeps those, replaces the fourth with its own choice, and has produced 4 tokens for the price of one large pass plus four cheap ones. If the first guess is wrong, it still gets 1 token, so the output is never worse, only the speed-up is lost. The method spends extra compute to cut latency, so it helps most when the GPU has spare capacity.
* **FlashAttention:** computes exact attention in a memory-efficient way on the GPU, by working in blocks that fit in fast on-chip memory. Same result, less memory, faster.
* **Multi-GPU:** tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs when a model does not fit on one. A 70B model at 140 GB in FP16 does not fit on one 80 GB GPU.

### Serving engines

| Engine | Best for | Remember |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ollama | Local development and prototyping | Simplest setup; not built for production scale |
| llama.cpp | CPU, laptops, edge devices | Runs GGUF quantized models almost anywhere |
| vLLM | High-concurrency production APIs | PagedAttention plus continuous batching; OpenAI-compatible API; broad hardware support |
| SGLang | Multi-turn chat, agents, structured output | RadixAttention reuses shared prefixes automatically; fast constrained decoding |
| TensorRT-LLM with Triton | Maximum performance on NVIDIA; multi-model pipelines | Needs a model compile step and MLOps skill |
| TGI | Existing deployments only | In maintenance mode since December 2025; Hugging Face recommends vLLM or SGLang for new work |

To serve many fine-tuned variants, keep one base model in memory and load a LoRA adapter (a small set of extra weights from fine-tuning) per request. This is multi-LoRA serving.

### Autoscaling and load testing

**Autoscaling.** Scale on queue depth, tokens in flight or TTFT, not CPU.

| Signal | What it tells you | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queue depth | Requests are waiting for a slot right now | The earliest warning; scale on it first |
| Tokens in flight | Prompt plus expected output tokens of all running and queued requests | Better than a request count, because one request can be 100 times larger than another |
| p95 TTFT | What users feel | It moves late, after the queue has already built up |
| CPU or GPU utilisation | Little | CPU stays low while the GPU is saturated; GPU utilisation reads high at almost any batch size |

Model loading is slow: a new replica must start a node, download tens of gigabytes of weights and load them into GPU memory. So keep a warm minimum of replicas, scale up early and scale down slowly. Put a gateway in front for rate limits, retries and fallback to another model.

**Load testing.** Replay prompts with a realistic length distribution, sweep concurrency upward, and record TTFT and TPOT percentiles at each level. The point where latency climbs sharply is your capacity per replica. Send requests at a fixed arrival rate as well as with a fixed number of simulated users: simulated users who wait for each reply slow down when the server does, which hides the queue that real traffic would build. Use the measured number in capacity planning, not a number from a blog post.

## Worked example

**KV cache for a 7B model.** Take 32 layers, 32 heads, head dimension 128 (hidden size 4,096) and FP16 values (2 bytes).

1. Per token: 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes, about 0.52 MB.
2. One request with 4,000 tokens of prompt plus output: 524,288 x 4,000 = 2.10 GB.
3. A batch of 16 such requests: 2.10 x 16 = 33.6 GB.
4. The FP16 weights are 14 GB. On a 48 GB GPU that leaves 34 GB, so 16 requests of this length fit. On an 80 GB GPU, 66 GB is left, so 31 fit.
5. Quantize the weights to 4-bit (3.5 GB) on a 24 GB GPU: 20.5 GB is left, so 9 requests fit. The cache, not the weights, now sets the limit.
6. With grouped-query attention and 8 KV heads, the cache is 4 times smaller: 0.52 GB per request.

Real servers also keep a few GB for activations, so treat these as upper bounds.

**Latency for one request.** Assume a 2,000-token prompt, 300 output tokens, 40 ms of queue wait, prefill at 10,000 tokens per second and a TPOT of 25 ms.

1. Prefill: 2,000 / 10,000 = 200 ms. TTFT = 40 + 200 = 240 ms.
2. Tokens per second: 1 / 0.025 = 40.
3. End to end: 0.240 + 299 x 0.025 = 7.715 s. Decode is 97% of it.
4. Halve the prompt: 7.615 s, a 0.1 s gain. Cap the output at 150 tokens: 0.240 + 149 x 0.025 = 3.965 s. Output length is the bigger lever.
5. Cache a 1,500-token prefix: prefill covers 500 tokens (50 ms), so TTFT falls from 240 ms to 90 ms.

**Latency against throughput.** Suppose 32 requests share the batch and TPOT rises to 40 ms. Each user now gets 25 tokens per second and the same request takes 0.240 + 299 x 0.040 = 12.2 s. The server produces 32 / 0.040 = 800 tokens per second, 20 times the single-request rate, for 1.6 times the per-token latency.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""Static vs continuous batching on one GPU, plus a memory calculator.

Time is counted in decode steps: one step produces one token for every
request in the running batch. Prefill is ignored and a step costs the same
at any batch size, so the numbers show the scheduling effect only.
Pure Python, no NumPy.
"""
import random

def static_batching(reqs, slots, max_wait):
    """Fire a batch when `slots` requests are waiting or the oldest has waited
    `max_wait` steps. Hold the whole batch until its longest request finishes."""
    pending = sorted(reqs, key=lambda r: r[1])
    t, busy, waits, latencies = 0, 0, [], []
    while pending:
        t = max(t, pending[0][1])                       # GPU is free; first request is here
        fire_at = max(t, pending[0][1] + max_wait)      # latest moment we may fire
        if len(pending) >= slots:
            fire_at = min(fire_at, max(t, pending[slots - 1][1]))   # batch is full earlier
        t = fire_at
        batch = [r for r in pending if r[1] <= t][:slots]
        pending = [r for r in pending if r not in batch]
        longest = max(out for _, _, out in batch)
        for _, arrival, out in batch:
            waits.append(t - arrival)
            latencies.append(t + longest - arrival)     # everyone returns together
            busy += out                                 # useful slot-steps
        t += longest
    return report(waits, latencies, busy, slots, t)

def continuous_batching(reqs, slots):
    """At every decode step, drop finished requests and admit waiting ones."""
    pending = sorted(reqs, key=lambda r: r[1])
    running = {}                                        # name -> (arrival, tokens left)
    t, busy, waits, latencies = 0, 0, [], []
    while pending or running:
        while pending and pending[0][1] <= t and len(running) < slots:
            name, arrival, out = pending.pop(0)
            running[name] = (arrival, out)
            waits.append(t - arrival)
        if not running:                                 # nothing to do: jump to next arrival
            t = pending[0][1]
            continue
        busy += len(running)
        t += 1                                          # one decode step for the whole batch
        for name, (arrival, left) in list(running.items()):
            if left == 1:
                latencies.append(t - arrival)
                del running[name]                       # slot is free for the next step
            else:
                running[name] = (arrival, left - 1)
    return report(waits, latencies, busy, slots, t)

def report(waits, latencies, busy, slots, end):
    n = len(waits)
    return {"avg_wait": sum(waits) / n, "avg_latency": sum(latencies) / n,
            "end": end, "gpu_busy": busy / (slots * end)}

def show(title, reqs, slots, max_wait):
    print(title)
    for name, r in (("static", static_batching(reqs, slots, max_wait)),
                    ("continuous", continuous_batching(reqs, slots))):
        print(f"  {name:<10} avg wait {r['avg_wait']:7.2f}  avg latency {r['avg_latency']:7.2f}"
              f"  done at step {r['end']:4d}  GPU busy {r['gpu_busy']:.1%}")

def weight_gb(params_billion, bits):
    return params_billion * 1e9 * bits / 8 / 1e9

def kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch, bytes_per_value=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_value

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # The six requests from the picture: (name, arrival step, output tokens).
    six = [("A", 0, 2), ("B", 0, 8), ("C", 0, 4), ("D", 0, 3), ("E", 0, 5), ("F", 0, 2)]
    show("Six requests, 3 slots, all arrive at step 0", six, slots=3, max_wait=0)
    s, c = static_batching(six, 3, 0), continuous_batching(six, 3)
    assert (s["end"], c["end"]) == (13, 9)
    assert abs(s["avg_wait"] - 4.0) < 1e-9 and abs(c["avg_wait"] - 11 / 6) < 1e-9

    rng = random.Random(7)
    lengths = [20, 40, 80, 160, 400]
    burst = [(f"b{i}", 0, rng.choice(lengths)) for i in range(200)]
    show("Burst: 200 requests waiting at step 0, 8 slots", burst, slots=8, max_wait=0)

    t, steady = 0, []
    for i in range(200):
        t += rng.randint(10, 50)                        # a new request every 10 to 50 steps
        steady.append((f"s{i}", t, rng.choice(lengths)))
    load = sum(out for _, _, out in steady) / (8 * t)
    show(f"Steady: 200 requests, 8 slots, offered load {load:.0%} of the GPU", steady, slots=8, max_wait=20)

    print("Weights")
    for params, bits, label in ((7, 16, "7B FP16"), (7, 8, "7B INT8"), (7, 4, "7B 4-bit"), (70, 16, "70B FP16")):
        print(f"  {label:<9} {weight_gb(params, bits):6.1f} GB")

    print("KV cache: 32 layers, 32 heads, head dim 128, FP16")
    per_token = kv_cache_bytes(32, 32, 128, seq_len=1, batch=1)
    per_request = kv_cache_bytes(32, 32, 128, seq_len=4000, batch=1)
    print(f"  per token                {per_token:,} bytes ({per_token / 1e6:.2f} MB)")
    print(f"  one 4,000-token request  {per_request / 1e9:.2f} GB")
    print(f"  batch of 16              {kv_cache_bytes(32, 32, 128, 4000, 16) / 1e9:.1f} GB")
    for gpu_gb, w in ((24, weight_gb(7, 4)), (48, weight_gb(7, 16)), (80, weight_gb(7, 16))):
        fit = int((gpu_gb - w) * 1e9 // per_request)
        print(f"  {gpu_gb} GB GPU, {w:.1f} GB weights: {fit} requests of 4,000 tokens fit")
    gqa = kv_cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 4000, 1)
    print(f"  with 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention): {gqa / 1e9:.2f} GB per request")
```

## Key takeaways

* Prefill is one parallel pass over the prompt and sets TTFT. Decode is one pass per output token and sets tokens per second.
* The KV cache stores keys and values for every past token in every layer. KV bytes = 2 x layers x heads x head dim x sequence length x batch x bytes per value.
* Weights = parameters x bytes per parameter: 7B is 14 GB in FP16 and 3.5 GB in 4-bit; 70B in FP16 is 140 GB.
* Latency = TTFT + (N - 1) x TPOT. Quote p95 or p99, not the average.
* Continuous batching refills a slot the moment a request finishes. Static batching holds every request until the longest one is done.
* PagedAttention stores the cache in small blocks to stop fragmentation; prefix caching skips prefill for a shared prompt prefix.
* Bigger batches raise throughput and lower cost per token, and raise per-request latency. Tune to the latency target, then scale out.
* Autoscale on queue depth, tokens in flight or TTFT, keep warm replicas, and find capacity per replica with a load test.

## Common mistakes

* Counting only the weights when sizing a GPU. At long contexts and high concurrency the KV cache is larger than the model.
* Quoting average latency. One slow request in twenty is invisible in the average and obvious to users.
* Autoscaling on CPU or GPU utilisation. Neither shows that requests are waiting; queue depth and TTFT do.
* Putting a timestamp or user id at the top of the prompt, which breaks prefix caching for everything after it.
* Shipping a 4-bit model after checking only public benchmarks, not your own eval set.
* Load testing with one short prompt repeated. Real traffic has mixed lengths, and long prompts are what break TTFT.

## Practice

* Run the code example, then change the six-request workload so every request needs 5 tokens and remove the two asserts that check the original workload. Confirm that static and continuous batching now finish at the same step, and explain why in one sentence.
* Take a model you can look up the shape of (layers, KV heads, head dimension). Compute its FP16 weight size and its KV cache per token, then the largest batch of 8,000-token requests that fits on a 24 GB GPU.
* Serve a small open model with vLLM or llama.cpp. Send the same 1,000-token prompt at concurrency 1, 4, 16 and 64, and record p50 and p95 TTFT and TPOT at each level. Mark the concurrency where p95 TTFT doubles.
* Add a fixed 1,500-token system prompt to every request, run the test with prefix caching on and off, and report the change in p95 TTFT.

## Interview questions (16)

1.What happens when a request reaches an LLM server?Easy

The text is tokenized and the request joins a queue. The scheduler adds it to the running batch as soon as a slot and cache memory are free. Prefill processes the prompt in one pass and fills the KV cache. Decode then loops: predict a token, sample, append, repeat until a stop token or the limit. Tokens are detokenized and streamed back as they are produced, and when the request ends its cache memory is freed for the next one in the queue.

2.What is the KV cache and why does it use so much memory?Medium

Without it, every new token would recompute attention over the full sequence. The cache stores keys and values for every past token, in every layer and head. So memory grows with sequence length, number of layers and number of concurrent requests. As a formula it is 2 x layers x heads x head dimension x sequence length x batch x bytes per value. For a 7B model with 32 layers and hidden size 4,096 in FP16 that is about half a megabyte per token, so one 4,000-token request holds about 2 GB and sixteen of them hold more than the 14 GB of weights.

3.What affects TTFT, and what affects tokens per second?Medium

TTFT depends on queue wait and prefill, so prompt length and load matter most. Prefix caching cuts it because cached tokens skip prefill. Tokens per second depends on model size, hardware, quantization and how many requests share the batch. The two are tuned separately: a server can have a fast TTFT and slow streaming, or the reverse, so I measure and report both.

4.Latency vs throughput: what is the trade-off?Medium

Larger batches raise total tokens per second and lower cost per token, but each request gets a smaller share of the GPU, so per-request latency rises. Tune batch limits to your latency target, then scale out. For example, going from 1 request at 25 ms per token to 32 requests at 40 ms per token gives 20 times the throughput for 1.6 times the per-token latency. That is a good trade for a chat product and a bad one for a voice agent with a tight response budget.

5.Give six ways to reduce latency.Easy

Shorten the prompt. Cache the prefix. Use a smaller or quantized model. Stream the output so users see tokens early. Add speculative decoding. Cap output tokens. Also: route easy requests to a small model and keep replicas warm. I would first ask which latency hurts. If it is the first token, I work on the prompt, the prefix cache and the queue. If it is total time, output length and model size matter most, because for long answers decode is most of the time.

6.What do you lose with quantization?Medium

Some accuracy, more at lower bit widths. 8-bit is usually near lossless. 4-bit is fine for many tasks but can hurt reasoning, maths and long outputs. Always compare on your own eval set, not only on public benchmarks. I would also say what you do not gain: quantizing weights does not shrink the KV cache, so a long-context workload can still run out of memory.

7.How does speculative decoding keep quality the same?Hard

The large model verifies every drafted token and rejects the ones it would not have produced. You only gain speed when the draft model guesses right often, so it works best on predictable text. In detail, the draft model proposes a few tokens, the large model scores all of them in one parallel pass, and each token is accepted with a probability based on the ratio of the two models' probabilities. At the first rejection a replacement is sampled from a corrected distribution, the large model's probabilities minus the draft's, renormalised, so the final output follows the large model's distribution exactly. If the acceptance rate is 0.8 and 4 tokens are drafted, each large-model pass yields about 3.4 tokens on average.

8.vLLM or SGLang?Medium

vLLM is the safe default: mature, well documented, wide hardware support. SGLang tends to win when requests share long prefixes, as in multi-turn chat and agents, and for structured output. Benchmark both on your real traffic. The reason is the cache design: SGLang's RadixAttention finds and reuses shared prefixes automatically, and agent traffic resends the same long context on every step.

9.How do you serve many fine-tuned variants cheaply?Medium

Keep one base model in memory and load LoRA adapters per request (multi-LoRA serving). You avoid one GPU per customer. An adapter is megabytes in size against gigabytes for the base model, so many fit beside it. Requests with different adapters can share a batch because the base weights are the same. I would keep hot adapters in GPU memory with least-recently-used eviction and load cold ones on demand.

10.How do you autoscale LLM serving?Medium

Scale on queue depth, tokens in flight or TTFT, not CPU. Model loading is slow, so keep a warm minimum of replicas and scale early. Put a gateway in front for rate limits, retries and fallback to another model. CPU is the wrong signal because the work is on the GPU, and GPU utilisation is misleading because it reads high at almost any batch size. I would also set the scale-up threshold below the real limit, since a new replica can take minutes to pull weights and load them.

11.How do you load test an LLM endpoint?Medium

Replay prompts with a realistic length distribution, sweep concurrency upward, and record TTFT and TPOT percentiles at each level. The point where latency climbs sharply is your capacity per replica. I would use logged production prompts where possible, include the long ones, and fix the output length distribution too, because output tokens drive the load. The result is a curve of p95 TTFT against concurrency, and the capacity number is the highest concurrency that still meets the latency target.

12.Design an inference batching system for one GPU while users wait.Hard

Requests enter a queue, and a scheduler fires a batch when either the maximum batch size or a short maximum wait window is reached. The wait window is my latency-throughput dial: a longer window fills bigger batches and adds waiting time. I group requests by length so padding does not dominate. I add backpressure when the queue grows: reject or shed load with a clear error once the wait would break the latency target. For token generation I would use continuous batching, where finished requests leave and waiting ones join at every decode step, so a short answer never waits for a long one. I would track queue wait, batch size and p95 TTFT to tune the window.

13.What is the difference between static and continuous batching?Easy

Static batching waits to fill a batch and holds every request until the longest one finishes, so slots sit idle after short requests end. Continuous batching checks at every decode step: finished requests leave and waiting ones take their slots, so the GPU stays busy. With six requests of 2, 8, 4, 3, 5 and 2 tokens on three slots, static batching needs 13 steps and continuous needs 9. Static batching is still fine for offline jobs and for models with fixed-size outputs, such as embeddings.

14.What problem does PagedAttention solve?Hard

Memory fragmentation in the KV cache. The server does not know how long an output will be, so older engines reserved one contiguous region per request sized for the maximum length. Most of it stayed unused, and free gaps between regions were too small for new requests. PagedAttention splits the cache into small fixed-size blocks, allocates a block only when a sequence grows into it, and keeps a table from each request to its blocks, like an operating system's page table. Waste falls to at most one partly filled block per request, so more requests fit in a batch. Blocks can also be shared between requests with the same prefix.

15.How do you write prompts so that prefix caching works?Medium

The cache matches from the first token, and one different token ends the match. So I order the prompt from most stable to least stable: system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples, then chat history, then the new user message. Anything that changes per request, such as the current time or a request id, goes at the end. In chat I append to the history and never rewrite earlier turns. I then check the cache hit rate in the server metrics, because a silent miss shows up only as a higher TTFT.

16.A 7B model runs in FP16 on a 24 GB GPU. Roughly how many 4,000-token requests fit at once?Medium

The weights take 7 billion x 2 bytes, about 14 GB, which leaves 10 GB. For a model with 32 layers and hidden size 4,096, the KV cache is 2 x 32 x 4,096 x 2 bytes, about 0.52 MB per token, so a 4,000-token request holds about 2.1 GB. Ten divided by 2.1 gives 4 requests, a little less after working memory. To fit more I would quantize the weights to 4-bit, which frees about 10 GB, or limit the context length, since the cache grows linearly with it.
