# LLM fundamentals - tokens, embeddings, decoding

An LLM (large language model) is a neural network trained to do one thing: predict the next token. This lesson follows a piece of text through the whole machine. Text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors, a stack of transformer blocks mixes those vectors, and a decoding rule picks the next token from the output probabilities. You will work each stage with small numbers.

tokenizationbpeembeddingstransformerdecodingsamplingcontext window

## Why it matters

Most GenAI interviews open here. "What is a token?", "Explain self-attention simply", "Temperature vs top-p?" and "Why do LLMs hallucinate?" are warm-up questions, and a weak answer colours the rest of the round. The same ideas decide real engineering work: token counts set your bill and your latency, the context window sets how much history and retrieved text fits, and decoding settings decide whether an extraction job returns the same JSON twice. If you can draw the next-token loop and one transformer block from memory, the later topics (RAG, fine-tuning, serving) become details added to a picture you already have.

Read first: [Neural networks and backprop](/ai/learn/neural-networks-backprop)

## Lesson

### One objective: predict the next token

An LLM is a neural network trained to predict the next token. Chat, code and reasoning all come from that one objective, trained at very large scale.

At run time the model works in a loop. Text is split into tokens. The network outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary. One token is chosen and appended to the input, and the loop runs again until a stop token appears. Every section below is one stage of that loop.

Run naively, each pass would recompute the whole sequence to produce one token. Real servers keep a KV cache: the attention keys and values of earlier tokens (defined in the self-attention section below) are stored, so each step computes only the new token.

### Tokens and BPE

A token is the unit the model reads, usually a word piece. Roughly 1 token is 0.75 English words, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words.

Why word pieces? A vocabulary of whole words can never cover every name, typo and new word. Single characters cover everything but make sequences very long. Word pieces sit between the two: a common word is one token, and a rare word splits into a few known pieces.

Tokenizers such as BPE (byte pair encoding) build a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent character pairs:

1. Start with every word split into single characters.
2. Count every adjacent pair of symbols across the corpus.
3. Merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol and add it to the vocabulary.
4. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the size you want.

Here is a tiny corpus, as word counts: play 5, plays 3, played 4, player 2, day 7, plan 2.

| Merge | Most frequent pair | Count | New token | "played" is now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | a + y | 21 | ay | p l ay e d |
| 2 | p + l | 16 | pl | pl ay e d |
| 3 | pl + ay | 14 | play | play e d |
| 4 | d + ay | 7 | day | play e d |

Check merge 1: "ay" occurs in play, plays, played, player and day, so 5 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 7 = 21. After four merges the unseen word "replay" encodes as r, e, play: three tokens and no "unknown word" symbol. To encode new text you apply the merges in the order they were learned. Real tokenizers run tens of thousands of merges and usually start from bytes, so any string can be encoded.

Two practical effects follow. The 0.75 ratio is for English prose: code and text in other languages usually need more tokens per word, so measure with the real tokenizer. And the model sees pieces, not letters, which is why "how many r's are in strawberry" is harder for it than it looks.

### The embedding table

A token ID is only an index, so the model needs numbers it can do maths on. The embedding table is a matrix with one row per vocabulary entry and `d_model` columns, where `d_model` is the length of every token vector inside the model. Token ID 4,821 selects row 4,821. That row is the token's vector, called its embedding.

The rows are learned during training. Tokens that appear in similar contexts end up with similar rows, so similar meanings sit close together in that vector space.

The table gives one fixed vector per token. "bank" gets the same row in "river bank" and "bank loan". It is the transformer blocks that mix in the neighbours and turn this fixed vector into one that fits the sentence.

The table is large. With a vocabulary of 50,000 and `d_model` = 4,096 it holds 50,000 x 4,096 = 204.8 million parameters. At the other end of the network, an output layer maps the final vector back to 50,000 scores called logits, one per vocabulary token.

### Position

Attention has no sense of order: shuffle the input tokens and each token still gets the same result. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical, so position is added.

| Method | How it works | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sinusoidal | Fixed sine and cosine waves of different frequencies, added to the token embedding | No parameters; used in the original transformer |
| Learned | One trainable vector per position, added to the token embedding | Simple; cannot go past the longest position seen in training |
| Rotary (RoPE) | Rotates query and key vectors by an angle that depends on position, inside every attention layer | The attention score depends on the distance between two tokens; most modern LLMs use it |

RoPE stands for rotary position embeddings. Because both the query and the key are rotated, their dot product depends on the difference of the two angles. The model learns "three tokens back", not "position 507".

### Self-attention

Self-attention is the step where tokens exchange information. Every token looks at every other token and decides how much each one matters. It builds a query, a key and a value per token. The query is compared with every key, and the scores decide how much of each value to take.

Formula

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QKT​)V

In a generating model a causal mask hides later tokens, so a token attends only to itself and what came before. The next lesson builds this formula step by step with numbers.

### The transformer block

A transformer block is multi-head attention, then a feed-forward layer, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer norm.

* **Multi-head attention** moves information between tokens. Several attention heads run in parallel.
* **Feed-forward layer:** two linear layers with a non-linearity between them, applied to each token on its own. It typically expands the vector to about 4 x `d_model` and brings it back.
* **Residual connection:** the input of a sub-layer is added to its output, x + f(x). Gradients get a direct path through the whole stack.
* **Layer norm:** rescales each token's vector to zero mean and unit variance, which keeps values in a stable range.

![One pre-norm decoder block: a residual path with an attention branch and a feed-forward branch](/ai/img/decoder-block-prenorm.svg)One pre-norm decoder block: a residual path with an attention branch and a feed-forward branch

Formula

h=x+Attention(Norm(x)),y=h+FFN(Norm(h))

This order is called pre-norm: normalise first, then run the sub-layer. The original transformer used post-norm, Norm(x + f(x)). Most modern LLMs use pre-norm because the residual path is never rescaled, and deep stacks train more stably. The input and output have the same shape, so you stack dozens of blocks.

Where do the parameters sit? Attention has four `d_model` x `d_model` matrices (query, key, value, output), so 4 x d\_model^2. A feed-forward layer with 4 x expansion has two matrices of size d\_model x 4 d\_model, so 8 x d\_model^2. With `d_model` = 4,096 that is about 67 million for attention and 134 million for the feed-forward layer: two thirds of a block's parameters are in the feed-forward part.

### Three architectures

| Architecture | What each token sees | One use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decoder-only (GPT style) | Causal mask: only earlier tokens | Generation: chat and code |
| Encoder-only (BERT style) | Both directions | Embeddings and classification |
| Encoder-decoder (T5 style) | The encoder reads the input in both directions; the decoder generates and attends to the encoder output | Translation and summarisation |

Most LLMs today are decoder-only.

### Training stages

1. **Pretraining on raw text (next-token prediction).** The label is the next token of the text itself, so no human labelling is needed. The loss at each position is the negative log of the probability given to the correct token: 0.69 if the model gave it 0.5, and 4.6 if it gave it 0.01. With a causal mask, a 1,000-token text gives 999 predictions in one pass. The result is a base model that continues text.
2. **Supervised fine-tuning on instructions.** Instruction and response pairs teach the model to answer a request, not just continue it.
3. **Preference alignment (RLHF or DPO).** RLHF is reinforcement learning from human feedback. DPO is direct preference optimisation. Both use human choices between two answers to push the model toward the preferred one.

Reasoning models add reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: the model is rewarded when a program can check the result, such as a correct final number or passing unit tests.

### Decoding

The model outputs a probability for every token. Decoding is the rule that picks one.

| Method | What it does | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Greedy | Picks the top token | No random choice; can repeat itself |
| Temperature T | Divides the logits by T before softmax | T below 1 sharpens the distribution, T above 1 flattens it |
| Top-k | Keeps the k most likely tokens | Cuts the tail at a fixed size |
| Top-p (nucleus) | Keeps the smallest set whose probability adds up to p | The set shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is unsure |

Formula

pi​=∑j​exp(zj​/T)exp(zi​/T)​

Here z is the logit vector. A common order is: apply temperature, filter with top-k or top-p, renormalise so the kept probabilities sum to 1, then sample. As T approaches 0 the result approaches greedy. The worked example below does all of this with real numbers.

### Context window

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one call, input plus output.

Treat it as a budget. Assume an 8,000-token window. A 600-token system prompt, 2,400 tokens of chat history and 6 retrieved chunks of 500 tokens use 600 + 2,400 + 3,000 = 6,000 tokens. That leaves 2,000 tokens for the answer, about 1,500 words. If each new turn adds 800 tokens of history, two more turns leave only 400 tokens for the answer and a third does not fit, so you must trim or summarise. Nothing is remembered between calls: anything the model should know must be inside the window again on the next call.

A longer window is not free. The cost of attention is quadratic in sequence length: doubling the tokens gives four times as many token pairs to score.

### Why hallucination happens

A hallucination is a fluent answer that is false. The model is trained to produce likely text, not verified facts: the training loss rewards a plausible next token, and no step checks truth. When knowledge is missing, outdated or ambiguous the model still produces a fluent answer, because every decoding step must output some token. "I don't know" appears only when it is the likely continuation.

Fixes: grounding with RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), asking for citations, lower temperature, letting the model say "I don't know", and evals that measure faithfulness.

### Mixture of experts

In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model the feed-forward layer is split into many expert networks, and a router sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many parameters but uses a small part per token, so quality rises without the same rise in compute. With 8 experts and a router that picks 2, each token runs a quarter of the feed-forward parameters. Many recent open-weight models use sparse MoE designs. The cost is memory: every expert must still be loaded.

### LLM vs SLM

An SLM is a small language model. Pick a small model for narrow, high-volume tasks such as routing, classification and extraction, or when you need low latency, low cost or on-device privacy. Use a large model for open-ended reasoning. A common production design uses both: the small model handles or routes the easy requests and the large one takes the hard ones.

## Worked example

**Decoding one token by hand.** The prompt is "I would like a cup of". Pretend the vocabulary has only five tokens, and the model gives these probabilities at temperature 1:

| Token | tea | coffee | water | milk | sugar |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| p | 0.50 | 0.20 | 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.05 |

**Greedy** picks "tea" every time.

**Temperature.** Dividing logits by T is the same as raising each probability to the power 1/T and renormalising.

* T = 0.5 means squaring: 0.25, 0.04, 0.0225, 0.01, 0.0025. The sum is 0.325. Divide each by 0.325.
* T = 2.0 means square roots: 0.7071, 0.4472, 0.3873, 0.3162, 0.2236. The sum is 2.0814. Divide each by 2.0814.

| Setting | tea | coffee | water | milk | sugar |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T = 0.5 | 0.769 | 0.123 | 0.069 | 0.031 | 0.008 |
| T = 1.0 | 0.500 | 0.200 | 0.150 | 0.100 | 0.050 |
| T = 2.0 | 0.340 | 0.215 | 0.186 | 0.152 | 0.107 |
| Top-k = 2 | 0.714 | 0.286 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Top-p = 0.9 | 0.526 | 0.211 | 0.158 | 0.105 | 0 |

**Top-k = 2** (at T = 1) keeps tea and coffee. Their sum is 0.70, so tea becomes 0.50 / 0.70 = 0.714 and coffee 0.20 / 0.70 = 0.286.

**Top-p = 0.9** (at T = 1) adds probabilities from the top: 0.50, 0.70, 0.85, 0.95. The total first reaches 0.9 at the fourth token, so four tokens stay and "sugar" is dropped. Divide by 0.95: 0.526, 0.211, 0.158, 0.105.

**What to notice.** The odd answer "sugar" has probability 0.05 at T = 1. It falls to 0.008 at T = 0.5, rises to 0.107 at T = 2.0, and is exactly 0 under top-p = 0.9. Temperature reshapes every probability but never removes a token. Top-k and top-p remove the tail but keep the ratios between the survivors: tea is still 2.5 times as likely as coffee.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""Temperature, top-k and top-p on the five-token distribution from the worked example."""
import numpy as np

TOKENS = ["tea", "coffee", "water", "milk", "sugar"]
PROBS = np.array([0.50, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05])
LOGITS = np.log(PROBS)          # any logits whose softmax gives PROBS

def softmax(z):
    z = z - np.max(z)           # stable: the largest exponent is 0
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

def with_temperature(logits, t):
    """Divide the logits by t, then softmax. t < 1 sharpens, t > 1 flattens."""
    return softmax(logits / t)

def top_k(probs, k):
    """Keep the k most likely tokens, zero the rest, renormalise."""
    keep = np.argsort(-probs)[:k]
    out = np.zeros_like(probs)
    out[keep] = probs[keep]
    return out / out.sum()

def top_p(probs, p):
    """Keep the smallest set of top tokens whose probability adds up to at least p."""
    order = np.argsort(-probs)
    cumulative = np.cumsum(probs[order])
    n_keep = int(np.searchsorted(cumulative, p)) + 1   # first index where the sum reaches p
    out = np.zeros_like(probs)
    out[order[:n_keep]] = probs[order[:n_keep]]
    return out / out.sum()

def show(label, probs):
    cells = "  ".join(f"{t}={x:.3f}" for t, x in zip(TOKENS, probs))
    print(f"{label:<12} {cells}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    show("T = 1.0", with_temperature(LOGITS, 1.0))
    show("T = 0.5", with_temperature(LOGITS, 0.5))
    show("T = 2.0", with_temperature(LOGITS, 2.0))
    show("top-k = 2", top_k(PROBS, 2))
    show("top-p = 0.9", top_p(PROBS, 0.9))

    # The numbers from the worked example.
    assert np.allclose(with_temperature(LOGITS, 0.5), PROBS ** 2 / np.sum(PROBS ** 2))
    assert np.allclose(with_temperature(LOGITS, 2.0).round(3), [0.340, 0.215, 0.186, 0.152, 0.107])
    assert np.allclose(top_k(PROBS, 2).round(3), [0.714, 0.286, 0, 0, 0])
    assert np.allclose(top_p(PROBS, 0.9).round(3), [0.526, 0.211, 0.158, 0.105, 0])

    # Sample 10,000 next tokens at each temperature and count how often "sugar" appears.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for t in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
        draws = rng.choice(len(TOKENS), size=10_000, p=with_temperature(LOGITS, t))
        print(f"T = {t}: 'sugar' sampled {np.mean(draws == 4):.3f} of the time")
    print("greedy pick:", TOKENS[int(np.argmax(PROBS))])
```

## Key takeaways

* An LLM predicts the next token. Generation is a loop: tokenize, run the network, pick a token, append, repeat.
* A token is a word piece, about 0.75 English words. BPE builds the vocabulary by merging the most frequent pair again and again.
* The embedding table has one row per token; a token ID selects its row. Position is added separately, and most modern LLMs use RoPE.
* A transformer block is attention plus a feed-forward layer, each with a residual connection and layer norm. Modern models normalise before the sub-layer (pre-norm).
* Decoder-only models generate, encoder-only models produce representations, encoder-decoder models map one sequence to another.
* Temperature reshapes the whole distribution; top-k and top-p cut the tail. Use low temperature for extraction and code.
* The context window counts input plus output tokens, and attention cost grows with the square of the length.
* Hallucination comes from the objective: likely text, not verified facts. Ground the model with retrieval and measure faithfulness.

## Common mistakes

* Counting words when the limit is in tokens. A 3,000-word document is about 4,000 tokens, not 3,000.
* Saying temperature 0 guarantees identical output. It removes sampling, not floating-point and batching differences.
* Forgetting that the context window includes the output. A prompt that fills the window leaves no room to answer.
* Describing top-p as "keep tokens with probability above p". It keeps the smallest set whose total reaches p.
* Saying attention knows word order. It does not; position has to be added.
* Mixing up the architectures: using a decoder-only model where an embedding (encoder) model is the right tool, or the reverse.

## Practice

* Train BPE by hand on the corpus play 5, plays 3, played 4, player 2, day 7, plan 2. Do merges 5 and 6 yourself and check them with a short script. Result: the two merged pairs and their counts.
* Run the code example, then add a function that applies temperature 0.7 followed by top-p 0.9. Result: the five final probabilities, summing to 1.
* Take any 500-word text, count its tokens with a real tokenizer, and report the words-per-token ratio. Compare it with 0.75, then repeat for Hindi or Tamil text and for Python code.
* Draw one pre-norm decoder block from memory, with shapes on every arrow. Result: a diagram a friend can check against the image in this lesson.

## Interview questions (16)

1.Explain self-attention simply.Easy

Each token asks a question (query) and every token offers a label (key) and content (value). The dot product of query and key gives a score, softmax turns scores into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of values. So each token's new representation is a mix of the tokens most relevant to it. For example, in "the animal did not cross the street because it was tired", the token "it" can put most of its weight on "animal" and pull that meaning into its own vector.

2.Why divide by the square root of d\_k?Medium

Dot products grow with vector size. If the entries of the query and key have variance 1, their dot product has variance d\_k, so with d\_k = 64 the scores are spread with a standard deviation of about 8. Large values push softmax into regions with tiny gradients, where one token gets almost all the weight. Dividing by the square root of d\_k brings the variance back to 1. Scaling keeps the scores in a stable range so training works.

3.Why multiple heads?Easy

Each head can learn a different relationship, for example syntax in one and coreference in another. Their outputs are concatenated, which gives a richer representation than one large head. A single head produces one set of weights per token, so it has to average all the relationships it cares about. The cost is about the same, because each head works in a smaller dimension: d\_model divided by the number of heads.

4.Why did transformers replace RNNs and LSTMs?Easy

RNNs process tokens one by one, so they cannot be parallelised and they forget long-range context. Information from token 1 has to survive hundreds of updates to reach token 500. Attention connects any two tokens directly, in one step, and trains in parallel on GPUs because every position in a sequence is processed at once. Parallel training is what made it practical to train on very large amounts of text.

5.What is the cost of attention, and why does it matter?Medium

It is quadratic in sequence length, because every token attends to every other token. With n tokens there are n squared scores per head, so doubling the context means four times the work. That is why long context is expensive in memory and latency, and why KV caching, FlashAttention and context compression exist. KV caching avoids recomputing earlier tokens during generation, FlashAttention computes the same result with less memory, and context compression sends fewer tokens in the first place.

6.Encoder-only vs decoder-only: when do you use each?Easy

Use an encoder model when you need a representation: embeddings, classification, reranking. It reads the text in both directions, so each token's vector uses the full sentence. Use a decoder model when you need to generate text. It has a causal mask, so each token sees only what came before, which matches generating left to right. Most LLMs today are decoder-only.

7.Temperature vs top-p vs top-k?Easy

Temperature rescales all probabilities; low is focused, high is varied. It divides the logits by T before softmax, so it never removes a token. Top-k and top-p cut off the unlikely tail before sampling: top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens, and top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability adds up to p, so the set adapts to how confident the model is. For extraction or code use low temperature; for creative writing raise it.

8.Why can output differ even at temperature 0?Medium

Floating-point operations on GPUs are not perfectly deterministic. Batching with other requests, different hardware and ties between near-equal tokens can change one token, and the rest of the output then follows a different path. Temperature 0 removes the random sampling step, but it does not make the arithmetic identical from run to run. If you need repeatable results, store the output and reuse it; do not rely on regenerating it.

9.Why do LLMs hallucinate?Medium

The model is trained to produce likely text, not verified facts. When knowledge is missing, outdated or ambiguous it still produces a fluent answer, because every decoding step must output some token and nothing in the loop checks truth. Fixes: grounding with RAG, asking for citations, lower temperature, letting the model say "I don't know", and evals that measure faithfulness.

10.What is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model?Medium

The feed-forward layer is split into many expert networks and a router sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many parameters but uses a small part per token, so quality rises without the same rise in compute. Many recent open-weight models use sparse MoE designs. The trade-off is memory: every expert must be loaded even though each token uses only a few, and the router has to be trained to spread tokens across experts.

11.LLM vs SLM: when would you pick a small model?Easy

Pick a small model for narrow, high-volume tasks such as routing, classification and extraction, or when you need low latency, low cost or on-device privacy. Use a large model for open-ended reasoning. A common production design uses both: a small model handles or routes the easy requests, and the large model takes the hard ones. Check the split on an eval set, because the saving is only real if quality holds.

12.How does BPE build its vocabulary, and what happens to a word it has never seen?Medium

It starts with single characters or bytes. It counts every adjacent pair of symbols in the training corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new symbol, and repeats until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The list of merges, in order, is the tokenizer. A new word is split into characters and the same merges are applied in the same order. So an unseen word breaks into known pieces, such as "replay" into "r", "e" and "play", and there is no need for an unknown-word token.

13.What is an embedding table, and how large is it?Easy

It is a matrix with one row per vocabulary token and d\_model columns. A token ID selects its row, and that row is the vector the first transformer block receives. The rows are learned in training, so tokens used in similar contexts get similar vectors. Its size is vocabulary times d\_model: 50,000 tokens at 4,096 dimensions is about 205 million parameters. The output layer does the reverse and turns the final vector into one logit per vocabulary token.

14.Sinusoidal, learned and rotary positions: what is the difference?Medium

Sinusoidal positions are fixed sine and cosine waves added to the token embeddings; they have no parameters. Learned positions are one trainable vector per position, also added at the input, and they stop at the longest position seen in training. Rotary positions, RoPE, do not add anything at the input. They rotate the query and key vectors inside every attention layer by an angle that depends on position, so the score between two tokens depends on how far apart they are. Most modern LLMs use RoPE.

15.What is pre-norm, and why do modern models use it?Medium

In a pre-norm block the layer norm sits before each sub-layer: h = x + Attention(Norm(x)), then y = h + FFN(Norm(h)). The original transformer used post-norm, where the norm comes after the addition. With pre-norm the residual path carries x through the whole stack without being rescaled, so gradients reach early layers directly and deep stacks train more stably. A final norm is applied once after the last block.

16.A user pastes a 3,000-word document. How many tokens is that, and why do you care?Easy

At roughly 0.75 words per token it is about 3,000 / 0.75 = 4,000 tokens. I care for three reasons. Cost: pricing is per token, for input and output. Latency: more input tokens take longer to process before the first output token appears. Fit: the context window counts input plus output, so I subtract the system prompt, the history and the space reserved for the answer before deciding whether the document fits whole or needs retrieval or summarising.

# LLM system design

LLM system design is the interview round where you design a whole product around a model: a chat service, document Q&A, a support agent or a serving platform. Almost every answer uses the same five layers and the same seven steps. This lesson gives you the layers, the steps, the arithmetic for capacity, cost and latency, and the points each common question expects.

system designcapacity planningcostlatency budgetcachinginterview framework

## Why it matters

This round decides the level you are hired at. The interviewer is not checking whether you know what RAG or vLLM is. They are checking whether you can turn a vague request into numbers, pick a model path and defend it, and say what breaks at 10 times the traffic. A fixed structure lets you spend your 45 minutes on the hard part and not on deciding what to draw. The same structure works at work: every design review for an LLM feature asks about traffic, tokens, latency, cost and evals.

Read first: [Vector DBs and RAG](/ai/learn/vector-dbs-rag), [Inference and serving - KV cache, batching, vLLM](/ai/learn/inference-serving), [Agents in depth - patterns, reliability, security](/ai/learn/agents-in-depth), [Evals, tracing and guardrails](/ai/learn/evals-tracing-guardrails)

## Lesson

Most LLM design questions use the same five layers. Draw them first, then go deep where the interviewer pushes.

### The five layers

![Five stacked layers of an LLM system with a data-and-tools box beside orchestration and an observability bar underneath](/ai/img/llm-system-five-layers.svg)Five stacked layers of an LLM system with a data-and-tools box beside orchestration and an observability bar underneath

| Layer | What sits in it |
| --- | --- |
| Client | Web or mobile app; tokens stream back to the user |
| API gateway | Auth, rate limits, model routing, response cache, fallback |
| Orchestration | Builds the context: prompt, retrieval, agent loop, guardrails |
| Model serving | vLLM or SGLang: continuous batching, KV cache, LoRA adapters |
| GPU nodes | Autoscaled on queue depth, with warm replicas |
| Data and tools (side box) | Vector DB and keyword index; MCP servers and external APIs; long-term memory store |

Observability and evals sit under every layer: traces, latency, cost and quality scores.

A request flows top to bottom; the orchestration layer is where RAG, agents and guardrails live, and it is where most of the design discussion happens. Orchestration is the only layer that talks to the data-and-tools box, and the link goes both ways: it reads chunks and memories, calls tools, and writes new memories back. If you use a hosted API, the provider runs the bottom two layers. You still own the top three, the data and the observability.

### The answer framework

1. **Clarify:** users, traffic, tokens per request, latency target, quality bar, data sensitivity, budget.
2. **Choose the model path:** hosted API or self-hosted open model, and why.
3. **Draw the layers** above and name what sits in each.
4. **Go deep on the hard part:** retrieval quality, agent reliability or serving capacity, depending on the question.
5. **Estimate capacity** with simple arithmetic.
6. **Add evals and monitoring:** what you measure offline and online.
7. **Cover failure and cost:** fallbacks, rate limits, caching, guardrails.

A workable split for a 45-minute round: clarify 5 minutes, model path 3, layers 5, the hard part 20, capacity 5, evals 4, failure and cost 3. Steps 1 to 3 are setup. Most of the time belongs to step 4.

### Step 1: what to ask, and why it changes the design

| Ask about | Why the answer changes the design |
| --- | --- |
| Users | Employees or the public? Public traffic needs moderation, abuse limits and stricter guardrails |
| Traffic | Peak requests per second sets the replica count and whether you need autoscaling at all |
| Tokens per request | Output tokens set GPU load and total latency; input tokens set prefill time, cost and whether prefix caching pays |
| Latency target | Decides streaming, model size and how many extra steps (reranker, guardrail, agent turns) fit |
| Quality bar | What does a wrong answer cost? Decides model size, citations, human approval and how strict the evals are |
| Data sensitivity | Personal or regulated data can rule out a public API and adds redaction and permission filters |
| Budget | A cost per request decides routing to small models, caching and the model path |

If the interviewer gives no numbers, state your own and move on: "I will assume 50 requests per second at peak and 500 output tokens."

### Step 2: hosted API or self-hosted

| Factor | Points to a hosted API | Points to self-hosting an open model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quality needed | Hardest reasoning, widest knowledge | A narrow task a small or fine-tuned model handles |
| Volume | Low or spiky; you pay per token | High and steady; GPUs stay busy |
| Data | May leave your network under a contract | Must stay inside your network |
| Control | Standard features are enough | You need LoRA adapters, constrained decoding or a fixed model version |
| Team | No GPU operations skill | Someone can run serving and be on call for it |
| Time | Launch this month | You can spend weeks on load tests and autoscaling |

A common answer is both: launch on a hosted API, then move the high-volume, simple requests to a small self-hosted model and keep the hosted model for hard requests and as a fallback.

### Step 4: find the hard part

| The question is about | The hard part | Go deep on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answering from documents | Retrieval quality | Chunking, hybrid search, reranking, permission filters, Recall@k on a labelled set |
| Taking actions for a user | Agent reliability | Tool design, step and cost limits, approval before risky actions, checkpoints, injection defence |
| Serving a model at scale | Serving capacity | KV cache memory, continuous batching, a load test, autoscaling signals, fallback |

If you are not sure which one the interviewer wants, ask: "Should I go deeper on retrieval or on serving?"

### Step 5: capacity arithmetic

A replica is one copy of the model server with its own GPU or GPUs. Headroom is spare capacity kept for spikes and for a replica that fails.

Formula

tokens per second=requests per second×output tokens per request

Formula

replicas=⌈tokens per second per replicatokens per second needed​×(1+headroom)⌉

**Capacity example (illustrative numbers):** peak load is 50 requests per second with 500 output tokens each, so you need 25,000 output tokens per second. If one replica sustains 2,500 tokens per second at your latency target, you need 10 replicas, or 13 with 30% headroom. Say that you would measure the per-replica number with a load test.

The per-replica figure is not a constant: it depends on model size, the GPU, the batch size, prompt length and the latency target. The inference lesson's example, one 7B replica with 32 requests in the batch at 40 ms per token, produces 32 / 0.040 = 800 tokens per second, while 2,500 assumes a replica that holds about 75 streams at 30 ms per token. Both are assumptions, and only a load test on your model, your GPU and your prompts gives the number to use.

Two more formulas help. Concurrent streams = requests per second x seconds each response stays open. This converts "1,000 concurrent users" into a rate. Daily tokens = requests per day x tokens per request, which feeds the cost estimate. Size for the peak, not the average: in the worked example below the peak is 3.5 times the daily mean.

### Cost

Formula

cost per request=106input tokens×pin​+output tokens×pout​​

Here p is the price per million tokens. At an assumed 0.50 USD per million input tokens and 1.50 USD per million output tokens, a request with 1,000 input and 500 output tokens costs (1,000 x 0.50 + 500 x 1.50) / 1,000,000 = 0.00125 USD.

For self-hosting, monthly cost = replicas x GPUs per replica x GPU-hour price x 720 hours. At an assumed 2.50 USD per GPU-hour, the 13 replicas above cost 13 x 2.50 x 720 = 23,400 USD a month. A GPU costs the same whether busy or idle, so utilisation decides the price per token: at 2,500 tokens per second, that GPU makes a million output tokens for 0.28 USD when always busy and 2.78 USD when 10% busy.

### Latency budget

Split the target across stages before choosing components. Here is an illustrative budget for a RAG chat whose p95 time to first token (TTFT) must be 1 second, meaning 95% of requests show their first token within that time:

| Stage | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| Gateway: auth, rate limit, cache lookup | 20 ms |
| Input guardrail | 50 ms |
| Embed the query | 30 ms |
| Hybrid search | 60 ms |
| Rerank 50 candidates | 150 ms |
| Queue wait at the model server | 100 ms |
| Prefill | 250 ms |
| Network | 40 ms |
| **Total** | **700 ms, leaving 300 ms spare** |

After the first token, time per output token takes over: 300 tokens at 30 ms each is another 9 seconds. Streaming is what makes that acceptable. Every extra model call before the first token (query rewriting, an LLM guardrail, an agent step) costs hundreds of milliseconds, so name the ones you can afford.

### Where caching goes

| Cache | Layer | Saves | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exact response cache | Gateway | The whole model call for a repeated prompt | Low hit rate outside FAQs |
| Semantic response cache | Gateway | The call for a similar question | A wrong match returns a wrong answer; never share across users with private data |
| Retrieval and embedding cache | Orchestration | Search time for popular queries | Stale results after re-indexing |
| Prefix (KV) cache | Model serving | Prefill for a shared system prompt or chat history | Breaks if the prompt start changes per request |

### Fallbacks and rate limits

* **Timeouts** on time to first token and on total time, so a stuck call fails fast.
* **Retries** with exponential backoff and jitter, only for errors that can succeed later (429, 5xx).
* **Fallback chain:** a second provider or model, then a smaller model, then a cached or fixed answer. Say that quality drops and how you would tell the user.
* **Rate limits in tokens per minute**, per user and per tenant, not only in requests. One request can cost 100 times another.
* **Backpressure:** when the queue is too long to meet the latency target, reject with a clear error; do not let every request get slow.
* **Guardrails** on input and output, and a cap on output tokens and agent steps.

### Evals and monitoring

Offline, before a change ships: a fixed eval set of real questions, task metrics, an LLM judge checked against human labels, and a gate that blocks a release when scores drop. Online, after it ships: p95 time to first token, time per output token, error and fallback rates, tokens and cost per request, cache hit rate, guardrail triggers, user feedback and the task metric (resolved tickets, accepted suggestions). Trace every request with one span per stage, and feed failed production cases back into the eval set.

### Common questions

| Question | Points your answer must include |
| --- | --- |
| Design a ChatGPT-like chat service | Token streaming, conversation store, context trimming and summarising, prefix caching, continuous batching, moderation, rate limits, autoscaling |
| Design document Q&A for an enterprise | Ingestion pipeline, chunking, hybrid search and reranking, permission filtering, citations, RAG evals, incremental re-indexing |
| Design a customer support agent | Tools for lookup and actions, approval before refunds, escalation to a human, customer memory, injection defence, task success as the metric |
| Serve an open model to 1,000 concurrent users | Engine choice, quantization, capacity maths, autoscaling on queue depth, multi-LoRA, gateway with fallback, a p95 TTFT target |
| Design a coding assistant | Small fast model for completion and a large one for chat, repository indexing, context selection, caching, test execution in a sandbox |
| Cut the cost of an LLM feature by half | Prompt trimming, caching, routing to smaller models, batching offline work, distilling or fine-tuning a small model, quality checks after each step |

### The serving question asked most often

"Design an inference batching system for one GPU while users wait" is reported again and again at AI labs. The expected answer: requests enter a queue, and a scheduler fires a batch when either the maximum batch size or a short maximum wait window is reached. Call the wait window your latency-throughput dial. Group requests by length so padding does not dominate, add backpressure when the queue grows, and mention continuous batching for token generation.

## Worked example

**A support assistant for a shopping app.** Assumptions: 2,000,000 requests a day, a peak of 80 requests per second, 1,500 input tokens per request (system prompt, retrieved chunks, history) and 300 output tokens.

1. **Check the peak.** The average is 2,000,000 / 86,400 = 23.1 requests per second, so the peak is about 3.5 times the average. Size for 80.
2. **Tokens per second.** 80 x 300 = 24,000 output tokens per second at peak.
3. **Replicas.** Assume one replica sustains 3,000 output tokens per second while p95 TTFT stays under 1 second, a number to confirm with a load test using these 1,500-token prompts. 24,000 / 3,000 = 8 replicas.
4. **Headroom.** 8 x 1.3 = 10.4, so 11 replicas.
5. **Cross-check with concurrency.** With a 0.5 s TTFT and 30 ms per token, one response stays open for 0.5 + 299 x 0.03 = 9.47 s. Concurrent streams = 80 x 9.47 = 758, or 69 per replica across 11. At 30 ms per token a replica producing 3,000 tokens per second carries 90 streams, so 69 fits.
6. **Daily tokens.** Input: 2,000,000 x 1,500 = 3.0 billion. Output: 2,000,000 x 300 = 0.6 billion.
7. **Hosted cost.** At an assumed 0.50 USD per million input tokens and 1.50 USD per million output tokens: 3,000 x 0.50 + 600 x 1.50 = 1,500 + 900 = 2,400 USD a day, 72,000 USD a month, 0.0012 USD per request.
8. **Self-hosted cost.** At an assumed 2.50 USD per GPU-hour with one GPU per replica, always on: 11 x 2.50 x 720 = 19,800 USD a month, 0.00033 USD per request.
9. **Decision.** On these assumptions hosting is 3.6 times the GPU bill. That gap has to pay for the engineers who run the serving stack, and it only holds if a small open model meets the quality bar. Scaling down at night widens the gap. If traffic were 10 times lower, the hosted bill would be 7,200 USD a month against 3,600 USD for 2 replicas, and a 3,600 USD saving does not pay for running a serving stack.

Say the last step aloud. The interviewer wants the decision and what would change it, not only the numbers.

## Runnable code

Python · standard library and NumPy only · prints its own checks

```
"""Capacity and cost calculator for an LLM service. Pure Python.

Every price and every per-replica throughput below is an assumption.
Replace them with your provider's price list and your own load test.
"""
import math

HOURS_PER_MONTH = 24 * 30

def capacity(peak_rps, output_tokens, replica_tps, headroom=0.30):
    """Replicas needed at peak. replica_tps = output tokens per second that one
    replica sustains at the latency target (measure it with a load test)."""
    need_tps = peak_rps * output_tokens
    base = need_tps / replica_tps
    with_headroom = math.ceil(round(base * (1 + headroom), 9))
    return {"need_tps": need_tps, "base": base, "replicas": with_headroom}

def concurrent_streams(peak_rps, output_tokens, ttft_s, tpot_s):
    """Streams open at once = arrival rate x time each request stays open."""
    duration = ttft_s + (output_tokens - 1) * tpot_s
    return duration, peak_rps * duration

def hosted_cost(requests_per_day, input_tokens, output_tokens, usd_in_per_m, usd_out_per_m):
    per_request = (input_tokens * usd_in_per_m + output_tokens * usd_out_per_m) / 1e6
    return {"per_request": per_request, "per_day": per_request * requests_per_day,
            "per_month": per_request * requests_per_day * 30}

def self_hosted_cost(replicas, usd_per_gpu_hour, requests_per_day, gpus_per_replica=1):
    per_month = replicas * gpus_per_replica * usd_per_gpu_hour * HOURS_PER_MONTH
    return {"per_month": per_month, "per_request": per_month / (requests_per_day * 30)}

def estimate(name, peak_rps, requests_per_day, input_tokens, output_tokens, replica_tps,
             ttft_s, tpot_s, usd_in_per_m, usd_out_per_m, usd_per_gpu_hour):
    cap = capacity(peak_rps, output_tokens, replica_tps)
    duration, streams = concurrent_streams(peak_rps, output_tokens, ttft_s, tpot_s)
    api = hosted_cost(requests_per_day, input_tokens, output_tokens, usd_in_per_m, usd_out_per_m)
    own = self_hosted_cost(cap["replicas"], usd_per_gpu_hour, requests_per_day)
    print(name)
    print(f"  output tokens per second at peak : {peak_rps} x {output_tokens} = {cap['need_tps']:,}")
    print(f"  replicas before headroom         : {cap['need_tps']:,} / {replica_tps:,} = {cap['base']:.1f}")
    print(f"  replicas with 30% headroom       : {cap['base'] * 1.3:.1f} -> {cap['replicas']}")
    print(f"  one response stays open          : {duration:.2f} s, so {streams:.0f} concurrent streams,"
          f" {streams / cap['replicas']:.0f} per replica")
    print(f"  tokens per day                   : {requests_per_day * input_tokens / 1e9:.2f} B input,"
          f" {requests_per_day * output_tokens / 1e9:.2f} B output")
    print(f"  hosted API (assumed prices)      : {api['per_request']:.5f} USD per request,"
          f" {api['per_day']:,.0f} USD per day, {api['per_month']:,.0f} USD per month")
    print(f"  self-hosted (assumed GPU price)  : {own['per_month']:,.0f} USD per month,"
          f" {own['per_request']:.5f} USD per request")
    print(f"  hosted / self-hosted             : {api['per_month'] / own['per_month']:.1f}x, before engineering cost")
    return cap, api, own

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 1. The guide's example: 50 requests per second, 500 output tokens,
    #    2,500 tokens per second per replica, 30% headroom -> 13 replicas.
    #    Requests per day, input tokens and prices are extra assumptions for the cost lines.
    cap, api, own = estimate("Guide example", peak_rps=50, requests_per_day=1_500_000,
                             input_tokens=1_000, output_tokens=500, replica_tps=2_500,
                             ttft_s=0.5, tpot_s=0.03, usd_in_per_m=0.50, usd_out_per_m=1.50,
                             usd_per_gpu_hour=2.50)
    assert (cap["need_tps"], cap["base"], cap["replicas"]) == (25_000, 10.0, 13)
    assert abs(api["per_request"] - 0.00125) < 1e-12 and round(own["per_month"]) == 23_400

    # 2. The worked example: shopping-app support assistant.
    cap, api, own = estimate("Worked example", peak_rps=80, requests_per_day=2_000_000,
                             input_tokens=1_500, output_tokens=300, replica_tps=3_000,
                             ttft_s=0.5, tpot_s=0.03, usd_in_per_m=0.50, usd_out_per_m=1.50,
                             usd_per_gpu_hour=2.50)
    assert (cap["need_tps"], cap["base"], cap["replicas"]) == (24_000, 8.0, 11)
    assert round(api["per_month"]) == 72_000 and round(own["per_month"]) == 19_800

    # 3. Cost per million output tokens on your own GPU depends on utilisation.
    print("Self-hosted cost per million output tokens at an assumed 2.50 USD per GPU-hour, 2,500 tokens/s:")
    for utilisation in (1.0, 0.5, 0.1):
        usd = 2.50 / 3600 / (2_500 * utilisation) * 1e6
        print(f"  GPU {utilisation:>4.0%} busy: {usd:.2f} USD")
    print("all checks passed")
```

## Key takeaways

* Five layers: client, API gateway, orchestration, model serving, GPU nodes. Data and tools sit beside orchestration; observability and evals sit under everything.
* Seven steps: clarify, choose the model path, draw the layers, go deep on the hard part, estimate capacity, add evals and monitoring, cover failure and cost.
* Tokens per second = requests per second x output tokens. Replicas = needed / per replica, plus headroom, rounded up. 50 x 500 = 25,000; / 2,500 = 10; with 30% headroom, 13.
* The per-replica number is an assumption until a load test measures it. Say so.
* Cost per request = (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price) / 1,000,000. A self-hosted GPU costs the same idle or busy, so utilisation decides.
* Give time to first token a budget per stage. After the first token, output length times time per token dominates.
* Each cache has a layer: response caches at the gateway, retrieval caches in orchestration, the prefix cache in the model server.
* Always end with fallbacks, token-based rate limits, guardrails and what you measure offline and online.

## Common mistakes

* Drawing boxes before asking about traffic, tokens, latency and data sensitivity. The design depends on all four.
* Giving no numbers. "It should scale" is not an answer; 25,000 tokens per second and 13 replicas is.
* Sizing for average traffic. Queues form at the peak, and the peak is often several times the mean.
* Treating the model as a box with fixed latency. Latency depends on prompt length, output length and how many requests share the GPU.
* Spending twenty minutes on the layer you know best while the interviewer keeps asking about another one.
* Stopping at the happy path: no evals, no fallback, no rate limits, no plan for a wrong or harmful answer.

## Practice

* Pick one of the six common questions and answer it aloud in 35 minutes using the seven steps. Record it, then check that you stated traffic, tokens per request, a latency target and a replica count.
* Run the calculator with your own product idea: choose requests per day, peak rate and tokens per request, and find the daily volume at which self-hosting becomes cheaper than the hosted price you assumed.
* Write a latency budget for a voice agent whose first audio must start within 800 ms. List every stage and decide which steps from the RAG budget you must drop.
* Draw the five layers from memory, then list for each layer one metric you would put on a dashboard and one failure you would alert on.

## Interview questions (13)

1.How do you structure an answer to an LLM system design question?Easy

Seven steps. First clarify: users, traffic, tokens per request, latency target, quality bar, data sensitivity and budget. Second, choose the model path, hosted API or self-hosted open model, and say why. Third, draw the five layers and name what sits in each. Fourth, go deep on the hard part, which is retrieval quality, agent reliability or serving capacity depending on the question. Fifth, estimate capacity with simple arithmetic. Sixth, add evals and monitoring, offline and online. Seventh, cover failure and cost: fallbacks, rate limits, caching and guardrails. I keep the first three steps to under fifteen minutes so the hard part gets most of the time.

2.Design a ChatGPT-like chat service.Hard

I would clarify scale and latency first, say a p95 time to first token under one second. The client holds a streaming connection and tokens stream back as they are generated. The gateway does auth, moderation of the input and per-user token rate limits. A conversation store keeps every turn. Orchestration builds the context: system prompt, then history, trimming old turns and summarising them when the window fills. I keep the prompt start stable so prefix caching works across turns. The model server uses continuous batching so short and long answers share the GPU. Output moderation runs on the stream. GPU replicas autoscale on queue depth with a warm minimum. I would then size it: requests per second times output tokens, divided by measured tokens per second per replica.

3.Design document Q&A for an enterprise.Medium

Two paths. Offline, an ingestion pipeline parses documents, chunks them on structure, embeds the chunks and writes them to a vector index and a keyword index, with the access groups stored on every chunk. Incremental re-indexing handles changes: hash each document, re-embed only what changed and delete stale chunks. Online, the query runs through hybrid search and a reranker, with permission filtering inside the search so restricted text never reaches the prompt. The model answers only from the retrieved chunks and returns citations. For RAG evals I measure retrieval and generation separately: Recall@k on a labelled set, then faithfulness and answer correctness. The hard part is retrieval quality, so that is where I would spend the time.

4.Design a customer support agent.Hard

The agent is a model in a loop with tools. Lookup tools read orders, accounts and policies. Action tools change things: cancel an order, issue a refund. Lookups run freely; any refund needs approval first, from a human or a strict policy check, and every action is logged. The agent escalates to a human when it is unsure, when the customer asks, or when it hits its step limit, and passes on a summary. Customer memory stores past issues and preferences so the customer does not repeat themselves. For injection defence I treat ticket text and tool results as data, not instructions, and give the agent only the permissions of the customer it serves. The metric is task success: issues resolved without a human and without a reopened ticket.

5.Serve an open model to 1,000 concurrent users.Hard

I start with a target, say p95 TTFT under one second and 30 tokens per second per stream. Engine choice: vLLM as the default, SGLang if requests share long prefixes. Quantization: FP16 if memory allows, 8-bit or 4-bit after checking my eval set. Capacity maths: 1,000 streams x 30 tokens per second is 30,000 tokens per second. If a load test shows 2,500 per replica at the target, that is 12 replicas, or 16 with 30% headroom. I autoscale on queue depth with warm replicas because loading a model is slow. If tenants have fine-tuned variants I use multi-LoRA on one base model. A gateway in front handles rate limits, retries and fallback to another model.

6.Design a coding assistant.Hard

There are two workloads. Inline completion fires on keystrokes and needs a reply in a few hundred milliseconds, so it uses a small fast model, short outputs and cancellation when the user keeps typing. Chat and agent requests can take seconds and use a large model. Both depend on context selection: I index the repository, with embeddings and a symbol index, and send the open file, nearby code and the most relevant definitions, not the whole repository. Caching matters twice: the prefix cache for the stable part of the prompt and a cache for repeated completions. When the assistant edits code, tests run in a sandbox with no access to secrets or the network, and failures go back to the model. I would measure suggestion acceptance rate and test pass rate.

7.Cut the cost of an LLM feature by half.Medium

First I measure where tokens go, per feature and per step. Then I work from cheapest to hardest. Prompt trimming: shorter instructions, fewer retrieved chunks, a cap on output tokens. Caching: prefix caching for the shared prompt and a response cache for repeated questions. Routing: send easy requests to a smaller model and keep the large one for hard ones. Batching offline work, such as summaries and evals, on a cheaper batch path. If volume is steady, distil or fine-tune a small model for the main task. After each step I rerun the eval set, because a saving that drops quality below the bar is not a saving.

8.Design an inference batching system for one GPU while users wait.Hard

Requests enter a queue, and a scheduler fires a batch when either the maximum batch size or a short maximum wait window is reached. The wait window is the latency-throughput dial: 5 ms gives small batches and low wait, 50 ms gives full batches and higher throughput. I group requests by length so padding does not dominate. I add backpressure when the queue grows: past a limit, new requests get an error with a retry hint so the ones already waiting still meet the target. For token generation I would use continuous batching, where finished requests leave and waiting ones join at every decode step. I would watch queue wait, batch size and p95 TTFT to tune the two limits.

9.Hosted API or a self-hosted open model: how do you decide?Medium

Five things decide it. Quality: the hardest reasoning usually needs a top hosted model, while a narrow task can run on a small open one. Volume: per-token pricing wins when traffic is low or spiky, and owned GPUs win when traffic is high and steady enough to keep them busy. Data: if it cannot leave the network, self-host or use a private endpoint. Control: adapters, constrained decoding or a pinned model version point to self-hosting. Team: someone has to run the serving stack and be on call. I usually propose a hosted API to launch, then a self-hosted small model for the high-volume path once the numbers justify it, with the hosted model as fallback.

10.Peak load is 50 requests per second with 500 output tokens each. How many replicas do you need?Medium

50 x 500 is 25,000 output tokens per second. I need one more number: what one replica sustains at my latency target. If that is 2,500 tokens per second, I need 10 replicas, and with 30% headroom for spikes and a failed node, 13. I would say clearly that 2,500 is an assumption and that I would measure it with a load test on real prompts, because it depends on the model, the GPU, the prompt lengths and the latency target. I would also check the prefill load, since long prompts take GPU time that an output-token count does not show.

11.Where do you put caches in an LLM system?Medium

Three places. At the gateway, a response cache: exact match on the normalised prompt, and optionally a semantic cache that matches similar questions by embedding. The semantic cache needs a strict similarity threshold, and the user or tenant in the key when answers depend on private data. In orchestration, I cache query embeddings and retrieval results for popular queries and clear them on re-index. In the model server, the prefix cache reuses the KV cache for a shared system prompt and chat history, which cuts time to first token. To make that work I put stable text first in the prompt. I report hit rate for each cache, because an unused cache is only extra risk.

12.The model provider is slow or down. What does your system do?Medium

It degrades in steps. Every call has a timeout on first token and on total time. Errors that can succeed later, such as 429 and 5xx, are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, a small number of times. A circuit breaker stops sending traffic to a provider that keeps failing. Then the fallback chain: a second provider or region, then a smaller model I host, then a cached or fixed answer that says the service is limited. For agents, a step that changes data is retried only if it is idempotent. I alert on the fallback rate, and I run the eval set on the fallback model in advance so I know how much quality drops.

13.What do you monitor after launch?Medium

Four groups. Latency: p95 and p99 time to first token and time per output token, plus queue wait. Reliability: error rate, timeout rate, fallback rate and rate-limit rejections. Cost: input and output tokens per request, cost per request and per user, cache hit rate. Quality: user feedback, the task metric such as resolved tickets or accepted suggestions, guardrail triggers, and a sampled LLM-judge score on production traffic. Every request has a trace with a span per stage, so a slow or wrong answer can be followed from the gateway to the model. Failed cases go into the offline eval set, which runs before every prompt or model change.

# LLMs on cloud - Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Vertex AI

Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI and Google Vertex AI each give you one managed API to many models inside your own cloud account. The product names differ, but the ideas are the same: pay per token or reserve capacity, live inside quotas, choose where data is processed, lock access down with cloud identity and private networking, and add managed retrieval, agents, guardrails, tuning and evals. This lesson teaches the shared ideas and when to self-host instead.

## Why it matters

Most companies do not call a model lab directly. They buy models through the cloud they already use, because billing, access control and compliance are already set up there. So interviewers ask what someone who has shipped on a cloud would know: on-demand or provisioned throughput, what a 429 means and what you do about it, how you keep data in one region, and when a GPU of your own is cheaper than tokens. You do not need to memorise three product catalogues. You need the six ideas that are common to all three, and one cost calculation you can do on a whiteboard.

Read first: [Inference and serving - KV cache, batching, vLLM](/ai/learn/inference-serving), [Evals, tracing and guardrails](/ai/learn/evals-tracing-guardrails), [LLM system design](/ai/learn/llm-system-design)

## Lesson

### Three clouds, one shape

Each cloud sells the same thing: a managed API, inside your cloud account, to models from several providers, on your normal cloud bill.

* **Amazon Bedrock** is a fully managed service for foundation models from Amazon and from other model companies.
* **Azure OpenAI** is how Azure serves OpenAI models. The documentation now places it inside a wider platform, Microsoft Foundry, and calls it "Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models". The same catalogue also holds models from other providers.
* **Vertex AI** is Google Cloud's platform. Its documentation now uses the name Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and has a page that maps each old Vertex AI name to the new one. Its Model Garden offers Google's own models such as Gemini, partner models and open models.

Interviewers still say "Azure OpenAI" and "Vertex AI". Know both names, and learn the ideas below, because names change and ideas do not.

### Three ways to pay

1. **On-demand (pay per token).** No commitment, and no cost when there is no traffic. Capacity is shared with other customers, so throughput and latency can vary.
2. **Reserved capacity (provisioned throughput).** You pay a fixed price for a fixed amount of throughput, used or not. You get steadier latency and a predictable bill. Bedrock sizes it in model units billed hourly, Azure in provisioned throughput units (PTUs) billed hourly, Google in generative AI scale units (GSUs) bought for a term such as a week or a month. On Bedrock and Azure a longer commitment lowers the hourly price.
3. **Batch.** You submit a file of requests and collect results later. All three list batch at 50 percent below the on-demand rate, Bedrock for the models that support batch. Azure and Google both state a 24-hour target turnaround, and Azure gives batch its own quota.

Bedrock and Google also offer a cheaper flex tier for work that tolerates slow responses, and a priority tier at a higher price. The usual production design reserves the steady baseline and lets peaks overflow to on-demand. Azure calls this spillover.

![Monthly cost against requests per day for on-demand tokens, batch tokens and two self-hosted GPUs, with the two break-even points marked](/ai/img/cloud-llm-break-even.svg)Monthly cost against requests per day for on-demand tokens, batch tokens and two self-hosted GPUs, with the two break-even points marked

The picture uses the assumed prices from the worked example below. The two token lines rise with volume and the GPU line is flat, so each token line crosses it once.

### Quotas, rate limits and the 429

On-demand capacity is limited per account, in tokens per minute (TPM) and often requests per minute (RPM).

* **Bedrock:** TPM per model, counting input plus output tokens, and a tokens-per-day cap across models. `max_tokens` is deducted from the quota when a request starts and corrected when it ends. For some models one output token counts as several.
* **Azure:** TPM is assigned per subscription, region, model and deployment type, and RPM is set in proportion to it. The TPM check uses an estimate made when the request arrives, and that estimate includes `max_tokens`. RPM is checked over windows of 1 or 10 seconds, so a burst is throttled even when the minute total is fine.
* **Google:** Standard PayGo gives an organisation a TPM threshold that rises with its spend over a rolling 30 days. Traffic above the threshold is served only when the shared pool has spare capacity, and is throttled first when demand is high.

When you pass a limit, or the shared pool is busy, you get HTTP 429. Retry with exponential backoff and random jitter, cap the retries, and obey the wait hint if there is one (Azure sends a `retry-after-ms` header). Then fix the cause: smooth bursts, lower `max_tokens`, request more quota, or reserve capacity. On Bedrock a 429 is your quota and a 503 is service capacity; for the 503 the docs suggest cross-Region inference.

### Regions and data residency

All three offer three routing scopes, and the wider the scope, the more capacity you get.

| Scope | Where inference can run | Named as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Narrowest | Bedrock: the Region you call. Azure: the Azure geography of your resource. Google: the country or jurisdiction of the region you call | Bedrock without a cross-Region inference profile; Azure Standard; Google locational (regional) endpoint |
| A geography | Any region inside US, EU or a similar zone | Bedrock Geographic cross-Region inference; Azure Data Zone; Google jurisdictional multi-region endpoint |
| Global | Any region the provider chooses | Bedrock Global cross-Region inference; Azure Global Standard; Google global endpoint |

Read the first row carefully. On Azure and Google the narrowest option promises a geography or a country, not one data centre region. If a rule names a single region, check the provider's wording before you promise it.

Separate data at rest from data being processed. Azure and Google keep data at rest in the location you chose whichever scope you call; only processing moves. Google's docs say the global endpoint gives no residency guarantee. Bedrock records the Region that served each cross-Region request in CloudTrail.

### Identity and private networking

Do not ship long-lived API keys. Use the cloud's identity system: IAM roles with temporary credentials on AWS, Microsoft Entra ID with managed identities and role-based access control on Azure, IAM on Google Cloud. Azure's docs say API keys cannot express a user identity and are not recommended for production. Keep traffic off the public internet with an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) or an Azure private endpoint with public network access disabled. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls put a perimeter around the API so data cannot leave it.

### The managed building blocks

| Need | Bedrock | Azure OpenAI | Vertex AI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay per token | On-demand | Standard deployment | Standard PayGo |
| Reserved capacity | Provisioned Throughput; Reserved tier | Provisioned deployment (PTUs) | Provisioned Throughput (GSUs) |
| Batch | Batch inference | Global Batch, Data Zone Batch | Batch inference |
| Managed retrieval | Knowledge Bases | Foundry IQ, built on Azure AI Search | RAG Engine |
| Managed agents | AgentCore | Foundry Agent Service | Agent Runtime, Agent Development Kit |
| Guardrails | Guardrails | Guardrails and controls | Model Armor |
| Customisation | Fine-tuning, distillation, Custom Model Import | Fine-tuning | Tuning |
| Evaluation | Evaluations | Evaluations | Evals, formerly Gen AI evaluation service |
| Open model on your own GPUs | SageMaker AI endpoint | Managed compute (preview) | Self-deployed model from Model Garden |

Managed retrieval runs the RAG pipeline for you: ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing and retrieval with citations. Guardrails check the prompt and the response. Bedrock Guardrails can also be called alone, without invoking a model, and Azure gives a model a default guardrail unless you assign your own. Fine-tuning on all three is supervised first, with preference or reinforcement methods as extras.

### Managed API or self-hosted on cloud GPUs

|  | Managed API | Self-hosted on cloud GPUs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing | Per token; nothing at zero traffic | Per GPU-hour, idle or busy |
| Capacity | Shared pool, quotas, 429s | Fixed by your GPUs; you queue or scale |
| Models | The provider's catalogue, closed models included | Any open weights, your fine-tunes and adapters |
| Control | Provider retires model versions on its schedule | You pin version, quantization and serving engine |
| Operations | Close to none | Autoscaling, upgrades, load tests, on-call |
| Wins when | Volume is low or spiky; you need the strongest models | Volume is steady and high; data rules are strict |

Self-host for three reasons: cost at steady high volume, control, and data rules. Otherwise use the managed API, because an idle GPU still costs money. Google's docs make the same trade: self-deployment can lower the total cost over an application's lifetime, and it needs a greater upfront engineering investment.
