# LoRA fine-tuning pipeline with an adapter registry

fine-tuningloraqloragpu schedulingevaluation gateadapter registryReported at OpenAI

## Problem statement

Design a fine-tuning platform for a company where 120 product teams adapt two open base models, a 7B and a 70B model, to their own tasks. A team uploads a dataset and gets back a LoRA adapter: a small set of trained weights added to a frozen base model. The platform validates the data, runs about 40 training jobs a day on a shared GPU pool, proves each adapter beats the base model before promotion, and rolls back in under a minute. It must also say when fine-tuning is the wrong tool.

## Requirements

### Functional

* Upload a versioned dataset of chat examples and get a validation report with a verdict: train, fix the data, or do not fine-tune.
* Submit a LoRA or QLoRA job (QLoRA is LoRA on a base model stored in 4 bits) with safe default hyperparameters, see the cost estimate, queue position and loss curve, and cancel it.
* Resume a job from its latest checkpoint after a GPU is taken away.
* Score every finished adapter against the base model on a held-out split and a general regression set. Only passing adapters can be promoted.
* Keep each adapter in a registry with its lineage: base model hash, dataset version, hyperparameters, eval scores and owner.
* Deploy an adapter behind a stable alias with a canary, and roll back to the previous adapter with one call.

### Non-functional

* 40 jobs per day on average and 100 per day at peak; p95 queue wait under 30 minutes for jobs under 2 GPU-hours.
* A preempted job (its GPU was taken back by the provider) loses at most 10 minutes of training work.
* Promotion gate: at least 3 points better than the base model with its best prompt on the held-out split, proven at 95% confidence, and at most 1 point worse on the general regression set.
* Rollback completes in under 60 seconds with no model reload.
* A standard 7B job costs under 10 USD including evaluation, and the estimate is shown before the job starts.
* A team's datasets and adapters are readable only by that team, and every promotion is written to an audit log.

## Back-of-the-envelope estimates

**A standard job.** 5,000 examples with 10% held out leave 4,500 x 800 tokens = 3.6M tokens. 3 epochs = 10.8M training tokens. At batch size 16 that is 4,500 x 3 / 16 = 844 steps.

**Memory.** 7B in 16-bit is 14 GB, so LoRA fits on one 80 GB GPU. 70B in 16-bit is 140 GB and does not fit. In 4-bit it is 35 GB, so 70B jobs use QLoRA.

**GPU time.** Assume 3,000 training tokens per second on the 7B base and 300 on the 70B. Training takes 10.8M / 3,000 = 3,600 s (1 hour) or 10.8M / 300 = 36,000 s (10 hours). Adding model load and evaluation, budget 1.5 and 12 GPU-hours.

**Fleet.** Average day: 36 small x 1.5 + 4 large x 12 = 102 GPU-hours, 4.25 GPUs busy. Peak day: 90 x 1.5 + 10 x 12 = 255 GPU-hours, 10.6 GPUs. Reserve 6 GPUs (144 GPU-hours, 71% used on an average day) and burst to 16 with preemptible GPUs (384 GPU-hours, 66% used at peak).

**Cost.** At an assumed 2.5 USD per GPU-hour, a small job costs 3.75 USD, a large one 30 USD. The eval gate judges 500 held-out cases for both models and 300 regression prompts for the adapter only (base scores are cached): 1,300 calls of 1,200 input and 100 output tokens, 1.56M and 0.13M tokens. At an assumed 1 USD and 5 USD per million: 1.56 + 0.65 = 2.21 USD, 60% of a small job's GPU cost.

**Storage.** A rank-16 adapter on the attention and MLP layers of the 7B model has about 40M values: 80 MB in 16-bit. A checkpoint stores each weight plus two Adam optimiser values in 32-bit: 40M x 12 bytes = 480 MB.

**Checkpoint interval.** 100 steps x 16 examples x 800 tokens = 1.28M tokens: 7 minutes on the 7B base, 71 on the 70B. So checkpoint every 100 steps or 10 minutes, whichever is first.

## API

```
POST /v1/datasets
  body: { team, task, format: "chat_jsonl" }        -> { dataset_id, upload_url }
POST /v1/datasets/{dataset_id}/validate
  -> { dataset_version, report: { examples, duplicates, template_errors,
       too_long, pii_hits, baseline_score },
       verdict: "train" | "fix_data" | "do_not_finetune", reasons: [] }

POST /v1/jobs
  body: { dataset_version, base_model, method?: "lora" | "qlora",
          hyperparams?: { rank, alpha, learning_rate, epochs },
          eval_suite_id, target_metric }
  -> { job_id, estimated_gpu_hours, estimated_cost_usd, queue_position }
GET  /v1/jobs/{job_id}
  -> { state, step, total_steps, train_loss, val_loss, preemptions, eta }
POST /v1/jobs/{job_id}/cancel
GET  /v1/jobs/{job_id}/eval
  -> { baseline, tuned, fixed_cases, broken_cases, z, regression_delta,
       gate: "pass" | "fail" | "not_proven" }

GET  /v1/adapters?team=&task=
POST /v1/aliases/{alias}/deploy     body: { adapter_id, canary_percent }
POST /v1/aliases/{alias}/promote
POST /v1/aliases/{alias}/rollback
```

## Data model

```
dataset_versions(dataset_version PK, dataset_id, team, content_hash,
                 examples, train_uri, heldout_uri, report_json,
                 verdict, created_at, deleted_at)

jobs(job_id PK, team, dataset_version FK, base_model_hash, method,
     rank, alpha, learning_rate, epochs, state, priority,
     est_gpu_hours, used_gpu_hours, preemptions, created_at)

checkpoints(job_id FK, step, uri, epoch, data_position, data_seed,
            complete BOOL, created_at)       -- adapter + optimiser state

eval_runs(eval_id PK, job_id FK, suite_version, judge_version,
          baseline_score, tuned_score, fixed, broken, z,
          regression_delta, gate, report_uri)

adapters(adapter_id PK, job_id FK, team, task, base_model_hash,
         dataset_version, rank, size_bytes, weights_uri,
         stage: candidate | canary | production | retired)

aliases(alias PK, team, current_adapter_id, previous_adapter_id,
        canary_adapter_id, canary_percent, updated_by, updated_at)
audit_log(id PK, actor, action, alias, adapter_id, at)
```

## High-level design

**Offline path (data to adapter)**

1. **Upload.** A team uploads chat examples as JSONL. The platform stores an immutable dataset version keyed by a content hash.
2. **Validate.** The validator checks the schema and roles, renders each example with the base model's chat template (the exact text format, with special tokens, that marks each turn), counts tokens, removes duplicates, scans for PII (personal data such as names and phone numbers), and then splits 90/10 into train and held-out.
3. **Advise.** The advisor runs the base model with the team's best prompt on the held-out split and returns a verdict: train, fix the data, or do not fine-tune.
4. **Queue.** A job gets a cost estimate and enters a fair-share queue. Defaults are rank 16, alpha 32 and 3 epochs.
5. **Schedule.** The scheduler picks a GPU. It uses LoRA when the 16-bit base fits with room to train, and QLoRA (a 4-bit base) when it does not.
6. **Train.** The trainer updates only the adapter, logs train and validation loss, and writes a checkpoint every 100 steps or 10 minutes. A preempted job goes back to the queue with a resume flag.
7. **Gate.** The eval runner scores the base model and the adapter on the held-out split and the regression set, case by case.
8. **Register.** A passing adapter enters the registry with its lineage. A failing one is kept 7 days for debugging and cannot be promoted.

**Online path (adapter to traffic)**

9. **Deploy.** Serving replicas keep the base model in memory and load the adapter beside it. An alias such as `support/triage:prod` sends 5% of its traffic to the new adapter first. This small first step is the canary.
10. **Watch.** The platform compares canary and current traffic on the team's online metric, then promotes or rolls back by changing the alias.
11. **Feed back.** Labelled production failures become examples in the next dataset version.

## Architecture diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Deep dives

### Validation, and when to say "do not fine-tune"

Most failed fine-tunes are data problems. The validator renders every example through the base model's chat template and rejects the upload if special tokens are missing, because a wrong template is the most frequent cause of an adapter that scores below the base. It removes exact and near duplicates before splitting, so no held-out example copies a training example. It flags over-long examples, empty outputs, and identical inputs with different labels.

The advisor then returns "do not fine-tune" when:

* there are fewer than about 500 clean examples;
* the task needs facts that change, such as prices or policies. That is knowledge, and retrieval supplies it without retraining;
* the base model with the team's best prompt already meets the target on the held-out split;
* the task definition is still changing, since every change means a new dataset;
* the only gain is a shorter prompt and traffic is low. Saving 1,700 prompt tokens on 1,000 requests a day is 1.7M tokens, or 1.70 USD a day at an assumed 1 USD per million.

Each verdict carries its evidence: the baseline score and the rejected examples.

### Scheduling GPUs: fair share, short jobs and preemption

Large jobs are 10% of the count and 47% of the GPU-hours on an average day (48 of 102). A first-in-first-out queue lets one 12-hour job block many 1.5-hour jobs. Two rules fix this. Fair share: each team has a weight, and the scheduler serves the team furthest below its share. Short jobs first inside a team, using the estimated GPU-hours. Reserved GPUs run jobs to completion. Burst GPUs can be taken away, so every job on them must be resumable.

A checkpoint holds the adapter weights, the optimiser state, the learning-rate schedule step, the data-order seed and the position in the epoch. Without the last two, a resumed job repeats or skips examples. Write the checkpoint under a temporary name and rename it when complete, so a preemption mid-write cannot leave half a file as "latest". After two preemptions, move the job to a reserved GPU.

### The evaluation gate

The gate asks one question: is this adapter better than what the team could ship without it? So the baseline is the base model with the team's best prompt, not a weak prompt. Three checks run:

1. **Held-out split.** Code checks where a program can decide (an exact label, valid JSON), and an LLM judge with a fixed rubric otherwise.
2. **General regression set.** 300 prompts per base model on general instruction following and safety refusals. This catches catastrophic forgetting: the model gains the new task and loses old skills.
3. **Memorisation probe.** Unrelated prompts must not return training examples word for word.

500 held-out cases are noisy. At 80% accuracy the standard error is sqrt(0.8 x 0.2 / 500) = 1.8 points, so two separate scores can differ by 3 points by chance. Compare both models on the same cases and count flips. If the adapter fixes 60 cases and breaks 30, the net gain is 6 points and z = (60 - 30) / sqrt(60 + 30) = 3.2, above the 1.96 needed for 95% confidence. If it fixes 20 and breaks 12, z = 1.4 and the gate says "not proven". The report lists the broken cases: they show what the adapter unlearned.

### Registry, deployment and rollback

An adapter only makes sense with the exact base weights it was trained on. The registry stores the base model's content hash, and serving refuses to load an adapter onto any other hash. A new base version means retraining every adapter, so the registry keeps each dataset version and job spec to make a retrain one call.

Deploy adapters unmerged on the shared base. Merging adds the adapter into the base weights and removes the small per-request overhead, but costs a 14 GB copy per adapter. Reserve it for a team whose traffic fills dedicated replicas.

Rollback is an alias change. The previous adapter stays loaded for 24 hours after a promotion, so flipping the alias back needs no reload. Lineage also handles deletion: when a dataset must be removed, the registry finds and retires every adapter trained on it.

## Evaluation

**Per adapter, offline.** The gate above: task metric on the 10% held-out split against the base model with its best prompt, a 300-prompt regression set, and a memorisation probe. Results are paired case by case, and the gate needs a net gain of 3 points with z above 1.96.

**Judge quality.** When an LLM judge scores the task, label 100 held-out outputs by hand and report agreement with the judge, including agreement on the failing cases alone. Recheck when the judge model or rubric changes.

**Per adapter, online.** The canary is an A/B test: 5% of the alias's traffic, randomised by user, compared on the team's own outcome metric (ticket resolved, edit accepted), thumbs-down rate, latency and tokens per request. Low-traffic aliases stay in canary until they have enough requests, not for a fixed number of hours.

**The platform itself.** p95 queue wait, job success rate, failures split by cause (data, out of memory, preemption), GPU utilisation, and time from upload to a promotable adapter. Two numbers show whether the checks are honest. Escaped regressions: adapters rolled back after promotion. Advisor precision: when a team overrides "do not fine-tune", how often does the adapter then pass the gate?

**Guardrails.** PII scan before training, base hash check before loading, and an audit log entry for every promotion and rollback.

## Bottlenecks & mitigations

* 70B QLoRA jobs: 10% of jobs and 47% of GPU-hours on an average day. They set the fleet size and the worst queue waits.
* Evaluation: 800 prompts generated per adapter plus 1,300 judge calls. Judge rate limits cap how many gates run at once, so cache base model outputs per dataset version.
* Loading base weights at job start: 14 GB or 35 GB per job unless each node keeps the bases on local disk.
* Canary duration for low-traffic adapters, which can need days to collect enough requests for a decision.
* Human labelling for judge calibration, which does not scale with GPU count.

## Failure modes

* **The adapter scores below the base model.** Usually a wrong chat template, a learning rate that is too high, or too many epochs on small data. Mitigation: template rendering in the validator, safe defaults, and the gate blocks promotion.
* **Held-out leak.** Near duplicates on both sides of the split inflate the score. Mitigation: remove duplicates before splitting, and split by group (customer or thread) when examples are related.
* **Out of memory mid-run.** One very long example lands in a batch. Mitigation: a token cap in the validator, batches grouped by length, and a smaller batch with gradient accumulation.
* **Preemption loop.** A job on burst GPUs is interrupted again and again. Mitigation: checkpoints every 10 minutes, and a move to reserved GPUs after two preemptions.
* **Catastrophic forgetting.** The adapter wins on the task and loses general skills. Mitigation: the regression set, fewer epochs, a lower learning rate, or general examples mixed into the data.
* **Adapter loaded on the wrong base version.** Outputs degrade with no error. Mitigation: the base hash check in the registry and in serving.
* **Passes the gate, fails in production.** The training data does not look like real inputs. Mitigation: canary with rollback, and production samples added to the next held-out split.
* **Private data memorised.** A customer's details appear in outputs for another user. Mitigation: PII scan at upload, the memorisation probe, and per-team isolation of adapters.

## Follow-up questions interviewers ask

* A team has 200 examples and insists on fine-tuning. What do you tell them, and what do you offer?
* The base model gets a new version. How do you move 300 adapters to it?
* Training loss falls but the eval score does not move. How do you debug it?
* How would you add preference tuning with DPO, or distillation from a larger model, as job types?
* When is a hyperparameter sweep worth its GPU cost, and how would the scheduler treat it?
* Two teams want one adapter for two related tasks. One adapter or two, and how do you decide?

# Guardrails and PII redaction layer

guardrailspiisafety classifierstreamingpolicyaudit logReported at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google

## Problem statement

Design the guardrail layer that sits between users and the LLM for a consumer company with three chat products: a general assistant, a homework helper for teenagers and a support bot. Together they handle 40 million messages a day. The layer masks personal data (PII) before it reaches the model or the logs, blocks unsafe and off-topic requests, checks the answer while it streams, and lets each product set its own policy. Users should not feel the delay.

## Requirements

### Functional

* Detect PII in each user message and replace every value with a typed placeholder that can be restored in the reply.
* Score each input for safety categories (self-harm, sexual content, violence, hate, prompt injection) and for off-topic requests, then act as the product's policy says.
* Check the model's output while it streams, and stop or replace an answer that fails.
* Store one policy per product: categories, thresholds, actions, PII types and stream mode, versioned and changeable without a deploy.
* Write an audit event for every verdict, with scores and versions and no raw PII.
* Let users report a wrong block, and feed those reports into labelling.

### Non-functional

* Input checks add under 40 ms at p95 before the model call.
* Output checks delay the first visible text by under 350 ms in strict mode and by 0 ms in optimistic mode.
* 40 million messages a day: 463 per second on average, 1,389 at peak.
* PII recall of at least 99% for structured types (card, phone, email, national id) and 95% for names and addresses.
* Safety: at least 90% recall per category with under 0.2% of normal messages blocked.
* Guardrail compute under 1% of LLM spend; a policy change is live within 60 seconds.

## Back-of-the-envelope estimates

**Traffic.** 5 million daily users x 8 messages = 40 million messages/day: 463 per second on average and 1,389 at a 3x peak.

**Input checks.** A message averages 120 tokens. A small encoder model on one GPU handles an assumed 48,000 tokens per second, so 400 messages per second. Peak needs 1,389 / 400 = 3.5, so 4 GPUs for the name-and-address model and 4 for the safety classifier.

**Output checks.** An answer averages 300 tokens. One check every 50 tokens, reading the last 100: 6 checks per answer, 240 million a day, 8,333 per second at peak. A GPU does 48,000 / 100 = 480 checks per second, so 18 GPUs.

**Cost.** 26 GPUs x 24 h x an assumed 1.5 USD per GPU-hour = 936 USD/day. The LLM uses 1,500 input and 300 output tokens per message. At an assumed 1 and 5 USD per million that is 0.0030 USD per message, 120,000 USD/day. The guardrails add 0.78%.

**Errors at one threshold.** Assume 0.5% of messages break policy: 200,000 a day. At 90% recall, 180,000 are caught and 20,000 are missed. A 0.2% false-block rate on 40 million is about 80,000 normal messages blocked. Precision is 180,000 / 260,000 = 69%, so about 1 block in 3 hits an innocent user.

**Grey band.** Send the 1% of messages with middle scores to a larger model: 400,000 a day, 4.6 per second. At 600 tokens each and an assumed 1 USD per million, that is 240 USD/day.

**Storage.** 8% of messages hold PII, 1.5 values each: 4.8 million vault entries a day x 200 bytes = 0.96 GB, 29 GB for 30 days. Audit: 2 events per message (one input verdict, one output verdict) = 80 million events x 300 bytes = 24 GB/day, 2.16 TB for 90 days.

## API

```
POST /v1/guard/input
  body: { product_id, conversation_id, message_id, text, locale }
  resp: { action: "allow" | "block" | "safe_reply" | "redirect"
                  | "second_check",
          masked_text,
          entities: [{ type, placeholder, start, end }],
          verdicts: [{ category, score, low, high }],
          policy_version, latency_ms }

STREAM /v1/guard/output/{message_id}
  in:   model tokens
  out:  { event: "release", text }            (placeholders restored)
        { event: "retract", category, fallback_text }

PUT  /admin/policies/{product_id}             (new version, reviewed)
POST /admin/policies/{product_id}/replay
  body: { candidate_policy, from, to }
  resp: { blocks_now, blocks_candidate, changed_examples[] }

GET  /admin/audit?product_id=&category=&action=&from=&to=
POST /v1/guard/reports   { message_id, reason: "wrong_block" }
```

## Data model

```
policies(product_id, version, created_by, live_from,
  pii:        { CARD: "mask", PHONE: "mask", EMAIL: "mask",
                NATIONAL_ID: "mask", PERSON: "mask", PINCODE: "pass" },
  categories: { self_harm: { low: 0.20, high: 0.60, action: "safe_reply" },
                hate:      { low: 0.50, high: 0.90, action: "block" },
                off_topic: { low: 0.70, high: 0.95, action: "redirect" } },
  stream_mode: "strict" | "optimistic")

pii_vault(conversation_id, placeholder, type, value_encrypted,
          expires_at)                 -- PK (conversation_id, placeholder)

audit_events(event_id PK, ts, product_id, conversation_id, message_id,
             direction: "input" | "output", check, category, score,
             low, high, action, policy_version, model_version,
             latency_ms, masked_text_ref)        -- never a raw value

labels(message_id, category, human_label, labeller_id, source:
       "sample" | "user_report" | "grey_band")
```

## High-level design

**Offline path**

1. Policy store. Each product owns a policy document. A new version is reviewed, replayed against last week's logged scores, then pushed to every gateway within 60 seconds.
2. Labelled sets. People label sampled traffic (masked), user reports and grey-band cases. The sets train the classifiers and give the precision and recall curves that thresholds are picked from.
3. A new classifier or policy runs in shadow mode on live traffic before it decides anything.

**Online path**

4. The gateway receives a message and reads the product's policy from memory.
5. Three input checks run in parallel: a pattern detector with checksums for structured PII, a named-entity model for names and addresses, and a multi-label safety classifier. The wait is the slowest of the three, about 25 ms.
6. The policy turns scores into an action. Above the high threshold: block, or send a safe reply (a self-harm message gets a supportive reply with helpline details). Between the thresholds: a larger model reads the message with the policy text. Below: allow.
7. Each PII value is replaced by a typed placeholder such as `<PHONE_1>`, and the mapping is saved in the vault for this conversation.
8. The masked prompt goes to the LLM, with one system line: copy placeholders exactly.
9. The output stream passes through the output guard: a pattern scan on a rolling buffer, and the classifier every 50 tokens. Strict mode holds each chunk until it passes. Optimistic mode releases at once and retracts on failure.
10. Placeholders are restored at the last hop, just before text leaves for the user. Traces and logs keep the masked text.
11. Each message writes two audit events: its input verdict and its output verdict. A sample goes to labelling, which closes the loop to step 2.

## Sequence diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Deep dives

### Reversible placeholders

Replace each value with a typed, numbered placeholder: `<PHONE_1>`, `<PERSON_2>`. The same value gets the same placeholder for the whole conversation, so the model can still reason: "send it to `<EMAIL_1>`, the address `<PERSON_1>` gave". The type keeps the sentence meaningful; a bare `[REDACTED]` does not. A one-shot request can keep the mapping in memory. A chat needs it on every later turn, so it lives in a vault: encrypted, keyed by conversation, expiring after 30 days. Restoring happens at the last hop, so the model provider and the trace store never hold the raw value.

Two limits. The model cannot compute on a masked value ("which city has this PIN code?"), so the policy lists types that pass unmasked per product. And a stream can split a placeholder across tokens, so the gateway holds text from an open `<` until the closing `>` arrives.

### Latency before and during the stream

Before the model call, checks run in parallel, so the cost is the slowest check (25 ms) and not the sum. Masking must finish before the prompt leaves, because a raw value sent to the model cannot be taken back. Safety scoring has no such limit. The 300 ms second check runs alongside the model call, and the answer is cancelled if the check fails.

During the stream, strict mode holds a chunk until it is checked. At an assumed 50 tokens per second a 50-token chunk appears 1 s late, so the first chunk is cut to 15 tokens: 0.3 s plus a 25 ms check. Optimistic mode shows tokens at once and checks behind them; on a failure it stops and replaces the message, and the user may already have read up to 50 tokens. The teen product runs strict. The general assistant runs optimistic.

### False blocks against misses

One threshold gives 80,000 false blocks and 20,000 misses a day. The two errors cost differently by category and product. A missed self-harm message in the teen product is far worse than a wrong block. A blocked medical question in the general assistant loses a user. So each category has its own thresholds per product, read from that product's precision and recall curve.

Use three bands. Below `low`: allow. Above `high`: act. Between: the second check by a larger model, which costs 240 USD/day because only 1% of traffic reaches it. PII is different: a wrongly masked order number is restored correctly anyway, so a false positive costs almost nothing. Tune PII detection for recall.

### Policy as data, and the audit trail

A policy is a versioned document, not code. Every audit event stores the score, both thresholds, the action, the policy version and the classifier version, so "why was this blocked in March" has an answer. Because scores are logged, a threshold change can be replayed over last week's events to predict the new block count before it ships, with no model run.

## Evaluation

**PII detection.** A labelled set of 5,000 messages with marked spans. Report span-level recall and precision per type. Include local formats (12-digit Aadhaar numbers with their checksum, 10-character PAN, UPI ids), Hindi-English mixed text, digits written as words, and names that are also common words.

**Leak test.** Send canary values through the whole pipeline, then search the model request log and the trace store. The count must be zero.

**Round trip.** Share of answers where every placeholder is restored exactly. Track how often the model changes one (`<PERSON 1>`); target under 0.1%.

**Safety classifiers.** For each category and product: recall on the harm and attack set, and false-block rate on 50,000 sampled normal messages, both at the live thresholds. Slice by language.

**Latency.** p50, p95 and p99 added by input checks, and time to first visible text in strict mode, under a load test at 1,389 messages per second.

**Human review.** Each week, label 500 blocked and 500 allowed messages per product. Misses are about 0.05% of traffic, so a random sample of allowed messages finds almost none: also sample just under the low threshold, where misses concentrate.

**Online.** Block rate by category and product, with an alert when it doubles. Wrong-block reports per 1,000 blocks, retractions per day in optimistic mode, grey-band volume and PII found in outputs.

**Rollout.** Shadow first and compare decisions with the live version. Then an A/B test on user outcomes: sessions abandoned right after a block, and session length.

## Bottlenecks & mitigations

* Output checks: 8,333 per second at peak use 18 of the 26 GPUs. One shared encoder with two heads (PII spans and safety labels) would cut the input side from 8 GPUs to 4.
* Vault reads on every released chunk. Cache the conversation's mapping in gateway memory for the life of the stream.
* Long pasted documents: a 6,000-token paste costs the name model as much as 50 average messages. Split it into windows, batch them and cap the size.
* The grey-band model takes about 300 ms. If an attack wave grows the band tenfold, queue depth explodes, so fall back to the stricter threshold.
* Audit volume of 24 GB a day needs partitioning by day and product.

## Failure modes

* **PII slips past detection.** A name that is a common word, or a phone number spelled out in words. Mitigation: normalise spelled digits, tune for recall, and scan the output side as a second chance.
* **The model changes a placeholder.** `<PERSON_1>` comes back as `<Person 1>` and cannot be restored. Mitigation: a tolerant restore pattern, the system instruction, and an alert on the mangle rate.
* **A user types a placeholder.** Text such as `<EMAIL_1>` in the input could be restored to a stored value. Mitigation: escape placeholder-shaped text on input; the vault is per conversation, so it holds only that user's data.
* **Retraction comes too late.** In optimistic mode harmful text is on screen before the check fails. Mitigation: strict mode for high-risk products, and a shorter check interval for severe categories.
* **A request split over turns.** Each message alone looks harmless. Mitigation: the classifier reads the last few turns, not only the newest message.
* **The guard service is down.** Mitigation: strict products fail closed with an apology; others fall back to pattern checks only and raise an alert.
* **A policy change spikes false blocks.** Mitigation: replay before release, roll out to 5% first, and roll back within 60 seconds.
* **The audit log becomes a PII store.** Mitigation: masked text and hashes only, access control, and 90-day retention.

## Follow-up questions interviewers ask

* A user asks for a letter that includes their own address. What does the model see, and what does the user see?
* The product must show the first word within 300 ms. Which stream mode do you choose, and what do you give up?
* Legal demands at most 1% misses for one category. What happens to false blocks, and how do you show the trade-off?
* How do you support 12 languages, including Hindi-English mixed text?
* The model provider already offers a moderation endpoint. Do you still need this layer?
* How does the design change for voice or image input?

# Hybrid retrieval and reranking service

hybrid searchbm25reciprocal rank fusioncross-encoderretrieval metrics

## Problem statement

Design a shared retrieval service for a product company. Several teams call it: site search, a support chatbot and an internal RAG assistant. Given a query and filters, it returns the 10 best passages out of 30 million, in under 200 ms. It combines keyword search (BM25) with embedding search, fuses the two result lists and reranks the fused candidates with a cross-encoder. Answer generation is out of scope: this service only finds and orders passages, and it must prove its quality with retrieval metrics.

## Requirements

### Functional

* Return the top k passages (default 10) for a text query, with tenant and metadata filters applied inside both searches.
* Run BM25 and dense search in parallel, fuse the two ranked lists, then rerank the fused candidates.
* Let callers choose a mode per request: `hybrid`, `bm25` or `dense`, with reranking on or off.
* Return a debug view: each passage's rank in every stage and the time each stage took.
* Accept passage upserts and deletes and keep both indexes in step.
* Store relevance judgments and run offline evaluations that report Recall@k, MRR and nDCG for any configuration.

### Non-functional

* End-to-end latency under 200 ms at p95; without reranking under 60 ms at p95.
* 2 million queries per day: about 23 QPS on average, 60 QPS at peak.
* Quality gates on the judged set: Recall@50 of at least 0.95 for the 50 fused candidates, nDCG@10 of at least 0.70 after reranking.
* A new or edited passage is searchable in both indexes within 60 seconds.
* 99.95% availability. If the reranker or one retriever fails, the service still answers in a degraded mode and says so in the response.
* Reranking cost under 0.0005 USD per query.

## Back-of-the-envelope estimates

**Traffic.** 2,000,000 queries / 86,400 s = 23 QPS on average. Plan for 60 QPS at peak.

**Dense index.** 30M passages x 768 dimensions x 4 bytes = 92 GB as float32. HNSW links (M = 32: up to 64 neighbour ids x 4 bytes = 256 bytes per vector) add 30M x 256 bytes = 7.7 GB, so about 100 GB. With 40% headroom for deletes, growth and filter fields that is 140 GB: 3 shards of about 47 GB each, on 64 GB nodes. Scalar quantization to int8 would cut the vectors to 23 GB.

**Keyword index.** 30M passages x 200 tokens x about 4 bytes = 24 GB of text. Plan the inverted index at the same order of size, split over the same 3 shards.

**Latency budget (p95 target 200 ms).**

| Stage | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| Embed the query | 15 ms |
| BM25 and dense search in parallel, top 100 each | 30 ms |
| Fuse the lists, keep 50 | 1 ms |
| Fetch 50 passage texts | 5 ms |
| Cross-encoder reranks 50 pairs | 120 ms |
| Total | 171 ms |

That leaves 29 ms for network and queueing. The reranker takes 120 of the 171 ms (70%), so it is the stage to design around.

**Reranker GPUs.** Peak load is 60 QPS x 50 pairs = 3,000 pairs per second. Assume one GPU scores 50 pairs in 120 ms (confirm with a load test). That is 50 / 0.12 = 417 pairs per second. 3,000 / 417 = 7.2, so 8 GPUs, and 10 with 25% headroom.

**Cost.** At an assumed 1.50 USD per GPU-hour, 10 GPUs x 24 h x 1.50 = 360 USD per day. Divided by 2M queries that is 0.00018 USD per query, inside the 0.0005 USD target.

## API

```
POST /v1/search
  body: { tenant_id, query, k = 10,
          mode = "hybrid" | "bm25" | "dense",
          rerank = true,
          filters?: { source?, lang?, updated_after? },
          debug = false }
  200:  { results: [{ passage_id, doc_id, text, score,
                      ranks?: { bm25, dense, fused, reranked } }],
          degraded: null | "no_rerank" | "bm25_only" | "dense_only",
          timings_ms?: { embed, bm25, dense, fuse, fetch, rerank } }

PUT    /v1/passages/{passage_id}     body: { tenant_id, doc_id, text, metadata }
DELETE /v1/passages/{passage_id}

POST /v1/judgments                   body: { query_id, passage_id, grade: 0..3 }
POST /v1/eval/runs                   body: { query_set, config }
GET  /v1/eval/runs/{run_id}  ->  { recall_at_50, mrr_at_10, ndcg_at_10, by_query_type }
```

## Data model

```
passages(passage_id PK, tenant_id, doc_id, text, token_count,
         metadata JSON, version, updated_at, deleted)

keyword_index(term -> postings[(passage_id, term_freq)])   -- BM25, filter fields stored
vector_index(passage_id, embedding VECTOR(768), tenant_id, metadata)   -- HNSW, cosine

query_log(query_id PK, tenant_id, query, mode, config_version,
          bm25_ids[], dense_ids[], fused_ids[], reranked_ids[],
          clicked_ids[], timings_ms JSON, created_at)

eval_queries(query_id PK, query, query_type)   -- id lookup, keyword, natural language
judgments(query_id, passage_id, grade)         -- graded relevance, 0 to 3
eval_runs(run_id PK, config JSON, recall_at_50, mrr_at_10, ndcg_at_10, created_at)
```

## High-level design

**Offline path (indexing)**

1. Callers upsert passages. An indexer consumes the change stream in order and writes each passage to the keyword index and, after embedding it, to the vector index.
2. Both writes carry `tenant_id`, the filter fields and a `version`, so the two indexes can be compared and repaired. A passage counts as searchable only when both writes have landed.

**Online path (search)**

3. The API validates the request and attaches the tenant filter. A caller cannot remove it.
4. Query analysis normalises the text and detects exact-match signals: quoted phrases, ids such as `E-4012`, version strings. These are kept as they are for BM25.
5. The query embedder (a bi-encoder, which embeds query and passage separately) produces one 768-dimension vector. Popular queries come from an embedding cache.
6. BM25 search and dense search run in parallel, each with the filters applied inside the index, and each returns its top 100.
7. Reciprocal rank fusion merges the two lists into at most 200 unique passages and keeps the best 50.
8. The service fetches the 50 texts and sends 50 query-passage pairs to the cross-encoder pool, truncating each passage to 256 tokens.
9. The reranker's order is final. The service returns the top 10 and, in debug mode, every stage's ranks and timings.
10. Each stage has its own timeout. If the reranker does not answer in 140 ms, the fused order is returned with `degraded: "no_rerank"`.

**Evaluation path**

11. Every request is logged with the ids each stage returned. The eval runner replays a judged query set against any configuration and reports metrics per stage, so a change is measured before it ships.

## Architecture diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Deep dives

### Two retrievers with different mistakes

Dense search matches meaning: "laptop will not switch on" finds "device does not power up". It blurs exact strings, so `E-4012` and `E-4021` land very close together. BM25 scores a passage by how often the query's words occur in it, with more weight for rare words. It finds the exact code and misses every paraphrase. Their errors barely overlap, so the union has higher recall than either list alone.

### Fusion: ranks, not raw scores

The two scores are not comparable. A BM25 score has no upper limit and grows with the number and rarity of the query terms, so 12 is a weak match for one query and a strong match for another. Cosine similarity lies between -1 and 1, and one model's results usually sit in a narrow band such as 0.60 to 0.85. Add them and BM25 decides everything.

A weighted sum works only if each list is rescaled per query (min-max or z-score) and the weight is tuned on labelled data. One outlier stretches the scale, and the weight goes stale when the embedding model changes.

Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) uses positions only: each passage scores the sum of 1 / (60 + rank) over the lists it appears in. A passage ranked 30th in both lists scores 2/90 = 0.0222. A passage ranked 1st in one list and absent from the other scores 1/61 = 0.0164. Agreement wins and nothing needs tuning. The price: RRF discards margins, so a runaway exact-id hit looks like any other rank 1. That is why the fused list is cut at a generous 50 and the reranker decides the final order.

### The cross-encoder and its budget

A cross-encoder reads the query and one passage together and outputs one score. Nothing can be precomputed, so cost = pairs x tokens per pair. The levers:

* Candidates: 50 pairs fit the budget. 100 pairs take about 240 ms on the same GPU.
* Length: truncate passages to 256 tokens. Halving the tokens at least halves the time.
* Model: a smaller distilled reranker trades some nDCG for speed. Check on the judged set.
* Batching: one batch per query, merged across concurrent queries on the GPU server.

### Reading the metrics

Take one query whose two relevant passages sit at ranks 2 and 5.

* Recall@k: share of relevant passages in the top k. Recall@10 = 2/2 = 1.0.
* MRR (mean reciprocal rank): 1 / rank of the first relevant result, averaged over queries. Here 1/2 = 0.5.
* nDCG@k: each hit is discounted by log2(rank + 1), then divided by the ideal order. DCG = 1/log2(3) + 1/log2(6) = 0.631 + 0.387 = 1.018. Ideal = 1 + 0.631 = 1.631. nDCG = 0.62.

Read them per stage. Low Recall@50 after fusion is a retrieval problem: the reranker cannot return a passage it never received. High recall with low nDCG@10 points at the reranker.

## Evaluation

**Judged set.** Sample 1,000 queries from the log, stratified by type: id lookups, short keyword queries and natural-language questions. For each query, pool the top 20 from BM25, dense and the current production order, and grade every pooled passage from 0 to 3. An LLM judge can do the first pass, checked against 200 human-graded pairs. Pooling matters: if only one system's results are judged, every new system looks worse because its new finds are unlabelled.

**Offline metrics, per stage.** Recall@100 for each retriever alone, Recall@50 after fusion, then nDCG@10 and MRR@10 after reranking. Report each by query type. An average can hide a collapse on id lookups.

**Ablations.** Run the same set with `bm25`, `dense`, hybrid without reranking and the full pipeline. Each stage has to earn its latency.

**Online.** Click-through rate on the top 3, mean reciprocal rank of the first click, zero-click rate, reformulation rate (a new query within 30 seconds) and the share of degraded responses.

**A/B setup.** For ranking changes, interleave: mix the results of the old and new ranker in one list and count which side gets the clicks. It needs far less traffic than a split by user. Change one stage at a time.

**Guardrails.** p95 latency per stage with alerts, a canary set of 50 id queries that must return the exact passage at rank 1, and a tenant-isolation test that runs on every deploy.

## Bottlenecks & mitigations

* The reranker pool: 3,000 pairs per second at peak fills 8 of the 10 GPUs, and reranking is 120 ms of every 171 ms. A slow GPU node shows up at once in p95.
* Dense search with a selective filter: when a tenant owns a tiny share of the 30M passages, the graph walk visits many nodes that fail the filter.
* Fetching 50 passage texts per query: 3,000 point reads per second at peak, so texts need an in-memory cache or a fast key-value store.
* Dual writes: the keyword and vector indexes drift apart when one write fails, and a passage found by one retriever only loses the agreement bonus in RRF.
* Query embedding on a cold cache adds 15 ms to every request and needs its own small GPU or CPU pool.

## Failure modes

* **Reranker pool overloaded or down.** GPU capacity is sized for 60 QPS and a traffic spike or node loss pushes latency past the budget. Mitigation: a 140 ms timeout (the 120 ms budget plus 20 of the 29 ms of slack), return the fused order with `degraded: "no_rerank"`, and shed load by reranking 20 candidates before skipping entirely.
* **Exact-match query answered with near matches.** The embedding model pulls in passages about similar ids and RRF rewards agreement. Mitigation: detect id-like tokens, require the BM25 exact hit to stay in the candidate set, and track the id-lookup slice of the judged set.
* **Index drift.** A passage is deleted from one index and still served by the other. Mitigation: one ordered change stream, a version on every write, and a nightly job that compares id sets and repairs differences.
* **Embedding model changed on one side only.** Queries are embedded with a new model while passages still hold old vectors, and dense recall drops with no error raised. Mitigation: store the model version in the index and reject a query vector whose version does not match.
* **Filter leak across tenants.** A code path searches without the tenant filter. Mitigation: the filter is added by the API layer, never by the caller, and a deploy-time test queries each tenant for another tenant's canary passage.
* **Reranker truncation hides the answer.** The relevant sentence sits after token 256 of a long passage. Mitigation: index shorter passages, or score overlapping windows and keep the best window's score.
* **Metrics look good and users are unhappy.** The judged set has aged and no longer matches live queries. Mitigation: refresh 10% of the set from recent logs every month and watch the online reformulation rate.

## Follow-up questions interviewers ask

* Recall@50 after fusion is 0.97 but nDCG@10 is only 0.55. What do you look at first?
* How would you weight BM25 and dense search differently for different query types, and how would you prove it helps?
* The product team wants p95 under 100 ms. What do you cut or change?
* How does a late-interaction model such as ColBERT compare with a bi-encoder plus a cross-encoder?
* The corpus grows from 30 million to 3 billion passages. Which stage breaks first?
* How do you build relevance judgments when you have no click data yet?

# Decoder with a KV cache

kv cachetransformerdecodinginferencenumpycausal mask

## Problem statement

Build a tiny decoder-only transformer in NumPy (random weights are fine) and write two greedy generation functions for it. The first pushes the whole sequence through the model at every step. The second keeps a KV cache, which stores the attention keys and values of every earlier token for every layer, and feeds in only the newest token. Prove that both return the same logits at every step, and show with counters and a timer how much work the cache saves.

## Requirements

### Functional

* `TinyDecoder.forward(ids, cache=None)` runs a pre-norm decoder stack: token and position embeddings, then per layer causal multi-head attention and an MLP, then logits.
* With a cache, `forward` treats `ids` as the next tokens after the cached ones, appends their keys and values, and returns logits for the new tokens only.
* `generate_no_cache(model, prompt, n_new)` recomputes the full sequence each step.
* `generate_with_cache(model, prompt, n_new)` does one prefill pass over the prompt, then one single-token pass per step.
* `KVCache` reserves its memory once and exposes its shapes and fill length.
* Self-checks print the logit gap, the work counters, the timings and the cache size.

### Non-functional

* The two functions return identical token ids, and logits that agree within 1e-9 at every step in float64.
* Work: for a prompt of P tokens and N new tokens, the cached path pushes P + N - 1 token positions through the stack; the uncached path pushes N x P + N x (N - 1) / 2. For P = 48 and N = 160 that is 207 against 20,400.
* Cache shape is `(n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head)` for keys and the same for values. Memory per token is 2 x 4 x 4 x 32 x 8 = 8,192 bytes for the default model in float64.
* Adding a token writes one slot per layer: 0 reallocations and 0 copies of older entries.
* The whole self-check, 160 generated tokens on both paths, finishes in under 10 seconds on a laptop CPU.

## API

```
def kv_bytes(layers, heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_value=2) -> int: ...

class KVCache:
    k: np.ndarray        # (n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head)
    v: np.ndarray        # (n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head)
    length: int          # number of filled slots (tokens seen so far)
    def append(self, layer: int, k_new: np.ndarray, v_new: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: ...
        # k_new, v_new: (n_heads, m, d_head) -> all keys and values so far: (n_heads, t + m, d_head)

class TinyDecoder:
    def __init__(self, vocab=96, d_model=128, n_heads=4, n_layers=4, max_len=256, seed=0): ...
    def new_cache(self) -> KVCache: ...
    def forward(self, ids: list[int], cache: KVCache | None = None) -> np.ndarray: ...
        # m token ids -> logits (m, vocab)

def generate_no_cache(model, prompt: list[int], n_new: int) -> tuple[list[int], np.ndarray]: ...
def generate_with_cache(model, prompt: list[int], n_new: int) -> tuple[list[int], np.ndarray, KVCache]: ...
    # ids: P + n_new tokens; step logits: (n_new, vocab)
```

## Data model

```
t = tokens already in the cache      m = new tokens in this call
no cache: t = 0, m = whole sequence  prefill: t = 0, m = P      decode: t grows, m = 1

ids        (m,)                       new token ids
x          (m, d_model)               tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[t : t+m]
q          (h, m, d_head)             queries of the new tokens; used once, never stored
k_new      (h, m, d_head)             written to cache.k[layer, :, t : t+m]
v_new      (h, m, d_head)             written to cache.v[layer, :, t : t+m]
k, v       (h, t+m, d_head)           everything this layer has seen, read from the cache
mask       (m, t+m) bool              row i (position t+i) may attend to columns 0 .. t+i
scores     (h, m, t+m)                q @ k^T / sqrt(d_head)
logits     (m, vocab)                 generation reads the last row only

cache.k    (L, h, max_len, d_head)    slots 0 .. length-1 filled, the rest are zeros
cache.v    (L, h, max_len, d_head)
```

## Approach

1. Write the model as one `forward(ids, cache)` function. Let t be the number of cached tokens (0 without a cache) and m the number of new tokens. A full pass, prefill and a decode step are then the same code with different t and m.
2. Embed the new tokens and add the position rows `t` to `t + m - 1`. The position of a new token is the cache length, not 0.
3. Build the mask with shape `(m, t + m)`: row i may attend to columns 0 to t + i. With t = 0 this is the usual lower triangle. With m = 1 it is a single row of all True.
4. In each layer, apply layer norm, then project the m new tokens to queries, keys and values.
5. Without a cache, attend over those keys and values. With a cache, write the new keys and values into slots `t` to `t + m - 1` of this layer and read back all `t + m`.
6. Compute scores of shape `(h, m, t + m)`, mask, softmax, multiply by the values, merge heads, project and add to the residual stream. Then apply layer norm and the MLP to the m new positions.
7. After the last layer, set `cache.length = t + m`. Do this once per call, not once per layer, or the second layer writes into the wrong slots.
8. `generate_no_cache` calls `forward(all_ids)` each step and reads the last row of logits.
9. `generate_with_cache` calls `forward(prompt, cache)` once (prefill), then `forward([new_token], cache)` per step (decode).
10. Count work inside `forward` (positions processed, attention scores computed) so the saving is a number, and compare the logits of the two paths at every step.

Rendering diagram…

## Deep dives

### Why the causal mask makes caching exact

In a decoder, the hidden state of token i at every layer depends only on tokens 0 to i. The mask stops attention from reading later tokens, and layer norm and the MLP work on one position at a time. So the key and value of token i are the same whether the sequence has i + 1 tokens or 10,000. Computing them once and storing them changes nothing. The self-check shows this directly: appending 20 tokens leaves the keys and values of the first 48 unchanged to 1e-12. A bidirectional encoder has no such property, because a new token changes every earlier hidden state. The two paths still differ by about 1e-15, because they group the same floating-point additions differently. In 16-bit floats on a GPU the gap is larger and can flip a near-tie between two tokens.

### What is cached, what is not, and what it costs

Stored: the key and value vectors of every past token, per layer and per head. Not stored: queries (a token uses its query once), attention weights, MLP activations and the hidden states themselves. Later tokens read earlier tokens only through keys and values, so nothing else is needed.

Formula

KV bytes=2×layers×heads×head dim×sequence length×batch×bytes per value

The toy model needs 2 x 4 x 4 x 32 x 8 = 8,192 bytes per token. A model with 32 layers, 32 heads and head dimension 128 in FP16 needs 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 bytes, about 0.52 MB per token, so a 4,000-token request holds about 2.1 GB. With grouped-query attention, count the KV heads only. Reserve the memory up front or in blocks: growing the arrays with `concatenate` copies the whole cache on every step.

### Prefill and decode

Prefill is the call with t = 0 and m = P. It is one parallel pass with a P x P score matrix per head, and it sets the time to first token. Decode is the call with m = 1: one row of t + 1 scores per head, plus the projections and the MLP for a single position. Over the 160 generated tokens of the self-check, the uncached path computes 47,077,120 attention scores and the cached path 362,496, about 130 times fewer. Per step, attention cost falls from O(n^2) to O(n).

### Position information with a cache

A decode step receives one token id and nothing else, so the code must supply its position. With learned or sinusoidal positions, add row t of the table, where t is the cache length. Adding row 0 is the classic bug: it runs and returns confident, wrong logits. With rotary positions (RoPE) nothing is added at the input. The query and key are rotated by an angle that depends on their absolute position, keys are normally stored already rotated, and the new query is rotated by position t. The score depends only on the distance between the two positions, so cached keys never need updating.

### Batching caches of different lengths

In a batch, requests have different cache lengths. The simple layout adds a batch axis, pads every cache to the longest, and needs two extra pieces: a per-request length for positions, and a key mask so that no query attends to a padded slot. Padding wastes memory, and a request that finishes leaves a hole. Serving engines store the cache in fixed-size blocks with a table from each request to its blocks, so a sequence takes a new block only when it grows into it and frees its blocks the moment it ends.

## Evaluation

**Correctness tests.**

* Equality: 160 greedy steps after a 48-token prompt. Token ids are identical and the largest logit difference is below 1e-9. The printed logit spread shows the logits are not all near zero, so the test means something.
* Work counters: positions pushed through the stack equal `sum(P + i)` without the cache and `P + N - 1` with it; attention scores equal `L x h x sum((P + i)^2)` and `L x h x (P^2 + sum(P + i))`.
* Timing: the wall time of both paths and their ratio are printed but not asserted. A timer on a busy machine is noisy; the counters are exact, so the test asserts on them.
* Cache: shapes are `(L, h, max_len, d_head)`, the fill length is `P + N - 1`, the bytes in the filled part equal the formula, and unfilled slots are still zero.
* Causality: keys and values of a prefix do not change when the sequence is extended.
* Prefill: one pass over the prompt, two chunks of 30 and 18 tokens, and P single-token passes all build the same cache and the same first logits. The chunked case is the only one with a non-empty cache and more than one new token.

**Complexity.** For sequence length n, model width d and L layers, one uncached step costs O(L (n^2 d + n d^2)). One cached decode step costs O(L (n d + d^2)). Generating n tokens costs O(L n^3 d) attention work without the cache and O(L n^2 d) with it. The cache takes O(L n d) memory.

**What a strong answer adds.** Explaining exactness from the mask before writing code, reserving memory instead of concatenating, noting that the last sampled token is not in the cache yet, stating the memory formula with a real model's numbers, and describing how positions and padding masks change in a batch.

## Bottlenecks & mitigations

* Cache memory grows linearly with sequence length, layers and batch size. At long contexts and high concurrency it is larger than the weights.
* Each decode step still reads every weight of the model to produce one token, which is why servers batch requests into one pass.
* Attention in decode is still O(n) per step, so the last tokens of a long answer are slower than the first.
* Reserving `max_len` slots per request wastes memory for short answers; block allocation fixes this.
* The uncached path redoes O(n^2) attention per step and is only useful as a reference for tests.

## Failure modes

* **Position restarts at 0.** The new token gets the first position row, the code runs, and the logits are wrong. Mitigation: use the cache length as the position; the equality test catches it.
* **Mask built as (m, m).** It is right for prefill and, by broadcasting, for single-token steps, so the bug hides until several tokens are appended to a non-empty cache. Mitigation: build the mask as `(m, t + m)` with the diagonal shifted by t, and test a chunked prefill.
* **Cache length updated inside the layer loop.** Layer 2 writes into the next slot and reads garbage. Mitigation: commit the length once after the last layer.
* **Feeding the whole sequence with a cache.** Earlier tokens are appended twice and attention double counts them. Mitigation: feed only tokens that are not in the cache; assert on `max_len`.
* **Growing the cache by concatenation.** Every step copies all earlier entries, so copying becomes O(n^2) and hides the speedup. Mitigation: reserve memory or allocate blocks.
* **Reusing a cache after the prefix changed.** Editing one early token invalidates every later key and value. Mitigation: reuse a cache only for an exact token-for-token prefix match.
* **Off-by-one after generation.** The last sampled token has not been fed, so the cache holds P + N - 1 tokens. Mitigation: track which tokens are cached, and feed the pending token before continuing a chat.
* **Padded slots attended in a batch.** Shorter requests read zeros as real keys and their outputs change with batch composition. Mitigation: a per-request key mask.

## Reference solution

Python · standard library and NumPy only · runs and prints its own checks

```
"""A tiny decoder-only transformer in NumPy, generated with and without a KV cache."""
import time

import numpy as np

def softmax(x):
    x = x - np.max(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def layer_norm(x, gain, bias, eps=1e-5):
    """Normalises each position on its own, so it never mixes tokens."""
    mean = x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    var = x.var(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return gain * (x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + bias

def kv_bytes(layers, heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, bytes_per_value=2):
    """KV cache size: the 2 is keys plus values."""
    return 2 * layers * heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_value

class KVCache:
    """Keys and values of every token seen so far, for every layer and head.

    k, v: (n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head). Only the first `length` slots are filled.
    Memory is reserved once, so adding a token is a write, not a copy of the whole cache.
    """

    def __init__(self, n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head):
        self.k = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head))
        self.v = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads, max_len, d_head))
        self.length = 0

    def append(self, layer, k_new, v_new):
        """Store (h, m, d_head) keys and values; return all t + m of them for this layer."""
        t, m = self.length, k_new.shape[1]
        self.k[layer, :, t:t + m] = k_new
        self.v[layer, :, t:t + m] = v_new
        return self.k[layer, :, :t + m], self.v[layer, :, :t + m]

class TinyDecoder:
    def __init__(self, vocab=96, d_model=128, n_heads=4, n_layers=4, max_len=256, seed=0):
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.vocab, self.d_model, self.max_len = vocab, d_model, max_len
        self.n_heads, self.n_layers, self.d_head = n_heads, n_layers, d_model // n_heads

        def w(rows, cols):                       # random weights are enough for this task
            return rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(rows), (rows, cols))

        self.tok_emb = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (vocab, d_model))
        self.pos_emb = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (max_len, d_model))   # learned absolute positions
        self.layers = [{
            "w_q": w(d_model, d_model), "w_k": w(d_model, d_model),
            "w_v": w(d_model, d_model), "w_o": w(d_model, d_model),
            "w_1": w(d_model, 4 * d_model), "w_2": w(4 * d_model, d_model),
            "g1": np.ones(d_model), "b1": np.zeros(d_model),
            "g2": np.ones(d_model), "b2": np.zeros(d_model),
        } for _ in range(n_layers)]
        self.g_out, self.b_out = np.ones(d_model), np.zeros(d_model)
        self.w_out = w(d_model, vocab)
        self.positions = 0        # work counter: token positions pushed through the stack
        self.scores = 0           # work counter: attention scores computed

    def new_cache(self):
        return KVCache(self.n_layers, self.n_heads, self.max_len, self.d_head)

    def _split(self, x):
        """(m, d_model) -> (h, m, d_head)."""
        return x.reshape(x.shape[0], self.n_heads, self.d_head).transpose(1, 0, 2)

    def forward(self, ids, cache=None):
        """Run m new tokens and return their logits, shape (m, vocab).

        cache=None: `ids` is the whole sequence and nothing is kept.
        With a cache holding t tokens: `ids` are the next m tokens, at positions t..t+m-1.
        Their keys and values are appended, and their queries attend to all t + m keys.
        """
        t = 0 if cache is None else cache.length
        m = len(ids)
        assert t + m <= self.max_len, "sequence is longer than max_len"
        x = self.tok_emb[ids] + self.pos_emb[t:t + m]            # (m, d_model)
        # Row i is the token at position t + i. It may attend to keys 0..t+i.
        mask = np.tril(np.ones((m, t + m), dtype=bool), k=t)     # (m, t + m)
        for i, p in enumerate(self.layers):
            h = layer_norm(x, p["g1"], p["b1"])
            q = self._split(h @ p["w_q"])                        # (h, m, d_head): used once
            k = self._split(h @ p["w_k"])                        # (h, m, d_head): only new tokens
            v = self._split(h @ p["w_v"])
            if cache is not None:
                k, v = cache.append(i, k, v)                     # (h, t + m, d_head)
            scores = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(self.d_head)   # (h, m, t + m)
            weights = softmax(np.where(mask, scores, -1e9))
            heads = weights @ v                                  # (h, m, d_head)
            x = x + heads.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(m, self.d_model) @ p["w_o"]
            h = layer_norm(x, p["g2"], p["b2"])
            x = x + np.maximum(h @ p["w_1"], 0.0) @ p["w_2"]     # MLP: one position at a time
            self.scores += self.n_heads * m * (t + m)
        if cache is not None:
            cache.length = t + m                                 # commit after the last layer
        self.positions += m
        return layer_norm(x, self.g_out, self.b_out) @ self.w_out

def generate_no_cache(model, prompt, n_new):
    """Greedy decoding that pushes the whole sequence through the model at every step."""
    ids, step_logits = list(prompt), []
    for _ in range(n_new):
        logits = model.forward(ids)[-1]          # only the last row is used
        step_logits.append(logits)
        ids.append(int(np.argmax(logits)))
    return ids, np.array(step_logits)

def generate_with_cache(model, prompt, n_new):
    """Greedy decoding with a KV cache: one prefill pass, then one token per step."""
    cache = model.new_cache()
    ids, step_logits = list(prompt), []
    new = list(prompt)                           # tokens that are not in the cache yet
    for _ in range(n_new):
        logits = model.forward(new, cache)[-1]   # first pass: prefill. Later passes: decode.
        step_logits.append(logits)
        new = [int(np.argmax(logits))]
        ids.append(new[0])
    return ids, np.array(step_logits), cache

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = TinyDecoder()
    L, H, D = model.n_layers, model.n_heads, model.d_head
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    P, N = 48, 160
    prompt = [int(i) for i in rng.integers(0, model.vocab, size=P)]

    # 1. Same tokens and same logits at every step.
    model.positions = model.scores = 0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ids_a, logits_a = generate_no_cache(model, prompt, N)
    time_a, pos_a, scores_a = time.perf_counter() - t0, model.positions, model.scores

    model.positions = model.scores = 0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ids_b, logits_b, cache = generate_with_cache(model, prompt, N)
    time_b, pos_b, scores_b = time.perf_counter() - t0, model.positions, model.scores

    assert ids_a == ids_b and logits_a.shape == logits_b.shape == (N, model.vocab)
    gap = float(np.max(np.abs(logits_a - logits_b)))
    assert gap < 1e-9, gap
    print(f"exact ok: {N} steps, same tokens, largest logit gap {gap:.1e} "
          f"(logit spread {float(np.ptp(logits_a)):.1f})")

    # 2. Less work, counted and timed.
    assert pos_a == sum(P + i for i in range(N)) and pos_b == P + N - 1
    assert scores_a == L * H * sum((P + i) ** 2 for i in range(N))
    assert scores_b == L * H * (P * P + sum(P + i for i in range(1, N)))
    assert pos_a > 50 * pos_b and scores_a > 100 * scores_b
    # Wall time is printed, not asserted: a timer on a busy machine is noisy, the counters are exact.
    print(f"positions through the stack: {pos_a:,} without the cache, {pos_b:,} with it")
    print(f"attention scores computed:   {scores_a:,} without, {scores_b:,} with")
    print(f"wall time: {time_a:.2f} s without, {time_b:.3f} s with ({time_a / time_b:.0f}x faster)")
    assert sum(range(2000, 2300)) == 644_850 and 2000 + 300 - 1 == 2299
    print("same formulas for a 2,000-token prompt and a 300-token answer: 644,850 vs 2,299")

    # 3. Cache shapes and memory.
    assert cache.k.shape == cache.v.shape == (L, H, model.max_len, D)
    assert cache.length == P + N - 1             # the last sampled token was never fed in
    used = cache.k[:, :, :cache.length].nbytes + cache.v[:, :, :cache.length].nbytes
    assert used == kv_bytes(L, H, D, cache.length, bytes_per_value=8)
    assert np.all(cache.k[:, :, cache.length:] == 0.0)
    print(f"cache ok: k and v are {cache.k.shape}, {cache.length} slots filled, "
          f"{used:,} bytes = 2 x {L} x {H} x {D} x {cache.length} x 8")
    assert kv_bytes(layers=32, heads=32, head_dim=128, seq_len=1) == 524_288
    print("formula ok: 32 layers, 32 heads, head dim 128, FP16 -> 524,288 bytes per token")

    # 4. Why it is exact: a token's keys and values do not depend on later tokens.
    short, long_ = model.new_cache(), model.new_cache()
    model.forward(ids_a[:P], short)
    model.forward(ids_a[:P + 20], long_)
    assert np.allclose(short.k[:, :, :P], long_.k[:, :, :P], atol=1e-12)
    assert np.allclose(short.v[:, :, :P], long_.v[:, :, :P], atol=1e-12)
    print("causal ok: 20 extra tokens leave the keys and values of the first", P, "unchanged")

    # 5. Prefill in one pass, in two chunks, or one token at a time: same cache, same logits.
    one_by_one, chunked = model.new_cache(), model.new_cache()
    for tok in prompt:
        last = model.forward([tok], one_by_one)[-1]
    model.forward(prompt[:30], chunked)
    last_chunked = model.forward(prompt[30:], chunked)[-1]      # 18 tokens on top of 30 cached
    for other, logits in ((one_by_one, last), (chunked, last_chunked)):
        assert other.length == P
        assert np.allclose(other.k, short.k, atol=1e-12) and np.allclose(other.v, short.v, atol=1e-12)
        assert np.allclose(logits, logits_a[0], atol=1e-9)
    print(f"prefill ok: one pass, chunks of 30 + 18, and {P} single-token passes build the same cache")
```

## Follow-up questions interviewers ask

* Add a batch dimension for prompts of different lengths. What changes in the mask and the positions?
* Replace the learned positions with RoPE. What exactly is stored in the cache?
* Two requests share a 1,500-token system prompt. How do you reuse the cache between them?
* The context window is full. Can you drop the oldest cache entries and keep generating?
* How does the cache change with grouped-query attention?
* How would beam search or speculative decoding fork and roll back a cache?
