markdown:
[DevOps roadmap](/devops) Cloud and IaCLesson #14SkimBeginner 1.5 h # Ansible and configuration management Configuration management is the job of making a fleet of machines match a written description: these packages, this config file, this service running. Ansible does it over SSH with no agent, from YAML playbooks whose tasks are idempotent: run them twice and the second run changes nothing. This lesson covers where Ansible still fits once you have containers and Terraform, its model (inventory, plays, tasks, modules, handlers, roles, vault) and the mistakes that make it dangerous. ansibleconfiguration managementidempotencysshlinuxvm fleets ## Why it matters Ansible is a SKIM topic because Kubernetes and image builds took over most of what it used to do. It still shows up in interviews at companies with VM fleets, on-prem racks or bastion hosts, and in the question "what is idempotency" which every DevOps interview asks in some form. In real work you will meet it when bootstrapping nodes, patching a hundred VMs, or inheriting a system built before containers. Knowing the model, and knowing when not to reach for it, is enough. Read first: [Linux for operators](/devops/learn/linux-for-operators), [Bash scripting and the terminal toolkit](/devops/learn/bash-and-terminal-toolkit), [Terraform - infrastructure as code](/devops/learn/terraform-infrastructure-as-code) ## Lesson ### What is left for configuration management Before containers, every server was configured in place: install the runtime, write the config, start the service. Configuration management tools did that repeatably. Puppet and Chef solved it with an agent on every machine pulling from a server; they are rarely chosen for new work now. Ansible won because it needs nothing on the target but SSH and Python. Today, containers carry their own configuration and Terraform creates the machines, so what is left is smaller but real: | Still Ansible's job | Why containers and Terraform do not cover it | | --- | --- | | VM fleets that run things outside Kubernetes: databases on EC2, legacy apps, Windows hosts | Something must install and configure the software on the box | | Bastion and jump hosts, build agents, on-prem servers | Few, long-lived, hand-tuned, and nobody will containerise them | | The node image itself (hardening, agents, kernel settings) | Built once with Packer, which calls Ansible as a provisioner | | Bootstrapping: the first config a fresh VM needs before anything else can run | Terraform hands over a bare machine | | One-off fleet operations: rotate a key on 200 hosts, patch a CVE, collect a file | An ad hoc loop over SSH, but with inventory, parallelism and a report | Anything Kubernetes already does, such as rolling out an application, scaling, restarts and health checks, is not Ansible's job. ### The model Ansible is **agentless**: a control machine (your laptop or a CI runner) connects over SSH to each host and runs small Python programs called **modules**. Nothing is installed on the targets. The parts, top down: * **Inventory** lists hosts in groups. Static INI or YAML, or a **dynamic** plugin that asks the AWS API, so new EC2 instances appear automatically. * A **playbook** is a YAML file of **plays**; each play targets a group of hosts and runs a list of **tasks** in order. * A **task** calls one module with parameters. The module checks the current state and changes only what differs, then reports `changed` or `ok`. That is **idempotency**: the second run is all `ok`. * A **handler** is a task that runs once at the end of the play, only if a task that `notify`s it reported `changed`. "Restart nginx only if the config changed" is the classic use. * **Variables** come from many places; the rule to remember is that role `defaults/` is the weakest, `group_vars` and `host_vars` sit in the middle, and `-e` extra vars on the command line always win. * **Templates** are Jinja2 files (`site.conf.j2`) rendered with variables, written by the `template` module. * A **role** is a reusable unit with a fixed layout: `tasks/main.yml`, `handlers/main.yml`, `templates/`, `files/`, `defaults/main.yml`, `vars/main.yml`, `meta/main.yml`. * **Collections** package roles, modules and plugins; Galaxy is the registry. `ansible-galaxy collection install community.general` gives you the `ufw` module used below. Modules are called by their full name, `ansible.builtin.apt`. * **ansible-vault** encrypts a whole vars file or one value (`ansible-vault encrypt_string`), which appears in YAML as `!vault |`; the password comes from `--ask-vault-pass` or `--vault-password-file`. * `--check` simulates a run and `--diff` shows the before and after of a template; `--tags config` runs a subset; `--limit web-3` restricts hosts; `serial: 1` makes a play finish on one host before starting the next, which is a rolling change. ### A complete playbook Inventory, `inventory/prod.ini`: ``` [webservers] web-1 ansible_host=10.0.1.11 web-2 ansible_host=10.0.1.12 web-3 ansible_host=10.0.1.13 [webservers:vars] ansible_user=ubuntu ``` Playbook, `site.yml`: installs Nginx, templates its config, opens the firewall and restarts the service only when the config changed, one host at a time. ``` - name: Configure web servers hosts: webservers become: true # sudo for every task; forgetting this is mistake number one serial: 1 # one host at a time: a bad config takes down one server, not three any_errors_fatal: true # stop the whole run at the first failed host vars: nginx_port: 80 site_root: /var/www/html tasks: - name: Install nginx ansible.builtin.apt: name: nginx state: present update_cache: true cache_valid_time: 3600 tags: [packages] - name: Template the site config ansible.builtin.template: src: templates/site.conf.j2 dest: /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default owner: root group: root mode: "0644" notify: Restart nginx # only fires if this task reports changed tags: [config] - name: Check the nginx config ansible.builtin.command: nginx -t changed_when: false # a read-only command must not report changed - name: Open the firewall community.general.ufw: rule: allow port: "{{ nginx_port }}" proto: tcp - name: Enable and start nginx ansible.builtin.systemd_service: name: nginx enabled: true state: started handlers: - name: Restart nginx ansible.builtin.systemd_service: name: nginx state: restarted ``` Template, `templates/site.conf.j2`: ``` server { listen {{ nginx_port }}; root {{ site_root }}; server_name {{ inventory_hostname }}; } ``` Run it: ``` ansible-playbook -i inventory/prod.ini site.yml --check --diff --limit web-1 # dry run on one host first ansible-playbook -i inventory/prod.ini site.yml # for real, serial: 1 ansible-playbook -i inventory/prod.ini site.yml --tags config # only the template task ``` The recap on the first run shows `changed=5` per host (four tasks plus the handler); the second run shows `changed=0` and the handler does not run, because nothing notified it. For AWS, replace the INI file with `inventory/aws_ec2.yml` (the file name must end in `aws_ec2.yml`): `plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2`, a `regions` list, `filters` such as `tag:Role: web`, and `keyed_groups` with `key: ec2_tags.Role` so instances land in groups by tag. ### Ansible next to Terraform and Packer | Question | Terraform | Ansible | Packer | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | What it does | Creates the machine, network, load balancer | Configures what is inside a running machine | Builds a machine image once | | Model | Declarative with a state file | Imperative tasks that are each idempotent; no state | Declarative build, runs provisioners (Ansible, shell) | | When it runs | On every infra change | On every config change, or on boot | Once per image version | | Typical pair | Terraform creates an ASG from a Packer AMI | Ansible, called by Packer, hardens the AMI | Immutable: replace the instance instead of patching it | The modern default is **immutable infrastructure**: bake the image with Packer and Ansible, roll new instances with Terraform, never SSH in to change a live box. Running Ansible against live fleets is for the cases in the first table, and for the one-off operations. ### Common mistakes * `ansible.builtin.shell: apt-get install -y nginx` reports `changed` every run and fires the handler every run. Use the `apt` module, or add `creates:` or `changed_when:` to a command. * Forgetting `become: true` and getting "Permission denied" halfway through a play, with the first tasks already applied. * Running against prod without `--limit` and `--check` first: an inventory typo makes `hosts: all` mean every machine in the account. * A handler that restarts a service on every host at once because the play has no `serial`. * Secrets in plain `group_vars` committed to Git instead of vault, or `--vault-password-file` pointing at a file inside the repo. * Using Ansible to deploy a container to Kubernetes. That is Helm and Argo CD's job; Ansible stops at the node. ## Diagram Rendering diagram… ## Worked example **Rolling a config change across 30 web servers.** The playbook above is run with `serial: 3` after the Nginx template changed in Git. Each host needs about 4 seconds for the five tasks over SSH, plus a 2-second Nginx restart from the handler. Step 1: batches. 30 hosts at 3 per batch is 10 batches. Inside a batch the 3 hosts run in parallel (the default `forks` is 5, so 3 fit), and the play, including the handler, finishes on the batch before the next one starts. Step 2: time. Per batch: 4 seconds of tasks plus 2 seconds of restart, about 6 seconds. 10 batches give about 60 seconds for the whole fleet. With `serial: 1` it would be 30 batches, about 3 minutes; with no `serial`, 30 hosts run through the default 5 forks, so about 6 waves of 6 seconds, roughly 36 seconds, but every host restarts Nginx within the same minute and a bad config takes all 30 down together. Step 3: capacity during the roll. With 3 hosts restarting at any moment, 27 of 30 serve traffic: 90 percent capacity, which is why batch size is chosen from the load headroom. If peak load needs 25 hosts, `serial: 3` is safe and `serial: 10` is not. Step 4: failure. The template on batch 2 renders a bad `listen` line. `nginx -t` fails on those 3 hosts and they drop out of the play. The docs say `serial` changes the scope of a failure to the batch, and with `any_errors_fatal: true` on the play Ansible stops the whole run at that point, so the other 24 hosts never receive the broken file. The handler never fired on the failing hosts because the play did not reach its end there, so even they still run the old config. Fix the template, rerun with `--limit` to the failed hosts first, then the rest; every unchanged host reports `ok` and nothing restarts twice. ## Runnable code Python · runs and prints its own checks ``` """A tiny idempotent configuration applier, the idea behind every Ansible module. Each task describes a desired state (a file's content, a package installed, a service enabled). Applying it means: look at the host, compare, change only if needed, and report 'changed' or 'ok'. Handlers run once at the end of the play, and only if a task that notifies them reported changed. Everything is in memory; no SSH, no network. Running the same play twice shows the point: changed on the first run, ok on the second, handler fires only once. """ class Host: """An in-memory machine: files, installed packages, services.""" def __init__(self, name): self.name = name self.files = {} # path -> content self.packages = set() # installed package names self.services = {} # name -> {"enabled": bool, "running": bool, "restarts": int} # Modules: each takes (host, params) and returns (changed, message). # The rule for every module is the same: read the current state first, # do nothing if it already matches, never blindly run the change. def file_module(host, params): path, content = params["path"], params["content"] if host.files.get(path) == content: return False, f"{path} already has the desired content" host.files[path] = content return True, f"wrote {path}" def package_module(host, params): name, state = params["name"], params.get("state", "present") installed = name in host.packages if state == "present" and installed: return False, f"{name} already installed" if state == "absent" and not installed: return False, f"{name} already absent" if state == "present": host.packages.add(name) return True, f"installed {name}" host.packages.discard(name) return True, f"removed {name}" def service_module(host, params): name = params["name"] svc = host.services.setdefault(name, {"enabled": False, "running": False, "restarts": 0}) changed = [] if "enabled" in params and svc["enabled"] != params["enabled"]: svc["enabled"] = params["enabled"] changed.append("enabled" if params["enabled"] else "disabled") state = params.get("state") if state == "started" and not svc["running"]: svc["running"] = True changed.append("started") elif state == "restarted": # like Ansible: restarted always changes svc["running"] = True svc["restarts"] += 1 changed.append("restarted") if not changed: return False, f"{name} already in desired state" return True, f"{name} {' and '.join(changed)}" def shell_module(host, params): """The non-idempotent trap: a raw command always reports changed.""" return True, f"ran: {params['cmd']}" MODULES = {"file": file_module, "package": package_module, "service": service_module, "shell": shell_module} def run_play(host, tasks, handlers): """Apply tasks in order, collect notifications, run notified handlers once at the end.""" counts = {"ok": 0, "changed": 0} notified = [] # ordered, no duplicates for task in tasks: changed, msg = MODULES[task["module"]](host, task["params"]) status = "changed" if changed else "ok" counts[status] += 1 print(f" TASK [{task['name']:<32}] {status:<8} {msg}") if changed and task.get("notify") and task["notify"] not in notified: notified.append(task["notify"]) for name in notified: changed, msg = MODULES[handlers[name]["module"]](host, handlers[name]["params"]) print(f" HANDLER [{name:<29}] changed {msg}") counts["changed"] += 1 print(f" RECAP {host.name}: ok={counts['ok']} changed={counts['changed']} handlers_run={len(notified)}") return counts, notified NGINX_CONF = "server { listen 80; root /var/www/html; }\n" TASKS = [ {"name": "Install nginx", "module": "package", "params": {"name": "nginx", "state": "present"}}, {"name": "Write nginx site config", "module": "file", "params": {"path": "/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default", "content": NGINX_CONF}, "notify": "Restart nginx"}, {"name": "Write index page", "module": "file", "params": {"path": "/var/www/html/index.html", "content": "

hello

\n"}}, {"name": "Enable and start nginx", "module": "service", "params": {"name": "nginx", "enabled": True, "state": "started"}}, ] HANDLERS = { "Restart nginx": {"module": "service", "params": {"name": "nginx", "state": "restarted"}}, } if __name__ == "__main__": web = Host("web-1") print("PLAY 1: fresh host") c1, n1 = run_play(web, TASKS, HANDLERS) assert c1 == {"ok": 0, "changed": 5}, c1 # 4 tasks changed + 1 handler assert n1 == ["Restart nginx"] assert web.services["nginx"]["restarts"] == 1 print("\nPLAY 2: same play again, nothing should change") c2, n2 = run_play(web, TASKS, HANDLERS) assert c2 == {"ok": 4, "changed": 0}, c2 assert n2 == [] # handler not notified, so not run assert web.services["nginx"]["restarts"] == 1 # still 1: no needless restart print("\nPLAY 3: config changed in Git, only the file task and the handler fire") tasks_v2 = [dict(t) for t in TASKS] tasks_v2[1] = dict(tasks_v2[1], params={"path": "/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default", "content": NGINX_CONF.replace("80", "8080")}) c3, n3 = run_play(web, tasks_v2, HANDLERS) assert c3 == {"ok": 3, "changed": 2}, c3 # 1 task + 1 handler assert web.services["nginx"]["restarts"] == 2 print("\nPLAY 4: the shell-task mistake, changed every time even though nothing changed") bad = [{"name": "Install nginx with a shell command", "module": "shell", "params": {"cmd": "apt-get install -y nginx"}, "notify": "Restart nginx"}] c4, n4 = run_play(web, bad, HANDLERS) assert c4["changed"] == 2 and web.services["nginx"]["restarts"] == 3 print("\nself-checks passed: idempotent modules report ok on the second run, the handler ran " "only when its notifying task changed, and the shell task restarted nginx for nothing") ``` ## Key takeaways * Configuration management puts a machine into a described state; Ansible does it over SSH with no agent on the target. * Idempotency is the whole point: a module compares desired with current state and reports changed or ok, so a second run is harmless. * Handlers run once at the end of a play and only when a notifying task changed; that is how you restart a service only when its config changed. * Inventory groups hosts; dynamic AWS inventory builds groups from EC2 tags; roles and collections make playbooks reusable; vault keeps secrets encrypted in Git. * `--check --diff --limit` before every prod run; `serial` for rolling changes so a bad config hits one batch, not the fleet. * Terraform creates machines, Packer bakes images, Ansible configures what is inside; Kubernetes workloads are not Ansible's job. * Puppet and Chef solved the same problem with agents and are rarely chosen for new work. ## Common mistakes * Shell and command tasks that are not idempotent, so every run reports changed and every run restarts services. * Missing `become: true`, discovered halfway through a play with the first tasks already applied. * Running against prod with `hosts: all` and no `--limit` or `--check`, after an inventory change nobody re-read. * No `serial`, so the handler restarts the service on every host in the same second. * Treating Ansible as a deployment tool for Kubernetes instead of stopping at the node. ## Practice * Run the applier script from this lesson, then add a `user` module that creates a login only if missing and confirm the second run reports ok. * Start two Ubuntu containers with SSH (or two Multipass VMs), write an INI inventory, and run the Nginx playbook with `--check --diff` first, then for real, then again; confirm the recap shows changed=0 the third time and the handler did not run. * Change the template port to 8080 and rerun with `--tags config`; confirm only the template task and the handler report changed, and curl the new port. * Encrypt a variable with `ansible-vault encrypt_string`, put it in `group_vars/webservers.yml`, and run the playbook with `--ask-vault-pass`; then try without it and read the error. ## Interview questions (7) 1.Ansible or Terraform: what is the difference and when do you use each?Easy Terraform provisions infrastructure: it creates VPCs, instances, databases and DNS records through cloud APIs, keeps a state file, and shows a plan of exactly what will change before it applies. It is declarative and best at the lifecycle of cloud resources, including deleting them. Ansible configures machines that already exist: it connects over SSH with no agent and runs tasks, such as installing packages, writing config files from templates and restarting services, in order. It has no state file; it checks the machine each time. They work together: Terraform creates the EC2 instances and outputs their addresses, and Ansible (through a dynamic inventory) configures them. In a container platform Ansible's role shrinks, because the image is built once (with Packer or a Dockerfile) and Kubernetes runs it, but it is still the right tool for VM fleets, bastions and one-off changes across many hosts. 2.What does idempotent mean in Ansible and why does it matter?Easy An idempotent task gives the same result however many times you run it, and only reports changed when it actually changed something. The apt module checks whether nginx is installed before installing; the template module compares the rendered file with the one on disk before writing. It matters for two reasons. You can rerun a playbook safely to converge a host that failed halfway, and handlers depend on it: if a task falsely reports changed every run, the service restarts every run. The common way to break it is a shell or command task; the fix is the proper module, or creates and changed\_when on the command. 3.How does a handler differ from a normal task?Easy A handler is defined in the handlers section and does not run on its own. A task names it with notify, and the handler runs only if that task reported changed. All notified handlers run once at the end of the play, after every task, even if five tasks notified the same one, so Nginx restarts once rather than five times. meta flush\_handlers runs them earlier if you need to. The typical pair is a template task that writes a config and notifies a restart handler, so a run that changes nothing restarts nothing. 4.When would you choose Ansible over Terraform, and when the reverse?Medium They answer different questions. Terraform creates and tracks cloud resources: VPCs, instances, load balancers, IAM. It is declarative with a state file, so it knows what to delete. Ansible configures what is inside a running machine: packages, config files, users, services. It has no state; each task is idempotent on its own. I use Terraform for everything the cloud API owns and Ansible for anything that needs SSH into a box, usually only VM fleets, bastions and on-prem. For most modern setups the box is a Packer image built with Ansible once and rolled out with Terraform, so Ansible never touches a live server. 5.You have to patch a package on 200 production VMs. How do you run it safely?Medium First a dry run: ansible-playbook with --check and --diff and --limit to one canary host, and read the output. Then run for real on that one host with --limit and verify the service. Then the fleet with serial set to a batch size the load headroom allows, perhaps 10 percent, so a failure stops the run after one batch instead of touching all 200. The play uses the apt or dnf module with a pinned version, not a shell task, so a rerun on failed hosts is safe and reports ok on the hosts already done. Secrets, if any, come from vault, and the run happens from a CI runner with a logged job, not from a laptop. 6.What does Ansible need on the target hosts, and how does it connect?Easy Only SSH access and a Python interpreter, which every common Linux image has. There is no agent. The control node reads the inventory, opens SSH connections in parallel, the default forks is 5, copies each module as a small Python program to a temporary directory on the host, runs it with the parameters from the task, reads the JSON result, and deletes it. Privilege escalation is become, which runs sudo on the host. For Windows it uses WinRM instead of SSH. This is why Ansible fits one-off fleet operations: nothing to install first. 7.Why is configuration management less central than it used to be?Medium Two shifts. Containers moved configuration into the image: the Dockerfile installs the packages and the config is a ConfigMap, so there is no running VM to converge. And immutable infrastructure replaced patching in place: build a new image with Packer, roll new instances, throw the old ones away. Kubernetes then handles rollout, scaling and restarts. What remains for Ansible is the layer below containers, the node image, bastions, databases on VMs, on-prem hardware, plus one-off fleet operations. Puppet and Chef, which needed an agent on every host, mostly disappeared with that shift. ## Quiz 1.A task uses ansible.builtin.shell to run apt-get install nginx. What happens on the second run? 2.When does a handler run? 3.Which combination is the safe first step before a production run? 4.Which part of the stack is NOT Ansible's job? 5.What is the lowest precedence source of a variable? ## Practice these problems * [OPSHigh load average and a process eating memory on a Linux hostMedium](/devops/problems/high-load-memory-leak-linux) * [CODEBash: safe deploy script with locking, rollback and trapsMedium](/devops/problems/bash-safe-deploy-script) * [CODETerraform: VPC and autoscaling group moduleMedium](/devops/problems/terraform-vpc-asg-module) ## Further reading * [Ansible documentationGuidedocs.ansible.com](https://docs.ansible.com/) * [Packer documentation: What is Packer?Guidedeveloper.hashicorp.com](https://developer.hashicorp.com/packer/docs/intro) * [systemd System and Service ManagerGuidefreedesktop.org](https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/) ## My notes ## Your notes Saved Autosaves to this browser. # AWS core - IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, load balancers, autoscaling

AWS is the cloud most Indian DevOps jobs ask for. This lesson covers the services every platform is built from and the one setting people get wrong in each: accounts and IAM (who may do what), VPC (where things live on the network), EC2 and Auto Scaling groups (the machines), load balancers (the front door), S3, RDS and Aurora (data), Route 53, CloudWatch, Systems Manager and Secrets Manager.

awsiamvpcec2autoscalingalbrds

## Why it matters

"Design a highly available web app on AWS" is the most common cloud design question in DevOps interviews, and the follow-ups are precise: why a NAT gateway per zone, why a role instead of an access key, what an explicit deny does, how target tracking picks a number. In real work the same facts decide whether a release is safe (instance refresh, health checks), whether the bill is sane (NAT data processing, cross-zone transfer) and whether an audit passes (no long-lived keys, IMDSv2, block public access). Kubernetes on EKS sits on top of all of this, so the next lesson assumes it.

Read first: [Linux for operators](/devops/learn/linux-for-operators), [Networking for DevOps - TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, SSH](/devops/learn/networking-for-devops), [Web servers, reverse proxies and TLS - Nginx, certificates, process managers](/devops/learn/nginx-reverse-proxy-tls)

## Lesson

### Accounts, regions and the shared responsibility model

An AWS **account** is the hard boundary for permissions, billing and blast radius. Put production in its own account, separate from dev and staging, and group accounts with **AWS Organizations**: a management account, organisational units (OUs) and **service control policies** (SCPs). An SCP sets the maximum permissions available in an account; it never grants anything. A classic SCP denies every region except the ones you use, so a leaked key cannot start miners elsewhere. One account per environment means a wrong `terraform destroy` in staging cannot touch production data.

A **region** (ap-south-1 is Mumbai) is a set of **Availability Zones** (AZs): separate data centres with separate power and network, close enough for synchronous replication. Everything here spreads across three AZs because losing one AZ is the failure AWS designs for.

The **shared responsibility model**: AWS is responsible for security *of* the cloud (hardware, regions, the hypervisor, the managed service software). You are responsible for security *in* the cloud: your data, IAM, OS patches on EC2, security groups and encryption settings. "RDS is managed" does not mean AWS chose your password or backup window.

### IAM: identities, policies and how a decision is made

* **Users** are long-lived identities with a password or access keys. Avoid them. Humans sign in through **IAM Identity Center** (formerly AWS SSO) with the company identity provider and get short-lived credentials for a **permission set** in an account; `aws configure sso` sets this up for the CLI.
* **Roles** are identities that are *assumed*, not logged into. An EC2 instance assumes its instance role through the metadata service, a CI job through OIDC, a Lambda function through its execution role. The credentials are temporary and rotate by themselves, so there is nothing to leak.
* **Identity-based policies** attach to users, groups and roles and say what that identity may do. **Resource-based policies** attach to a resource (an S3 bucket policy, a KMS key policy, a role's trust policy) and say who may use it.

The evaluation logic, in the order AWS applies it. Everything starts as an implicit deny. Then:

1. An explicit `Deny` in any applicable policy (SCP, resource policy, identity policy, permissions boundary, session policy) ends it as Deny. Nothing overrides an explicit deny.
2. The organisation's SCPs (and resource control policies, if used) must allow the action.
3. A resource-based policy that allows the principal can be enough on its own within the same account.
4. Otherwise an identity-based policy must allow it.
5. A permissions boundary on the identity, and a session policy passed at assume time, must each allow it too.

The interview version: "explicit deny wins, then the request needs an allow from every layer that applies, and the default is deny."

**Least privilege** is a practice, not a flag. Start from an AWS managed policy, let IAM Access Analyzer generate a policy from what the identity actually used, scope `Resource` to ARNs, and add conditions such as `aws:RequestedRegion` or `s3:prefix`.

**CI through OIDC, no keys.** You create an OIDC identity provider in IAM for `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with audience `sts.amazonaws.com`. The role's trust policy allows `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` only for a `sub` claim such as `repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main`. The workflow sets `permissions: id-token: write` and calls `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume`. No secret is stored anywhere.

### VPC: the network you own

A **VPC** is a private network in one region with an IPv4 range from /16 to /28. Pick a /16 (65,536 addresses) that does not overlap any VPC or office network you may ever peer with. A **subnet** is a slice of it in one AZ; AWS reserves the first four and the last address of every subnet, so a /24 has 251 usable addresses. Three tiers per AZ:

![A VPC across three Availability Zones with public subnets holding ALB nodes and NAT gateways, private subnets holding Auto Scaling group instances, and database subnets holding an RDS primary and its synchronous standby](/devops/img/aws-three-az-vpc-layout.svg)A VPC across three Availability Zones with public subnets holding ALB nodes and NAT gateways, private subnets holding Auto Scaling group instances, and database subnets holding an RDS primary and its synchronous standby

* **Public subnets** have a route table whose default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) points at the **internet gateway** (one per VPC). Only load balancer nodes and NAT gateways live here.
* **Private subnets** have a default route to a **NAT gateway**, so instances can reach the internet (package updates, third-party APIs) without being reachable from it.
* **Database subnets** have no default route at all.

A NAT gateway is zonal. If every private subnet routes to the NAT in zone a and zone a fails, zones b and c lose internet access too, so the documented pattern is one NAT gateway per AZ with each private route table pointing at its own zone's NAT. NAT gateways are billed per hour and per GB processed (an assumed 0.045 USD per hour and 0.045 USD per GB), which adds up when nodes pull images through them. Two cheap fixes: a **gateway VPC endpoint** for S3 (free, one route table entry) and **interface endpoints** for ECR (`ecr.api` and `ecr.dkr`, billed hourly). Image layers live in S3, so ECR needs the S3 gateway endpoint as well.

**Security groups** are stateful firewalls on network interfaces: allow rules only, return traffic allowed automatically, and a rule can reference another security group ("allow 8080 from the ALB's security group") so you never hard-code IPs. **Network ACLs** are stateless rules on a subnet, evaluated in number order, with allow and deny; being stateless, they need the ephemeral return ports opened by hand. Use security groups for almost everything and NACLs as a coarse second layer, such as denying a known bad range at the subnet edge.

**VPC peering** joins two VPCs one-to-one with non-overlapping CIDRs and is not transitive; **Transit Gateway** is the hub for many VPCs or an on-premises link.

### EC2: the machines

An **instance type** name encodes family, generation and options: `m6i.xlarge` is general purpose (m), generation 6, Intel (i), size xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB). `c` is compute optimised, `r` memory optimised, `t` burstable (fine for dev, a trap for steady load because it runs out of CPU credits); after the generation, `g` means Graviton (Arm), `a` AMD, `d` local NVMe disk, `n` more network. An **AMI** is the disk image an instance boots from; build your own with Packer, or take Amazon Linux 2023 and configure it with **user data**, a script run once on first boot as root.

The **instance metadata service** at `169.254.169.254` is how a process on the instance learns its own ID, region and, most importantly, the temporary credentials of the instance role. **IMDSv2** requires a session token from a PUT request, and the default hop limit of 1 stops a container or an SSRF through a proxy from reaching it. Always set `HttpTokens=required` in the launch template.

```
# IMDSv2: get a token (TTL up to 21600 s), then use it
TOKEN=$(curl -sX PUT 169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600")
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id
# require IMDSv2 on an existing instance
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 --http-tokens required
```

**EBS** volumes are network-attached disks in one AZ. Use **gp3**: 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s are included and you can raise either independently of size (gp2 ties IOPS to size, 3 per GiB, and bursts from credits). **Snapshots** are incremental copies to S3 and the basis of AMIs and backups. **Placement groups**: *cluster* packs instances for low latency, *spread* puts each on separate hardware (up to 7 per AZ), *partition* splits a fleet into groups that share no racks.

### Auto Scaling groups

An **Auto Scaling group** (ASG) keeps a fleet of instances built from a **launch template** (AMI, instance type, security groups, instance role, user data, IMDSv2 setting) across the subnets you give it, with **min**, **desired** and **max** counts, replacing instances that fail health checks. EC2 status checks are on by default; turn on **ELB health checks** too so an instance whose app is dead but whose kernel is fine is replaced. The **health check grace period** (300 s in the console, 0 through the CLI) stops a slow-booting instance being killed before it is up; the **default instance warmup** keeps a new instance's CPU out of the group average until it settles.

* **Target tracking** is the one to use. You name a metric and a target (`ASGAverageCPUUtilization` at 60, or `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` at a number you measured); AWS creates the CloudWatch alarms and computes the capacity. The metric must move in proportion to instance count (CPU per instance does; total request count does not). Scale-out is fast; scale-in is deliberately slow and gradual.
* **Step scaling** adds N instances when an alarm crosses a threshold; **simple scaling** is the old form with a cooldown (default 300 s). **Scheduled** actions handle the 9 am ramp you know is coming.

```
# target tracking: hold average CPU near 60 percent
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --policy-name cpu60 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{"TargetValue": 60.0,
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {"PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"}}'
```

**Lifecycle hooks** pause an instance in `Pending:Wait` (configure before it serves) or `Terminating:Wait` (drain, ship logs) until you call `complete-lifecycle-action` or the heartbeat timeout (default 1 hour) expires. **Instance refresh** rolls a new launch template version through the group in batches, keeping at least `MinHealthyPercentage` (default 90) of desired capacity in service and growing to at most `MaxHealthyPercentage` (default 100); set 100 and above to launch before terminating, and turn on `AutoRollback` so failed health checks revert it. Vertical scaling (a bigger instance) is a restart with a ceiling; horizontal scaling (more instances behind a load balancer) is what an ASG gives you. Building one yourself is the week 29 project: a loop that reads a metric, computes a desired count, and starts or stops VMs.

### Load balancers

|  | Application Load Balancer | Network Load Balancer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layer | 7 (HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket) | 4 (TCP, UDP, TLS) |
| Routing | listener rules on host, path, header, query, source IP | one target group per listener port |
| IPs | DNS name, IPs change | static IP or Elastic IP per AZ |
| Cross-zone | on by default; off only per target group | off by default |
| Pick when | web apps, APIs, one entry for many services | raw TCP, fixed IPs for allow-lists, very high packet rates |

A **target group** holds the targets (instances, IP addresses, or a Lambda) and the **health check**: HTTP GET on a path every 30 s, timeout 5 s, healthy after 5 passes, unhealthy after 2 failures, success on 200 by default. If every target is unhealthy the ALB fails open and sends traffic to all of them. **Deregistration delay** (default 300 s) lets in-flight requests finish before removal. **Sticky sessions** pin a client to one target with a cookie; session state in Redis is the better fix. An ALB needs subnets in at least two AZs, each /27 or larger with eight free addresses.

### S3

An S3 **bucket** has a globally unique name and lives in one region. Objects have keys; "folders" are prefixes. Turn on **versioning** (overwrites and deletes become recoverable) and add **lifecycle rules**: logs to `STANDARD_IA` after 30 days, to `GLACIER_IR` or `DEEP_ARCHIVE` after 90, expire after 400, abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days. **Intelligent-Tiering** moves objects between tiers for a small fee. Keep **Block Public Access** on at the account level; a public website goes behind CloudFront with origin access control. A **presigned URL** lets a client upload or download one object for a limited time with the signer's permissions: up to 7 days with IAM user keys, but one signed with a role's temporary credentials dies when those credentials expire, the usual surprise.

### RDS and Aurora

**RDS** runs PostgreSQL, MySQL and others on an instance you size. **Multi-AZ** keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ; it serves no reads, and on failure RDS flips the DNS record to the standby in typically 60 to 120 seconds, so the app must reconnect and must not cache DNS forever. A **read replica** is asynchronous and serves reads: scaling, not failover. **Backups**: daily snapshots plus transaction logs for point-in-time restore within the retention window. A **parameter group** is the engine config (`max_connections`, `shared_buffers`, `log_min_duration_statement`); the default `max_connections` is derived from instance memory, which is why a small instance falls over at a few hundred connections and why PgBouncer or RDS Proxy sits in front of it.

**Aurora** separates compute from a storage layer replicated across three AZs; up to 15 replicas share that storage, failover promotes a replica fast, and there is a **writer endpoint** and a **reader endpoint** (which points at the writer if there are no replicas). For the profile this site targets (many services, one shared relational database, strict availability), Aurora PostgreSQL is the default answer: three-AZ durability without an idle standby, fast failover, and read scaling through the reader endpoint.

### Route 53, CloudWatch, Systems Manager, Secrets Manager

**Route 53** hosts a **hosted zone** per domain. An **alias record** points a name, even the zone apex `example.com`, at an AWS resource (ALB, CloudFront, S3 website) and is free to query; a CNAME cannot sit at the apex. **Routing policies**: simple, weighted (5 percent to a new stack), latency, failover (health check on the primary), geolocation, multivalue.

**CloudWatch** holds **metrics** (EC2 sends CPU, network and disk every 5 minutes; **detailed monitoring** makes it 1 minute for a charge; memory and disk usage need the **CloudWatch agent** inside the instance), **logs** (log groups with retention, shipped by the agent), **alarms** (a metric over a threshold for N periods triggers SNS, an ASG policy or EventBridge) and **dashboards**.

**Systems Manager Session Manager** gives a shell on an instance through the SSM agent and IAM, with no inbound port 22, no bastion and no key pairs, and sessions can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch: `aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0`. **Parameter Store** holds configuration as a path hierarchy (`/prod/api/db_host`), `SecureString` encrypted with KMS, standard tier free up to 4 KB per value. **Secrets Manager** is for credentials: it rotates them with a Lambda function, replicates across regions, and costs per secret per month, so non-secret config stays in Parameter Store.

**The CLI and profiles.** `~/.aws/config` holds `[profile name]` sections with region, output and the SSO session; `~/.aws/credentials` holds `[name]` sections with keys and should be nearly empty on a modern laptop. `--profile prod` or `AWS_PROFILE=prod` selects one; run `aws sts get-caller-identity` before anything destructive.

### The one setting people get wrong

| Need | Service | The setting people get wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App needs AWS permissions | IAM role | an IAM user with access keys; the keys end up in a repo |
| CI deploys | IAM OIDC provider + role | a trust policy without a `sub` condition, so any repo can assume it |
| Humans in console and CLI | IAM Identity Center | per-account IAM users with passwords and no MFA |
| Private instances need internet | NAT gateway | one NAT for all zones; image pulls through it instead of VPC endpoints |
| Firewall for instances | security group | port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0; use Session Manager |
| Instance credentials | IMDSv2 | `HttpTokens` left optional, so IMDSv1 and SSRF still work |
| Scale a fleet | ASG target tracking | no ELB health check, grace period 0, no instance warmup |
| Roll a new AMI | instance refresh | terminating by hand; set MinHealthyPercentage and AutoRollback |
| HTTP entry point | ALB | health check on `/` returns 200 while the database is down |
| Object storage | S3 | public ACLs for convenience; keep Block Public Access on |
| Relational database | RDS Multi-AZ or Aurora | a read replica as the HA plan; it is asynchronous |
| DNS to a load balancer | Route 53 alias | a CNAME at the zone apex, which DNS does not allow |
| Memory on a dashboard | CloudWatch agent | expecting EC2 to report memory; the hypervisor cannot see it |
| Database password | Secrets Manager | a `SecureString` parameter with no rotation, value in Terraform state |

## Diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Worked example

**Subnet plan.** VPC `10.20.0.0/16` in ap-south-1, three AZs, three tiers. Private subnets carry the instances and later the EKS pods, so they get the big blocks: `10.20.0.0/20`, `10.20.16.0/20`, `10.20.32.0/20`, each 4,096 addresses, 4,091 usable after the five AWS reserves. Public subnets hold only ALB nodes and a NAT gateway: `10.20.100.0/24`, `10.20.101.0/24`, `10.20.102.0/24` (251 usable each, well above the eight free addresses an ALB needs per subnet). Database subnets: `10.20.110.0/24` to `10.20.112.0/24`. Total used: 3 x 4,096 + 6 x 256 = 13,824 of 65,536, leaving 51,712 addresses for pod subnets or a second cluster. None of the nine blocks overlap, and the /16 does not overlap the office range `192.168.0.0/16`, so peering later is possible.

**ASG sizing.** Peak is 2,000 requests per second. A load test shows one m6i.xlarge handles 300 requests per second before p99 latency climbs. Raw need: 2,000 / 300 = 6.67, so 7 instances. Add 30 percent headroom so a traffic spike or a slow deploy does not push instances to their limit: 2,000 x 1.3 / 300 = 8.67, so 9 instances, 3 per AZ. That is `desired = 9`.

Express the same thing as a target-tracking target: 300 / 1.3 = 230 requests per target. With `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` at 230, the policy computes 2,000 / 230 = 8.7 and rounds up to 9, the same number, and at night with 400 requests per second it computes 400 / 230 = 1.7, rounded up to 2, which the `min = 3` below holds at 3.

Set `min = 3` (one per AZ, so the service is never in one zone) and `max = 20` (about twice the peak need, a ceiling against a runaway loop).

Now the AZ-loss test. Lose one zone and 6 instances remain: 6 x 300 = 1,800 requests per second, 200 short of the peak. Two choices: accept that the ASG will add instances in the surviving zones within about 5 minutes (launch plus warmup), or set `desired = 15` (5 per AZ) so any two zones carry 10 x 300 = 3,000. At an assumed 0.192 USD per hour, 9 instances cost 9 x 0.192 x 730 = 1,261 USD per month and 15 cost 2,102 USD; the difference, 841 USD, is the price of surviving a zone loss at peak without waiting for a scale-out. Most teams choose 9 and a fast scale-out; a payment system chooses 15.

## Runnable code

Python · runs and prints its own checks

```
"""A model of an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a target-tracking policy on CPU.

No network, no AWS. The point is to see how target tracking behaves minute by
minute: scale-out is quick, scale-in is slow, new instances warm up before they
count, and min/max bound everything. The numbers (3 minutes above target to
scale out, 15 minutes below to scale in) are this model's assumptions, chosen
to look like the CloudWatch alarms the real policy creates; tune them and watch.
"""
import math

CAPACITY_RPS = 300.0      # one instance at 100 percent CPU handles 300 req/s
TARGET_CPU = 60.0         # the target-tracking target value (percent)
WARMUP_MIN = 3            # default instance warmup: new instances serve no traffic
SCALE_OUT_AFTER = 3       # minutes above target before a scale-out
SCALE_IN_AFTER = 15       # minutes below target before a scale-in
SCALE_IN_COOLDOWN = 5     # minutes after any activity before a scale-in may start

def traffic_curve():
    """Requests per second for each minute of a 3-hour window: a quiet start,
    a sharp ramp to a 2,000 req/s peak, a plateau, and a slow decline."""
    curve = []
    for minute in range(180):
        if minute < 30:
            rps = 400
        elif minute < 45:
            rps = 400 + (2000 - 400) * (minute - 30) / 15   # ramp over 15 minutes
        elif minute < 100:
            rps = 2000
        else:
            rps = max(400, 2000 - (minute - 100) * 25)      # decline 25 req/s per minute
        curve.append(rps)
    return curve

def cpu_percent(rps, in_service):
    """Average CPU of the instances that actually serve traffic."""
    if in_service == 0:
        return 100.0
    return min(100.0, rps / in_service / CAPACITY_RPS * 100)

def simulate(curve, minimum, maximum, desired, verbose=True):
    # Each instance is a dict with the minute it was launched.
    instances = [{"launched": -WARMUP_MIN} for _ in range(desired)]  # already warm
    above = below = 0
    last_activity = -SCALE_IN_COOLDOWN
    peak = len(instances)
    overloaded_minutes = 0
    if verbose:
        print(f"{'min':>3} {'req/s':>6} {'total':>5} {'warm':>4} {'cpu%':>5}  action")
    for minute, rps in enumerate(curve):
        warm = [i for i in instances if minute - i["launched"] >= WARMUP_MIN]
        cpu = cpu_percent(rps, len(warm))
        if cpu >= 95:
            overloaded_minutes += 1
        action = ""
        # Track consecutive minutes above and below target, like an alarm.
        above = above + 1 if cpu > TARGET_CPU else 0
        below = below + 1 if cpu < TARGET_CPU else 0
        total = len(instances)
        if above >= SCALE_OUT_AFTER:
            # Proportional estimate of what is needed, counting warming instances
            # against desired capacity so the group does not overshoot.
            needed = math.ceil(len(warm) * cpu / TARGET_CPU)
            needed = min(maximum, max(needed, total))
            if needed > total:
                for _ in range(needed - total):
                    instances.append({"launched": minute})
                action = f"scale out {total} -> {needed}"
                last_activity = minute
                above = 0
        elif (below >= SCALE_IN_AFTER and minute - last_activity >= SCALE_IN_COOLDOWN
              and len(warm) == total):
            needed = math.ceil(total * cpu / TARGET_CPU)
            needed = max(minimum, min(needed, total))
            if needed < total:
                # Scale in gradually: one instance per activity, then wait for
                # the cooldown. The alarm stays in ALARM while CPU is below target,
                # so the 15-minute wait is not paid again.
                instances.pop()
                action = f"scale in {total} -> {total - 1}"
                last_activity = minute
        peak = max(peak, len(instances))
        if verbose and (action or minute % 10 == 0):
            print(f"{minute:>3} {rps:>6.0f} {len(instances):>5} {len(warm):>4} {cpu:>5.0f}  {action}")
    return peak, overloaded_minutes, len(instances)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    curve = traffic_curve()
    print("target-tracking on CPU, target 60 percent, min 3, max 20, desired 3\n")
    peak, hot, final = simulate(curve, minimum=3, maximum=20, desired=3)
    print(f"\npeak instances: {peak}; minutes at 95 percent CPU or more: {hot}; final size: {final}")

    # Self-checks: the model must reach the arithmetic from the worked example.
    ideal = math.ceil(2000 / (CAPACITY_RPS * TARGET_CPU / 100))  # 2000 / 180 -> 12
    assert peak == ideal, (peak, ideal)
    assert final == 3, final                     # scaled all the way back to min
    assert hot > 0, "a 15-minute ramp with a 3-minute warmup should overload briefly"

    # Same curve with a larger minimum: the overload disappears, the peak is the same.
    peak2, hot2, final2 = simulate(curve, minimum=6, maximum=20, desired=6, verbose=False)
    assert peak2 == ideal and hot2 == 0 and final2 == 6
    print(f"with min 6: peak {peak2}, overloaded minutes {hot2}; the floor absorbs the ramp")

    # A max below the need: the group is capped and stays hot at the plateau.
    peak3, hot3, _ = simulate(curve, minimum=3, maximum=6, desired=3, verbose=False)
    assert peak3 == 6 and hot3 > hot
    print(f"with max 6: peak {peak3}, overloaded minutes {hot3}; max is a hard ceiling")
    print("\nself-checks passed")
```

## Key takeaways

* Production gets its own account; SCPs cap what any identity in it can do; one region deny-list SCP stops most key-leak damage.
* IAM: explicit deny wins, then every applicable layer must allow, and the default is deny. Roles with temporary credentials for everything; OIDC for CI; Identity Center for humans; no long-lived keys.
* A VPC is three tiers across three AZs: public (ALB, NAT), private (instances, pods), database (no internet route). One NAT gateway per AZ, VPC endpoints for S3 and ECR.
* Security groups are stateful and reference each other; NACLs are stateless and rarely needed.
* IMDSv2 required, gp3 volumes, user data for bootstrap, an instance role instead of keys.
* An ASG with a launch template, target tracking on CPU or ALB requests per target, ELB health checks, a warmup, and instance refresh for AMI rollouts is the "autoscaling orchestrator".
* ALB for HTTP with listener rules and health checks; NLB for TCP and static IPs; cross-zone is on by default for ALB (off only per target group) and off by default for NLB.
* RDS Multi-AZ is for availability (synchronous, no reads); read replicas are for scaling (asynchronous); Aurora gives both with shared storage across three AZs.

## Common mistakes

* Answering "I would create an IAM user for the app and put the keys in a Secret". The answer is an instance role, Pod Identity, or an OIDC role.
* Saying a read replica is the high-availability plan. It is asynchronous and must be promoted by hand; Multi-AZ is the HA plan.
* One NAT gateway for the whole VPC, or no VPC endpoints, so a zone failure cuts outbound traffic and image pulls run up the NAT bill.
* An ASG with EC2 health checks only and a health check on `/` that returns 200 while the app's database is unreachable, so broken instances stay in service.
* Forgetting that security groups are stateful and writing outbound rules for every inbound rule, or treating NACLs as the main firewall.
* Caching the RDS endpoint's IP in the application (JVM DNS cache set to forever), so a Multi-AZ failover that took 90 seconds becomes an outage until restart.

## Practice

* In a free-tier account, build the three-tier VPC from the worked example with the console or Terraform: three AZs, public, private and database subnets, one internet gateway, one NAT gateway (or three if you accept the cost for an hour), and an S3 gateway endpoint. Launch a t3.micro in a private subnet with no key pair, connect with Session Manager, and prove `curl https://s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com` works while the NAT route is removed. Delete everything after.
* Create a launch template with IMDSv2 required and user data that installs nginx returning the instance ID, an ASG with min 2 and max 4 across two AZs behind an ALB with a health check on `/`, and a target-tracking policy on CPU at 50 percent. Run `stress-ng` on one instance and time how long until a third instance is in service. Then publish a new template version and run an instance refresh with MinHealthyPercentage 100; watch the target group during the refresh.
* Set up GitHub Actions OIDC to a role that may only list one S3 bucket; run `aws sts get-caller-identity` from a workflow, then change the `sub` condition to a different branch and confirm the job fails with AccessDenied.
* Run the code example, then change `WARMUP_MIN` to 1 and `SCALE_OUT_AFTER` to 1 and compare the peak instance count and the overloaded minutes; explain in two sentences why the real policy is deliberately slower to scale in than to scale out. Then write your own autoscaling orchestrator (the 100xDevs exercise) in about 40 lines of Python: a loop that reads a fake metric each tick, computes `desired = ceil(current * usage / target)`, clamps it between min and max, applies a cooldown so it does not scale twice inside 5 ticks, and calls a fake `scale(n)` function that prints the change. Feed it a usage series that rises from 20 to 90 percent and back, and check that the instance count never changes more than once per cooldown.

## Interview questions (12)

1.Why is production in a separate AWS account, and how do you keep that account safe?Easy

An account is the hardest boundary AWS has: separate IAM, separate limits, separate bill, and a mistake in one cannot reach another. A destroy in staging cannot touch production tables. I put every environment in its own account under AWS Organizations, attach service control policies to the production OU that deny regions we do not use and deny deleting CloudTrail, and give humans access through IAM Identity Center permission sets with MFA instead of IAM users. Cross-account access for CI is a role with a trust policy, not shared keys.

2.Explain how AWS decides whether a request is allowed.Medium

Everything starts as an implicit deny. First AWS looks for an explicit deny in any policy that applies: SCPs, resource policies, identity policies, permissions boundaries, session policies. One matching deny ends it; nothing overrides it. Then the SCPs must allow the action. Then a resource-based policy that names the principal can allow it on its own within the same account; otherwise an identity-based policy must allow it. If a permissions boundary or a session policy exists, each must allow it too. So the short version is: explicit deny wins, then you need an allow from every layer that applies, and the default is deny.

3.How does a GitHub Actions job deploy to AWS without a stored secret?Medium

Through OIDC. In IAM I create an identity provider for `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with audience `sts.amazonaws.com`. I create a role whose trust policy allows `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` only when the token's `sub` claim equals `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main`, so only the main branch of that one repository can assume it. The workflow sets `permissions: id-token: write`, and `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` exchanges the GitHub token for temporary credentials. No access key exists anywhere, and the credentials expire with the job. The common mistake is leaving out the `sub` condition, which lets any repo in the organisation assume the role.

4.Draw the VPC for a three-tier web app and explain the route tables.Medium

A /16 VPC, three Availability Zones, three subnets per zone. Public subnets have a route table with `0.0.0.0/0` to the internet gateway; only ALB nodes and NAT gateways live there. Private subnets hold the application instances or pods; each zone's private route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to the NAT gateway in the same zone, so a zone failure does not cut outbound traffic for the other zones. Database subnets have no default route at all. I add a gateway endpoint for S3 and interface endpoints for ECR so image pulls and object traffic never cross the NAT. Security groups chain: the database allows 5432 only from the app security group, the app allows 8080 only from the ALB security group.

5.Security groups versus network ACLs: when do you use which?Easy

Security groups are stateful and attach to network interfaces. They have allow rules only, return traffic is allowed automatically, and a rule can reference another security group instead of an IP range, which is how you say "only the load balancer can reach the app". Network ACLs are stateless, attach to a subnet, have numbered allow and deny rules evaluated in order, and need the ephemeral return ports opened explicitly. I use security groups for all real access control and keep the default NACL open, adding a deny rule only for a coarse case like blocking a known abusive range at the subnet edge.

6.What is IMDSv2 and why do you require it?Medium

The instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254 hands out the instance's role credentials to any process that asks. With IMDSv1 a simple GET works, so a server-side request forgery bug in the app can fetch the credentials. IMDSv2 requires a PUT to get a session token first and then that token in a header on each GET, and the token response has a hop limit of 1 by default so it cannot pass through a container's NAT or a proxy. I set `HttpTokens=required` in the launch template and the SDKs use it transparently.

7.How does a target-tracking scaling policy decide how many instances to run?Medium

I give it a metric that moves in proportion to the number of instances, like average CPU or ALB requests per target, and a target value. AWS creates the CloudWatch alarms and, when the metric is above target for a few minutes, computes the capacity that would bring it back, roughly current count times metric over target, rounded up, bounded by min and max. New instances sit out of the average during the warmup period so their startup CPU does not cause a second scale-out. Scale-in is slower and more gradual on purpose, so a short dip does not drop capacity right before the next spike. For 2,000 requests per second with 230 per target it settles at 9 instances.

8.You have a new AMI. How do you roll it through an Auto Scaling group with no downtime?Medium

Publish a new launch template version with the AMI and start an instance refresh. It replaces instances in batches while keeping at least MinHealthyPercentage of the desired capacity in service, 90 by default; with MinHealthyPercentage 100 and MaxHealthyPercentage above it, the group launches each replacement before terminating the old one. Each new instance must pass the ELB health check and finish the instance warmup before the next batch starts. With AutoRollback on, a failed batch reverts to the old template. I would also set a Terminating lifecycle hook so an instance drains from the target group before it is killed.

9.ALB or NLB for this service?Easy

ALB when the traffic is HTTP: it terminates TLS, routes on host, path and headers, supports WebSockets and gRPC, integrates with WAF, and one ALB can front many services. NLB when I need layer 4: raw TCP or UDP, a static IP or Elastic IP per zone for a customer's allow-list, very high connection rates, or TLS passthrough to the backend. Cross-zone is on by default for an ALB, and can only be turned off per target group, while it is off by default for an NLB, which matters when targets are unevenly spread across zones.

10.Multi-AZ RDS versus a read replica: what is each for?Easy

Multi-AZ is availability. RDS keeps a synchronous standby in another zone; it cannot serve reads, and when the primary fails RDS points the same DNS name at the standby in about 60 to 120 seconds. The app just needs to reconnect and not cache DNS. A read replica is scaling. It replicates asynchronously, serves read queries on its own endpoint, and can lag; promoting it is a manual, lossy operation. Aurora blurs the two: replicas share the storage layer, so a replica can be promoted in seconds and the reader endpoint load-balances reads across them.

11.An EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot reach the internet. What do you check?Medium

First the route table of its subnet: is there a `0.0.0.0/0` route and does it point at a NAT gateway, not at an internet gateway, which does nothing for an instance with no public IP. Then the NAT gateway itself: is it in a public subnet whose route table points at the internet gateway, does it have an Elastic IP, is it in the same zone or at least reachable. Then the security group's outbound rules and the NACL's outbound and inbound ephemeral ports. Then DNS: `enableDnsSupport` on the VPC. If it only needs S3 or ECR, I add VPC endpoints and avoid the NAT entirely.

12.How do you get a shell on a production instance without opening SSH?Easy

Systems Manager Session Manager. The SSM agent on the instance makes an outbound connection to the SSM service, so no inbound port is open, no bastion exists and no key pairs are distributed. Access is an IAM permission on `ssm:StartSession` scoped to tagged instances, and the session commands can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3. From the laptop it is `aws ssm start-session --target i-...`, and port forwarding through the same channel reaches an RDS instance in a private subnet for a one-off query.

# AWS managed platforms - EKS, ECS, Fargate, Lambda, SQS, ElastiCache, CloudFront

AWS offers five ways to run a workload: EC2 with an Auto Scaling group, ECS, EKS, Fargate, and Lambda. This lesson is about choosing between them and about EKS as an AWS product: node groups and Auto Mode, the VPC CNI, Pod Identity, access entries, add-ons and the load balancer controller. It also covers the services that sit beside the cluster: SQS and SNS, ElastiCache, CloudFront, and Secrets Manager through the External Secrets Operator.

eksecsfargatelambdasqselasticachecloudfront

## Why it matters

Interviewers rarely ask "what is EKS". They ask "ECS or EKS for this team, and why", "how does a pod get AWS permissions", "why are your pods stuck Pending with no IPs", "what happens to a message when the consumer crashes". Each has a precise answer tied to a specific AWS feature. On the job, the same features decide the monthly bill (control plane, NAT, extended support), the upgrade plan (support windows, node group rollouts) and whether a traffic spike turns into a queue backlog or a cold-start storm. The resume this site targets lists EKS, ECS, Aurora, ElastiCache and Cloudflare at the edge; this lesson is that list.

Read first: [Containers and Docker](/devops/learn/containers-and-docker), [AWS core - IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, load balancers, autoscaling](/devops/learn/aws-core-for-devops)

## Lesson

### Choosing a compute platform

| Platform | Ops burden | Cost shape | Scaling | Pick it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EC2 + ASG | you own the OS, the deploy tool and the AMI pipeline | per instance-hour; cheapest per vCPU with Reserved or Spot | ASG target tracking, minutes | one or two stateful or legacy services, GPU boxes, very high steady load |
| ECS on Fargate | no servers; task definitions and services | per task vCPU-second and GB-second, 1-minute minimum | service auto scaling, about a minute per task | a few to a few dozen containers, a small team, no Kubernetes skills needed |
| ECS on EC2 | you patch the instances; ECS schedules tasks on them | instance-hours, denser packing than Fargate | capacity providers scale the ASG | ECS with GPUs, daemon tasks, or cost pressure at scale |
| EKS | the cluster, add-ons, upgrades, IAM mapping; large ecosystem | control plane per hour plus nodes (or Fargate per pod, or Auto Mode fee) | HPA plus Karpenter, under a minute for pods, 1 to 2 minutes for nodes | many services and teams, Helm and GitOps, operators, portability, a platform team |
| Lambda | none; code and configuration only | per request and per GB-second; free when idle | automatic, 1,000 concurrent per Region by default | event-driven glue, bursty or rare work, short tasks under 15 minutes |

The honest rule: a team of three with five services should not run EKS; ECS on Fargate gives them rolling deploys, load balancing and logs with a tenth of the surface area. A company with 30 services, several teams, Helm charts and operators needs the Kubernetes API and should pay the EKS tax. Lambda is for the edges of a system (webhooks, S3 triggers, scheduled jobs), not for a long-running API at a steady 500 requests per second, where it costs more than a few Fargate tasks.

### ECS: enough for most teams

An ECS **cluster** is a logical group. A **task definition** is the unit of deployment: one or more containers with image, CPU and memory, ports, environment, secrets (from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store by ARN), the log driver and the **task role** (the IAM role the application uses) plus the **execution role** (the role ECS uses to pull the image and fetch secrets). A **task** is a running copy. A **service** keeps N tasks running, registers them in a load balancer target group, and replaces failed ones. The **launch type** is Fargate (AWS runs the hosts, one task per micro VM, you pick a CPU and memory pair such as 1 vCPU with 2 GB) or EC2 (your instances join the cluster through the ECS agent). Images come from **ECR**; private subnets need the `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr` and S3 gateway endpoints to pull without a NAT, and Fargate tasks logging with `awslogs` need the CloudWatch Logs endpoint too.

Rolling updates are controlled by `minimumHealthyPercent` and `maximumPercent` (defaults 100 and 200 for a replica service), and the **deployment circuit breaker** stops a deployment whose tasks keep failing and rolls back to the last good revision. Since July 2025, ECS also has a built-in blue/green strategy with lifecycle hooks, so CodeDeploy is no longer required for it. **Service Connect** gives tasks a service mesh style DNS name and metrics without a sidecar you manage. The week 30 project is exactly this: push an image to ECR, write a task definition, create a service behind an ALB, and watch it roll.

```

### EKS as a product

![EKS control plane in an AWS-owned account above a customer VPC that holds a managed node group, a Fargate profile, an ALB created by the load balancer controller, and a Pod Identity path from a pod to an IAM role and on to S3 and SQS](/devops/img/eks-control-plane-and-data-plane.svg)EKS control plane in an AWS-owned account above a customer VPC that holds a managed node group, a Fargate profile, an ALB created by the load balancer controller, and a Pod Identity path from a pod to an IAM role and on to S3 and SQS

**Control plane.** EKS runs at least two API server instances and three etcd instances across three AZs, in an account AWS owns, and creates two to four network interfaces in your subnets so it can reach kubelets and admission webhooks. Your subnets must span at least two AZs with at least six free IPs each (16 recommended). The control plane costs a flat hourly fee (an assumed 0.10 USD per hour, about 73 USD a month) and the API endpoint can be public, private, or both; production uses private plus a public endpoint restricted to office and CI ranges.

**Versions and support.** A Kubernetes minor version gets 14 months of standard support on EKS, then 12 months of **extended support** at a higher hourly price (an assumed 0.60 USD per hour), and a cluster that is still on the version when extended support ends is upgraded automatically with no notice. Extended support is on by default; turn it off if you would rather be forced to upgrade than pay six times the control plane fee. Upgrade order: control plane one minor at a time, then add-ons, then nodes.

**Where nodes come from.**

| Option | Who manages the EC2, OS, AMI and Kubernetes version | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Managed node group | you choose the instance types; AWS runs the ASG, rolls new AMIs with `maxUnavailable` (default 1), cordons and drains respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, fails after 15 minutes of blocked eviction unless `--force` | the default for most clusters |
| Self-managed nodes | you, entirely | custom AMIs, special kernels, rarely worth it now |
| Fargate profile | AWS; one micro VM per pod, selected by namespace and labels | no DaemonSets, no EBS, no privileged pods, private subnets only, IRSA not Pod Identity, ALB target type must be `ip` |
| EKS Auto Mode | AWS: Bottlerocket nodes, Karpenter-based scaling, pod networking, load balancing, EBS storage, DNS, GPU drivers, patching with a 21-day maximum node life, no SSH or SSM to nodes | a per-instance management fee on top of EC2; you still own the VPC, the cluster config and your apps |

**Networking: the VPC CNI.** Every pod gets a real VPC IP from the node's subnet. A node can only attach so many network interfaces and each interface only so many IPs, so an m6i.xlarge is capped at a few dozen pods and a cluster can run out of subnet addresses long before it runs out of CPU. **Prefix delegation** fixes both: the CNI attaches `/28` blocks (16 addresses) instead of single IPs, so the pod limit per node rises to the managed node group cap of 110 (250 for instances with 30 or more vCPUs). It needs Nitro instances and contiguous free `/28` blocks in the subnet, which is why pod subnets are large and separate.

```
kubectl set env daemonset aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true
kubectl describe node ip-10-20-5-17.ap-south-1.compute.internal | grep -E 'pods|PrivateIPv4Address'
```

**Identity.** Humans and CI get into the cluster through **access entries**: an IAM principal is mapped to a Kubernetes group or to an AWS access policy (`AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy`, `AmazonEKSAdminPolicy`, `AmazonEKSEditPolicy`, `AmazonEKSViewPolicy`), managed through the EKS API and Terraform, with the authentication mode `API` or `API_AND_CONFIG_MAP`. This replaces the `aws-auth` ConfigMap, whose one typo could lock everyone out. Pods get AWS permissions in one of two ways:

* **IRSA** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): the cluster has an OIDC issuer; a role's trust policy names that issuer and the service account; the pod gets a projected token that the SDK exchanges for credentials. Works on Fargate and outside EKS, but every new cluster means editing every trust policy.
* **Pod Identity**: install the `eks-pod-identity-agent` add-on, create a role whose trust policy names `pods.eks.amazonaws.com` once, and create an association between the role and a service account. The agent on each node hands out credentials at `169.254.170.23`. Simpler, one trust policy for every cluster, but EC2 nodes only.

```
aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name prod \
  --namespace payments --service-account api \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/payments-api
```

**Add-ons.** `vpc-cni`, `coredns` and `kube-proxy` are installed on every cluster; `aws-ebs-csi-driver` (PersistentVolumes on EBS, one AZ each), `aws-efs-csi-driver` (shared ReadWriteMany), `eks-pod-identity-agent`, `amazon-cloudwatch-observability` and `adot` are AWS add-ons you turn on, and `metrics-server`, `cert-manager`, `external-dns` and `kube-state-metrics` are community add-ons managed the same way. The **AWS Load Balancer Controller** is installed with Helm (an IAM policy plus Pod Identity for its service account): an `Ingress` with `ingressClassName: alb` becomes an ALB, a `Service` of type `LoadBalancer` becomes an NLB, and `alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip` sends traffic straight to pod IPs across any node. Subnets need the tags `kubernetes.io/role/elb=1` (public) and `kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1` (private) for discovery. **Karpenter** runs on a small managed node group or Fargate (never on nodes it manages) and launches right-sized instances from a `NodePool` and `EC2NodeClass`, with consolidation and Spot interruption handling; Auto Mode is Karpenter run by AWS.

**Logging and cost.** Control plane logs (`api`, `audit`, `authenticator`, `controllerManager`, `scheduler`) are off by default; turn on at least `audit` and `authenticator` and they land in `/aws/eks/<cluster>/cluster`. The bill is control plane plus nodes plus the NAT and load balancers around them; the control plane is the smallest line. **eksctl** creates a working cluster in one command and is fine for a lab; production clusters are Terraform, so the VPC, IAM, access entries and add-ons are reviewed in a pull request.

### Kubernetes concept to AWS resource

| Kubernetes concept | On EKS it is | Owned by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node | EC2 instance in a managed node group, or a Fargate micro VM | you (node group) or AWS (Fargate, Auto Mode) |
| Pod IP | a VPC IP from the subnet, via the VPC CNI (`aws-node` DaemonSet) | VPC CNI add-on |
| Service type LoadBalancer | NLB created by the AWS Load Balancer Controller | controller, Helm |
| Ingress / Gateway | ALB with listener rules | controller, Helm |
| PersistentVolume, ReadWriteOnce | EBS gp3 volume in one AZ | `aws-ebs-csi-driver` add-on |
| PersistentVolume, ReadWriteMany | EFS file system | `aws-efs-csi-driver` add-on |
| ServiceAccount with cloud permissions | IAM role via Pod Identity association or IRSA | `eks-pod-identity-agent` add-on or OIDC provider |
| kubectl user and RBAC group | access entry mapped to an IAM role | EKS API |

| Control plane logs | CloudWatch log group `/aws/eks/<name>/cluster` | EKS |
