## Worked example

**An upgrade that fails and the rollback timeline.** The `api` release is at revision 4, chart 0.3.0, image tag 1.7.2, 3 replicas, with `maxUnavailable: 0`. At 10:00 CI runs:

```
helm upgrade --install api oci://123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/api \
  --version 0.3.1 -n shop -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.8.0 \
  --wait --timeout 5m --rollback-on-failure
```

Step 1 (10:00:00). Helm merges values: values.yaml from chart 0.3.1, then values-prod.yaml, then the `--set`. Schema passes. It renders 7 manifests and finds one `pre-upgrade` hook, the migrate Job with weight -5.

Step 2 (10:00:02). Helm creates the Job and waits. The migration adds an index and finishes in 40 seconds with exit code 0. Policy `hook-succeeded` deletes the Job.

Step 3 (10:00:42). Helm applies the manifests. Only the Deployment changed (new image, new chart label), so the API server starts a rolling update: new ReplicaSet, 1 surge pod.

Step 4 (10:00:42 to 10:05:42). The new pod starts, but 1.8.0 reads a config key that does not exist in prod and exits. CrashLoopBackOff. Because `maxUnavailable` is 0, the 3 old pods stay ready and users see nothing. `--wait` keeps polling the Deployment: it wants 3 ready replicas on the new ReplicaSet and never gets them.

Step 5 (10:05:42). The 5 minute timeout fires. Helm marks revision 5 as failed and, because of `--rollback-on-failure`, performs a rollback: it writes revision 6 with the manifests of revision 4 (image 1.7.2) and applies them. The Deployment's pod template is now identical to the old ReplicaSet, so Kubernetes scales it back to 3 and deletes the crashing ReplicaSet. No pre-rollback hooks exist, so the migration is not reversed; adding an index is backwards compatible, which is the rule for migrations that run before a rollout.

Step 6 (10:05:50). `helm history api -n shop` shows: 4 deployed-then-superseded, 5 failed, 6 deployed with description "Rollback to 4". Total user-facing impact: zero errors, about 6 minutes of CI time.

Count the cost of the alternative. Without `--wait`, Helm returns "deployed" at 10:00:43, CI goes green, and the broken ReplicaSet sits in the cluster until a human reads `kubectl get pods`. Without `maxUnavailable: 0`, the controller could have removed one old pod first and run on 2 of 3 for 5 minutes, which is a 33 percent capacity cut during the window. The flags and the Deployment strategy together are what made the failure invisible.

## Runnable code

Go · gofmt and go vet clean · runs and prints its own checks

```
// A tiny "helm template" in Go, standard library only.
//
// Helm templates are Go text/template files with extra functions. This
// program defines the few functions a Deployment template needs (default,
// quote, indent, nindent, toYaml), merges a base values map with a
// per-environment override (what -f values-prod.yaml does), renders the
// same template for dev and prod, and prints a diff summary. Running it
// shows that one chart plus two values files gives two different manifests.
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"sort"
	"strings"
	"text/template"
)

// deploymentTemplate is what templates/deployment.yaml looks like in a chart.
// {{- and -}} trim the whitespace around an action, exactly as in Helm.
const deploymentTemplate = `apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
    app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount | default 1 }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
        app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
          ports:
            - containerPort: {{ .Values.service.port }}
          {{- if .Values.env }}
          env:
            {{- range $k, $v := .Values.env }}
            - name: {{ $k }}
              value: {{ $v | quote }}
            {{- end }}
          {{- end }}
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
`

// Values is a nested map, like the result of parsing values.yaml.
type Values map[string]any

// merge copies overrides on top of base, recursing into nested maps.
// This is the same rule Helm uses when it layers -f files: a later file
// wins per key, and maps are merged rather than replaced.
func merge(base, overrides Values) Values {
	out := Values{}
	for k, v := range base {
		out[k] = v
	}
	for k, v := range overrides {
		if bm, ok := out[k].(Values); ok {
			if om, ok := v.(Values); ok {
				out[k] = merge(bm, om)
				continue
			}
		}
		out[k] = v
	}
	return out
}

// toYaml renders a value as YAML. It handles the three shapes a values file
// uses: scalars, lists, and nested maps, with keys sorted for stable output.
func toYaml(v any) string {
	var b strings.Builder
	writeYaml(&b, v, 0)
	return strings.TrimRight(b.String(), "\n")
}

func writeYaml(b *strings.Builder, v any, depth int) {
	pad := strings.Repeat("  ", depth)
	switch t := v.(type) {
	case Values:
		keys := make([]string, 0, len(t))
		for k := range t {
			keys = append(keys, k)
		}
		sort.Strings(keys)
		for _, k := range keys {
			switch t[k].(type) {
			case Values, []any:
				fmt.Fprintf(b, "%s%s:\n", pad, k)
				writeYaml(b, t[k], depth+1)
			default:
				fmt.Fprintf(b, "%s%s: %v\n", pad, k, t[k])
			}
		}
	case []any:
		for _, item := range t {
			fmt.Fprintf(b, "%s- %v\n", pad, item)
		}
	default:
		fmt.Fprintf(b, "%s%v\n", pad, t)
	}
}

// The function map: what Helm adds on top of text/template (a subset).
var funcs = template.FuncMap{
	// default takes the fallback FIRST so it works in a pipeline: {{ x | default 1 }}
	"default": func(def any, val any) any {
		if val == nil || val == "" || val == 0 {
			return def
		}
		return val
	},
	"quote": func(v any) string { return fmt.Sprintf("%q", fmt.Sprint(v)) },
	"indent": func(n int, s string) string {
		pad := strings.Repeat(" ", n)
		return pad + strings.ReplaceAll(s, "\n", "\n"+pad)
	},
	"nindent": func(n int, s string) string {
		pad := strings.Repeat(" ", n)
		return "\n" + pad + strings.ReplaceAll(s, "\n", "\n"+pad)
	},
	"toYaml": toYaml,
}

// render is the core of "helm template": build the context (.Release, .Chart,
// .Values), parse the template with the function map, and execute it.
func render(releaseName string, values Values) (string, error) {
	tmpl, err := template.New("deployment.yaml").Funcs(funcs).Parse(deploymentTemplate)
	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}
	ctx := map[string]any{
		"Release": map[string]any{"Name": releaseName, "Namespace": "shop"},
		"Chart":   map[string]any{"Name": "api", "Version": "0.3.0", "AppVersion": "1.7.2"},
		"Values":  values,
	}
	var buf bytes.Buffer
	if err := tmpl.Execute(&buf, ctx); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}
	return buf.String(), nil
}

// diffLines is the "helm diff" idea in ten lines: report lines that differ.
func diffLines(a, b string) []string {
	al, bl := strings.Split(a, "\n"), strings.Split(b, "\n")
	n := len(al)
	if len(bl) > n {
		n = len(bl)
	}
	var out []string
	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
		var x, y string
		if i < len(al) {
			x = al[i]
		}
		if i < len(bl) {
			y = bl[i]
		}
		if x != y {
			out = append(out, fmt.Sprintf("line %2d: dev  %q\n         prod %q", i+1, strings.TrimSpace(x), strings.TrimSpace(y)))
		}
	}
	return out
}

func replicasOf(manifest string) string {
	for _, line := range strings.Split(manifest, "\n") {
		if strings.HasPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(line), "replicas:") {
			return strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(line), "replicas:"))
		}
	}
	return ""
}

func main() {
	// values.yaml: sane defaults that work for a developer laptop.
	base := Values{
		"replicaCount": 1,
		"image":        Values{"repository": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/api", "tag": ""},
		"service":      Values{"port": 8080},
		"env":          Values{"LOG_LEVEL": "debug"},
		"resources": Values{
			"requests": Values{"cpu": "100m", "memory": "128Mi"},
			"limits":   Values{"memory": "256Mi"},
		},
	}
	// values-prod.yaml: only the keys that differ in production.
	prodOverrides := Values{
		"replicaCount": 3,
		"env":          Values{"LOG_LEVEL": "info"},
		"resources": Values{
			"requests": Values{"cpu": "500m", "memory": "512Mi"},
			"limits":   Values{"memory": "1Gi"},
		},
	}

	dev, err := render("api-dev", base)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	prod, err := render("api-prod", merge(base, prodOverrides))
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Println("# helm template api-dev ./api")
	fmt.Print(dev)
	fmt.Println("---")
	fmt.Println("# helm template api-prod ./api -f values-prod.yaml")
	fmt.Print(prod)
	fmt.Println("---")
	fmt.Println("# diff summary (dev vs prod)")
	changes := diffLines(dev, prod)
	for _, c := range changes {
		fmt.Println(c)
	}

	// Self-checks: the things an interviewer would ask you to prove.
	if got := replicasOf(dev); got != "1" {
		panic("dev replicas should be 1, got " + got)
	}
	if got := replicasOf(prod); got != "3" {
		panic("prod replicas should be 3, got " + got)
	}
	if !strings.Contains(dev, `image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/api:1.7.2"`) {
		panic("empty image.tag should fall back to Chart.AppVersion")
	}
	if !strings.Contains(prod, "memory: 1Gi") || !strings.Contains(dev, "memory: 256Mi") {
		panic("resources override did not merge per key")
	}
	if strings.Contains(prod, "containerPort: 8080\n\n") {
		panic("whitespace control failed: blank line after ports")
	}
	fmt.Printf("\nself-check OK: dev replicas=1, prod replicas=3, %d lines differ, image tag fell back to appVersion\n", len(changes))
}
```

## Key takeaways

* A chart is templates plus defaults; a release is one installed copy of a chart with a numbered history stored as Secrets in its namespace.
* Chart `version` changes on every edit and becomes the OCI tag; `appVersion` is only the software version and the default image tag.
* Values merge left to right across `-f` files, `--set` wins, maps merge per key and lists are replaced; `values.schema.json` validates the final result.
* `{{-` and `nindent` are how you control whitespace; `include` not `template`; `required` and `default` for safety.
* `helm upgrade --install --wait --timeout 5m --rollback-on-failure` is the CI invocation; a rollback is a new revision, never a deleted one.
* Hooks run Jobs at lifecycle points by weight; hook resources are not part of the release, so set a delete policy.
* A ConfigMap change only restarts pods if a checksum annotation puts it into the pod template.
* Argo CD renders charts with `helm template` and applies them itself: no release secrets, rollback by Git revert, values in the GitOps repo.

## Common mistakes

* Using `indent` where `nindent` is needed, or forgetting `{{-`, and shipping YAML with a value on the wrong line or an empty line inside a list.
* Changing the labels in `spec.selector` of a Deployment in a chart upgrade. Selectors are immutable; the upgrade fails and the usual fix is uninstall and reinstall, which is downtime.
* Putting `replicas` in the Deployment while an HPA manages it, so every upgrade snaps the count back to the value in values.yaml.
* Committing passwords in values-prod.yaml. They end up in Git history and in every release secret.
* Not bumping `version` in Chart.yaml, so `helm push` to ECR overwrites a tag that other teams have already pulled.
* Running `helm upgrade` without `--wait` in CI and treating a green pipeline as a successful deploy.

## Practice

* Run `helm create api`, replace the templates with the chart from this lesson, and confirm `helm template api ./api -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -` passes on a kind cluster. Count the rendered documents with and without `ingress.enabled=true`.
* Install the chart, change LOG\_LEVEL in values, upgrade, and prove with `kubectl get pods -w` that pods restarted because of the checksum annotation. Remove the annotation, repeat, and confirm they do not.
* Add a pre-upgrade Job hook that runs `exit 1`, upgrade with `--rollback-on-failure --wait --timeout 60s`, and read `helm history` to see the failed revision and the rollback revision. Measure how long Helm waited.
* Write a values.schema.json that requires image.repository and limits replicaCount to 1 through 20, then run `helm lint` with a values file that sets replicaCount to 50 and confirm the error message names the field.

## Interview questions (11)

1.How do you deploy the same application to dev, staging and prod with Helm without copying YAML?Easy

One chart, three small values files. The chart's values.yaml holds defaults that work on a laptop: one replica, no ingress, small resources. Each environment file overrides only what differs, so values-prod.yaml sets replicaCount 3, autoscaling on, the real hostname and the production resource sizes. The install command is the same everywhere with a different `-f` file, and CI passes the image tag with `--set image.tag=`. I keep a values.schema.json so a typo in an environment file fails `helm lint` before it reaches a cluster, and I run `helm template` with each file in CI and diff the output so a chart change is reviewed as rendered YAML, not as template syntax.

2.What happens, step by step, when you run helm upgrade?Medium

Helm loads the chart, merges values from the chart defaults, the `-f` files left to right and `--set`, validates them against the schema, and renders every template into manifests. It reads the last release secret to get the previous manifest, fetches the live objects, and computes a three-way merge so fields other controllers added survive. If there are pre-upgrade hooks it creates them in weight order and waits for the Jobs to finish; a failing Job fails the upgrade. It then applies the manifests through the API server. With `--wait` it polls until the workloads are ready or the timeout expires. Finally it writes a new revision secret, `sh.helm.release.v1.NAME.vN`, with status deployed or failed. With `--rollback-on-failure` a failure triggers a rollback that creates one more revision copying the last good one.

3.Where does Helm store release state, and what does that mean for access control?Easy

In Secrets in the release's own namespace, one per revision, named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<N>` with type `helm.sh/release.v1`, holding the chart, the values and the rendered manifests compressed and base64-encoded. There is no server component since Helm 3 removed Tiller, so Helm acts with the caller's kubeconfig and RBAC: if I cannot create Secrets and Deployments in the namespace, I cannot install there. Two consequences: anything in values ends up readable by anyone who can read Secrets in that namespace, so real secrets must come from an external manager, and `--history-max` matters because each revision is another Secret in etcd.

4.Your ConfigMap changed and helm upgrade succeeded, but pods still show the old config. Why?Medium

A Deployment only rolls its pods when the pod template changes. The ConfigMap object was updated, but the pod template still references it by name, which is unchanged, so no rollout happens. Pods that mount it as a volume will see the new file eventually, but environment variables from `envFrom` are read at container start and never change. The fix is a checksum annotation on the pod template, `checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}`, so any change to the rendered ConfigMap changes the template and triggers a rolling update. The alternative is a tool like Reloader that watches ConfigMaps and restarts Deployments, but the annotation is the standard Helm answer.

5.What is the difference between chart version and appVersion, and when do you bump each?Easy

`version` in Chart.yaml is the version of the chart itself: the templates, the defaults, the dependencies. It follows semver and must change whenever any file in the chart changes, because it becomes the tag of the packaged artifact in the registry; pushing a different chart under the same version breaks every consumer who cached it. `appVersion` is the version of the application the chart deploys, is only informational, and in the standard template is the default image tag. Releasing a new application build bumps appVersion and usually the chart patch version too; fixing a template bug bumps only the chart version.

6.How do Helm hooks work, and what would you use one for?Medium

A hook is any template carrying the `helm.sh/hook` annotation with a lifecycle point: pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade, pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback or test. Helm creates hook resources at that point, in `helm.sh/hook-weight` order from lowest to highest, and for Jobs and Pods it waits for completion; a failure fails the release. The common use is a pre-upgrade Job that runs database migrations before the new pods start. Hook resources are not tracked as part of the release, so I always set `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy`, usually `before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded`, so a finished Job is cleaned up and a stale one from a failed run is replaced next time.

7.An upgrade fails with "field is immutable" on a Deployment selector. What happened and how do you fix it?Hard

Someone changed the labels that feed `spec.selector.matchLabels`, often by changing the chart name or by adding a version label to the selector template. Kubernetes does not allow a Deployment's selector to change after creation, so the apply is rejected and Helm marks the revision failed. The clean fix is to never put mutable labels in the selector: only `app.kubernetes.io/name` and `app.kubernetes.io/instance`, never the version. To recover, there are two paths. For a stateless service with little traffic, uninstall and reinstall, which is downtime. For production, create the new Deployment under a new name in the chart first, let it become ready behind the same Service selector, then remove the old one in a second release. Argo CD users can set the Replace sync option, which deletes and recreates the object, with the same downtime.

8.How does Argo CD use Helm differently from running helm install yourself?Medium

Argo CD treats the chart as a manifest generator. The repo server runs `helm template` with the values from the Application spec (valueFiles, values, valuesObject and parameters, in rising precedence) and the application controller applies the rendered manifests and tracks them with its own labels. Nothing calls `helm install`, so no release secret exists and `helm ls` shows nothing. Helm hooks are mapped onto Argo CD hooks: pre-install and pre-upgrade both become PreSync, hook-weight becomes a sync wave, and test hooks are skipped. Rollback is a Git revert, not `helm rollback`. The benefit is that the values for every environment live in the GitOps repo and every change is a reviewed commit; the cost is that Helm's own features that depend on release state, such as `lookup` and the three-way merge from the last release, do not apply.

9.You are given a third-party chart that hardcodes something you need to change. What are your options?Medium

First check whether a value already covers it, since large charts expose almost everything; `helm show values chart` lists them. If not, the options in order of preference: a post-renderer, which is any program that reads the rendered manifests on stdin and writes patched ones to stdout, usually Kustomize, so I keep the upstream chart unchanged and apply a small patch; wrapping the chart as a dependency of my own chart and adding the extra objects I need next to it; and last, forking the chart, which means I now own its upgrades. I would also open an issue or pull request upstream to turn the hardcoded field into a value, which is the kind of small contribution that gets people started in open source.

10.What goes in values.yaml and what must never go there?Easy

Everything a template reads should have a default in values.yaml that produces a working install: image repository, an empty tag that falls back to appVersion, ports, probes, resource requests, feature switches like ingress.enabled and autoscaling.enabled, and the structures the templates pipe through toYaml such as resources and nodeSelector. What must never be there is any secret: database passwords, API keys, TLS private keys. Values files sit in Git and are copied into every release secret, so a password in values is a password in the repo history and in etcd twice. The chart should instead render an ExternalSecret that pulls from AWS Secrets Manager, or reference a Secret created outside the chart by name.

11.How would you publish a chart so other teams can install it, and how do they get upgrades?Medium

I bump the chart version, run `helm lint` and `helm template` in CI, package it with `helm package`, and push it to an OCI registry: on AWS that is an ECR repository with the same name as the chart, after `aws ecr get-login-password | helm registry login --username AWS --password-stdin`. The pipeline runs `ct lint-and-install` against a kind cluster on every pull request so a broken template never gets a version. Consumers install with `helm install name oci://account.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/api --version 0.3.0` or list it as a dependency with a version range in their Chart.yaml. Upgrades are a version bump in their values or Chart.yaml, reviewed as a pull request, and `helm diff upgrade` in CI shows exactly what will change in the cluster.

## Quiz

1.Which file must change on every edit to a chart's templates?

2.Values are given as `-f base.yaml -f prod.yaml --set replicaCount=5`. prod.yaml sets replicaCount 3. What is the rendered value?

3.Where does Helm 3 and later store the history of a release?

4.A pre-upgrade hook Job fails. What happens to the release?

5.Why does a Deployment template omit replicas when autoscaling is enabled?

# Interview playbook, what is new in 2026, revision sheet

This is the last stop before an interview. It lists the rounds a DevOps, SRE or platform candidate faces in 2026 and what each one tests, gives a fixed structure for troubleshooting and design answers, a table of what changed recently and a line to say about each, a 42-term revision sheet, the 15 questions Indian service and product companies ask most, how to talk about projects, and a one-week plan.

interviewrevisiontroubleshootingsystem designkubernetes2026india

## Why it matters

Most candidates fail interviews they could have passed, not because they lacked knowledge but because they answered a troubleshooting scenario by guessing, a design question without numbers, and "tell me about an outage" without a structure. The content of the earlier lessons is necessary; this lesson is about delivery. Interviewers at Infosys, Capgemini and TCS report asking the same ten things again and again, and product companies add design and incident rounds. Knowing the format lets you spend your nervous energy on the answer instead of on the surprise.

Read first: [Kubernetes in production - resources, autoscaling, RBAC, upgrades, EKS](/devops/learn/kubernetes-in-production), [GitOps with Argo CD and progressive delivery](/devops/learn/gitops-argocd-progressive-delivery), [Observability - Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, logs and alerting](/devops/learn/observability-prometheus-grafana-otel), [SRE practice - SLOs, error budgets, incidents and postmortems](/devops/learn/sre-slos-incidents-postmortems), [Troubleshooting playbook - Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, network, pipelines](/devops/learn/troubleshooting-playbook), [Security and DevSecOps - secrets, least privilege, supply chain, policy as code](/devops/learn/security-and-devsecops)

## Lesson

### The rounds and what each one tests

| Round | Length | What it tests | What a pass looks like |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | 30 min | Resume fundamentals: Linux, Git, Docker, one cloud, one CI tool | Short correct answers; no "I think" on basics |
| Linux and scripting | 45 min, shared screen | `ps`, `ss`, `journalctl`, `df`, `top`, permissions, a script task such as "count 5xx per minute from this log" | You type without a search engine and explain each flag |
| Kubernetes | 45 to 60 min | Two or three scenarios (CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, 502, HPA not scaling), sometimes "write the Deployment YAML live" | Symptom to object to event; YAML with requests, probes, a matching selector |
| CI/CD and IaC design | 45 min | Push to production, Terraform state and modules, secrets, rollbacks | Stages drawn, tests and approvals placed, a bad build stopped |
| System or platform design | 60 min | "Design the platform for 50 services on EKS", "design an uptime monitor"; the DESIGN problems here | Requirements, numbers, diagram, trade-offs, failure modes, operations |
| Incident and behavioural | 30 to 45 min | "Tell me about an outage you handled", on-call habits, disagreement, learning | A timeline, your own actions, the root cause, what changed |

Service companies (Infosys, Wipro, Capgemini, TCS) usually run screening, one technical round mixing Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and a CI tool, then a manager round. Product companies add the design and incident rounds and go deeper on Kubernetes. Jenkins still appears in service-company questions; GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are what newer teams use, and the answer structure is the same for all three.

### How to answer a troubleshooting scenario

Six steps; say each name out loud so the interviewer can follow.

1. **Scope.** One pod, one service or the cluster? Since when? What changed: a deploy, a config, a node?
2. **Protect.** Mitigate before diagnosing: roll back, scale up, fail over, disable the flag. Say that order explicitly.
3. **Follow the path.** Client to pod: DNS, load balancer, Ingress or Gateway, Service, EndpointSlice, pod, container, dependency. Name the command for each hop.
4. **Evidence.** `kubectl describe` events, `kubectl logs --previous`, the exit code, the PromQL, the target health.
5. **Fix through the proper path.** Git and the pipeline, not a hand edit; the exception is a live `kubectl rollout undo` during an outage, and Git is made to match afterwards.
6. **Prevent.** The alert, test, probe, policy or budget that would have caught it earlier.

### How to answer a design question

1. **Clarify** in two or three questions: users, scale, what exists, what "done" means.
2. **Requirements**: three functional, three non-functional with numbers (latency, availability, RPO and RTO, cost).
3. **Numbers**: requests per second, pods, nodes, GB per day, monthly cost. Say the arithmetic.
4. **Design**: boxes in the order traffic flows, then the control plane around them (CI, GitOps, observability, secrets).
5. **Trade-offs**: for each big choice, the one you did not pick and why (EKS vs ECS, Karpenter vs node groups, canary vs blue-green).
6. **Failure modes**: a zone down, a bad deploy, a slow dependency, a leaked secret.
7. **Operations**: who is on call, which SLOs page, how upgrades and cost reviews happen.

No numbers and no failure modes is the most common reason a strong candidate is marked "junior".

### What is new in 2026 and a line you can say

Dated claims were checked on the official pages during writing; everything else is undated.

| Topic | What it is | Why it matters | A line you can say |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Platform engineering, internal developer platforms | A platform team ships golden paths (templates, a Backstage portal, self-service environments) instead of tickets | DORA's 2024 report covers it; job titles say "platform engineer" | "Treat the platform as a product; measure time to first deploy" |
| GitOps as the default | Git is the desired state; Argo CD or Flux pulls it in and reports drift | Auditable rollbacks, no cluster credentials in CI | "Rollback is a revert; Argo CD shows OutOfSync when someone edits live" |
| OpenTelemetry as the standard | One SDK and one Collector for traces, metrics and logs; traces and metrics are Stable in Go, Java, Python and more on the OpenTelemetry status page | Vendor-neutral; interviewers expect "OTel Collector" by name | "Instrument once with OTel, export anywhere through the Collector" |
| Gateway API replacing Ingress for new work | Gateway, GatewayClass and HTTPRoute, GA (v1) since the v1.0 release | The Kubernetes blog says Ingress NGINX best-effort maintenance ends in March 2026 and recommends Gateway API | "HTTPRoute is owned by the app team, the Gateway by the platform team" |
| Karpenter and EKS Auto Mode | Karpenter launches right-sized nodes per pending pod and consolidates; Auto Mode runs it for you with immutable nodes replaced within 21 days | Cheaper and faster than fixed node groups | "NodePool with consolidation, spot for stateless, PDBs to make it safe" |
| eBPF with Cilium | Kernel programs replace iptables; Cilium can fully replace kube-proxy; Hubble shows flows | Policy, load balancing and visibility without sidecars | "L7 network policy and per-flow metrics with no agent in the pod" |
| Supply chain security as a hiring filter | SBOM per image, cosign signatures, SLSA provenance (the spec lists v1.2) | "How do you know the image you run is the one you built" | "SBOM and signed image at build; Kyverno rejects unsigned images at admission" |
| Policy as code at admission | Kyverno or Gatekeeper, and built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (stable since Kubernetes v1.30) with CEL | Enforced rules instead of review comments | "Requests, labels and no latest tag are policy, not convention" |
| FinOps in engineering | Tags, showback with OpenCost (CNCF incubating since October 2024), Infracost on PRs | Cost questions appear in platform rounds | "Right-size, then spot, then commit; Infracost diff on every Terraform PR" |
| AI assistants in CI/CD and incidents | Assistants draft pipeline fixes, summarise alerts and propose runbook steps; a human approves each change | DORA's 2025 research calls AI an amplifier of the surrounding system | "The assistant drafts, a human approves, the pipeline gate stays" |
| GPU and LLM inference as tenants | GPU node pools, the NVIDIA GPU Operator, vLLM or KServe, Dynamic Resource Allocation (stable in Kubernetes v1.35) | Inference is a normal tenant with quotas and SLOs | "A GPU tenant gets a tainted NodePool, a ResourceQuota and a latency SLO" |
| Jenkins giving way to GitHub Actions and GitLab CI | Pipelines as YAML in the repo, runners you can scale, OIDC to the cloud | Jenkins remains common in Indian IT services; newer teams expect Actions or GitLab | "Same stages; what changes is YAML in the repo and OIDC instead of stored keys" |

### The revision sheet: 42 terms, one line each

![The six roadmap modules as horizontal bands, each holding the revision terms that belong to it, with the Kubernetes band highlighted](/devops/img/roadmap-revision-map.svg)The six roadmap modules as horizontal bands, each holding the revision terms that belong to it, with the Kubernetes band highlighted

| Term | One-line answer |
| --- | --- |
| container vs VM | A process isolated by namespaces and cgroups on the host kernel; a VM brings its own kernel |
| image layers | Each Dockerfile instruction is a cached read-only layer; the container adds one writable layer |
| Pod | Smallest scheduled unit: containers sharing an IP and volumes; disposable, replaced not repaired |
| Deployment | Owns ReplicaSets, rolls out within maxSurge and maxUnavailable; `rollout undo` is the fastest rollback |
| Service types | ClusterIP inside, NodePort on every node, LoadBalancer via the cloud, ExternalName as a DNS alias |
| Ingress vs Gateway API | Ingress: host and path rules plus controller annotations; Gateway API: Gateway for the platform team, HTTPRoute for app teams, typed fields |
| requests vs limits | Requests are reserved by the scheduler; limits are enforced: OOM kill for memory, throttling for CPU |
| QoS | Guaranteed when requests equal limits, Burstable when some are set, BestEffort when none; evicted in reverse order |
| probes | Readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts, startup protects slow starters |
| HPA formula | desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / targetMetric), checked every 15 seconds by default |
| PDB | minAvailable or maxUnavailable that voluntary disruptions such as drain must respect |
| taints | A node repels pods without a matching toleration: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute |
| RBAC | A Role lists verbs on resources; a RoleBinding gives it to a user, group or ServiceAccount |
| IRSA vs Pod Identity | IRSA maps a ServiceAccount to an IAM role through the cluster OIDC provider; Pod Identity uses an agent add-on and an association, no per-cluster OIDC trust |
| CNI | The plugin that gives pods IPs: VPC CNI on EKS (real VPC IPs), Cilium (eBPF) |
| EndpointSlice | The ready pod IPs behind a Service, split into slices; replaced Endpoints |
| PV vs PVC | PV is the disk, PVC is the request for one, a StorageClass creates PVs on demand |
| StatefulSet | Stable names, ordered start, one PVC per pod; for databases and Kafka |
| Helm release | One installed chart in a namespace with a revision history; `helm rollback` |
| Argo CD sync | Compare live with Git; OutOfSync means they differ; sync applies, prune deletes extras, selfHeal reverts live edits |
| canary | A small share of traffic goes to the new version; promote on metrics or abort |
| blue-green | Two full environments; switch all traffic at once, switch back to roll back |
| Terraform state | Maps config to real resource IDs; keep it in S3 with locking (`use_lockfile`) |
| drift | Real infrastructure differs from state or config; `terraform plan` shows it |
| module | A reusable Terraform unit with variables and outputs; pin versions by tag |
| OIDC | CI gets a short-lived token and swaps it with AWS STS for a role; no stored keys |
| SLI | A measured indicator: fraction of good requests, latency under a threshold |
| SLO | A target for an SLI over a window: 99.9 percent over 30 days |
| error budget | 1 minus the SLO: 0.1 percent of 30 days is about 43 minutes |
| burn rate | How fast the budget goes; 14.4 for 1 hour spends 2 percent of a 30-day budget |
| RED | Rate, Errors, Duration for every request-driven service |
| golden signals | Latency, traffic, errors, saturation |
| cardinality | Distinct label combinations on a metric; user IDs as labels blow it up |
| histogram\_quantile | `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))` gives p99 |
| trace | One request across services as spans sharing a trace ID; traceparent carries it |
| SBOM | Every package in an image (SPDX or CycloneDX), generated at build and scanned |
| cosign | Signs and verifies images, keyless via Sigstore; a policy checks it at admission |
| Kyverno | YAML policy engine that validates, mutates or generates at admission |
| DORA metrics | Deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time (was MTTR) |
| RPO and RTO | How much data you may lose; how long you may be down |
| token bucket | Tokens refill at a rate up to a capacity; a request spends one or is rejected; capacity is the burst |
| idempotency | Twice gives the same result as once; needed for retries, `kubectl apply`, Terraform |

### The 15 questions Indian DevOps interviews ask most

Confirmed from candidate reports on the Glassdoor pages for Infosys, Capgemini and TCS in the resources, and the bregman-arie exercises.

1. **Docker vs Kubernetes.** Docker builds and runs one container on one host. Kubernetes schedules many containers across hosts, restarts, scales and addresses them. Docker makes the image; Kubernetes runs the fleet through containerd.
2. **Explain your CI/CD pipeline end to end.** Push triggers lint and tests, an image build tagged with the commit SHA, a scan, a signature, a push to the registry. CD updates the tag in the GitOps repo; Argo CD syncs staging, smoke tests run, a canary reaches production. Rollback is a revert.
3. **A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff; debug it.** `kubectl describe pod` for the exit code and events, `kubectl logs --previous` for the crash output. Usual causes: a missing env or secret, a wrong command, a failing migration, OOMKilled, a liveness probe too strict. Fix in Git, redeploy, confirm restarts stop.
4. **Requests vs limits.** Requests are what the scheduler reserves and the HPA measures against; limits are enforced at run time. Memory over the limit is OOM-killed; CPU over it is throttled. Memory requests equal limits; CPU requests from measurement.
5. **Where is the Terraform state file?** In S3 with versioning and encryption, locking on with `use_lockfile` (the DynamoDB method is deprecated). One state per environment, never in Git. Locking stops two applies at once.
6. **What is an init container?** It runs to completion before the app containers start: wait for a database, run a migration, fetch config. If it fails the pod restarts it, so the app never starts half-configured.
7. **Kubernetes deployment strategies.** RollingUpdate (default, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable) and Recreate; above the Deployment, blue-green and canary with Argo Rollouts or weighted HTTPRoutes. Pick canary when you can measure errors per version.
8. **What happens when a developer pushes to GitHub?** The webhook starts the workflow; a runner checks out the commit, tests and builds; on success it pushes the image and updates the manifest. Branch protection blocks the merge until checks pass.
9. **CMD vs ENTRYPOINT.** ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs; CMD gives default arguments that `docker run` can override. Use exec form so signals reach the process: `ENTRYPOINT ["python","app.py"]`, `CMD ["--port","8080"]`.
10. **How does a Service find its pods?** By label selector; the EndpointSlice controller lists ready pod IPs; kube-proxy or Cilium forwards the virtual IP to them. No endpoints means a selector typo or failed readiness.
11. **PV vs PVC.** The PV is the storage; the PVC is the pod's request for size and access mode. A StorageClass creates PVs dynamically (EBS CSI on EKS). The reclaim policy decides whether the disk survives.
12. **Autoscaling and path routing in production.** HPA on CPU or a custom metric for pods, Karpenter for nodes, and an Ingress or HTTPRoute sending `/api` and `/web` to different Services. PDBs so scale-down never drops below the minimum.
13. **AWS load balancer types.** ALB for HTTP with host and path routing and WAF; NLB for TCP and UDP with static IPs; Gateway Load Balancer for inline appliances. On EKS the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates them.
14. **Linux troubleshooting.** `top` and `free -m`, `df -h`, `ss -tlnp` for ports, `journalctl -u name` for a service, `dmesg` for the kernel. Then the process itself. Fix, then write the alert.
15. **A shell script that saved time.** Problem, what it did, the number: "a log analyser counting 5xx per endpoint per minute cut triage from 20 minutes to 1". Add `set -euo pipefail`, a temp dir and a dry-run flag.

### Talking about projects and open source

Five beats for any project: the **problem** in one sentence, the **design** as a 30-second diagram, the **numbers** (requests, nodes, cost, time saved), **what broke** and how you found it, **what you would change** now. For open source, add the review: what the maintainer asked for and why. "I fixed a nil check" is weak; "the reconciler panicked when the status subresource was missing, I added the check and a test, and the maintainer asked me to return an error so the item is requeued" shows you understood the control loop.

## Worked example

**"A deploy went out and error rate jumped from 0.1 to 4 percent. What do you do?"** A 3-minute answer, as you would say it.

"First I scope it. I check whether the jump lines up with the deploy time and whether it is this service only: `kubectl rollout history deployment/checkout -n payments` shows revision 14 went out at 14:02, and the error rate in Grafana rises at 14:03. One service, one change: the deploy is the prime suspect.

Second, I protect users before I diagnose. Four percent errors on checkout is money, so I roll back now: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/checkout -n payments`, then `kubectl rollout status deployment/checkout -n payments` to watch it finish. If Argo CD manages this app I also revert the commit in the GitOps repo, otherwise Argo CD will sync the bad version straight back. I confirm with the PromQL I already have on the dashboard: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",code=~"5.."}[2m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[2m]))` should fall back under 0.1 percent within two minutes.

Third, with users safe, I look for the cause. `kubectl get pods -n payments -l app=checkout` tells me if the new pods were crashing or healthy. If they were Running with no restarts, the errors came from inside the app: `kubectl logs deployment/checkout -n payments --since=10m | grep -c ' 500 '` and the first stack trace. Typical causes: a new config key the pods could not read, a database migration that ran ahead of the code, a timeout to a dependency that the new version calls more often. If pods were restarting, `kubectl describe pod` for the exit code and `kubectl logs --previous`.

Fourth, I fix it through the pipeline: the fix is a commit, it goes through CI, and it ships as revision 16. No hand edits in the cluster.

Fifth, I prevent it. This should have been caught before 4 percent: a canary with an analysis template that compares 5xx rate of the new version with the stable one over five minutes and aborts automatically, a readiness probe that fails if the config is missing, and an alert on 5xx ratio with a 2-minute window so a human sees it in one minute, not ten.

I would close with: the deploy caused it, we rolled back within three minutes, the fix was X, and from now on a canary gate stops this at 1 percent of traffic."

## Key takeaways

* Know the round before you enter it: screening, Linux and scripting, Kubernetes scenarios, CI/CD and IaC, design, incident. Each has a different pass condition.
* Troubleshooting answers follow scope, protect, follow the path, evidence, fix through the proper path, prevent. Say the step names.
* Design answers need numbers, trade-offs and failure modes, or you will be graded as junior.
* The 2026 defaults to say by name: GitOps, OpenTelemetry, Gateway API, Karpenter, Cilium, SBOM and cosign, policy at admission, FinOps, human-approved AI assistance, GPU tenants, GitHub Actions and GitLab CI.
* Indian service-company rounds repeat the same 15 questions; prepare three-line answers and the one command that proves each.
* Tell a project as problem, design, numbers, what broke, what you would change.
* Mitigate before you diagnose, and fix through Git afterwards; interviewers listen for that order.
* Rehearse out loud with a timer; reading is not practice.

## Common mistakes

* Starting a troubleshooting answer with a guess ("it is probably DNS") instead of scoping and protecting first.
* Giving a design with no numbers, no cost and no failure modes.
* Saying "Kubernetes runs Docker", "Secrets are encrypted" or "liveness probe removes the pod from the Service".
* Describing a project without a number: no requests per second, no time saved, no cost.
* Claiming tools you cannot demonstrate; interviewers follow up on every tool in your resume.
* Fixing the scenario with a hand edit in the cluster and never mentioning Git or the pipeline.

## Practice

* Run the flashcard drill for the kubernetes module with count 10, say each answer before reading it, and record how many you got right; repeat daily until 10 of 10.
* Record yourself answering the deploy scenario in the worked example in under 3 minutes, then listen for the six step names; redo it until all six are said out loud.
* In a kind cluster, break a Deployment three ways (wrong image tag, missing ConfigMap key, liveness probe on the wrong port) and time yourself from symptom to root cause using only describe, logs and events; target under 5 minutes each.
* Write your three projects in the five-beat format (problem, design, numbers, what broke, what you would change) in under 120 words each and have a friend ask one follow-up per beat.

## Interview questions (10)

1.Tell me about an outage you handled.Medium

I give a timeline. "At 14:02 a deploy of the checkout service went out; at 14:05 the 5xx alert fired at 4 percent. I was on call. I checked rollout history, saw the deploy matched the time, and rolled back at 14:08; error rate was back under 0.1 percent by 14:10. The cause was a config key renamed in the new version with no default, so half the requests failed on a nil value. The fix went through a PR with a test for the missing key, and we added a canary step with automatic analysis on 5xx ratio, so the same bug now stops at 5 percent of traffic. The postmortem was blameless and the action items are closed." Timeline, my action, root cause, prevention.

2.Pods are Pending after you scaled a Deployment. What do you check first?Easy

`kubectl describe pod` and read the Events: the scheduler writes why it could not place the pod. The usual messages are insufficient cpu or memory, no nodes matched a nodeSelector or affinity, an untolerated taint, or a PVC that cannot bind in that zone. If it is capacity, I check whether Karpenter or the Cluster Autoscaler is adding a node and whether the NodePool limits or the account quota block it. If it is a selector or taint, I fix the manifest in Git. I never fix Pending by deleting pods; the scheduler will produce the same result.

3.How would you design a CI/CD pipeline for 30 microservices in one repo?Hard

I clarify languages, deploy target and how often teams ship. Then: a monorepo pipeline that detects changed paths so only affected services build; each build runs lint and unit tests, builds a multi-stage image tagged with the commit SHA, scans it, generates an SBOM and signs it with cosign, and pushes to ECR using OIDC rather than stored keys. CD is GitOps: the pipeline updates the image tag in a config repo, Argo CD syncs staging, smoke tests run, then a canary in production with automatic analysis. Numbers: 30 services, maybe 200 builds a day, so caching and self-hosted runners matter. Failure modes: a flaky test blocks everyone, so I quarantine flaky tests; a bad base image breaks every build, so I pin digests.

4.What is new in Kubernetes networking that you would use on a new cluster?Medium

Gateway API instead of Ingress for anything new: Gateway and GatewayClass owned by the platform team, HTTPRoute owned by each app team, with typed fields for header matching and traffic weights instead of controller-specific annotations. The Kubernetes project announced that Ingress NGINX best-effort maintenance ends in March 2026, so new work should not start on it. For the CNI I would consider Cilium, which can replace kube-proxy with eBPF and gives L7 network policy and per-flow observability through Hubble. On EKS I would keep VPC CNI if the team already knows it and add Cilium only when policy or observability demands it.

5.Why GitOps rather than kubectl apply from the pipeline?Easy

With GitOps the cluster pulls its desired state from Git through Argo CD or Flux, so the pipeline never needs cluster credentials, every change is a reviewed commit, rollback is a revert, and drift is visible: if someone edits live, the app shows OutOfSync and selfHeal can revert it. With kubectl apply from CI you have cluster-admin tokens in the CI system, no record of what is actually running beyond the last successful job, and no way to detect hand edits. The cost is one more repo and the discipline to change nothing by hand.

6.How do you talk about an open-source contribution in an interview?Easy

Problem, design, numbers, what broke, what I would change, plus the review. For example: "Karpenter logged a misleading message when a NodePool limit was hit; I traced it to the consolidation path, added the limit name to the log and a unit test, and the maintainer asked me to use structured fields instead of string formatting. The PR took three rounds over two weeks." That shows I can read a Go controller, write a test, and take review. I would avoid listing a one-line typo fix as a contribution unless I can explain the code around it.

7.A design question: an uptime monitor for 10,000 URLs checked every minute. Walk me through it.Hard

Clarify: check type (HTTP status and latency), regions, alert channels. Numbers: 10,000 checks a minute is 167 per second, trivially small; the hard part is false alerts, so each failure is confirmed from a second region before alerting. Design: a scheduler that pushes due checks to a queue (Redis Streams or SQS), stateless workers in three regions that run checks and write results to a time-series store, an alert evaluator that applies "down if 2 regions fail twice in a row", and a web app. Failure modes: a worker region loses the internet and reports everything down, so quorum; a slow target holds a worker, so timeouts; the queue backs up, so a lag metric and autoscaling on it. Operations: SLO on check delay, cost per million checks.

8.What does a strong answer to "requests vs limits" sound like?Easy

Requests are what the scheduler reserves when placing the pod and what the HPA uses for its percentage; limits are enforced at run time by the kernel, OOM-kill for memory and CFS throttling for CPU. Requests also decide the QoS class, which decides eviction order under node pressure. My defaults: memory requests equal limits so the pod is never killed for someone else's spike, CPU requests from the measured p95, and I am careful with CPU limits because throttling shows up as latency that is hard to see. Then the follow-up they want: no requests at all means BestEffort and first to be evicted.

9.What do you do in the first minute of an incident?Medium

Acknowledge the page so nobody else gets woken, open the dashboard for the service, and answer three questions: what is the user impact, when did it start, and what changed. If a deploy or config change lines up with the start, I roll it back before any deeper diagnosis, because mitigation beats root cause while users are affected. I post a one-line status in the incident channel with the impact and what I am doing. Only then do I open logs and events. If the impact is large or spreading I ask for an incident commander so I can focus on the technical work.

10.What is new in 2026 that you have actually used?Medium

Be honest and specific. "I used Gateway API with HTTPRoutes on a kind cluster and on EKS with the AWS Load Balancer Controller; I ran Karpenter with a NodePool that consolidates and uses spot; I instrumented a Go service with the OpenTelemetry SDK and sent traces through the Collector to Tempo; and I signed images with cosign and blocked unsigned ones with a Kyverno policy." Then one thing you have only read about, said as such: "I have read the EKS Auto Mode docs but have not run it." Interviewers trust a candidate who draws the line between done and read.

# Kubernetes architecture and core objects

Kubernetes runs containers across a fleet of machines. You describe the state you want in YAML (three copies of this image, reachable on port 80) and a set of control loops makes the cluster match it and keeps it matched when things fail. This lesson covers the control plane, the worker node, the core objects (Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace) and the kubectl commands interviewers expect you to know cold.

kubernetespodsdeploymentsservicescontrol planekubectleks

## Why it matters

Kubernetes appears in almost every DevOps, SRE and platform engineering job post, and in Indian interviews it is the topic most likely to decide the outcome. The questions are rarely "what is a pod". They are "what happens when you run kubectl apply", "why does the pod say Running when the app is broken", "what does a Service actually do". Every one of those has a precise answer that comes from the architecture, and every troubleshooting scenario in later lessons starts from the same picture. Learn the picture once and the rest follows.

Read first: [Containers and Docker](/devops/learn/containers-and-docker), [Networking for DevOps - TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, SSH](/devops/learn/networking-for-devops), [AWS managed platforms - EKS, ECS, Fargate, Lambda, SQS, ElastiCache, CloudFront](/devops/learn/aws-managed-platforms-eks-ecs)

## Lesson

### What Kubernetes is for

Docker runs one container on one machine. Production needs more: run many copies, spread them over machines, restart them when they die, replace them during a release, give them a stable address, and scale them with load. Kubernetes (K8s, with 8 letters between the K and the s) is the system that does all of that. It grew out of two Google systems, Borg and Omega, which had done the same job for Google's own services for a decade.

The core idea is declarative state. You do not tell Kubernetes "start a container". You write down the state you want and Kubernetes keeps the cluster in that state. If a machine dies, the system notices that the real state no longer matches the desired state and starts replacements elsewhere. You never issue the repair command.

### The control plane

![Kubernetes control plane components above two worker nodes, with every component talking to the API server](/devops/img/kubernetes-architecture.svg)Kubernetes control plane components above two worker nodes, with every component talking to the API server

The control plane is the set of processes that hold the desired state and run the control loops. On a managed service such as Amazon EKS, AWS runs these for you and you only see an API endpoint. On a self-managed cluster they run on three machines so the cluster survives one failing.

| Component | What it does | What breaks if it is down |
| --- | --- | --- |
| kube-apiserver | The front door. Every read and write of cluster state is an HTTP request here. It authenticates, authorises (RBAC), runs admission checks and writes to etcd | kubectl stops working; running pods keep running but nothing can change |
| etcd | A consistent key-value store that holds every object. It uses the Raft consensus algorithm, so it needs an odd number of members (3 or 5) | Everything freezes; this is the one component that must be backed up |
| kube-scheduler | Watches for pods with no node assigned and picks a node for each one, based on resource requests, affinities, taints and tolerations | New pods stay Pending; existing pods are unaffected |
| kube-controller-manager | Runs the built-in control loops: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, EndpointSlice and many more | Pods are not replaced when they die; scaling and rollouts stop |
| cloud-controller-manager | Talks to the cloud API: creates load balancers for Services, labels nodes with zones, removes nodes the cloud deleted | New LoadBalancer Services never get an address |

The single rule that explains the whole design: nothing talks to etcd except the API server, and every other component is a client of the API server. The scheduler, the controllers and every kubelet all do the same thing: watch for objects they care about and act when they change.

### The worker node

A worker node is a machine (an EC2 instance in an EKS node group, a VM, or a bare-metal host) that runs pods. Three processes live on every node.

* **kubelet** registers the node with the API server, watches for pods assigned to that node, asks the container runtime to start them, runs the liveness and readiness probes, and reports pod status back.
* **container runtime** does the actual work of pulling images and starting containers. Kubernetes talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI); containerd is the usual runtime today. Docker as a runtime was removed from the kubelet in version 1.24, which is why "Kubernetes runs Docker" is now a wrong answer.
* **kube-proxy** programs the node's networking (iptables rules by default, nftables as the newer mode) so that traffic to a Service's virtual IP is sent to one of the healthy pods behind it. Some network plugins (Cilium) replace it with eBPF programs.

### The Pod

A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP address, one set of ports) and can share volumes. Most pods have one container. A second container in the same pod is a sidecar: a log shipper, a proxy, an agent. Containers in a pod are always scheduled together on the same node.

Pods are disposable. A pod is never moved or repaired; when its node dies, the pod is gone and a controller creates a new one with a new name and IP. This is why you almost never create a bare pod by hand and why nothing should depend on a pod's IP.

The pod lifecycle, as `kubectl get pods` shows it:

| Phase or status | Meaning | First thing to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pending | Accepted but not yet running: no node chosen, or the image is still pulling | `kubectl describe pod`: Events at the bottom |
| ContainerCreating | Node chosen, kubelet is pulling the image and mounting volumes | Events; image size; volume attach |
| Running | At least one container started | Readiness: is it in the Service's endpoints? |
| CrashLoopBackOff | The container keeps exiting and kubelet is waiting longer between restarts | `kubectl logs --previous` |
| ImagePullBackOff | The image name, tag or registry credentials are wrong | Events: the exact pull error |
| OOMKilled (in last state) | The container used more memory than its limit | Limits and the app's real usage |
| Completed / Error | A Job or one-shot pod finished | Exit code in describe |

"Running" means a process started. It says nothing about whether the application works. That is what probes are for.

### Deployments and ReplicaSets

A **ReplicaSet** keeps N identical pods running. Its controller counts pods matching a label selector; too few, it creates; too many, it deletes. A **Deployment** owns ReplicaSets and handles change. When you update the image in a Deployment, the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods from old to new in steps, bounded by two settings.

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  labels:
    app: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1          # up to 4 pods during the rollout
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never drop below 3 ready pods
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/api:1.4.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 10
```

Three parts of this file matter in every interview. The `selector` must match the `template` labels, or the Deployment cannot find its own pods. `requests` are what the scheduler uses to place the pod and `limits` are what the kernel enforces. The readiness probe decides whether the pod receives traffic; the liveness probe decides whether kubelet restarts it. A liveness probe that is too aggressive is the classic self-inflicted outage: the app is slow to start, liveness fails, kubelet restarts it, and it never finishes starting.

`kubectl rollout status deployment/api` follows a rollout, `kubectl rollout history` lists revisions, and `kubectl rollout undo` goes back one revision, which is the fastest rollback in Kubernetes because the old ReplicaSet still exists at zero replicas.

### Services: a stable address for disposable pods

Pods come and go with new IPs, so clients need something stable. A **Service** is a virtual IP and a DNS name that load-balances across the pods selected by a label. The EndpointSlice controller keeps the list of ready pod IPs behind the Service current; kube-proxy turns that list into forwarding rules on every node. Only pods that pass their readiness probe are in the list.

| Service type | Reachable from | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ClusterIP (default) | Inside the cluster only, at `name.namespace.svc.cluster.local` | Service-to-service calls |
| NodePort | A fixed port (30000 to 32767) on every node | Rarely in production; demos and some on-prem setups |
| LoadBalancer | A cloud load balancer the cloud controller creates (on EKS, an NLB through the AWS Load Balancer Controller; an ALB comes from an Ingress, not a Service) | Exposing one service to the internet |
| ExternalName | A DNS alias to a name outside the cluster | Pointing at an RDS endpoint by a short name |

Most clusters expose many HTTP services through one load balancer plus an **Ingress** (or the newer Gateway API), which routes by host and path. That is the next lesson.

### ConfigMaps, Secrets and Namespaces

A **ConfigMap** holds non-secret configuration (key-value pairs or whole files) and a **Secret** holds credentials. Both reach a pod as environment variables or as files in a mounted volume. A Secret is base64-encoded in the API, which is encoding, not encryption: anyone with read access to Secrets in a namespace can read every value. Real protection comes from RBAC, from encrypting etcd at rest, and from pulling secrets from a manager such as AWS Secrets Manager with the External Secrets Operator.

A **Namespace** is a scope for names and for access control. `api` in `payments` and `api` in `search` are different objects. Namespaces are where you attach RBAC roles, resource quotas and network policies, so one team's mistake stays inside its namespace.

Other objects you will meet soon: **DaemonSet** (one pod per node, used for log and metrics agents), **StatefulSet** (pods with stable names and their own disks, for databases and Kafka), **Job** and **CronJob** (run to completion), **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** (change `replicas` from metrics), **PersistentVolumeClaim** (ask for a disk).

### What happens when you run kubectl apply

This is the question that separates people who have used Kubernetes from people who understand it. The sequence diagram below is the answer; in words:

1. kubectl reads your YAML, authenticates with the cluster from your kubeconfig, and sends a request to the API server.
2. The API server authenticates and authorises you, runs admission controllers (which can reject or mutate the object), validates the schema and writes the Deployment to etcd.
3. The Deployment controller sees a new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet controller sees it and creates three Pod objects with no node assigned.
4. The scheduler sees three unscheduled pods, filters nodes that have room and match constraints, scores the rest and writes the chosen node name into each pod.
5. The kubelet on each chosen node sees a pod assigned to it, pulls the image through containerd, sets up networking through the CNI plugin, starts the containers and begins probing.
6. Once a pod's readiness probe passes, the EndpointSlice controller adds its IP behind the Service, kube-proxy updates the rules on every node, and traffic flows.

Nothing in that chain is a direct call from one component to the next. Each step is a component noticing a change in the API server and acting on it. That is why a crashed controller does not lose work: when it restarts, it reads the current state and continues.

### The kubectl commands to know cold

```
kubectl get pods -n payments -o wide            # phase, restarts, node, IP
kubectl describe pod api-7d9f6b7c5-x2k4p         # events at the bottom tell you why
kubectl logs api-7d9f6b7c5-x2k4p --previous      # logs of the last crashed container
kubectl exec -it api-7d9f6b7c5-x2k4p -- sh       # a shell inside the container
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp      # what the cluster did recently
kubectl rollout status deployment/api            # follow a release
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api              # fastest rollback
kubectl scale deployment/api --replicas=5
kubectl get svc,endpointslices -n payments       # is anything behind the Service?
kubectl top pods                                 # CPU and memory, needs metrics-server
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy         # built-in reference for any field
```

### Backing up and restoring etcd on a self-managed cluster

On EKS you never touch etcd. On a cluster you run yourself (kubeadm, on-prem, CKA exam style), backing it up is your job, because losing etcd means losing every object in the cluster. The client tool is `etcdctl`; since etcd 3.5 the offline tasks (checking and restoring a snapshot) moved to `etcdutl`, and the `etcdctl` versions of those commands are deprecated.

```
# Take a snapshot from a running member (kubeadm certificate paths)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db

# Check the file: hash, revision, number of keys, size
etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status /backup/etcd-2026-11-04.db

# Restore into a NEW data directory, then point etcd at it
etcdutl --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore snapshot restore /backup/etcd-2026-11-04.db
# kubeadm: edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml so the etcd-data hostPath
# is /var/lib/etcd-restore; kubelet restarts the static etcd pod by itself
```

Three rules matter. Restore into a new directory, or stop etcd and delete the old one first. Copy snapshots off the machine, because a backup on the node that died is no backup. And test a restore on a scratch cluster, since a snapshot nobody restored is only a hope. A snapshot holds Secrets, so encrypt it and treat it like a credential.

### Where EKS differs

On Amazon EKS, AWS runs the control plane across three availability zones and you pay a flat hourly fee for it. You choose how worker nodes run: managed node groups (EC2 instances AWS creates and upgrades for you), self-managed nodes, or Fargate (no nodes at all; each pod gets its own micro VM). Identity is tied to IAM: your kubectl token comes from your AWS credentials, and pods get AWS permissions through IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) or the newer EKS Pod Identity, so a pod can read an S3 bucket without any access key in a Secret. Networking uses the VPC CNI plugin, which gives each pod a real VPC IP address. The details are in the production lesson; for now, remember that the architecture is identical and only who operates each part changes.
