# Platform engineering, service mesh and eBPF

Platform engineering treats the internal tooling that developers use to ship software as a product with customers. This lesson covers what an internal developer platform (IDP) is, golden paths, Backstage and Crossplane, and how to measure a platform. It then covers the two technologies platform teams are asked about most: service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) with their real costs, and eBPF with Cilium, which moves networking, policy and observability into the kernel.

platform engineeringbackstagecrossplaneistiociliumebpfservice mesh

## Why it matters

"Platform engineer" is now a job title at most companies that run more than a few teams on Kubernetes, and the interview for it is different from a DevOps interview. You are asked how you would reduce the work a developer does to ship a service, how you would decide whether a mesh is worth its cost, and what eBPF changes about networking and security. These are judgment questions with numbers behind them. A candidate who can say "a sidecar per pod costs about this much, and here is when I would not pay it" stands out from one who only lists tool names.

Read first: [Kubernetes networking and storage](/devops/learn/kubernetes-networking-storage), [Kubernetes in production - resources, autoscaling, RBAC, upgrades, EKS](/devops/learn/kubernetes-in-production), [GitOps with Argo CD and progressive delivery](/devops/learn/gitops-argocd-progressive-delivery)

## Lesson

### Platform engineering is a product discipline

A platform team builds and runs the internal developer platform (IDP): the set of tools, templates and services that a product team uses to build, deploy and operate software. The difference from a traditional operations team is the stance. The platform team's customers are the developers. The platform is a product with a roadmap, documentation, support hours and a measure of success. Nobody is forced to use it; it wins by being the easiest way to do things right.

The problem it solves is cognitive load. A developer who wants to ship one small service today must know Dockerfiles, Helm, Argo CD, IAM, alert rules, dashboards, secrets, network policies and cost tags. Each is learnable. All of them together, for every team, is a tax paid again and again. The platform's job is to take that load off the developer without taking away control.

The tool for that is the **golden path** (also called a paved road): a supported, documented, opinionated way to do a common task, from "create a new Go service" to "get a Postgres database". You can leave the path, but then you own the result. A good platform API hides the parts that are the same for everyone and exposes only the decisions that belong to the team.

What the API looks like in practice: a developer opens one pull request that adds a short service manifest to a repository. Merging it creates a namespace with quotas and a NetworkPolicy, a CI pipeline, a Grafana dashboard with the RED panels, alert rules against the team's SLO, an IAM role for the pod, and an Argo CD Application that watches the service's own repository. The developer never wrote any of those objects.

```
# service.yaml: everything the developer decides. Everything else comes from the template.
apiVersion: platform.example.org/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  team: payments            # owner, on-call rotation, cost tag
  language: go              # picks the pipeline and the base image
  tier: 2                   # picks the SLO target, 99.9 for tier 2
  database: postgres        # provisions a database through Crossplane
  publicIngress: true
```

### The tools: Backstage, Port, Crossplane, Score

| Tool | What it is | What it gives the platform |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backstage | Open source developer portal from Spotify, a CNCF Incubation project | Software Catalog (every service with owner, docs, links), Software Templates (scaffold a repository from a form), TechDocs (docs-as-code next to the code), plugins |
| Port | A commercial developer portal with the same catalog and self-service ideas | Faster to set up than Backstage, less to run |
| Crossplane | A CNCF control plane framework that provisions cloud resources through Kubernetes APIs | A team asks for a database as a Kubernetes object; the platform decides what that means in AWS |
| Score | A CNCF Sandbox workload specification | Describe a workload once, render it to Compose for a laptop or to Kubernetes for production |
| Argo CD | GitOps delivery (lesson 19) | The reconciler that applies everything the template generated |

Crossplane deserves one more paragraph because interviewers compare it with Terraform. In Crossplane, a provider installs managed resources (an RDS instance, an IAM role) as Kubernetes custom resources. A **Composition** describes how a high-level object such as `PostgresDatabase` is built from managed resources, and a composition function (written in Go or Python) can compute that build. A **composite resource** (XR) is an instance of that high-level type; since Crossplane v2 an XR is namespaced by default, and a composition can compose any Kubernetes resource, a Deployment as much as an RDS instance. **Claims**, the namespaced hand-off object of Crossplane v1, exist only for legacy cluster-scoped XRs. The difference from Terraform is not the resources, it is the loop: Terraform runs plan and apply when someone runs it and stores state in a file; Crossplane reconciles forever, so a security group changed by hand in the console is put back within minutes, and access is Kubernetes RBAC rather than a pipeline's credentials. Many platforms use both: Terraform for the cluster and the account, Crossplane for what teams ask for day to day.

### Measuring a platform

A platform without measurement becomes a tooling team that ships features nobody asked for. Four numbers tell you whether it works.

| Metric | How to measure | What a good number looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adoption | Share of services created through the golden path | Rising; teams choosing the path without being told |
| Time to first deploy | Minutes from "new service" to the first production deploy | Under one hour on the path, days off it |
| DORA metrics per team | Deploy frequency, lead time, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time | Teams on the platform beat teams off it |
| Cognitive load | A survey, plus the number of tools a developer must touch to ship | Falling release over release |

Report these per team, because the platform's job is to make the median team fast, not to make the best team faster.

### Service mesh: what it solves and what it costs

A service mesh puts a proxy in the path of every service-to-service call and controls those proxies from one place. That gives you mutual TLS (mTLS, both sides present certificates) between all pods without touching the code, retries and timeouts set by policy, traffic shifting for canaries (send 5 percent of calls to v2), and uniform telemetry: latency, error rate and a trace span for every hop.

The cost is real. In the classic sidecar mode, every pod gets an Envoy proxy container, so every request crosses two extra proxies. Istio's own performance page reports, measured with Istio 1.24 at 1000 requests per second with 1 KB payloads, about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB of memory per sidecar with 2 worker threads. Multiply by pods. Add the latency of two proxy hops per call, the YAML of VirtualService and DestinationRule objects, and the upgrade of a proxy inside every pod when the mesh version changes.

![Three data paths for a request between two pods: a sidecar proxy in every pod, a per-node ztunnel with an optional waypoint, and eBPF programs in the kernel](/devops/img/mesh-sidecar-ambient-ebpf.svg)Three data paths for a request between two pods: a sidecar proxy in every pod, a per-node ztunnel with an optional waypoint, and eBPF programs in the kernel

**Istio ambient mode** removes the sidecar. A per-node Rust proxy called **ztunnel** handles the Layer 4 work: mTLS, L4 authorization and telemetry, without parsing HTTP. Where a team needs Layer 7 features (retries, header routing, traffic shifting) it adds a **waypoint**, an Envoy deployment that runs per namespace, outside the application pods, and is scaled and upgraded on its own. Istio's feature status page, as of its 1.31 release, lists both ztunnel core and waypoints core as Stable. The same Istio page reports a ztunnel at about 0.06 vCPU and 12 MB under the test above, and that is per node, not per pod. Installation is `istioctl install --set profile=ambient` and a namespace joins the mesh with the label `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient`. Sidecar and ambient workloads can share one mesh, so migration can be gradual.

**Linkerd** is the other common mesh: a CNCF graduated project with a small, purpose-built Rust proxy (linkerd2-proxy) as the sidecar, fewer features than Istio and much less configuration.

When should a team not adopt a mesh? When it has under about ten services, when it only needs mTLS (Cilium can encrypt node-to-node traffic and a cert-manager-issued certificate at the ingress may be enough), when nobody on the team has run Envoy before, or when the main pressure is cost. Retries and timeouts can live in the client library; metrics can come from OpenTelemetry. A mesh pays off when many teams need the same traffic policy, security policy and telemetry and you cannot change every codebase.

### eBPF and Cilium

**eBPF** lets you run small programs inside the Linux kernel, attached to events such as a packet arriving, a system call, or a function being entered, without changing the kernel or loading a module. A verifier checks each program before it loads (bounded loops, memory access only through checked helpers, a size limit), so a bad program is rejected instead of crashing the machine. The programs are then JIT-compiled and run at native speed.

**Cilium** is the CNI plugin built on eBPF and the usual answer when an interviewer asks what eBPF changes in Kubernetes:

* **Networking without kube-proxy.** With the Helm value `kubeProxyReplacement=true`, Cilium implements ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer Services in eBPF, at the socket level for pod-originated traffic, so there are no iptables chains to walk and no kube-proxy DaemonSet.
* **NetworkPolicy and more.** Standard NetworkPolicy plus CiliumNetworkPolicy with identity-aware rules at L3 to L7, including DNS-name and HTTP-path rules.
* **Hubble observability.** Flow logs, service maps and drop reasons for every connection, exported to Prometheus, with no change to the application.
* **Mesh-like features without sidecars.** Transparent encryption between nodes (WireGuard or IPsec), L7 policy, and Gateway API support, with an Envoy proxy only where L7 handling is required.

```
# Install Cilium on a cluster that was created without kube-proxy
helm install cilium cilium/cilium --namespace kube-system \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
  --set k8sServiceHost=${API_SERVER_IP} \
  --set k8sServicePort=${API_SERVER_PORT}
cilium status                                 # agent, operator and Hubble health
hubble observe --namespace payments --verdict DROPPED   # who is being blocked and why
```

Two other eBPF tools to know by name: **Pixie** (CNCF Sandbox) collects request-level telemetry from Kubernetes applications with no instrumentation, and **Falco** (CNCF graduated) watches system calls through an eBPF probe and raises an alert when a container does something it should not, such as spawning a shell or reading `/etc/shadow`.

### Multi-cluster and multi-region in one paragraph

Past a certain size you run a fleet of clusters, not one: one per region, per environment, or per blast-radius boundary. The fleet is managed the same way as the services on it. Terraform or Crossplane creates each cluster from the same module, Argo CD registers every cluster and an ApplicationSet with the cluster generator stamps the platform add-ons and each team's applications onto every cluster whose Secret carries the right labels. A global load balancer (Route 53 latency or failover records, or Cloudflare in front of regional load balancers) sends users to the nearest healthy region, and a service mesh or Cilium cluster mesh lets services find each other across clusters when they must. The rule that makes this work: no cluster is special, so any cluster can be rebuilt from Git.

## Worked example

**What a sidecar mesh costs for 300 pods, against ambient and eBPF.** Every price and size here is an assumption for the arithmetic; replace them with your own.

Assume 300 application pods and a sidecar that reserves 0.1 vCPU and 128 MiB per pod. The mesh adds 300 x 0.1 = 30 vCPU and 300 x 128 MiB = 38,400 MiB = 37.5 GiB of memory that must come from somewhere.

Assume the cluster runs 4 vCPU, 16 GiB nodes and that, after the kubelet, the CNI agent and the system reservation, each node has 3.6 vCPU and 14 GiB allocatable. CPU needs 30 / 3.6 = 8.33, so 9 extra nodes. Memory needs 37.5 / 14 = 2.68, so 3 nodes. CPU is the binding constraint: 9 nodes. At an assumed 0.192 USD per node-hour and 730 hours a month, that is 9 x 0.192 x 730 = 1,261 USD a month, before the latency of two proxy hops on every call.

Now the ambient alternative. The 300 pods at about 8 pods per node sit on about 38 nodes; call it 40. A ztunnel runs once per node. Assume it reserves the same 0.1 vCPU and 128 MiB: 40 x 0.1 = 4 vCPU and 40 x 128 MiB = 5 GiB, which is 4 / 3.6 = 1.1 nodes, so 2 nodes, or 2 x 0.192 x 730 = 280 USD a month. Add waypoints only for namespaces that need L7 features: assume 8 such namespaces with one 0.5 vCPU waypoint each, 4 vCPU, another 2 nodes and 280 USD. Ambient total: about 560 USD, less than half of sidecar, and most pods have no proxy to upgrade.

The eBPF alternative, Cilium with encryption and Hubble: the Cilium agent already runs on every node as the CNI, so the L4 work adds CPU inside an existing DaemonSet rather than new pods. Assume 0.05 vCPU extra per node: 2 vCPU, which fits in the headroom of the existing nodes, so about 0 extra nodes. You give up Istio's L7 traffic policy unless you add Cilium's Envoy for those services.

| Option | Extra vCPU | Extra nodes | Assumed monthly cost | What you lose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sidecar | 30 | 9 | 1,261 USD | Nothing in features; latency and upgrade pain |
| Ambient | 8 | 4 | 560 USD | Per-pod L7 only where a waypoint exists |
| eBPF (Cilium) | 2 | 0 | about 0 USD | Istio's L7 policy model, unless Envoy is added |

The interview point: 300 pods is small. At 3,000 pods the sidecar line is 300 vCPU, 84 nodes and 11,773 USD a month, and the ambient line barely moves, because ztunnel scales with nodes, not pods.

## Runnable code

Python · runs and prints its own checks

```
"""A golden-path template in 120 lines, with no network.

Input: a service manifest, the only thing a developer writes.
Output: the platform objects a merge would create (namespace, pipeline,
dashboard, alert rules, IAM role, optional database request), as dicts,
each validated against a small schema before it is printed.

The point: the developer decides 5 things; the template decides the other 40.
"""
import json

SERVICE_SCHEMA = {
    "name": {"type": str, "pattern": "kebab"},
    "team": {"type": str},
    "language": {"type": str, "enum": ["go", "python", "node"]},
    "tier": {"type": int, "enum": [1, 2, 3]},
    "database": {"type": bool},
}

# SLO targets and alert windows the platform owns; a team only picks a tier.
TIER_SLO = {1: 99.95, 2: 99.9, 3: 99.5}
LANG_IMAGE = {"go": "golang:1.25-alpine", "python": "python:3.13-slim", "node": "node:22-alpine"}

def validate(obj, schema, label):
    """Reject anything that would fail later in a cluster, at PR time instead."""
    errors = []
    for key, rule in schema.items():
        if key not in obj:
            errors.append(f"{label}: missing field {key}")
            continue
        val = obj[key]
        if not isinstance(val, rule["type"]) or isinstance(val, bool) and rule["type"] is int:
            errors.append(f"{label}: {key} must be {rule['type'].__name__}")
        if "enum" in rule and val not in rule["enum"]:
            errors.append(f"{label}: {key} must be one of {rule['enum']}, got {val!r}")
        if rule.get("pattern") == "kebab" and not all(c.islower() or c.isdigit() or c == "-" for c in val):
            errors.append(f"{label}: {key} must be kebab-case, got {val!r}")
    extra = set(obj) - set(schema)
    if extra:
        errors.append(f"{label}: unknown fields {sorted(extra)}")
    return errors

def render(svc):
    """Turn one validated manifest into the set of platform objects."""
    name, team, tier = svc["name"], svc["team"], svc["tier"]
    slo = TIER_SLO[tier]
    error_budget = round(100 - slo, 3)
    objects = {
        "namespace": {
            "kind": "Namespace", "name": name,
            "labels": {"team": team, "tier": str(tier), "cost-center": team},
            "quota": {"cpu": "8", "memory": "16Gi"} if tier == 1 else {"cpu": "4", "memory": "8Gi"},
            "networkPolicy": "default-deny-ingress-except-ingress-controller",
        },
        "pipeline": {
            "kind": "Workflow", "name": f"{name}-ci",
            "baseImage": LANG_IMAGE[svc["language"]],
            "steps": ["test", "build", "trivy-scan", "cosign-sign", "push-ecr", "bump-gitops-tag"],
            "ecrRepository": f"platform/{team}/{name}",
        },
        "dashboard": {
            "kind": "GrafanaDashboard", "name": f"{name}-red",
            "panels": ["rate", "errors", "duration p50 p95 p99", "saturation cpu memory"],
            "datasource": "prometheus",
        },
        "alerts": {
            "kind": "PrometheusRule", "name": f"{name}-slo",
            "sloTarget": slo, "errorBudgetPercent": error_budget,
            "rules": [
                {"name": "FastBurn", "burnRate": 14.4, "window": "1h", "severity": "page"},
                {"name": "SlowBurn", "burnRate": 3.0, "window": "6h", "severity": "ticket"},
            ],
        },
        "iamRole": {
            "kind": "PodIdentityAssociation", "name": f"{name}-role",
            "serviceAccount": f"{name}/{name}",
            "policies": ["AllowReadOwnSecrets", "AllowWriteOwnLogs"]
            + (["AllowConnectOwnRds"] if svc["database"] else []),
        },
    }
    if svc["database"]:
        objects["database"] = {
            "kind": "PostgresDatabase", "apiVersion": "platform.example.org/v1alpha1",
            "name": f"{name}-db", "namespace": name,
            "size": "small" if tier == 3 else "medium", "multiAz": tier == 1,
        }
    return objects

OBJECT_SCHEMA = {"kind": {"type": str}, "name": {"type": str, "pattern": "kebab"}}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    good = {"name": "orders-api", "team": "payments", "language": "go", "tier": 2, "database": True}
    bad = {"name": "Orders_API", "team": "payments", "language": "rust", "tier": 2, "database": "yes", "region": "x"}

    print("validating bad manifest:")
    errs = validate(bad, SERVICE_SCHEMA, "service")
    for e in errs:
        print("  reject:", e)
    assert len(errs) == 4, errs

    print("\nvalidating good manifest:", validate(good, SERVICE_SCHEMA, "service") or "ok")
    objs = render(good)
    for key, obj in objs.items():
        problems = validate({"kind": obj["kind"], "name": obj["name"]}, OBJECT_SCHEMA, key)
        assert not problems, problems
    print(f"generated {len(objs)} platform objects from 5 developer decisions:\n")
    print(json.dumps(objs, indent=2))

    # Self-checks: tier drives SLO and budget; database flag drives IAM and the XR.
    assert objs["alerts"]["sloTarget"] == 99.9 and objs["alerts"]["errorBudgetPercent"] == 0.1
    assert "AllowConnectOwnRds" in objs["iamRole"]["policies"] and "database" in objs
    no_db = render({**good, "database": False, "tier": 1})
    assert "database" not in no_db and no_db["alerts"]["sloTarget"] == 99.95
    print("\nself-checks passed: tier 2 gives 99.9 SLO, database flag adds the XR and the IAM policy")
```

## Key takeaways

* A platform is a product: its customers are developers, its metric is cognitive load, and adoption is voluntary.
* A golden path turns one short manifest into every object a service needs; the developer decides only what belongs to the team.
* Backstage gives the catalog, templates and docs; Crossplane provisions cloud resources through Kubernetes APIs with a loop that never stops reconciling, unlike Terraform's plan and apply.
* Measure a platform with adoption, time to first deploy and DORA metrics per team.
* A sidecar mesh costs a proxy per pod; Istio ambient costs a ztunnel per node plus waypoints only where L7 is needed; Cilium does L4 in the kernel with no proxy.
* Do not adopt a mesh for a handful of services or for mTLS alone; adopt it when many teams need the same traffic and security policy.
* eBPF runs verified programs in the kernel; Cilium uses it to replace kube-proxy, enforce identity-aware policy and observe every flow with Hubble.

## Common mistakes

* Building a platform nobody asked for: shipping a portal before the golden path for the most common task exists.
* Treating Crossplane as "Terraform in YAML" and missing the real difference, the continuous reconcile loop and Kubernetes RBAC.
* Adopting Istio in sidecar mode for ten services, then paying a proxy per pod and an upgrade per pod for a feature set the team never uses.
* Saying ambient mode "has no proxies": it has one ztunnel per node and an Envoy waypoint wherever L7 features are turned on.
* Describing eBPF as "a kernel module": it is verified, sandboxed bytecode attached to kernel hooks, and that is why it is safe to run in production.
* Reporting platform success as features shipped instead of time to first deploy and DORA numbers per team.

## Practice

* On a kind cluster created with `kubeProxyMode: none` in the kind config, install Cilium with `kubeProxyReplacement=true`, confirm no kube-proxy pods exist, and use `hubble observe` to watch a request between two pods and then a request blocked by a default-deny CiliumNetworkPolicy.
* Install Istio with the ambient profile on kind, label a namespace `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient`, and compare `kubectl top pods` for the application pods before and after: there should be no new container in them. Then add a waypoint for one namespace and measure its CPU.
* Write the golden-path generator from this lesson as a GitHub Actions job: on a PR that adds `services/*.yaml`, render the objects into a `generated/` folder and post a comment listing what will be created. Time how long a new service takes from PR to a running pod on your cluster.
* Install Backstage locally with the create-app scaffold, register one of your repositories in the Software Catalog with a `catalog-info.yaml`, and add a TechDocs page. Note how many steps a new teammate would skip because the catalog answers "who owns this".

## Interview questions (8)

1.What is an internal developer platform, and how is a platform team different from an operations team?Easy

An internal developer platform is the set of tools, templates and services a product team uses to build, deploy and run software: the portal, the golden-path templates, the GitOps repo, the clusters and the observability stack behind them. The difference is the stance. An operations team receives tickets and does work for teams. A platform team ships a product whose customers are developers, measures adoption and time to first deploy, and wins by being the easiest way to do things right rather than by being mandatory. The metric it optimises is the cognitive load a developer carries to ship one service.

2.Describe a golden path for creating a new service. What does the developer write and what does the platform generate?Medium

The developer writes one short manifest: service name, owning team, language, tier and whether it needs a database. That goes in a pull request to the platform repository. On merge, a template renders everything else: a namespace with quota, RBAC and a default-deny NetworkPolicy; a CI workflow for that language with scanning and signing; an ECR repository; a Grafana dashboard with RED panels; SLO burn-rate alerts set from the tier; an IAM role bound to the service account through Pod Identity; a Crossplane composite resource for the database; and an Argo CD Application watching the service repo. The developer then pushes code and the first deploy happens without a ticket.

3.How does Crossplane differ from Terraform, and when would you use each?Medium

Both create cloud resources from declarations. Terraform runs when someone runs it, in a pipeline, and keeps state in a file; drift is found at the next plan. Crossplane runs as a controller inside Kubernetes: managed resources are custom resources, a Composition defines how a high-level type like PostgresDatabase is built from them, and the controller reconciles forever, so a hand-made change in the console is reverted automatically. Access is Kubernetes RBAC rather than pipeline credentials, so a team can request a database by applying a namespaced object. I would use Terraform for the account, VPC and cluster, and Crossplane for the resources teams request day to day on top of that cluster.

4.What problems does a service mesh solve, and what does it cost?Medium

It puts a proxy in every service-to-service call and controls the proxies centrally, which gives mTLS between all pods without code changes, retries and timeouts by policy, traffic shifting for canaries, and uniform latency, error and trace telemetry per hop. The cost in sidecar mode is a proxy per pod: Istio's own measurements put a sidecar at roughly a fifth of a vCPU and 60 MB at 1000 requests per second, plus two proxy hops of latency on every call, a lot of routing YAML, and a proxy upgrade inside every pod. Ambient mode moves the L4 work to one per-node ztunnel and keeps Envoy only as per-namespace waypoints for L7 features, which cuts the cost most teams actually feel.

5.A team with eight microservices asks you to install Istio so they get mTLS. What do you say?Hard

I ask what they actually need. If it is only encryption in transit, a mesh is the expensive answer: Cilium can encrypt node-to-node traffic with WireGuard, and TLS at the ingress plus NetworkPolicy may already meet the requirement. If they also need retries, timeouts and canary traffic shifting across all eight services and cannot change the code, a mesh starts to make sense, and I would propose Istio ambient or Linkerd rather than sidecars, so they pay per node rather than per pod. I would also check whether anyone has run Envoy before, because the operational cost of a mesh is the on-call cost when it misbehaves. For eight services run by one team, client-side retries and OpenTelemetry usually win.

6.What is eBPF and what does Cilium do with it in a Kubernetes cluster?Medium

eBPF lets you attach small programs to events inside the Linux kernel, such as a packet arriving or a system call, without a kernel module. A verifier checks every program before it loads, so it cannot loop forever or read arbitrary memory, and it is then JIT-compiled to run at native speed. Cilium uses it as the CNI: with kubeProxyReplacement it implements Services in eBPF at the socket level and removes kube-proxy and its iptables chains; it enforces NetworkPolicy and identity-aware L3 to L7 rules; Hubble exports every flow and drop reason for observability; and it can encrypt and apply L7 policy without a sidecar in each pod.

7.How would you measure whether your platform is succeeding?Easy

Four numbers, reported per team. Adoption: the share of new services created through the golden path, which should rise without anyone being forced. Time to first deploy: minutes from "new service" to the first production deployment, which should be under an hour on the path. DORA metrics: deploy frequency, lead time, change fail rate and failed deployment recovery time, where teams on the platform should beat teams off it. And cognitive load: a short survey plus a count of the tools a developer must touch to ship, which should fall every release. If adoption is flat, the path is wrong, not the developers.

8.What changes operationally when you go from one cluster to a fleet of clusters across regions?Hard

The clusters themselves become cattle. Every cluster comes from the same Terraform module or Crossplane composition, so any one can be rebuilt from Git. Argo CD registers each cluster, and an ApplicationSet with the cluster generator stamps the platform add-ons and team applications onto every cluster whose Secret has the matching labels, so adding a region is adding a labelled cluster. Traffic is steered by a global layer, Route 53 latency or failover records or Cloudflare, in front of regional load balancers, and health checks remove a bad region. Cross-cluster service discovery, if you need it, comes from a mesh or Cilium cluster mesh. The hard parts are data, because databases do not fail over as easily as stateless pods, and keeping the fleet on the same versions.

# Projects - pipeline, cluster, observability, operator

Five portfolio projects that together cover the whole roadmap: a service shipped to a VM by hand and then automated, a complete CI/CD pipeline, a production-shaped Kubernetes platform, an observability stack with a game day, and a Kubernetes operator in Go. Each has a one-to-two-week scope, numbered build steps, a measurable acceptance test, and the mistakes that make it look weak. The lesson ends with how to present a project in two minutes.

projectsportfolioci/cdkubernetesobservabilityoperatorinterview

## Why it matters

Early-career DevOps interviews in India are mostly conversations about what you have built. A certificate says you watched a course; a repository with a README, a diagram and numbers says you can do the job. Interviewers ask "tell me about a project" and then push: why that choice, what broke, what would you change. A project built the way this lesson describes gives you an answer to every one of those, and the numbers in the README are what separate "I deployed an app" from "I cut the pipeline from 14 to 6 minutes and deployed 14 times a week".

Read first: [CI/CD with GitHub Actions and GitLab CI](/devops/learn/ci-cd-github-actions-gitlab), [GitOps with Argo CD and progressive delivery](/devops/learn/gitops-argocd-progressive-delivery), [Observability - Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, logs and alerting](/devops/learn/observability-prometheus-grafana-otel), [Kubernetes internals and operators in Go](/devops/learn/kubernetes-internals-operators-go)

## Lesson

### How to pick a problem that is yours

Pick something you will actually use or that annoys you: a tool for your college club, a bot, a status page for a friend's site. Ownership shows in interviews because you know the details. Keep each project to one or two weeks of evenings; a finished small project beats an unfinished large one. Every project must end with a number you measured, a diagram you drew, and a README written for someone who has never seen the repo. The five projects below build on each other; do them in order if you can.

| Project | Proves which skill | The number to report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Ship to a VM, then automate it | Linux, Nginx, TLS, systemd, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions | Deploy time by hand vs by pipeline; TLS grade; uptime over a week |
| 2. CI/CD for a monorepo | Change detection, caching, scanning, signing, deploy by digest | Pipeline minutes before and after; images blocked by the scanner |
| 3. Production-shaped Kubernetes platform | Terraform, Argo CD, ingress, secrets, policy, HPA, PDB, canary | Time to rebuild the cluster from Git; canary abort time on a bad release |
| 4. Observability stack and game day | Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, OpenTelemetry, SLOs, postmortem | Time to detect and time to diagnose in the game day |
| 5. Operator in Go | kubebuilder, reconcile loop, envtest, Helm packaging, open source | Test coverage of the reconciler; the merged upstream PR |

### Project 1: ship a service to a VM the manual way, then automate it

**Goal.** Understand everything a platform hides by doing it once by hand: a small API (any language) on one Linux VM, reachable over HTTPS, surviving a reboot, deployed by a pipeline.

**Scope.** One free-tier EC2 instance or any small VM, one domain or a free subdomain, one service with a `/healthz` endpoint.

1. Create the VM, lock SSH to key auth, open only ports 22, 80 and 443 in the security group.
2. Run the service under systemd (or PM2 for Node) with `Restart=always`; confirm it comes back after `sudo reboot`.
3. Put Nginx in front as a reverse proxy; get a certificate from Let's Encrypt with certbot and confirm auto-renewal with `certbot renew --dry-run`.
4. Write a GitHub Actions workflow that, on push to main, builds, copies the artifact over SSH, restarts the unit and curls `/healthz`. Time it.
5. Repeat the deploy with Docker Compose: the service plus Nginx as containers, the certificate in a volume. Compare the two.

**Acceptance test.** `curl -I https://your.domain/healthz` returns 200 with a valid certificate; the service is back within 30 seconds of a reboot; a push to main is live in under 3 minutes with no manual step.

**What to show.** A README with the two deploy times, the SSL Labs grade, the systemd unit and the Nginx config, and a diagram of the request path (DNS, Nginx, service).

**Weak signs.** Secrets in the repo; a service started by hand in a tmux session; HTTP only; no rollback step in the pipeline.

### Project 2: a complete CI/CD pipeline for a small monorepo

**Goal.** A pipeline a reviewer would trust: only changed services build, every image is scanned and signed, and deploys use digests, never tags.

**Scope.** Two or three services in one repo, GitHub Actions, GHCR or ECR, a target from project 1 or 3.

1. Add path-based change detection so a commit touching only `services/api` builds only that service.
2. Cache dependencies and Docker layers; measure the pipeline before and after.
3. Scan each image with Trivy and fail the job on critical findings; record what was blocked.
4. Sign each image with cosign keyless and verify the signature before deploy.
5. Deploy by digest (`image@sha256:...`) by updating a manifest or a Helm value in a commit, and keep `main` protected behind required checks.

**Acceptance test.** A commit touching one service builds only that service; a deliberately vulnerable base image is blocked; an unsigned image is refused at deploy; the pipeline runs in under 6 minutes for a one-service change.

**What to show.** Pipeline duration before and after caching, the scanner's finding count, a signed-image verification log, and a flowchart of the stages.

**Weak signs.** `latest` tags; a workflow that rebuilds everything on every push; secrets printed in logs; no branch protection.

### Project 3: a production-shaped Kubernetes platform

**Goal.** A cluster that looks like the one in the design problems: created from code, configured from Git, with the guardrails a real team needs.

**Scope.** kind on a laptop, or a small EKS cluster you destroy at night. Terraform for the cluster, Argo CD for everything on it.

1. Terraform the cluster (kind provider or the EKS module), with a remote state backend if on AWS.
2. Install Argo CD and an app-of-apps that installs: the AWS Load Balancer Controller on EKS (or Envoy Gateway on kind; ingress-nginx is retired, so do not start on it), cert-manager with TLS, external-secrets backed by AWS Secrets Manager or a local secret store, Kyverno, metrics-server.
3. Add Kyverno policies: no `latest` tags, resources required, Pod Security Standards baseline. Show a denied deploy.
4. Deploy the monorepo services with an HPA, a PodDisruptionBudget, and an Argo Rollouts canary (`setWeight` 10, pause, 50, pause, 100) with an analysis that aborts on a 5xx rate.
5. Destroy and rebuild the whole thing from Git. Time it.

**Acceptance test.** `terraform destroy` then `terraform apply` plus one Argo CD sync brings every application to Healthy in under 20 minutes; a release with a failing readiness probe is aborted by the canary with no user-facing errors; `kubectl drain` of a node does not take the service below its PDB.

**What to show.** The rebuild time, the Argo CD application tree, the Kyverno denial, the Rollouts timeline of an aborted canary, and a diagram of the platform layers.

**Weak signs.** Manifests applied with kubectl by hand; secrets in Git; an HPA with no resource requests; no PDB; canary with no analysis.

### Project 4: an observability stack and a game day

**Goal.** Metrics, logs and traces through one pipeline, dashboards someone else can read, alerts that page on SLO burn, and a written postmortem of a failure you caused.

**Scope.** On the cluster from project 3: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, and the OpenTelemetry Collector in front of all three.

1. Instrument one service with the OpenTelemetry SDK; send traces, metrics and logs to a Collector; route them to Tempo, Prometheus and Loki.
2. Build a RED dashboard (rate, errors, duration) per service, plus a saturation row.
3. Define an SLO (99.9 percent of requests under 300 ms) and write multi-window burn-rate alerts (14.4x over 1 hour, 6x over 6 hours).
4. Run a game day: inject a fault (kill the database, add 500 ms latency with a sidecar or `tc`, fill a disk) without telling your future self the time. Note when the alert fired and when you found the cause from the dashboard, logs and a trace.
5. Write a blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, root cause, what went well, action items.

**Acceptance test.** A trace from the ingress to the database is visible in Tempo with the matching log lines in Loki by trace id; the fast-burn alert fires within 5 minutes of the fault; time to diagnose from the dashboard is under 15 minutes.

**What to show.** Time to detect and time to diagnose, the dashboard screenshot, the alert rules, the postmortem, and a diagram of the telemetry pipeline.

**Weak signs.** Dashboards nobody could read without you; alerts on CPU instead of the SLO; a postmortem that blames a person; no action items.

### Project 5: a Kubernetes operator in Go, and a first open source PR

**Goal.** The WebApp CRD from lesson 25 built for real: a controller that turns one custom object into a Deployment, a Service and an Ingress, tested, packaged, and a first contribution to a CNCF project.

**Scope.** kubebuilder, envtest, a Helm chart, one small upstream PR.

1. Scaffold with `kubebuilder init` and `kubebuilder create api`; define `WebApp` with image, replicas, host and a status with ready replicas and conditions.
2. Write the reconcile loop: create or update the three owned objects, set owner references, update status, requeue on error with backoff.
3. Test the reconciler with envtest: a WebApp creates its objects, changing replicas updates the Deployment, deleting the WebApp garbage-collects everything.
4. Package the CRD and controller as a Helm chart with a `templates/tests/` check; install it on the project 3 cluster through Argo CD.
5. Find a `good first issue` in a CNCF project (Kubernetes, Argo CD, Helm, Cilium, Kyverno), fix it, and get the PR merged. Link it in the README.

**Acceptance test.** `go test ./...` passes with envtest at over 70 percent coverage of the controller package; `helm install` on a fresh cluster followed by `kubectl apply` of a WebApp yields a reachable site within 60 seconds; one upstream PR is merged.

**What to show.** Coverage, the reconcile diagram, the CRD YAML, the chart, and the merged PR.

**Weak signs.** A controller with no tests; status never updated; objects without owner references, so they leak; a PR that only fixes a typo.

### Optional project 6: an uptime monitor

A BetterStack-style monitor from the 100xDevs cohort: users register URLs; probe workers in two or three regions check them every minute; results flow through Redis Streams from the API to the workers and on to "pusher" processes that alert and update a public status page. It proves async design with queues, consumer groups and a public page under load. The number to report: probes per minute sustained and the time from a site going down to the alert.

### How to present a project in two minutes

Problem (15 seconds): who needed what. Design (30 seconds): the diagram in words, three components, the data flow. Trade-offs (30 seconds): two choices you made and what you gave up. Numbers (20 seconds): before and after. What broke (15 seconds): one real failure and how you found it. What you would change (10 seconds): one honest improvement. Practise it aloud, timed. The interviewer will interrupt; that is good, it means they are interested.

## Diagram

Rendering diagram…

## Worked example

**A README skeleton for project 2, filled with illustrative numbers.** The numbers are examples, not measurements; yours will differ.

```
# orders-monorepo pipeline

## What it does
Builds, scans, signs and deploys three services (api, worker, web) from one repo
with GitHub Actions. Only changed services build. Deploys use image digests.

## Numbers (example values)
| Metric                              | Before   | After    | Change        |
| ----------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ------------- |
| Pipeline time, one-service change   | 14.2 min | 6.1 min  | -8.1 min, -57% |
| Deploys per week                    | 3        | 14       | +11, +367%     |
| Images blocked by Trivy (4 weeks)   | 0 (no scan) | 7     | new control    |
| Unsigned images that reached deploy | n/a      | 0        | verified       |

## Design
[diagram: push -> change detection -> build matrix -> trivy -> cosign -> push -> bump digest in gitops repo -> Argo CD]

## Trade-offs
- Keyless cosign signing needs an OIDC identity in CI; simpler than key management, but
  the verify step must pin the issuer and the workflow identity or it proves nothing.
- Change detection by path misses a shared library change; the fix is to map library
  paths to every dependent service, which is in paths-filter.yaml.

## What broke
- The first digest bump committed to the gitops repo from CI triggered the pipeline
  again (a loop). Fixed by ignoring the gitops path and using a bot identity.

## What I would change
- Move to a merge queue so two digest bumps cannot race.
```

How those example numbers were produced, so you can reproduce yours. Pipeline time: run the same one-file change ten times before and after caching and take the median; 14.2 to 6.1 minutes is an 8.1 minute cut, and 8.1 / 14.2 = 57 percent. Deploys per week: count merged pull requests that reached production; 3 to 14 is plus 11, and 11 / 3 = 367 percent. Blocked images: the count of pipeline runs failed by the scanner over four weeks, which is a new control so there is no "before". The interviewer's follow-up will be "why did deploys go up": because the pipeline got fast enough that people stopped batching changes, which is the DORA argument in one sentence.

## Runnable code

Python · runs and prints its own checks

```
"""Before and after comparison for a project README.

Give it two dictionaries of metrics and it prints a table with absolute and
relative change, marking whether the change is an improvement. For some metrics
lower is better (pipeline minutes, p95 latency, cost, time to restore); for
others higher is better (deploys per week, coverage). The direction is declared
per metric so the script never guesses.
"""

# metric name -> (unit, lower_is_better)
METRICS = {
    "pipeline_minutes": ("min", True),
    "deploys_per_week": ("/wk", False),
    "p95_latency_ms": ("ms", True),
    "monthly_cost_usd": ("USD", True),
    "time_to_restore_min": ("min", True),
    "test_coverage_pct": ("%", False),
}

def compare(before, after):
    """Return rows of (metric, before, after, abs_change, rel_change_pct, verdict)."""
    rows = []
    for name, (unit, lower_better) in METRICS.items():
        if name not in before or name not in after:
            continue
        b, a = before[name], after[name]
        delta = a - b
        rel = (delta / b * 100) if b else float("inf")
        improved = delta < 0 if lower_better else delta > 0
        verdict = "better" if improved else ("same" if delta == 0 else "worse")
        rows.append((name, b, a, unit, delta, rel, verdict))
    return rows

def fmt(x):
    return f"{x:.1f}" if isinstance(x, float) and not x.is_integer() else f"{int(x)}"

def print_table(rows):
    print(f"{'metric':<22} {'before':>8} {'after':>8} {'unit':<5} {'change':>10} {'relative':>9}  verdict")
    for name, b, a, unit, delta, rel, verdict in rows:
        sign = "+" if delta > 0 else ""
        rel_s = "n/a" if rel == float("inf") else f"{sign}{rel:.0f}%"
        print(f"{name:<22} {fmt(b):>8} {fmt(a):>8} {unit:<5} {sign}{fmt(delta):>9} {rel_s:>9}  {verdict}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    before = {"pipeline_minutes": 14.2, "deploys_per_week": 3, "p95_latency_ms": 820,
              "monthly_cost_usd": 212, "time_to_restore_min": 48, "test_coverage_pct": 41}
    after = {"pipeline_minutes": 6.1, "deploys_per_week": 14, "p95_latency_ms": 410,
             "monthly_cost_usd": 148, "time_to_restore_min": 9, "test_coverage_pct": 72}
    rows = compare(before, after)
    print_table(rows)

    # Self-checks against hand-computed values.
    by_name = {r[0]: r for r in rows}
    assert round(by_name["pipeline_minutes"][5]) == -57
    assert round(by_name["deploys_per_week"][5]) == 367
    assert round(by_name["p95_latency_ms"][5]) == -50
    assert round(by_name["monthly_cost_usd"][5]) == -30
    assert all(r[6] == "better" for r in rows)
    # A regression must be called out, not hidden.
    worse = compare({"p95_latency_ms": 400}, {"p95_latency_ms": 520})
    assert worse[0][6] == "worse" and round(worse[0][5]) == 30
    print("\nself-checks passed: directions respected, a regression is reported as worse")
```

## Key takeaways

* A project counts when it has a README with measured numbers, a diagram and a story of what broke.
* Build in order: ship by hand, automate the pipeline, build the platform, observe it, extend it with an operator.
* Every project needs an acceptance test you can run in front of someone: a rebuild time, a blocked image, an aborted canary, an alert that fired.
* Weak projects share the same signs: secrets in Git, latest tags, no tests, no rollback, no numbers.
* Two minutes, six beats: problem, design, trade-offs, numbers, what broke, what you would change.
* A merged upstream PR, however small, is the strongest line on an early-career resume.

## Common mistakes

* Ten half-finished repos instead of two finished ones with numbers.
* A README that lists technologies ("Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform") without saying what the project does or what was measured.
* Copying a tutorial exactly, so the first "why did you choose X" question has no answer.
* Leaving the cluster running and paying for it, then having no cost number because the bill was a surprise.
* Presenting only successes; interviewers trust the candidate who describes the deploy loop they caused and how they found it.

## Practice

* Pick project 1 and finish it this week: a VM, HTTPS, a systemd unit and a pipeline. Record the by-hand deploy time and the pipeline deploy time in the README.
* Take any repository you already have and write its README in the skeleton from the worked example, with real measured numbers; run the comparison script on them.
* Record yourself presenting one project in two minutes, then answer three follow-up questions a friend asks. Cut anything that is not problem, design, trade-off, number, failure or change.
* Find one `good first issue` in a CNCF Go project, reproduce it locally, and post a comment with your reproduction before writing the fix.

## Interview questions (7)

1.Tell me about a project you built. You have two minutes.Easy

I built a CI/CD pipeline for a three-service monorepo. The problem was that every push rebuilt everything and took fourteen minutes, so people batched changes. The design: GitHub Actions with path-based change detection, a build matrix per changed service, Trivy scanning, cosign keyless signing, and a digest bump into a GitOps repo that Argo CD syncs. Trade-offs: path filters miss shared-library changes, so I map library paths to dependents; keyless signing needs the verify step to pin the OIDC issuer. Numbers: a one-service change went from 14 to 6 minutes and deploys rose from 3 to 14 a week. What broke: the digest-bump commit retriggered the pipeline in a loop; I fixed it with a path ignore and a bot identity. Next I would add a merge queue.

2.Why do you deploy by image digest instead of by tag?Medium

A tag is a mutable pointer: `api:1.4.2` can be re-pushed and point at different bytes tomorrow, and `latest` changes constantly, so a rollback by tag may not restore what was running. A digest is the content hash of the image; `api@sha256:...` is exactly one set of layers forever. Deploying by digest makes the GitOps repo a true record of what ran, makes rollback a revert, and is what the cosign signature actually covers, so the verify step at deploy time proves the exact image was signed by the pipeline. The cost is readability, which I solve by keeping the tag in a comment next to the digest.

3.What did your game day find, and what did you change afterwards?Medium

I added 500 ms of latency to the database connection with tc on the database pod. The fast-burn alert fired after about four minutes: with every request now over the 300 ms threshold the 1-hour window crosses 14.4x in about a minute, and the rest was scrape interval and the rule's `for` duration. Diagnosis took longer than I wanted: the RED dashboard showed duration up and errors flat, so it looked like the service itself; only the trace showed the time was inside the database span. Afterwards I added a dependency-latency row to the dashboard, a log line with the trace id on slow queries so Loki and Tempo link, and an action item to set a client-side timeout so slowness becomes a fast error rather than a pile-up. The postmortem is in the repo.

4.How does your operator avoid leaking objects when a WebApp is deleted?Medium

Every Deployment, Service and Ingress the controller creates gets an owner reference pointing at the WebApp, set with controllerutil.SetControllerReference. When the WebApp is deleted, the Kubernetes garbage collector deletes everything owned by it; the controller does not need to run. The envtest suite checks this: create a WebApp, assert the three objects exist, delete it, assert they are gone. For anything outside the cluster, say a DNS record, owner references cannot help, so I would add a finalizer that cleans up and then removes itself, and test that the object is not deleted while the finalizer is present.

5.How would you rebuild your platform from scratch if the cluster was lost?Medium

Everything is in two repositories. Terraform recreates the cluster, the node pool and the IAM pieces; that is one apply. Then I install Argo CD and apply the single app-of-apps Application; Argo CD pulls the rest from Git: ingress, cert-manager, external-secrets, Kyverno, and the team applications. Secrets come back from AWS Secrets Manager through external-secrets, so nothing secret was in the cluster alone. In my test the full rebuild to every application Healthy took under twenty minutes, and the only manual step was the Argo CD bootstrap. The thing that would not come back is stateful data, which is why the database lives outside the cluster or has Velero backups.

6.What is the smallest useful open source contribution, and how did you find yours?Easy

The smallest useful one fixes something a maintainer has already marked as wanted: a `good first issue` or `help wanted` label. I filtered a CNCF project's issues by those labels, picked one touching code rather than only docs, read the contributor guide, reproduced the bug locally, wrote a test that failed, fixed it, ran the project's own lint and test commands, and opened a PR that linked the issue and explained the change in three sentences. Then I answered review comments quickly. A typo fix counts but proves little; a test plus a fix proves you can work in a large Go codebase.

7.Your pipeline got faster but deploys went up fivefold. Why does that matter to a hiring manager?Hard

Because deploy frequency and lead time are two of the four DORA metrics, and they move together with change failure rate and time to restore when batches get smaller. A fourteen-minute pipeline made people bundle several changes into one deploy, so each failure was bigger and harder to bisect. At six minutes, people shipped one change at a time; failures were smaller, rollback was a one-commit revert, and time to restore fell from 48 to 9 minutes in my measurements. A hiring manager hears that I understand the pipeline is not the goal, the delivery performance is, and that I measured the thing that matters rather than only the thing I changed.

## Quiz

2.In project 2, what does deploying by digest protect against?

# Python and Go for automation and tooling

A DevOps engineer needs two languages. Python is for scripts, checks, data and glue between APIs: fast to write, already installed everywhere. Go is for anything that ships as a single binary, does many things at once, or lives in the CNCF world, where Kubernetes, Helm, Argo CD, Prometheus and Terraform are written. This lesson shows the shape of a good Python ops script, the one page of Go a Python person needs, the worker-pool pattern with channels and context, and the mistakes that make Go tools leak.

pythongoautomationcliconcurrencytestingcncf

## Why it matters

Interviews for DevOps and SRE roles now include a coding round. The common tasks are "write a health checker with retries", "parse these logs and find the top errors", "call this API with pagination and summarise". Python answers them fastest. Platform and CNCF-adjacent roles add Go: "write a worker pool", "what is a goroutine leak", "how would you read client-go". LFX Mentorship and GSoC projects in Kubernetes, Argo, Prometheus or Cilium require Go on day one. Knowing which language to reach for, and the standard shape of a program in each, is what the interviewer is checking.

Read first: [Linux for operators](/devops/learn/linux-for-operators), [Bash scripting and the terminal toolkit](/devops/learn/bash-and-terminal-toolkit), [Networking for DevOps - TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, SSH](/devops/learn/networking-for-devops)

## Lesson

### Why two languages

|  | Python | Go |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best at | Scripts, checks, data, glue between APIs, quick CLIs | Services, operators, CLIs shipped as binaries, concurrent tools |
| Startup time | Tens of milliseconds for the interpreter plus imports | Single-digit milliseconds |
| Shipping | Needs an interpreter and a virtualenv or a container | One static binary, cross-compiled from any machine |
| Binary size | Not applicable; a container image is often 100 MB or more | Typically 5 to 15 MB, a scratch or distroless image of about the same |
| Concurrency | Threads limited by the GIL for CPU work; asyncio for I/O | Goroutines and channels, parallel across all cores |
| Typing | Dynamic, optional hints checked by mypy | Static, compiler-enforced |
| Error handling | Exceptions | Errors as return values |
| Ecosystem for us | boto3, requests, PyYAML, pytest, Ansible modules | client-go, controller-runtime, cobra, Prometheus client, Terraform providers |
| Where it wins | Anything you will write in an hour and run from a laptop or a CronJob | Anything others will install, that runs for months, or that talks to the Kubernetes API in volume |

The honest division of labour: write the health check, the cost report and the log parser in Python. Write the controller, the admission webhook, the kubectl plugin and the agent in Go. If a Python script grows a long-running loop and a concurrency problem, that is the signal to rewrite it in Go.

### The shape of a good Python ops script

Every ops script you write in Python should have the same skeleton: `argparse` for flags including `--dry-run`, `logging` to stderr so stdout stays parseable, `subprocess.run` with `check=True` and a `timeout`, HTTP calls with retries and backoff, `pathlib` for files, and explicit exit codes. The reader of your script is the on-call engineer at 3 a.m., and the shape tells them where to look.

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Drain a node safely: cordon, wait for pods to leave, with dry-run and timeouts."""
import argparse
import json
import logging
import subprocess
import sys
import time
import urllib.request
import urllib.error
from pathlib import Path

log = logging.getLogger("drain")

def run(cmd, timeout=30, dry_run=False):
    """Run a command; raise on non-zero exit; never hang forever."""
    log.info("run: %s", " ".join(cmd))
    if dry_run:
        return ""
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
    return result.stdout

def get_json(url, retries=3, backoff=0.5, timeout=5):
    """GET with retries and exponential backoff; retry only on 5xx and network errors."""
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as resp:
                return json.load(resp)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            if e.code < 500:
                raise  # 4xx is our bug, do not retry
            log.warning("attempt %d: HTTP %d", attempt + 1, e.code)
        except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError) as e:
            log.warning("attempt %d: %s", attempt + 1, e)
        time.sleep(backoff * 2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError(f"gave up on {url} after {retries} attempts")

def main(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("node")
    p.add_argument("--timeout", type=int, default=300, help="seconds to wait for pods to leave")
    p.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.INFO,
                        format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s", stream=sys.stderr)
    try:
        run(["kubectl", "cordon", args.node], dry_run=args.dry_run)
        run(["kubectl", "drain", args.node, "--ignore-daemonsets", "--delete-emptydir-data",
             f"--timeout={args.timeout}s"], timeout=args.timeout + 10, dry_run=args.dry_run)
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
        log.error("command failed (%d): %s", e.returncode, e.stderr.strip())
        return 2
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        log.error("drain did not finish in %d s", args.timeout)
        return 3
    Path("/tmp/last-drained").write_text(args.node)
    print(json.dumps({"node": args.node, "drained": not args.dry_run}))
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

Things to notice. `check=True` turns a failed command into an exception instead of a silent zero. `timeout` means a hung `kubectl` cannot hang your CronJob. The retry loop retries only on 5xx and network errors, because retrying a 403 just wastes time. Logs go to stderr and the one line of real output goes to stdout as JSON, so the next tool in the pipe can read it. Exit codes are distinct, so the caller can tell "command failed" from "timed out". For YAML, `import yaml` and `yaml.safe_load` (never `yaml.load` without a Loader) cover Kubernetes manifests and Helm values; `requests` with a `Session` and a `Retry` adapter is the usual upgrade from `urllib` when the package is available.

### Calling cloud APIs from Python

boto3 is the AWS SDK. Three rules. First, never put keys in code or in the repository: boto3 reads credentials from the environment, then from the pod's web identity token (IRSA on EKS), then from an SSO session, then from `~/.aws/credentials`, and last from the container or instance role (Pod Identity on EKS, an EC2 instance profile), in that order. Second, every list call is paginated and the default page hides the rest, so use a paginator. Third, pass a region explicitly in tooling that runs in CI.

```
import boto3

ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name="ap-south-1")
paginator = ec2.get_paginator("describe_instances")
untagged = []
for page in paginator.paginate(Filters=[{"Name": "instance-state-name", "Values": ["running"]}]):
    for reservation in page["Reservations"]:
        for inst in reservation["Instances"]:
            tags = {t["Key"]: t["Value"] for t in inst.get("Tags", [])}
            if "owner" not in tags:
                untagged.append(inst["InstanceId"])
print(len(untagged), "running instances have no owner tag")
```

Testing scripts like these is where most candidates stop, and where you can stand out. `pytest` plus `unittest.mock` lets you test the logic without a cluster:

```
from unittest.mock import patch
import subprocess
import drain  # the script above, importable because the logic is in main()

def test_dry_run_does_not_call_kubectl():
    with patch("drain.subprocess.run") as fake:
        assert drain.main(["node-1", "--dry-run"]) == 0
        fake.assert_not_called()

def test_failed_drain_returns_2():
    err = subprocess.CalledProcessError(1, ["kubectl"], stderr="node not found")
    with patch("drain.subprocess.run", side_effect=err):
        assert drain.main(["node-1"]) == 2
```

Mock the boundary (subprocess, HTTP, boto3 client), not your own functions. For boto3, `botocore.stub.Stubber` replays canned responses.

### Contracts first: OpenAPI specs and generated clients

An **OpenAPI spec** is a YAML or JSON document that describes an HTTP API: every path, method, parameter, request body, response schema and status code. It is the contract between the team that owns the service and everyone who calls it. Ops tooling should not hand-write `requests.get(f"{base}/v1/nodes/{name}")` calls against such an API. Generate a client from the spec instead: `oapi-codegen` produces Go client code, server stubs and typed models from an OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 document, and `openapi-python-client` produces a typed Python package with one function per endpoint and a class per schema. A generated client gives you the field names, the types and the enum values at compile time or in your editor, and when the service changes its spec, regenerating the client shows you every call that broke, instead of a 400 at runtime. The same spec is what an API gateway or a middleware validates incoming requests against: a body with a missing required field is rejected at the edge, before your handler runs. Keep the spec in the repo, lint it in CI and treat a spec change like a schema migration.

### Go in one page for a Python person

Go is small. Everything you need for ops tooling fits in one page of differences.

```
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"os"
)

// A struct is a typed record. Fields that start with a capital letter are exported.
type Target struct {
	Name string
	URL  string
	Tags map[string]string // maps must be made before use: make(map[string]string)
}

// Methods attach to a type. The receiver (t Target) is like self.
func (t Target) String() string { return t.Name + " -> " + t.URL }

// An interface is satisfied by any type that has the methods. No "implements" keyword.
type Checker interface {
	Check(t Target) error
}

// Errors are values. The caller must look at them; nothing is thrown.
var ErrNoURL = errors.New("target has no URL")

func validate(t Target) error {
	if t.URL == "" {
		return fmt.Errorf("validate %s: %w", t.Name, ErrNoURL) // %w wraps, errors.Is can find it
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	targets := []Target{{Name: "api", URL: "https://api.example.com"}, {Name: "bad"}} // a slice
	targets = append(targets, Target{Name: "db", URL: "tcp://db:5432"})

	f, err := os.CreateTemp("", "report")
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	defer os.Remove(f.Name()) // defer runs when main returns, in reverse order
	defer f.Close()

	for i, t := range targets { // range gives index and copy of the value
		if err := validate(t); err != nil {
			if errors.Is(err, ErrNoURL) {
				fmt.Printf("%d: skipped: %v\n", i, err)
			}
			continue
		}
		fmt.Fprintln(f, t) // uses String() because Target satisfies fmt.Stringer
	}
}
```

The translation table: `list` is a slice (`[]T`, grows with `append`), `dict` is a map (`map[K]V`, must be `make`d), `class` is a struct plus methods, duck typing is an interface (satisfied implicitly), `try/except` is `if err != nil`, `with` is `defer`, and `None` is `nil`. Unused imports and variables are compile errors, `gofmt` decides the formatting, and there are no exceptions, no inheritance and no generics tricks you need for tooling. Go has had generics since 1.18, and you will see `[T any]` in library code, but ops tools rarely need to write them.

### Goroutines, channels, context and the worker pool

![A Go worker pool: a producer sends jobs into a channel, four worker goroutines read them, each check honours a context deadline, results flow through a buffered channel to the main goroutine which waits on a WaitGroup](/devops/img/go-worker-pool-channels-context.svg)A Go worker pool: a producer sends jobs into a channel, four worker goroutines read them, each check honours a context deadline, results flow through a buffered channel to the main goroutine which waits on a WaitGroup

A **goroutine** is a function running concurrently, started with the keyword `go`. It costs a few kilobytes, so ten thousand of them are fine. A **channel** is a typed queue that goroutines use to hand values to each other; sending on an unbuffered channel blocks until someone receives. A **WaitGroup** counts running goroutines so `main` can wait for them. A **context** carries a deadline and a cancel signal down every call; every function that might block takes `ctx context.Context` as its first argument and gives up when `ctx.Done()` fires.

The worker pool is the pattern you will write most: N workers read jobs from one channel and write results to another. It bounds concurrency (you do not open 10000 connections to the API server), it collects results without locks, and with a context it has a hard deadline. The code example implements it with four workers over twelve checks, and the standard library `net/http` client takes the same context through `http.NewRequestWithContext`, so a real version is a small change.

### The standard library, modules and building

Go's standard library covers most of an ops tool: `net/http` for clients and servers (`http.ListenAndServe` and `http.HandleFunc` give you a `/healthz` endpoint in five lines), `encoding/json`, `os/exec` for running commands with a context (`exec.CommandContext`), `flag` for simple flags, `log/slog` for structured logs, `time`, `sync`. A **module** is a directory with a `go.mod` file naming the module path and the Go version; `go mod tidy` records every dependency with its exact version and hash in `go.sum`, so builds are reproducible.

```
go mod init github.com/you/checker        # creates go.mod
go build -o checker .                     # a static binary for this OS and CPU
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o checker-linux-arm64 .   # cross-compile, stripped
go vet ./... && go test ./...             # the two commands every CI job runs
```

`CGO_ENABLED=0` makes the binary fully static, which is what lets it run `FROM scratch` or distroless in a container. A real CLI with sub-commands, help text and shell completion is usually built with the `cobra` library (the one behind `kubectl`, `helm` and `gh`): a root command, `AddCommand` for each sub-command, flags bound to variables, and a `RunE` function that returns an error. You do not need it for a single-purpose tool; `flag` is enough.

### Measure before you argue: benchmarking languages

"Go is faster than Python" is a claim, not a number. Write the same hello handler (return `{"ok":true}` with a 200) in Node, Python and Go, run each on the same machine, and point one load generator at them in turn: `wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s --latency` against the local port prints requests per second and a latency distribution, and k6 reports `http_req_duration` with a threshold such as `p(99)<300`. Record requests per second and the p99 for each, with the CPU count, the framework and the flags used. Any number you quote in an interview or a design doc is from your own run and labelled as such ("on my 4-core laptop, Go stdlib served N requests per second"). Numbers copied from a blog post describe someone else's machine.

### Table-driven tests

Go tests live in `_test.go` files, use the `testing` package, and are run with `go test`. The idiom is a slice of cases and one loop:

```
func TestParseCIDR(t *testing.T) {
	cases := []struct {
		name    string
		in      string
		wantN   int
		wantErr bool
	}{
		{"slash24", "10.0.0.0/24", 256, false},
		{"slash28", "10.0.0.0/28", 16, false},
		{"garbage", "not-a-cidr", 0, true},
	}
	for _, tc := range cases {
		t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			n, err := countAddresses(tc.in)
			if (err != nil) != tc.wantErr {
				t.Fatalf("err = %v, wantErr %v", err, tc.wantErr)
			}
			if n != tc.wantN {
				t.Errorf("got %d, want %d", n, tc.wantN)
			}
		})
	}
}
```

`go test -race ./...` runs the race detector, which finds the data races that only show up under load in production. Use it in CI for anything with goroutines.

### Common Go mistakes in ops tools

| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goroutine leak | A worker blocks forever on a channel nobody reads or closes; memory and goroutine count climb for weeks | Close the jobs channel; buffer the results channel to the number of jobs; select on `ctx.Done()`; watch `runtime.NumGoroutine()` or the Go runtime metrics in Prometheus |
| Unbounded channels or goroutines | `go check(x)` in a loop over 50000 items opens 50000 connections | Worker pool with a fixed N; or a semaphore channel of size N |
| Ignoring errors | `resp, _ := client.Do(req)` then a nil-pointer panic at 3 a.m. | Handle every `err`; `errcheck` and `go vet` in CI |
| No context timeout | An HTTP call to a dead endpoint blocks forever; the whole tool hangs | `context.WithTimeout` on every outbound call, `http.Client{Timeout: ...}` as a backstop |
| Not closing `resp.Body` | Connections are never returned to the pool; file descriptors run out | `defer resp.Body.Close()` right after checking `err` |
| Shared map from goroutines | "concurrent map writes" fatal error | A mutex, or collect through a channel |
| Capturing the loop variable in a goroutine | All goroutines see the last value (Go before 1.22) | Pass it as an argument; Go 1.22 and later give each iteration its own variable |

### Reading client-go

Kubernetes controllers in Go all look the same once you know the shape: a `clientset` (or a controller-runtime `Client`) talks to the API server, an **informer** keeps a local cache of objects and calls your handler on add, update and delete, a **work queue** holds the keys of objects to reconcile, and a **reconcile** function reads the current object, compares it with the desired state, and makes one change. The reconcile function must be idempotent, because the same key is delivered again after errors and on every resync. The `go-reconcile-loop` problem has you write that function without client-go; lesson 25 shows the real thing with controller-runtime and Kubebuilder.
