## Worked example

**Sizing a worker pool for a health checker.** You must check 1200 endpoints every minute from one pod. Each check is an HTTP GET with a p50 of 150 ms and a p99 of 2 s, and 3 percent of endpoints are down and take the full timeout.

Step 1, serial time. 1200 checks at an average of about 200 ms (the mean sits above the median because of the slow tail) is 240 s. A 60 s cycle is impossible serially; you need at least 4 times parallelism just to break even.

Step 2, choose the timeout. The p99 is 2 s, so a 3 s context timeout loses almost nothing. The 36 down endpoints (3 percent of 1200) will each take 3 s.

Step 3, workers. With N workers the cycle takes roughly (total work) / N. Total work is 1164 x 0.2 s plus 36 x 3 s, which is 232.8 s plus 108 s, which is 340.8 s. For a 30 s cycle (half the budget, leaving room for jitter) N must be at least 340.8 / 30, which is 11.4, so 12 workers. Choose 16 for headroom.

Step 4, the channels. The jobs channel can be unbuffered: the producer blocks until a worker is free, which is the back-pressure you want. The results channel is buffered to 1200, so a worker never blocks on sending while `main` is still feeding jobs; a deadlock here is the classic leak. One WaitGroup counts 16 workers; `main` closes jobs after the last send, waits on the group, then closes results and reads them.

Step 5, memory and connections. 16 goroutines at about 8 KB each is trivial. 16 in-flight HTTP connections is fine for any target. If the targets share a few hosts, set `http.Transport.MaxConnsPerHost` so you do not become the DDoS.

Step 6, the Python comparison. The same design in Python uses `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16)`, which works because the checks are I/O bound and release the GIL. It is a fine choice if the checker runs as a CronJob. It becomes the wrong choice when the checker also exposes `/metrics`, keeps state across cycles and runs for months: then the Go version's static binary, race detector and goroutine metrics pay for themselves. The code example runs the Go design at small scale and proves the goroutine count returns to its starting value.

## Runnable code

Go · gofmt and go vet clean · runs and prints its own checks

```
// A worker pool that checks 12 fake endpoints with 4 goroutines, a context
// timeout, a results channel and a leak check. Standard library only.
//
// The shape is the one you will see in real ops tools: a bounded number of
// workers read jobs from a channel, every check takes a context so it can be
// cancelled, results flow back through one channel, and the main goroutine
// waits for everything to finish before it prints a summary.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"math/rand"
	"runtime"
	"sort"
	"sync"
	"time"
)

// result is what one check produces. Err is nil when the endpoint was healthy.
type result struct {
	name    string
	latency time.Duration
	err     error
}

// endpoint is a fake HTTP check: it sleeps for a while and sometimes fails.
// A real tool would call http.Client.Do with a request built from ctx.
type endpoint struct {
	name    string
	latency time.Duration
	fails   bool
}

var errUnhealthy = errors.New("status 503")

// check honours the context: if the deadline passes before the fake latency
// elapses, it returns ctx.Err() instead of blocking the worker forever.
func check(ctx context.Context, ep endpoint) result {
	start := time.Now()
	select {
	case <-time.After(ep.latency):
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return result{name: ep.name, latency: time.Since(start), err: ctx.Err()}
	}
	if ep.fails {
		return result{name: ep.name, latency: time.Since(start), err: errUnhealthy}
	}
	return result{name: ep.name, latency: time.Since(start)}
}

// runPool starts `workers` goroutines that pull endpoints from a channel and
// push results to another. It returns when every endpoint has a result.
func runPool(ctx context.Context, endpoints []endpoint, workers int) []result {
	jobs := make(chan endpoint)                  // unbuffered: workers pull at their own pace
	results := make(chan result, len(endpoints)) // buffered: workers never block on send
	var wg sync.WaitGroup

	for w := 0; w < workers; w++ {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func(id int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			for ep := range jobs { // exits when jobs is closed
				results <- check(ctx, ep)
			}
		}(w)
	}

	// Feed the jobs, then close the channel so the workers' range loops end.
	// If the context is cancelled mid-way we still send every job: the
	// workers return ctx.Err() immediately, so nothing blocks.
	for _, ep := range endpoints {
		jobs <- ep
	}
	close(jobs)

	wg.Wait()      // every worker has returned
	close(results) // safe: no more senders

	var out []result
	for r := range results {
		out = append(out, r)
	}
	sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool { return out[i].name < out[j].name })
	return out
}

func makeEndpoints(n int, seed int64) []endpoint {
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewSource(seed)) // fixed seed: same "random" failures every run
	eps := make([]endpoint, 0, n)
	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
		eps = append(eps, endpoint{
			name:    fmt.Sprintf("svc-%02d", i+1),
			latency: time.Duration(50+rng.Intn(400)) * time.Millisecond, // 50 to 449 ms
			fails:   rng.Intn(4) == 0,                                   // about 1 in 4
		})
	}
	return eps
}

func main() {
	const workers, n = 4, 12
	endpoints := makeEndpoints(n, 42)

	before := runtime.NumGoroutine()
	fmt.Printf("goroutines before: %d\n", before)

	// Run 1: a generous timeout, every check finishes.
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
	start := time.Now()
	res := runPool(ctx, endpoints, workers)
	cancel() // always call cancel, even after success, to free the timer
	elapsed := time.Since(start)

	var ok, failed, timedOut int
	for _, r := range res {
		status := "ok"
		switch {
		case errors.Is(r.err, context.DeadlineExceeded):
			status = "timeout"
			timedOut++
		case r.err != nil:
			status = "FAIL " + r.err.Error()
			failed++
		default:
			ok++
		}
		fmt.Printf("  %-7s %4d ms  %s\n", r.name, r.latency.Milliseconds(), status)
	}
	var serial time.Duration
	for _, ep := range endpoints {
		serial += ep.latency
	}
	fmt.Printf("run 1: %d checks, %d ok, %d failed, %d timed out, wall %d ms "+
		"(serial would be %d ms)\n", len(res), ok, failed, timedOut,
		elapsed.Milliseconds(), serial.Milliseconds())

	// Run 2: a timeout shorter than most latencies, to show cancellation.
	ctx2, cancel2 := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 120*time.Millisecond)
	res2 := runPool(ctx2, endpoints, workers)
	cancel2()
	timedOut2 := 0
	for _, r := range res2 {
		if errors.Is(r.err, context.DeadlineExceeded) {
			timedOut2++
		}
	}
	fmt.Printf("run 2: 120 ms budget, %d of %d checks returned context deadline exceeded\n",
		timedOut2, len(res2))

	// Leak check: after both pools have drained, the goroutine count must be
	// back where it started. A forgotten close(jobs) or a worker stuck on an
	// unbuffered results channel would show up here.
	time.Sleep(20 * time.Millisecond) // let timers from time.After settle
	after := runtime.NumGoroutine()
	fmt.Printf("goroutines after: %d\n", after)

	// Self-checks.
	if len(res) != n {
		panic(fmt.Sprintf("expected %d results, got %d", n, len(res)))
	}
	if failed == 0 || ok == 0 {
		panic("the fixed seed should give a mix of healthy and failing endpoints")
	}
	if timedOut != 0 {
		panic("nothing should time out with a 5 s budget")
	}
	if elapsed >= serial {
		panic("the pool should be faster than running the checks one by one")
	}
	if timedOut2 == 0 {
		panic("the 120 ms budget should cancel the slow checks")
	}
	if after != before {
		panic(fmt.Sprintf("goroutine leak: %d before, %d after", before, after))
	}
	fmt.Println("self-checks passed: all results collected, pool faster than serial, " +
		"timeouts honoured, no goroutine leak")
}
```

## Key takeaways

* Python for scripts, checks, data and glue; Go for binaries, long-running tools, concurrency and anything in the CNCF ecosystem.
* A good Python ops script has argparse with a dry-run flag, logging to stderr, subprocess with check=True and a timeout, retries with backoff only on retryable errors, and distinct exit codes.
* Never hard-code cloud keys; let the SDK find credentials from the environment or the pod identity, and always paginate list calls.
* Test scripts by mocking the boundary (subprocess, HTTP, the boto3 client), not your own logic.
* Go basics for ops: structs, slices, maps, errors as values with %w and errors.Is, defer, implicit interfaces.
* The worker pool: a jobs channel, N goroutines, a buffered results channel, a WaitGroup, and one context carrying the deadline.
* Every outbound call in Go gets a context timeout; every goroutine has a known way to exit; every resp.Body is closed.
* CGO\_ENABLED=0 go build gives a static binary for a scratch image; go vet and go test -race belong in CI.

## Common mistakes

* Writing a 400-line Bash script that should have been a 100-line Python script with argparse and tests.
* `subprocess.run` without `check=True`, so a failed kubectl is reported as success, or without `timeout`, so a hung command hangs the job.
* Retrying every HTTP error, including 401 and 403, which turns a config bug into a slow config bug.
* Starting a goroutine per item in a loop with no bound, no context and no way to stop it, then wondering why memory grows for a week.
* Forgetting `close(jobs)` or using an unbuffered results channel, so workers block forever and `wg.Wait()` never returns.
* Ignoring the error from `client.Do` or `json.Unmarshal` because "it always works".

## Interview questions (10)

1.When would you write a tool in Python and when in Go?Easy

Python when the tool is a script someone runs from a laptop or a CronJob, is mostly I/O and text, and will be written in an afternoon: health checks, reports, log parsing, calling AWS and the Kubernetes API through boto3 or the client. Go when the tool ships to other people as a binary, runs for months, needs real concurrency, or lives in the Kubernetes ecosystem: controllers, admission webhooks, kubectl plugins, agents, anything that would contribute to a CNCF project. The tell for a rewrite is a Python script that has grown a long-running loop and a concurrency bug.

2.What does a well-structured Python ops script look like?Easy

argparse for flags, including `--dry-run` and `--verbose`; logging configured to stderr so stdout stays machine-readable; `subprocess.run` with `check=True`, `capture_output=True`, `text=True` and a `timeout`; HTTP calls through a function that retries with exponential backoff only on 5xx and network errors; `pathlib` for files; `yaml.safe_load` for manifests; a `main(argv)` function that returns an exit code so tests can call it; and distinct exit codes for distinct failures. Credentials come from the environment or the pod identity, never from the file.

3.Explain goroutines and channels to someone who knows Python threads.Medium

A goroutine is a function started with `go f()`; the Go runtime multiplexes thousands of them over a few OS threads, and unlike Python threads they run in parallel on all cores. A channel is a typed, thread-safe queue: `ch <- v` sends, `v := <-ch` receives, and an unbuffered channel blocks the sender until a receiver is ready, which gives you back-pressure for free. `sync.WaitGroup` is how `main` waits for goroutines to finish. Instead of sharing a list protected by a lock, you send results through a channel. The closest Python analogue is `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a `queue.Queue`, but Go's version is cheaper and parallel.

4.What is a goroutine leak and how do you find one?Medium

A goroutine that can never exit: usually blocked sending on a channel nobody reads, receiving from a channel nobody closes, or waiting on an HTTP call with no timeout. Each one holds its stack and whatever it references, so memory and the goroutine count climb slowly until the pod is OOM-killed. I find it with `runtime.NumGoroutine()` in a test before and after the work, the `go_goroutines` metric in Prometheus trending up, or the `/debug/pprof/goroutine` endpoint, which shows exactly which line each goroutine is stuck on. The fixes are closing the jobs channel, buffering the results channel, selecting on `ctx.Done()`, and a context timeout on every outbound call.

5.Why does every Go function in an ops tool take a context as its first argument?Medium

Context carries a deadline, a cancel signal and request-scoped values down the call chain. When the top-level operation has a 30 s budget, every HTTP call, exec and database query under it inherits that budget through `context.WithTimeout`, and when the caller cancels, every goroutine below sees `ctx.Done()` and stops. Without it, a tool that calls a dead endpoint blocks forever and all its workers pile up behind it. The convention is `func Do(ctx context.Context, ...)`, always first, never stored in a struct, and always with `defer cancel()` after creating one so the timer is released.

6.How do you make sure a Python script that calls kubectl is tested without a cluster?Medium

I keep the logic in functions that take arguments and return values, with `main(argv)` returning an exit code, and I put every external call behind a small function like `run(cmd)`. In pytest I patch `subprocess.run` with `unittest.mock.patch`: `assert_not_called()` proves that `--dry-run` runs nothing, `side_effect=CalledProcessError(...)` proves the script returns the right exit code when kubectl fails, and `return_value` with a canned `stdout` tests the parsing. For boto3 I use `botocore.stub.Stubber` to replay responses. The rule is to mock the boundary, not my own functions, so the test still exercises the real logic.

7.Describe the worker-pool pattern and the two channel mistakes that deadlock it.Hard

One producer sends jobs into a channel, N worker goroutines range over it and send results into a second channel, a WaitGroup counts the workers, and main closes the jobs channel after the last send, waits on the group, then closes and drains results. The first deadlock is forgetting to close the jobs channel: the workers' `range` loops never end, `wg.Wait()` never returns. The second is an unbuffered results channel with main not reading until after `wg.Wait()`: every worker blocks on its first send, nobody finishes, main waits forever. The fix is a results buffer of at least the number of jobs, or a separate goroutine that drains results while the workers run. I also give every check a context so a slow endpoint cannot hold a worker.

8.How do you build and ship a Go tool so it runs in a minimal container?Easy

`CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o tool .` produces a static binary with no libc dependency and the symbol table stripped, usually under 15 MB. The Dockerfile is a two-stage build: a Go image compiles it, then `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static` or `FROM scratch` copies in the binary and CA certificates and runs as a non-root user. Cross-compiling for arm64 is just `GOARCH=arm64`, which matters for Graviton nodes. `go mod tidy` and the committed `go.sum` make the build reproducible, and CI runs `go vet`, `go test -race` and a linter before the image is pushed.

9.What does reading a Kubernetes controller in Go look like, at a high level?Medium

Every controller has the same parts. A client (clientset or controller-runtime Client) talks to the API server. An informer watches one resource type, keeps a cached copy of every object, and calls handlers on add, update and delete; the handlers do nothing except push the object's namespace-and-name key onto a work queue. Workers pop keys and call Reconcile, which reads the current object from the cache, reads whatever it owns, compares with the desired state, and makes one change through the client, then returns an error to be retried with backoff. Reconcile must be idempotent because the same key arrives many times. Once you see that shape, client-go code stops looking mysterious.

10.Compare Python's concurrency options with Go's for an I/O-heavy checker.Medium

In Python, threads work well for I/O because the GIL is released during network waits, so `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16)` gives a fine health checker; asyncio with `aiohttp` scales further for thousands of connections but forces every library to be async. CPU-bound work needs multiprocessing. In Go, goroutines handle both I/O and CPU in parallel, the worker pool is a few lines, context gives cancellation everywhere, and the race detector finds shared-state bugs in tests. For a CronJob that checks 1200 endpoints once a minute, Python is enough. For a service that checks continuously, exposes metrics and runs for months, Go is the better long-term choice.

# Scaling and resilience - caching, queues, rate limiting, DDoS, DR

Scaling is making a system handle more load; resilience is making it keep working when parts fail. Both come from the same layered design: stateless replicas behind a load balancer, state pushed into databases, caches, object storage and queues, limits and timeouts at every hop, and a tested plan for losing a zone or a region. This lesson covers each layer with the numbers interviewers expect: cache hit ratios, queue semantics, rate limiter algorithms, retry budgets, connection pools, RPO and RTO.

scalingcachingqueuesrate limitingddosdisaster recoverywebsockets

## Why it matters

"How would you scale this" and "what happens if this fails" are the two questions behind every system design round, and the DevOps version is more concrete than the developer version: which layer absorbs which failure, what setting makes it do so, and what you measured. Job posts for platform roles list rate limiting, quotas, abuse controls, Redis, Aurora, Cloudflare edge and WebSocket scaling, and the 100xDevs cohort spends five weeks on queues, WebSockets, rate limiting, captchas and DDoS. The worked example on 200,000 WebSocket connections is the kind of estimate you will be asked to do on a whiteboard.

Read first: [Networking for DevOps - TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, SSH](/devops/learn/networking-for-devops), [Web servers, reverse proxies and TLS - Nginx, certificates, process managers](/devops/learn/nginx-reverse-proxy-tls), [AWS core - IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, load balancers, autoscaling](/devops/learn/aws-core-for-devops), [Kubernetes in production - resources, autoscaling, RBAC, upgrades, EKS](/devops/learn/kubernetes-in-production), [SRE practice - SLOs, error budgets, incidents and postmortems](/devops/learn/sre-slos-incidents-postmortems)

## Lesson

### Vertical and horizontal scaling, and where state goes

Vertical scaling is a bigger machine: more vCPUs, more memory. It is the first move because it needs no code change, and the last one available, because the largest instance is a hard ceiling and a single machine is a single failure. Horizontal scaling is more machines behind a load balancer. It has no ceiling but one condition: a request must be able to land on any replica, so the replica holds no state between requests. Sessions go to Redis, files to S3, work-in-progress to a queue, records to the database. An Auto Scaling group or a Kubernetes HPA can add replicas in a minute, but only if the new replica needs nothing from the old one.

Load balancing and health checks are the glue. The load balancer sends traffic only to targets that pass a health check and removes a failing replica after interval times threshold (an assumed tuning: 10 s and 3). The check must test what the service does, not just that a port is open, or a replica with a dead database connection keeps receiving traffic.

![A resilient request path from edge CDN and WAF through rate limiter, load balancer, stateless replicas, cache, queue and workers to a database with replicas, with the failure each layer absorbs and the setting that makes it work](/devops/img/resilient-request-path.svg)A resilient request path from edge CDN and WAF through rate limiter, load balancer, stateless replicas, cache, queue and workers to a database with replicas, with the failure each layer absorbs and the setting that makes it work

### Caching

A cache answers repeated reads from memory instead of the database. **Cache-aside** is the pattern you will be asked about: the app checks the cache, on a miss reads the database, writes the value into the cache with a TTL (time to live), and returns it. Writes go to the database and either delete the cache key (invalidation) or overwrite it. Redis and its open-source fork Valkey are the usual in-memory stores; ElastiCache runs both on AWS. A CDN is a cache at the edge for HTTP responses: static files always, and any GET with a `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` header that is the same for every user.

Two numbers describe a cache: hit ratio and p99 latency. A 90 percent hit ratio means the database sees 10 percent of reads; raising it to 95 percent halves the database load again. The failure mode is the **cache stampede**: a hot key expires, 2,000 requests in the same 50 ms all miss, and all 2,000 go to the database at once. The fix is **single-flight**: the first miss takes a short lock (`SET lock:key 1 NX EX 5`), loads and fills the cache, and the others wait for the fill or serve the stale value. Add jitter to TTLs (`300 + random(0, 60)` seconds) so keys set together do not expire together.

| Cache concern | Setting or pattern | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staleness | TTL per key type: 60 s for prices, 1 day for a product name | the business decides how old a value may be |
| Invalidation | delete the key on write, never try to update it in two places | a delete is idempotent; a stale overwrite races with a read |
| Stampede | single-flight lock plus serve-stale | one loader per key per expiry |
| Hot key | local in-process cache for 1 s in front of Redis | one key can saturate one Redis shard |
| Memory | `maxmemory` with `allkeys-lru` eviction | a full cache that refuses writes is worse than one that evicts |

### Queues and async work

A queue sits between the API and the workers so the API answers in 20 ms with `202 Accepted` while the real work (send the email, call the payment provider) happens later. It absorbs bursts (the queue grows, workers catch up), isolates failures (workers can be down for ten minutes and nothing is lost), and lets the two sides scale separately.

The semantics decide the design. Almost every queue gives **at-least-once delivery**: a worker that crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging will see the message again. So consumers must be **idempotent**: processing the same message twice gives the same result, usually by storing the message id with the result and skipping duplicates. Messages that fail repeatedly go to a **dead-letter queue** (DLQ) after N attempts so they stop blocking the others and a human can look. **Backpressure** is the queue telling the producer to slow down: a bounded queue, a 429 from the API when depth is above a threshold, or simply the lag metric that the autoscaler reads.

| Option | Delivery model | Scaling consumers | Best for | Watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Redis streams with consumer groups (the 100xDevs weeks 42 and 43 design: API pushes to a stream, workers `XREADGROUP`, pushers fan results out to clients) | at-least-once; `XACK` per message; `XPENDING` and `XAUTOCLAIM` recover a dead consumer's messages | add consumers to the group; each message goes to one consumer | low latency, you already run Redis, moderate volume | memory: trim with `XADD ... MAXLEN ~ 100000`; Redis failover loses un-replicated entries |
| Amazon SQS | at-least-once (FIFO queues: exactly-once processing within a window); visibility timeout default 30 s, up to 12 hours | any number of pollers; `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` drives scaling | managed, no servers, DLQ built in with `maxReceiveCount` | the visibility timeout must exceed the job time or the job runs twice |
| Kafka | at-least-once per partition, ordered within a partition; consumer offsets | one consumer per partition at most, so partitions set the ceiling | high volume, replay, many consumers reading the same events | operations load; use MSK or a hosted service |

```
# Redis streams: the 100xDevs worker pattern in redis-cli
XGROUP CREATE jobs workers $ MKSTREAM                        # create the stream and group
XADD jobs MAXLEN ~ 100000 * type email user 42               # producer: trim to about 100k entries
XREADGROUP GROUP workers w1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS jobs >   # worker: 10 new messages, wait up to 5 s
XACK jobs workers 1699999999999-0                            # done; without this the entry stays pending
XPENDING jobs workers - + 10                                 # what is stuck, and for how long
XAUTOCLAIM jobs workers w2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10                # w2 takes over entries idle for over 60 s
```

### Scaling WebSocket servers

An HTTP request lasts milliseconds; a WebSocket connection lasts hours and lives in one process's memory. That changes three things. First, **sticky routing**: the load balancer keeps a connection on the node that holds it, and the 100xDevs week 44 pattern routes by room or user id so one node holds everyone in a room. Second, **fan-out across instances**: when a message must reach users spread over 17 nodes, the sender publishes once to Redis pub/sub or a stream, every node subscribes, and each node delivers to the connections it holds. Third, **limits per node**: each connection costs a file descriptor and memory (an assumed 20 to 50 KB in Go or Node with buffers), so a node has a connection ceiling set by `ulimit -n`, memory and the CPU needed for ping frames; keep it at 60 percent so one node's loss fits on the others.

A deploy must **drain gracefully**: the pod stops accepting new connections, sends a close frame to existing ones at a limited rate, and clients reconnect with jittered backoff to the other pods. Without the rate limit and the jitter, a deploy of one pod becomes a reconnect storm that overloads the rest. Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to cover the drain (60 to 120 seconds), use a `preStop` hook to flip readiness first, and use a PodDisruptionBudget so nodes drain one pod at a time.

### Rate limiting, abuse controls and DDoS

Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make, to protect the service and to make abuse expensive. Two algorithms cover the interview:

* **Token bucket**: a bucket of capacity B refills at R tokens per second; each request takes one token; an empty bucket means 429. It allows a burst of B and a steady rate of R. NGINX `limit_req` with `burst=20 nodelay` is one; so is the AWS API Gateway throttle. Most edge limiters are token buckets.
* **Sliding window**: count requests in the last W seconds (a log of timestamps, or two fixed windows weighted by overlap); above N, refuse. It is strict about the rate with no burst allowance, and after a burst it refuses everything until the window passes, which the code example below shows.

Apply limits at three places: **at the edge** per IP (Cloudflare or AWS WAF rate-based rules, the first line, cheap, catches scrapers), **at the gateway** per API token or user (the fair-share line, 1,000 requests per minute per token as an assumed quota), and **per operation** for expensive endpoints (5 password resets per hour per account). Quotas are limits over a day or a month, enforced from a counter in Redis (`INCR` with `EXPIRE`). Abuse controls beyond rate: a captcha or a managed bot score on signup and login, device and IP reputation, and a kill switch per token. The 100xDevs weeks 45 and 47 cover exactly this chain: rate limit, captcha, then DDoS.

A **DDoS** (distributed denial of service) sends traffic from thousands of sources, so per-IP limits do not help. Volumetric floods (tens of Gbps of UDP) can only be absorbed at the edge: an anycast CDN spreads the traffic over many points of presence and drops it there; AWS Shield Standard does this for every customer, Shield Advanced adds application-layer detection and a response team; Cloudflare does both. Application-layer floods (millions of valid-looking HTTP requests) need the WAF: managed bot rules, challenge pages, and rate rules keyed on a fingerprint rather than an IP. The rule for your own architecture: nothing with a public IP except the edge, so there is nothing else to hit.

```
# NGINX token bucket per client IP: 10 requests per second, bursts of 20 served without delay, then 429
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;
limit_req_status 429;
server {
    location /api/ {
        limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay;
        proxy_pass https://app;
    }
}
```

### Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads

Every remote call needs a **timeout**, both to connect and to read, set from the dependency's measured p99 plus a margin; without one, a slow dependency holds every thread and the slowness spreads. **Retries** recover from transient failures but are selfish: each retry is extra load on a service that is already failing. The **retry storm** is three layers each retrying three times, which turns one request into 27 at the bottom, and a brief blip into an outage. The rules: retry only idempotent calls, at one layer, a small number of times, with **exponential backoff and jitter** (wait `random(0, base * 2^attempt)`, capped), and with a retry budget (retries may be at most 10 percent of requests). A **circuit breaker** counts failures per dependency: after N failures it opens and fails fast without calling, after a cooldown it goes half-open and lets one trial call through, and closes again on success. It turns a dead dependency from a timeout on every request into an instant error, and gives the dependency room to recover. **Bulkheads** isolate resources per dependency: a separate connection pool or goroutine limit for each, so a slow payment provider cannot consume the pool the search endpoint needs.

The **Tail at Scale** idea: at fan-out, latency is decided by the slowest call. If a page calls 100 backends and each has a 1 percent chance of a slow (p99) response, the page is slow 63 percent of the time (1 minus 0.99 to the power 100). That is why p99 matters more than the average for anything that fans out, and why **hedged requests** help: send the same request to a second replica after the p95 delay and take the first answer, which cuts the tail for a few percent of extra load.

### Database scaling

The database holds the state, so it is the hardest layer to scale. In order of cost: **connection pooling** first. Each Postgres connection is a process with memory, and `max_connections` is often 100 to 500. A pool in the app (10 connections per pod) or a pooler in front (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) keeps the count fixed. The classic incident: a deploy with `maxSurge` doubles the pod count for a minute, every new pod opens its 10 connections, 40 pods times 10 is 400, the limit is 300, and the new pods crash on `too many connections`, so the rollout stalls. Size pools so pods times pool size plus surge stays under the limit, or put RDS Proxy in front. Next, **read replicas**: Aurora gives a writer endpoint and a reader endpoint that balances across up to 15 replicas; the app sends SELECTs that tolerate replica lag to the reader. Then **caching** in front of reads, then **sharding**, which splits rows across databases by a key such as tenant id, moves joins across shards into the application, and is a multi-quarter project; do it when a single writer cannot keep up after the cheaper moves.

### Multi-AZ, multi-region and disaster recovery

| Scope | What it survives | Design | RPO and RTO (typical, label as assumptions) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Multi-AZ | one data center: power, network, a bad EBS rack | replicas across 3 AZs, Aurora with a reader in another AZ, ALB across AZs | RPO 0, RTO about 1 to 2 minutes (Aurora failover) |
| Multi-region active-passive | a whole region, a regional service outage | the second region has infrastructure from the same Terraform, Aurora Global Database replicates with about 1 s lag, Route 53 health checks fail over DNS | RPO about 1 s, RTO 10 to 30 minutes including the promotion and the DNS TTL |
| Multi-region active-active | the same, with no failover step | both regions serve traffic; needs a database that writes in both (DynamoDB global tables, or Aurora Global with write forwarding) and conflict rules | RPO near 0, RTO near 0, cost about double, complexity high |

**RPO** (recovery point objective) is how much data you may lose, as time since the last good copy; **RTO** (recovery time objective) is how long until service is back. The business sets them; the design follows. **Backups** are the floor: automated snapshots daily with a 7 to 35 day retention, point-in-time recovery enabled, copied to another region, and **restored on a schedule** into a scratch account, because an untested backup is a guess. **DNS failover with Route 53**: a health check (request interval 30 s by default, 10 s for fast; failure threshold 3 by default) on the primary endpoint, and a failover record set that answers with the secondary when the check fails; keep the TTL at 60 s so clients move within a minute of the DNS change. The **DR runbook** is the list of commands, in order, with the person who runs each and the expected time, rehearsed every quarter: freeze writes, promote the secondary database, repoint DNS, scale the secondary region, verify with synthetic checks, announce.

### Capacity planning and chaos testing

Plan from numbers: peak requests per second (the busiest hour of the busiest day plus growth over the planning horizon), the measured capacity of one replica at the latency target (load test one pod: say 400 requests per second at p99 under 200 ms), then replicas equals peak divided by per-replica capacity, divided by a utilisation target of 0.6 to 0.7, plus one zone's worth so losing an AZ does not drop below peak. Do the same for connections, queue depth and database IOPS. Then test the plan: chaos testing kills a pod, a node, an AZ or a dependency on purpose, with a small blast radius, and checks that the system did what the design said. Start cheap: delete a pod and confirm no errors; add 300 ms of latency to the database with Toxiproxy and confirm the breaker opens; cordon every node in one AZ and confirm the PDBs keep the service up.

## Worked example

**A WebSocket service with 200,000 concurrent connections.**

Step 1, connections per node. One Go pod handles an assumed 20,000 connections comfortably: at 40 KB per connection that is 800 MB of memory, plus ping frames every 30 s, which is 20,000 / 30 = 667 small writes per second, trivial CPU. Set the file descriptor limit above 25,000.

Step 2, nodes needed with headroom. The bare minimum is 200,000 / 20,000 = 10 pods. Run at 60 percent utilisation so a lost AZ (one third of pods) or a deploy surge fits: 200,000 / (20,000 x 0.6) = 16.7, so 17 pods, about 11,765 connections each. Spread over 3 AZs with a topology spread constraint; losing one AZ leaves 12 pods holding 16,667 each, under the 20,000 ceiling.

Step 3, fan-out for a message to 10 percent of users. 20,000 recipients, 1 KB payload. The publisher writes once to Redis pub/sub; Redis sends one copy to each of the 17 subscribed pods: 17 KB out of Redis. Each pod delivers to its own share, 20,000 / 17 = 1,176 connections, 1.2 MB of client egress per pod. At 50 such messages per second, Redis egress is 50 x 17 KB = 850 KB/s, under 1 MB/s, and client egress across the fleet is 50 x 20,000 x 1 KB = 1,024 MB/s, which is 8.2 Gbit/s, about 0.48 Gbit/s per pod: the client side, not Redis, is the bandwidth cost, and node network capacity is what you size.

Step 4, drain time on a deploy. A pod holds 11,765 connections. Closing them all at once makes 11,765 clients reconnect in the same second. Instead the pod closes 500 per second: 11,765 / 500 = 23.5 seconds to drain. Clients reconnect with a random 0 to 30 s delay, so the reconnect rate on the other pods is about 11,765 / 30 = 392 per second, which a fleet of 16 pods absorbs. With `maxSurge: 25%` (25 percent of 17 is 4.25, rounded up to 5) the rollout replaces about 5 pods per wave: ceil(17 / 5) = 4 waves, each 24 s of drain plus about 30 s for the new pod to be Ready, about 216 seconds, 3.6 minutes for the full rollout. `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` must be at least 24 s plus margin; set 60.

## Runnable code

Python · runs and prints its own checks

```
"""Two rate limiters on the same burst, then a circuit breaker on a flaky dependency.

Part 1: a token bucket (capacity 10, refill 5 per second) and a sliding window
log (10 requests per 2 seconds) see the same 60-request timeline: a burst of
30 at t=0, then 30 spread evenly over the next 6 seconds. Both allow the same
long-run rate (5 per second) but treat the burst differently.

Part 2: a circuit breaker (closed, open, half-open) sits in front of a fake
dependency that is down from t=5 s to t=22 s. We count how many calls the
breaker refused instead of sending them into a dead service.
"""
from collections import deque

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_s):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.refill = refill_per_s
        self.tokens = float(capacity)
        self.last = 0.0

    def allow(self, now):
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.refill)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

class SlidingWindowLog:
    def __init__(self, limit, window_s):
        self.limit = limit
        self.window = window_s
        self.log = deque()  # timestamps of allowed requests

    def allow(self, now):
        while self.log and self.log[0] <= now - self.window:
            self.log.popleft()
        if len(self.log) < self.limit:
            self.log.append(now)
            return True
        return False

def request_timeline():
    """30 requests at t=0 (a burst), then 30 requests spread over 6 seconds."""
    return [0.0] * 30 + [0.2 * i for i in range(1, 31)]

class CircuitBreaker:
    """closed: calls pass. open: calls are refused for cooldown seconds.
    half-open: one trial call decides whether to close again or reopen."""

    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=3, cooldown_s=5.0):
        self.state = "closed"
        self.failures = 0
        self.threshold = failure_threshold
        self.cooldown = cooldown_s
        self.opened_at = None
        self.transitions = []
        self.saved = 0  # calls we refused instead of sending to a broken dependency

    def _go(self, state, now):
        self.transitions.append((now, self.state, state))
        self.state = state

    def call(self, fn, now):
        if self.state == "open":
            if now - self.opened_at >= self.cooldown:
                self._go("half-open", now)
            else:
                self.saved += 1
                return "refused"
        try:
            fn(now)
        except RuntimeError:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.state == "half-open" or self.failures >= self.threshold:
                self.opened_at = now
                self._go("open", now)
            return "failed"
        self.failures = 0
        if self.state == "half-open":
            self._go("closed", now)
        return "ok"

def flaky_dependency_factory(down_from=5.0, down_until=22.0):
    calls = {"n": 0}

    def dep(now):
        calls["n"] += 1
        if down_from <= now < down_until:  # every call in this window fails
            raise RuntimeError("503 from dependency")
    return dep, calls

if __name__ == "__main__":
    timeline = request_timeline()
    bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=10, refill_per_s=5)
    window = SlidingWindowLog(limit=10, window_s=2)
    tb = [bucket.allow(t) for t in timeline]
    sw = [window.allow(t) for t in timeline]

    print("Part 1: same 60 requests, two limiters (both allow 5 per second on average)")
    print(f"  burst of 30 at t=0:     token bucket allowed {sum(tb[:30])}, sliding window allowed {sum(sw[:30])}")
    print(f"  30 spread over 6 s:     token bucket allowed {sum(tb[30:])}, sliding window allowed {sum(sw[30:])}")
    print(f"  total allowed:          token bucket {sum(tb)}, sliding window {sum(sw)}")
    assert sum(tb[:30]) == 10 and sum(sw[:30]) == 10
    # After the burst the bucket refills 1 token per 0.2 s, exactly the arrival rate: every
    # later request passes. The window stays full until t=2 (9 requests at 0.2 .. 1.8 s are
    # refused) and then admits 5 per second: 21 of the 30 pass.
    assert sum(tb[30:]) == 30
    assert sum(sw[30:]) == 21
    print("  the window refuses everything for 2 s after a burst; the bucket recovers smoothly")

    print("\nPart 2: circuit breaker in front of a dependency that is down from t=5 s to t=22 s")
    dep, calls = flaky_dependency_factory()
    cb = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3, cooldown_s=5.0)
    results = []
    now = 0.0
    for i in range(80):  # 40 s of traffic
        now += 0.5  # one client call every 500 ms
        results.append(cb.call(dep, now))
    for t, old, new in cb.transitions:
        print(f"  t={t:5.1f}s  {old:>9} -> {new}")
    print(f"  calls attempted by client: {len(results)}")
    print(f"  calls that reached the dependency: {calls['n']}")
    print(f"  calls refused by the open breaker (saved): {cb.saved}")
    print(f"  final state: {cb.state}")
    assert cb.state == "closed"
    assert cb.saved > 0 and calls["n"] + cb.saved == len(results)
    assert [s for _, _, s in cb.transitions][:3] == ["open", "half-open", "open"]
    print("  self-checks passed: breaker opened on the 3rd failure, probed every 5 s, closed when the dependency recovered")
```

## Key takeaways

* Horizontal scaling needs stateless replicas; state goes to the database, Redis, S3 and a queue, and the health check must test real work.
* Cache-aside with TTLs and delete-on-write; single-flight and jittered TTLs stop stampedes; hit ratio and p99 are the two numbers.
* Queues give at-least-once delivery, so consumers are idempotent, failures go to a DLQ, and the visibility timeout exceeds the job time.
* WebSockets scale by routing connections to a node, fanning out through pub/sub, capping connections per node at about 60 percent, and draining at a limited rate with jittered client reconnects.
* Token bucket allows bursts and recovers smoothly; sliding window is strict; apply limits at the edge per IP, at the gateway per token, and per expensive operation; DDoS is absorbed only at the edge.
* Timeouts on every call, retries only idempotent and only at one layer with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers to fail fast, bulkheads to isolate pools; p99 decides fan-out latency.
* Pool connections so pods times pool plus deploy surge stays under max\_connections; then read replicas, then cache, then shard.
* Multi-AZ is the default; multi-region is a business decision expressed as RPO and RTO; backups count only when restored on a schedule; the DR runbook is rehearsed.

## Common mistakes

* Retrying at every layer with no backoff, which multiplies a blip into a retry storm.
* A health check that only opens a TCP port, so a replica with a dead database connection keeps receiving traffic.
* Updating a cache value on write instead of deleting it, and losing the race with a concurrent read that writes the old value back.
* Sizing a connection pool per pod without counting the deploy surge, so every rollout hits max\_connections.
* A per-IP rate limit as the only DDoS defence; floods come from thousands of IPs and must be dropped at the edge.
* Backups that have never been restored, and a DR plan that exists only as a diagram.

## Practice

* Run Redis in Docker, implement cache-aside for a slow function in Python with a 10 s TTL, hit it with 200 parallel requests at the moment the key expires, count database calls, then add a SET NX single-flight lock and count again; the second number should be 1.
* Create a Redis stream and consumer group, run two workers that crash randomly after processing but before XACK, prove duplicates with a counter, then add an idempotency set keyed by entry id and prove the count is exact. Use XPENDING and XAUTOCLAIM to recover a killed worker's entries.
* Put the NGINX `limit_req` block from this lesson in front of a local app, send 100 requests in one second with a load tool, and record how many return 429 at `rate=10r/s burst=20`; then change to `burst=0` and compare.
* On kind, deploy a 3-replica app with a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable 2 and a preStop sleep, run a load test, drain a node, and confirm zero failed requests; then remove the PDB and the preStop hook and measure the difference.

## Interview questions (10)

1.How would you scale a web API from one server to handle ten times the traffic?Easy

First measure: requests per second at peak, p99 latency, and what one server can do before latency breaks. Then make the API stateless: sessions to Redis, uploads to S3, long jobs to a queue, so any replica can take any request. Put replicas behind a load balancer with a health check that exercises real work, and autoscale on CPU or requests per replica with a 60 to 70 percent target. Add a cache for repeated reads and a CDN for static and cacheable responses. Then look at the database, which is now the bottleneck: pool connections, move reads to replicas, and only consider sharding after that. At every step, the number that proves it worked is p99 at the new peak.

2.What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?Medium

A hot key expires, and in the next few milliseconds hundreds of requests all miss the cache and all go to the database for the same value, which can take the database down at exactly the moment it is most needed. Prevention is single-flight: the first request that misses takes a short lock in Redis with SET NX and a few seconds of expiry, loads the value and fills the cache, and the other requests either wait briefly or serve the previous value if we keep a stale copy. Jittered TTLs stop many keys expiring in the same second, and refreshing hot keys in the background before they expire removes the miss entirely.

3.Why put a queue between an API and its workers, and what changes in the worker code?Medium

The queue lets the API respond in milliseconds with 202 Accepted while slow work happens later, absorbs bursts because the queue grows while workers catch up, and isolates failures because workers can be down without losing requests. It also lets the two sides scale on different signals: API on request rate, workers on queue depth. The worker code changes because delivery is at-least-once: a crash after the work but before the acknowledgement redelivers the message, so the worker must be idempotent, usually by recording the message id with the result and skipping repeats. It must acknowledge only after success, give up to a dead-letter queue after a few attempts, and finish within the visibility timeout or extend it.

4.Compare the token bucket and sliding window algorithms. Which do you use at the edge?Medium

A token bucket has a capacity and a refill rate; a request spends a token, so it allows a burst up to the capacity and then a steady rate, and it recovers smoothly because tokens keep arriving. A sliding window counts requests in the last N seconds and refuses above a limit; it is strict with no burst allowance, and after a burst it refuses everything until the window slides past, which feels harsh to clients. At the edge I use a token bucket per IP because real traffic is bursty and a page load is a burst of a dozen requests. Sliding windows fit quotas, such as 1,000 requests per minute per API token, where fairness over the window matters more than burst tolerance.

5.A dependency is slow and your whole service goes down with it. What do you add?Medium

Three things. Timeouts on every call to it, connect and read, set from its measured p99 plus margin, so a slow call cannot hold a thread forever. A circuit breaker that counts failures and opens after a threshold, so calls fail fast for a cooldown instead of waiting for the timeout, then half-opens to test recovery with a single call. A bulkhead, meaning a separate connection pool or concurrency limit for that dependency, so it cannot consume the resources other endpoints need. On top, retries only for idempotent calls, only at one layer, with exponential backoff and jitter and a retry budget, because retries against a struggling dependency are what turn slowness into an outage.

6.How does a deploy exhaust database connections, and how do you prevent it?Medium

Each pod opens a pool of, say, 10 connections at start. With 30 pods that is 300, right at a max\_connections of 300. A rolling update with maxSurge 25 percent starts 8 new pods before the old ones stop, so 38 pods try to hold 380 connections, the new ones fail with too many connections, never become Ready, and the rollout stalls or flaps. Prevention: size pools so pods times pool size plus the surge stays under the limit with margin; put a pooler such as RDS Proxy or PgBouncer in front so thousands of client connections share a fixed set of server connections; and alert on connection count as a percentage of the limit so you see it at 80 percent, not at 100.

7.Explain RPO and RTO and how they change the design.Easy

RPO, recovery point objective, is how much data the business accepts losing, measured as time since the last copy: an RPO of one hour means hourly backups are enough; an RPO of seconds means continuous replication. RTO, recovery time objective, is how long the service may be down: hours allows restoring from a backup into fresh infrastructure; minutes needs a warm standby with replication and DNS failover; near zero needs active-active in two regions. Each step down in RPO and RTO roughly doubles cost and complexity, so I ask the business for the numbers first and design the cheapest architecture that meets them, then prove it with a rehearsed restore and failover.

8.How do you scale a WebSocket service, and what makes a deploy dangerous?Hard

Connections are long-lived and live in one process, so three things differ from HTTP. Routing: the load balancer keeps a connection on its node, and we route by room or user so related connections share a node. Fan-out: a message for users across many nodes is published once to Redis pub/sub or a stream, every node subscribes, and each delivers to its own connections. Limits: each connection costs a file descriptor and tens of kilobytes, so each node has a ceiling and we run at about 60 percent so losing an AZ fits. A deploy is dangerous because draining a pod disconnects thousands of clients at once, and if they all reconnect immediately the remaining pods get a storm. So the pod flips readiness, closes connections at a limited rate within a long grace period, clients reconnect with jittered backoff, and a PodDisruptionBudget keeps node drains to one pod at a time.

9.What is the Tail at Scale argument and what do you do about it?Hard

When a request fans out to many backends, its latency is the slowest of them. If each of 100 backends is slow one percent of the time, the fan-out request is slow 63 percent of the time, because the chance that all 100 are fast is 0.99 to the power 100. So the average latency of a backend tells you nothing; p99 does. The responses are to reduce variance at the source (avoid garbage collection pauses, background jobs and head-of-line blocking), and to tolerate it: hedged requests send the same call to a second replica after the p95 delay and take the first answer, costing a few percent extra load; tied requests cancel the loser; and fan-out can return partial results after a deadline rather than wait for the slowest shard.

10.How would you protect an API from a DDoS attack?Medium

Volumetric floods can only be absorbed before they reach me, so the only public entry is an anycast edge, Cloudflare or CloudFront with AWS Shield, which spreads the traffic over many locations and drops it there; the origin accepts traffic only from the edge's IP ranges. For application-layer floods, the WAF applies managed bot rules, challenges suspicious clients, and rate-based rules keyed on more than the IP. Behind that, a token bucket per IP and per token at the gateway, quotas per customer, and a captcha on signup and login. Inside, autoscaling with a ceiling and a budget alarm so the attack does not become a bill, and a kill switch to shed expensive endpoints first. The measure of success is origin request rate during the attack staying flat.

# Security and DevSecOps - secrets, least privilege, supply chain, policy as code

DevSecOps means security is a property of the pipeline and the platform, not a review at the end. This lesson covers the controls a DevOps engineer owns: short-lived identity for humans, CI and pods; secrets that never touch Git; a supply chain where every image is scanned, pinned, signed and verified at admission; hardened pods and clusters enforced by policy as code; cloud hardening with private endpoints and audit logs; and the edge controls (TLS, WAF, rate limits, SSRF protection) that stop abuse before it reaches the application.

securitysecretsiamsupply chainkyvernopod securityoidc

## Why it matters

Security questions are in every DevOps interview now, and they are concrete: "how does your pipeline get AWS credentials", "where do your secrets live", "what stops someone deploying a root container", "what do you do when a key leaks". A candidate who answers "we use IAM" loses to one who says "GitHub Actions assumes a role through OIDC, the trust policy pins the repo and branch, no key exists to leak". The same controls are what a platform team is hired to build. Audits (an access review, a SOC 2 or ISO question, a customer security questionnaire) ask for the table at the end of this lesson, layer by layer.

Read first: [CI/CD with GitHub Actions and GitLab CI](/devops/learn/ci-cd-github-actions-gitlab), [AWS core - IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, load balancers, autoscaling](/devops/learn/aws-core-for-devops), [Kubernetes architecture and core objects](/devops/learn/kubernetes-architecture-core-objects), [Kubernetes in production - resources, autoscaling, RBAC, upgrades, EKS](/devops/learn/kubernetes-in-production), [GitOps with Argo CD and progressive delivery](/devops/learn/gitops-argocd-progressive-delivery)

## Lesson

### Shift left: security as a pipeline property

"Shift left" means the check happens where the change is made, as a failing build, not as a finding six weeks later. The order of controls follows the artifact: secret scanning on every push, dependency and image scanning on every build, policy checks on every manifest and every Terraform plan, signature verification at admission, detection at runtime. Each control is cheap on its own; together they make the common attacks (a leaked key, a vulnerable base image, a root container with the node's disk mounted) impossible to deploy by accident.

![The software supply chain from commit through CI, dependencies, build and scan, SBOM and signing, registry, admission and runtime, with the security control and the verification command at each step](/devops/img/supply-chain-controls.svg)The software supply chain from commit through CI, dependencies, build and scan, SBOM and signing, registry, admission and runtime, with the security control and the verification command at each step

### Identity and access: short-lived credentials everywhere

Least privilege means every identity (human, pipeline, pod) can do exactly what its job needs and nothing more. The second rule matters as much: no long-lived keys. A static access key in a CI secret is a credential that never expires, is copied into logs and laptops, and is the first thing an attacker looks for. The replacement is a token that proves identity to the cloud and is exchanged for credentials that expire in an hour.

| Who | Old way | 2026 way | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Humans | IAM users with access keys | SSO through IAM Identity Center, MFA, roles | the login gives a session of 1 to 12 hours; `aws sso login` |
| CI jobs | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in repository secrets | OIDC federation | the job presents a signed JWT from GitHub or GitLab; `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` returns 1-hour credentials |
| Pods on EKS | node instance role shared by every pod, or keys in a Secret | EKS Pod Identity (or IRSA) | a ServiceAccount is mapped to an IAM role; the SDK gets credentials from the Pod Identity agent on the node |
| Pods to the API server | the default ServiceAccount with a cluster-admin binding | a ServiceAccount per workload, RBAC Roles with named verbs | `automountServiceAccountToken: false` unless the pod talks to the API |
| Database | one shared password in a ConfigMap | IAM database authentication or a rotated secret from Secrets Manager | the token lives 15 minutes; rotation is a Lambda the secret owns |

The CI side in GitHub Actions: the workflow requests a token with `permissions: id-token: write`, and the AWS role's trust policy pins the subject claim so only one repository and branch can assume it.

```
# .github/workflows/deploy.yaml (the job that touches AWS)
permissions:
  id-token: write    # required to request the OIDC JWT
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<40-character-commit-sha>   # pin every action by commit SHA, not by a movable tag
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e3dd6a429d7300a6a4c196c26e071d42e0343502
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-shop-deploy
          aws-region: ap-south-1
```

```
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"},
      "StringLike": {"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:shop-org/shop-api:ref:refs/heads/main"}
    }
  }]
}
```

Without the `sub` condition, any GitHub repository in the world could assume the role. That single line is the most common OIDC mistake.

### Secrets management

A secret is anything that grants access: passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys, certificates, database connection strings with a password inside, webhook signing secrets, and the kubeconfig itself. Rules: a secret lives in one place (AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault), is written to Git never, reaches the workload at runtime, and rotates on a schedule.

| Need | Tool | How the secret reaches the pod |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sync from Secrets Manager into a Kubernetes Secret | External Secrets Operator (ESO) | an `ExternalSecret` names the remote key; ESO creates and refreshes the Secret; the pod mounts it as usual |
| Mount directly without a Kubernetes Secret object | Secrets Store CSI driver with the AWS provider | files appear in a volume; nothing is stored in etcd |
| Keep an encrypted secret in Git for GitOps | SOPS with a KMS key, or Sealed Secrets | the file in Git is ciphertext; Argo CD or the controller decrypts in-cluster |
| Rotation | Secrets Manager rotation Lambda, or Vault dynamic secrets | the app re-reads the file or restarts; ESO `refreshInterval` picks up the new value |

```
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: payments-provider
  namespace: payments
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: payments-provider        # the Kubernetes Secret ESO creates
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: PAYMENT_PROVIDER_KEY
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/payments/provider  # the name in Secrets Manager
        property: api_key
```

Scan every repository for leaked secrets, in CI and on the history: `gitleaks detect --source . --redact` fails the build on a match, and GitHub secret scanning with push protection blocks the push itself. **When a key leaks: rotate first, then investigate.** The order matters because the investigation takes hours and the attacker needs minutes. Revoke the key, issue a new one, deploy it, then read CloudTrail for every call the old key made (`aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIA...`), then remove it from Git history and write the incident note. Deleting the commit is not rotation; the key is already in a dozen clones.

### Supply chain security

The supply chain is every step between a developer's commit and a running container. Each step can be attacked: a typosquatted package, a compromised CI action, a registry tag that someone re-pushed. The controls, in pipeline order:

* **SBOM** (software bill of materials): a list of every package in the image, generated at build time with `trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json IMAGE` and attached to the image as an attestation. When the next log4j happens, you query SBOMs instead of rebuilding everything to find out.
* **Image scanning**: the gate policy is fail on CRITICAL, warn on HIGH. `trivy image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 IMAGE` in CI fails the build on a fixable critical vulnerability, and a second run with `--severity HIGH --exit-code 0` prints HIGH findings as warnings; ECR scan-on-push catches images that arrive another way. Scan the base image and the Terraform and Kubernetes manifests too (`trivy config .`).
* **Pinning by digest**: `FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:...` and `uses: actions/checkout@<40-char SHA>`. A tag can be moved; a digest cannot. Renovate or Dependabot updates the pins with a pull request you can review.
* **Signing and verification**: `cosign sign IMAGE@DIGEST` in CI uses keyless signing, where the signature is tied to the CI job's OIDC identity and recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. At admission, Kyverno verifies: `cosign verify IMAGE --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/shop-org/shop-api/' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
* **SLSA levels** (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, build track, from the v1.2 specification): **L0** no guarantees; **L1** provenance exists, generated by the build platform, showing how the package was built (prevents mistakes, trivial to forge); **L2** builds run on a hosted platform that generates and signs the provenance, and consumers validate it (forging requires an explicit attack); **L3** a hardened hosted platform that prevents builds from influencing one another and keeps the signing secrets away from user-defined build steps. GitHub Actions with the official SLSA generator workflow reaches L3 for provenance.

**Dependency confusion and typosquatting.** Dependency confusion is when a package manager configured with both a private and a public registry fetches a public package with the same name as your internal one, because the public version number is higher. Typosquatting is a public package named `reqeusts` or `colourama` that someone installs by mistake. Both are stopped by a lockfile with hashes, a private registry that proxies and pins the public one, scoping internal names (`@shop/` in npm), and `go mod verify` or `pip install --require-hashes`.

### Container and Kubernetes hardening

The Pod Security Standards define three profiles: privileged, baseline, restricted. The restricted profile is what every application namespace should enforce, through the namespace label `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A pod that passes it:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true                 # the image must declare a non-root USER
    runAsUser: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault             # the runtime's default syscall filter
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/api@sha256:9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # no setuid binaries gain root
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # writes go to an emptyDir, not the image layer
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]                  # add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE if you must bind 80
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}
        limits: {memory: 512Mi}
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
  volumes:
    - {name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}
```

Beyond the pod: **no privileged pods** (`privileged: true` is root on the node), **no hostPath** (mounting `/` or the container socket is the standard container escape), **no hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC**, **NetworkPolicy default deny** per namespace with explicit allow rules for DNS, the services the app calls, and the ingress controller. Admission policies with Kyverno enforce all of this and more (a required registry, no `latest` tag, required labels, signature verification):

```
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-digest-from-ecr
spec:
  rules:
    - name: image-from-ecr-by-digest
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        failureAction: Enforce         # Audit only writes a PolicyReport
        message: "images must come from our ECR and be pinned by digest"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/*@sha256:*"
```

The **OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten** (2025 edition) as a checklist, with the control for each: K01 insecure workload configurations (restricted profile), K02 overly permissive authorization (RBAC with named verbs, no cluster-admin for workloads), K03 secrets management failures (ESO, etcd encryption, no secrets in env dumps), K04 lack of cluster-level policy enforcement (Kyverno or Gatekeeper), K05 missing network segmentation (NetworkPolicy default deny), K06 overly exposed components (private API endpoint, no public kubelet or dashboard), K07 misconfigured and vulnerable components (upgrade cadence, add-on versions), K08 cluster-to-cloud lateral movement (block IMDS from pods, Pod Identity with least privilege), K09 broken authentication (SSO, no static tokens), K10 inadequate logging and monitoring (audit logs on, Falco, CloudTrail).

### Cloud hardening

* **Private clusters and VPC endpoints**: the EKS API endpoint is private (or public with a CIDR allow-list), nodes have no public IP, and traffic to ECR, S3, STS and Secrets Manager goes through VPC endpoints so it never crosses the internet and the NAT bill drops.
* **Security groups** are stateful allow-lists per ENI: the database group allows 5432 from the node or pod security group only, not from a CIDR.
* **Encryption at rest with KMS**: EBS volumes, S3 buckets, RDS and Aurora, and EKS Secrets envelope encryption, each with a customer-managed key so you control rotation and the key policy.
* **CloudTrail** records every API call in every region to an S3 bucket with object lock; **GuardDuty** reads CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and DNS logs and raises findings such as a credential used from an unusual IP or an EKS pod talking to a known bad host. Both are on in every account, by Organizations policy.
* **IMDSv2 and the hop limit**: a pod that can reach `169.254.169.254` can read the node's IAM credentials. Set the node launch template to `http_tokens = "required"` and `http_put_response_hop_limit = 1`, so the metadata response does not survive the extra hop into the pod network. Workloads then get credentials only through Pod Identity.

### Application-side controls DevOps owns

TLS everywhere: cert-manager issues certificates from Let's Encrypt or a private CA, the ingress or Gateway terminates TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, and inside the cluster a mesh or application TLS covers service-to-service traffic. A **WAF** (AWS WAF or Cloudflare) in front of the load balancer blocks known injection patterns and bots. **Rate limits** at the edge and the gateway, per IP and per API token, with quotas per customer, are the first abuse control; the full design is in the scaling lesson. **SSRF protection** (server-side request forgery, where the app is tricked into making a request on the attacker's behalf) is partly application code and partly network: block pod egress to the metadata endpoint and to the VPC CIDR except the services the app needs, through NetworkPolicy and the IMDS hop limit. A typical application security audit covers exactly these: cross-tenant access (a request with tenant A's token reading tenant B's rows, found by replaying requests with swapped IDs), SSRF through a URL parameter, and reconnect storms where clients hammered a recovering service; the fixes were authorization checks at the data layer, egress policy, and jittered reconnect backoff with a rate limit.

### Policy as code, runtime detection, compliance

| Tool | Writes policy in | Best at | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kyverno | YAML, Kubernetes-native | validate, mutate, generate, verify images; easy to read | the ClusterPolicy above |
| OPA Gatekeeper | Rego | complex logic, the same engine reused outside Kubernetes | `deny[msg] { input.review.object.spec.hostNetwork }` |
| Checkov | built-in rules for Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Dockerfiles | shift-left on IaC in CI | `checkov -d infra/ --check CKV_AWS_19` (S3 encryption) |
| Falco | YAML rules over syscalls | runtime detection: a shell in a container, a write to `/etc`, an outbound connection from a pod that never makes them | alert to Slack or an incident |

Compliance basics the auditor asks for: audit logs enabled (EKS control plane audit logs to CloudWatch, CloudTrail, application access logs) with a stated retention (90 days hot, one year cold is a common choice; label it as yours); quarterly access reviews where every IAM role, GitHub team and RBAC binding has an owner who confirms it is still needed; and evidence, which means the policy report, the scan output and the review ticket, not a promise.

### Layer, control, how to verify

| Layer | Control | How to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | branch protection, signed commits, secret scanning | `gh api repos/ORG/REPO/branches/main/protection`; `gitleaks detect` on the history |
| CI | OIDC with a pinned `sub`, actions pinned by SHA, least-privilege role | `aws sts get-caller-identity` in the job shows the role; grep workflows for `@v` tags |
| Dependencies | lockfiles with hashes, private registry, Renovate | `go mod verify`; `npm ci` fails on a lockfile mismatch |
| Image | non-root, pinned base, scanned, SBOM, signed | `trivy image`; `cosign verify` with identity and issuer; `docker inspect -f '{{.Config.User}}'` |
| Registry | private ECR, immutable tags, scan on push, VPC endpoint | `aws ecr describe-repositories --query 'repositories[].imageTagMutability'` |
| Admission | Pod Security restricted, Kyverno verifyImages and validation | apply a root pod and read the denial; `kubectl get policyreport -A` |
| Runtime | NetworkPolicy default deny, read-only fs, Falco | `kubectl exec` a pod and try `wget 169.254.169.254` (must time out); a Falco alert fires on the exec |
| Cloud | private endpoint, security groups, KMS, CloudTrail, GuardDuty | `aws eks describe-cluster --query 'cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.endpointPublicAccess'`; GuardDuty sample findings |
| Secrets | Secrets Manager plus ESO, rotation, no secret in Git | `kubectl get externalsecret -A` all `SecretSynced`; `aws secretsmanager describe-secret` shows `RotationEnabled` |
| Edge | TLS 1.2+, WAF, rate limits, IMDSv2 hop limit 1 | `openssl s_client -tls1_1` fails; a burst of 200 requests returns 429 after the limit |
